Data is the critical technical infrastructure necessary to build AI systems. It can determine performance, fairness, robustness, safety, and scalability of AI systems. Paradoxically, for AI researchers and developers, data work is often the least glamorized and incentivized aspect viewed as operational relative to the lionized work of building models. Data is often viewed as a databases, legal, or licensing issue, but we believe that HCI has an important role to play in elevating data work as a first-class citizen of AI systems. In this paper, we examine data quality practices and challenges among AI practitioners working in high-stakes domains, where there are safety impacts on living beings, such as maternal health, road safety, and climate change. Our primary contribution is to present empirical evidence and conceptualization around data cascades in AI systems. Our method involves semi-structured interviews with 53 AI practitioners working in high-stakes domains including researchers, engineers, and data scientists based out of India, USA, and Eastern and Western African countries. We observe and define data cascades as compounding events causing negative downstream effects from data issues That result in technical debt. Over time in our study, 92 % of our participants reported experiencing at least one cascade. and. And 45 % reported experiencing two or more data cascades. Data cascades are complex, long-term, occur frequently and persistently in our study. They're opaque in their diagnosis and manifestation. They're triggered when conventional AI practices are applied in high-stakes domains, like viewing data as operations, moving fast to proof of concept, or hacking model performance without consideration for data quality, or undervaluing domain expertise and data labor. Data cascades have negative impacts on the AI development and deployment processes leading to harm to beneficiary communities, burnout of relationships, discarding entire data sets, and performing costly iterations. High-stakes AI systems are typically brittle, closely interacting with previously undigitized environments like air quality sensing, ocean sensing, or ultrasound scanning, leading to several reasons for a model to break, like limited training data, complex underlying phenomena, or volatile domains. Now, data cascades here can appear in the form of hardware, environmental, or human knowledge trips. Artifacts like fingerprints, shadows, dust on the lens, improper lighting, and pen markings were reported to affect predictions. A conventional AI practice of training on pristine data but deployed in the messy real world appeared to trigger these cascades. reference: Hello, my name is Saba Kawas and I'm a PhD candidate at the University of Washington. I'm here to present, on behalf of my co-authors, our paper titled, When Screen Time Is Not Screen Time, Tensions and Needs Between Tweens and Their Parents During Nature-Based Exploration. Tweens is a vulnerable stage of development and undergo a critical transitional phase from childhood to adolescent. Tweens begin to separate from their parents, acquiring their sense of autonomous self and. and they start to spend more time with their peers. In the midst of this shift, when tweens are negotiating their relationship with their parents and demand their independence, many parents decide to give their tween children their first smartphone. The phone often becomes the tension object in parent-tween relationships. In addition to condemning smartphones as the cause of this tension, popular media often places the blame on technologies for keeping tweens indoors and decreasing their time spent outside in nature. In our peer of work, using the interest centered design framework, we co designed with tweens, the Nature Collections app to promote their interest and connectedness to Nature. The app encourages tweens to go outside and allows them to take photographs of things they see in nature, classify the plants and animals in their photographs, and organize them in themed photo albums such as birds, insects, and trees. The app lets tweens personalize their experience by tailoring their nature challenges based on their interests. In peer research studies, we evaluated the app use in situ with tweens and confirmed its ability to successfully promote tweens' interest and connectedness to nature. In this current study, we examined parents and tweens' shared experiences using the NC app in the broader context of parent-tween tech-related tensions. We asked the following question, how do parents experience their tweens' Nature Collections app engagement and outdoor exploration during their tweens' transitional stage of tech use? And how could design be used Be used to support family needs around joint parent tween, outdoor explorations. The study was part of a larger app deployment experiment study to evaluate multiple dimensions of tweens' Nature Collections app use. We recruited 23 tweens, including 8 sibling pairs ages 9-12 from 15 unique families to use Nature Collections for two weeks. Here we analyzed the parents' interviews post-app use and in-app audio recordings of tweens and their families' real-time interactions during app use. Two overarching themes emerged in our results. Family experiences of their tweens' Nature Collections app use during nature-based explorations and the concerns and tensions during tweens' transitional tech use. Many parents noticed that the app increased tweens' attention and engagement with nature. Additionally, tweens and their parents worked together to make sense of nature elements. And some parents incorporated their pre existing knowledge and interest in App nature activities. One mother shared how often she visited their local peat patch with her tweens and noted how they engaged differently while using the NC app. It was the first time they had really looked around and asked specific questions about the plants around them, considering, hey, what are other people are growing and what is this called? Parents described the tensions they face around screen time rules with their tweens as they transition from childhood. However, parents reported making exceptions to screen time limits when technology use facilitated a valued family activity. Parents explained that they positively viewed and valued their tweens using the NC app. As this parent explains, most of the screen time they use is a personal thing. They sit with YouTube or whatever and it's just them and the screen. The Nature Collections app just encouraged more sharing, especially between the two of them. They would go out together and they would just talk about what they were going to take pictures of. They would show each other their pictures. So that was definitely different. Despite these valued outcomes, tensions around tweens, independence, use of the phone and the NC app outdoors emerged As this parent, that explained the general lack of familiarity with the concept of tweens using technology outside. To me, spending time outside and technology don't go together just because devices can get damaged because my children play outside. It's all about being in motion. Additionally, tweens often negotiated geographic limitations Limitations during the App use, which impacted where they could use the Nc app and their ability to venture out to new places without their parents. Based on our findings, we present a set of recommendations for designing technology-based experiences to support family bonding in nature. Designer can consider facilitating digital experiences that mind the context gap by supporting features to recall photo related nature information and provide nature prompts to support family conversation during their joint nature explorations. Designer could also consider facilitating joint family activities by including co-play features and support remote interaction features for parents to engage with their tweens shared nature photos. The paper also highlight opportunities for technology to reduce family screen time tension, such as facilitating features that guide clear limit setting and elicit a meaningful rationale for those limits. On behalf of my co-authors, we would like to thank all children and their parents for participating in our study. Thank you. And I'd be happy to answer any questions.

reference: Hello, my name is Sanjar Kozubaev. This is Cracking Public Space Open, designed for public librarians. This research was done in collaboration with Dr. Karl DeSalvo, who is my advisor and co-author on this paper. I'd like to start with a short story. In 2018, Forbes published an article titled, Amazon Should Replace Local Libraries to Save Taxpayers' Money. The article generated so much outrage and controversy that Forbes pulled the article a few days later and apologized for publishing such a misinformed opinion about libraries. But it also underscores, exemplifies rather, a paradox of sorts that can be seen in public libraries, at least in the U.S. On the one hand, libraries are irrelevant and should be disposed of, and on the other hand, they have never been more vital to community life. Libraries are often seen just as a service that you get in exchange for taxes that you pay. On the other hand, they're seen as a cornerstone of a functional democracy. On the one hand, libraries are sites of liberation and openness, and on the other hand, they can be exploitative and oppressive to the people who work there. And this is intensified by the ongoing decline of public spaces, austerity policies, as well as market logics that seem to penetrate all aspects of public life. These sets of conditions motivated our research, where we wanted to reframe libraries and librarians to account for these paradoxes, opposing forces, and the daily reality of public librarians. And in this paper, we propose to do that through the notion of infrastructuring, which has been taken up in HCI and CSTW research in quite productive ways in recent years. The concept of infrastructuring understands technological change by focusing away from things towards relations that they enable. In that sense, it's always ongoing, situated, contextual, and contingent. Our research was conducted with the Fulton County Library System, which is an urban library spanning over 30 locations and serving hundreds of thousands of people in the Atlanta metro area in the state of Georgia. When we engaged with this library, they were undergoing a series of renovations and new construction, which stimulated conversations around the future of libraries and the theme of constant change and adaptability to change. So let's look at some of the themes that we've uncovered around infrastructuring in libraries. The first theme speaks to the idea that collection management, specifically of physical books, can be used as nurturing and fostering community identity. So it's not just a simple transaction of exchange. The 2nd theme speaks to the libraries as sites of political activities. In many ways, public libraries are still contested spaces and libraries are in a position often to mediate this contestation in various ways. The third theme speaks to the growing number of programs and services that libraries have to design and deliver, not only within the library walls, but also outside of them in the community in different areas. The fourth theme is about influence of commercial interest and market logics in not only in the technologies and tools that librarians use, but also in their daily practice. I'd like to share two examples that That demonstrate how these themes come together. The 1st is friends groups. So these are very loosely affiliated networks of people, usually volunteers. that engage with different activities to support libraries. So in this case, the example is a book sale. So this is a way for volunteers to raise additional funds and resources outside of normal budgetary processes and city politics. The second is a library in the park. And this is an example where librarians worked with city administration and used their own professional and social networks to allow to design a program, in this case, a storytime for children in a public state like a park. So they're drawing these resources together in ways that haven't been before. Through these themes and examples, we propose several design provocations under the umbrella of the term called Cracking Public Space Open. The first provocation is a design for everyday heterogeneity and contingency. The second is designing for quasi-legitimacy. And the 3rd is designing for longevity at a small scale. In the paper, we go into greater detail about around these provocations, and how Hci design. can contribute to improve the conditions of librarians and public libraries in general. I invite you to read the paper and look forward to hearing more of your feedback and comments. Thank you.

So how do we do that? In this paper, we take a first step to create a design framework for what we call embodied algebra. We also have implemented the framework as a sketch interface where users can draw iconic elements and functions to define algebraic relations using a visually descriptive medium like sketch. We chose sketching as the primary medium because this medium is flexible to convey complex concepts, and we can iteratively work on any sketched structure. They're also widely used in the sciences, engineering, and math to communicate concepts. On the other side of the spectrum, there is the composition of abstract algebraic expressions. We'd want to be able to construct and deconstruct abstract formulations in the sketch interface, which is something that we currently do on paper or using computer algebra systems. However, we somehow have to be able to define variables and functional relationships by sketching too. Together, the iconic elements and functions create an embodied math representation. And by manipulating the iconic elements and functions, we generate algebraic expressions. So how do we do this? In a nutshell, we have designed a few brushes that let us draw objects, collections, and functions. The iconic element brush can be used to create different categories of objects like circles, rectangles, and stick figures. Once we have the iconic elements, a list brush lets me draw lists which can count the number of elements inside it. Since these are brushes, any collection or function can be drawn in any shape or form. In this case, I'm basically drawing mathematical sets in the form of houses. Mathematical functions can be drawn using a function brush. Here, I'm drawing a function container in the form of a strip that contains these houses and adds their outputs. All elements are manipulable, so an algebraic expression can be formed by bringing the list inside the function. An important characteristic of each of these compositions is that they can be explored in three layers of mathematical abstractions. In this case, we can see that the function can be displayed as the iconic representation or the symbolic formula representation. We also demonstrated that using the brushes shown so far, we can cover a good portion of the American Common Core school-level mathematics. What that means is a lot of our abstract symbol manipulation exercises could be converted into drawing-based math exercises. In this example, I demonstrate how we can calculate pi using Buffon's Needle formula. The formula relies on how many times a matchstick has crossed some lines and derives pi from the probability calculation. Every time it crosses, I draw an object inside a list representing the line. And instead of calculating the probabilities in a symbolic formula, here we have a visual drawing activity, which is also the algebraic formula itself. This is an example from physics, an example of a transformer coil and how we calculate voltage as we add more turns in a coil. This example shows that books and research papers can be made more interactive and personalizable based on how users draw on top of them. reference: Hi, I'm Wolf from Facebook Reality Labs. I'm going to present our work on ElectroRing, a wearable device for pinch-and-touch detection. This is joint work with Eric Whitmire, Chris Rittaler and Hrvoje Benko. Increased user mobility requires new ways to interact with computers, beyond touchscreens, mice and keyboards. Chris Harrison introduced a promising paradigm in 2011 with OmniTouch. Using a projector and a Kinect depth camera, OmniTouch can turn any real-world surface, including the user's body, into a touchscreen. The effectiveness of this approach hinges on the system's ability to detect precisely when the user's finger is in contact with the uninstrumented surface. reference: Hello, my name is Alina Steiner, and this work is on understanding audience participation in game live streaming on sites like Twitch. In the era of COVID-19, audiences are returning to live streaming sites for rich experiences that connect people all over the world. We present a theme map of participatory live streaming as an emerging design space. So the capacity to alter experiences has empowered audiences beyond traditional roles, and has led to a dissolution of traditional audiencehood. A growing trend in live streaming shifts focus away from passive spectatorship towards active participation. Live streaming platforms are driving a new wave of media experiences. An emerging trend in live streaming shifts emphasis from spectatorship to social interactions, allowing viewers to respond to content, streams, and one another via text chat, emojis, and GIFs. In complement, remote audiences are given greater participatory roles. In Twitch Plays Pokemon, for example, the gameplay is driven by the audience. Meanwhile, in Choice Chamber, the streamer is driving the game, but the audience is affecting the game mechanics. Game live streaming is a particularly interesting space because games are inherently interactive. They offer many ways for audiences to engage, participate, and become emotionally invested. So, our contributions are a theme map diagramming a design space for audience participation, accompanying instructions for the theme map, empirical findings that validate the theme map, and articulations of three sensitizing concepts. So, to create the theme map, we conducted a thematic analysis of eight student projects from a Twitch audience participation design course. The final product was a set of 19 themes divided into 58 sub-themes. The map is organized by three sensitizing concepts, agency, pacing, and community, that encapsulate the themes and sub-themes from our analysis. The goal of the map was to support design reflection, reflection in action that occurs while working through design actions, and reflection on action, analyzing existing experiences by understanding their form, features, or an organization. Now, we were excited to present this work to you live in Yokohama, but of course that's not currently possible. While the map was derived from game live streaming, it contains elements that are applicable to many live streaming experiences such as this one, the CHI 2021 conference we're currently participating in. As a fun exercise, we thus asked ourselves, how could we learn from game live streaming to inform a more interactive streaming experience? And we wondered if we could spark a conversation about how to design conferences to be more participatory using our theme map. Now, a time that seems like long ago, this is what attending CHI used to look like. In-person presentations, interactivity demos, posters, and of course social events. Now, unfortunately, due to the COVID-19 pandemic, these rich social interactions have been reduced to a chat log on a screen. So, to map the conference, we interpreted the sub-themes in context of virtual conferences. Then, we identified prevalent themes and sub-themes in current virtual conference experiences. And finally, we envisioned what themes and sub-themes could make virtual conferences more engaging and participatory for audiences. So, here is our mapping of the current experience. Broadly, the focus here is on pacing and community themes, such as streamer-viewer relationships, communication, and scheduling. Now, in turquoise, we've added new themes that envision what would make virtual conferences more engaging for audiences. These new themes include choice, live streaming, agency, and roles and identity. And here is the opportunity space. Now, we'll zoom in on some sub-themes that can spark inspiration for redesigning the conference experience. One sub-theme we identified was sharing identity between conference participants. Inspired by emotes from Twitch channels, an engaging concept we envisioned was to identify conference-goers by their interests. A design concept was thus to have users customize their profile and the text chat with stickers of sessions they attended. A second sub-theme was chatting during off-times. Inspired by Battle Royale games, we conceptualized a virtual lobby that allows kind participants to connect to each other by engaging in cooperative mini-games. Finally, the third sub-theme was about the feeling of the game world. Inspired by survival games like Don't Starve with day and night cycles, our concept was to create a shared interpretation of a particular place and time. In this design concept, participants can customize their backgrounds to reflect the time of day in Yokohama, so that everyone feels that they're sharing a space together. And now, it's your turn to respond. Has our map sparked any ideas about improving live streaming experiences? Thank you so much for your time.

reference: In this presentation, I'm going to share our research, AI as social glue, uncovering the roles of deep generative AI during social music composition. This work is done by Mia Seo, Emily Youngbloom from Google, and Michael Terry and Carrie Cai from Google Research. AI now enables individuals to do various forms of creative work, such as auto-completing a paragraph, fleshing out a hand-drawn sketch, or co-composing whole sections of music. However, recent studies point out that it can be still challenging to partner with AI for creative work. This challenge might be more nuanced and complex when we consider that people's creative needs and practices are socially experienced. A growing body of work has focused on human-AI collaborations, but much less is known about what roles AI could play in human-human collaboration. This motivated us to seek to answer the research question, what kinds of roles can AI play in human-human collaboration for creative work? So, we conducted qualitative studies with 15 pairs. During the session, they composed music together twice, once without AI and once with AI in counterbalanced order. We found that AI played 5 primary roles in human-human collaboration for creative work. Due to the time constraints, I will focus on the three major themes, but I do encourage you to read our paper for the rest of the themes and details. We found that AI provided a psychological safety net. When AI was not present, participants felt more judged or socially pressured. One participant said they were slightly embarrassed after their first attempt to compose music, and another said they were worried if their music sounded weird to their partner. On the other hand, in the AI condition, participants felt less responsible to make something that sounded cool. Participants were nicely surprised at what AI could do, encouraging them to try out something new, which ultimately made their experiences more playful. We also found that AI was a mitigator of interpersonal friction in co-composition of music. When AI was not present, participants felt tensions like, this is how I see the world, and I want to make you to see it like I do. However, they were hesitant to fully express their feelings or differences in opinion because those may sound rude to their human partner. However, this notion was somewhat smoothed out in the AI condition. AI's presence naturally put two human partners together on the same team, which shifted from judging each other's ideas to judging AI's ideas. As AI would not get hurt or upset, the teams of two humans were able to have a more positive experience in their collaboration without worrying about the possibility of offending each other. In the meantime, we also observed that AI could reduce the depth of collaboration in their creative work. A majority of participants reported that they were more engaged in creating music when there was no AI. In AI condition, participants felt like AI was the composer and two humans were co-curators or producers, which indicates that the change of humans' roles In Co composition, when Ai was present to summarize, we found that Ai increased the ease of human human collaboration. but it decreased the depth of their co-creative activity. The findings provide various implications for how to design AI for human-human collaboration, but I want to empathize that AI can be designed as a social glue in co-creative activities. AI could help build on each other's ideas while helping maintain cordiality and forward momentum. Also, designers could note that potential shortcomings of AI of easing or deepening human-human collaboration and tailor technologies to best support specific goals and tasks. Thanks for listening to the presentation and you can find more details from our paper.

AI now enables individuals to do various forms of creative work, such as
auto-completing a paragraph, fleshing out a hand-drawn sketch, or co-composing whole sections of music.
However, research studies point out that it can be still challenging to partner with AI for creative work.
This challenge might be more nuanced and complex when we consider that people's creative needs and practices are socially experienced.
A growing body of work has focused on human AI collaborations, but much less is known about
what roles AI could play in human-human collaboration. This motivated us to seek to answer the
research question, what kinds of roles can AI play in human-human collaboration for creative work?
So we conducted qualitative studies with 15 pairs. During the session they composed music together twice,
once without AI and once with AI in counterbalanced order. We found that AI played five primary roles in
human-human collaboration for creative work. Due to the time constraints, I will focus on the three major
things, but I'd encourage you to read our paper for the rest of the themes and
details. We found that AI provided a psychological safety net. When AI was
not present, participants fell more judged or socially pressured. One participant
said they were slightly embarrassed after their first attempt to compose
music, and another said they were worried if their music sounded weird to
their partner. On the other hand, in the AI condition, participants felt less
responsible to make something that sounded cool. Participants were nicely
surprised at what AI could do, encouraging them to try out something new,
which ultimately made their experiences more playful. We also found that AI
was a mediator of interpersonal friction in co-composition of music. When AI
was not present, participate in the failed tensions like, this is how I see the word, and I want
to make you to see it like I do. However, they were hesitant to fully express their feelings or
differences in opinion because those may sound rude to their human partner. However, this notion
was somewhat smoothed out in the AI condition. AI's presence naturally put two human partners
together on the same team, which shifted from judging each other's ideas to judging
AI's ideas.
As AI would not get hurt or upset, the teams of two humans were able to have a more positive
experience in their collaboration without worrying about the possibility of offending
each other.
In the meantime, we also observed that AI could reduce the depth of collaboration in their
creative work.
A majority of participants reported that they were more engaged in creating music when
there was no AI.
In AI condition, participants felt like AI was the composer, and two humans were co-curators
or producers, which indicates that the change of humans' roles in co-composition when AI
was present.
To summarize, we found that AI increased the ease of human human collaboration, but
it decreased the depth of their co-creative activity.
The findings provide various implications for how to design AI for human human collaboration,
but I want to empathize that AI can be designed as social glue in co-creative activities.
AI could help build on each other's ideas, while helping maintain cordiality and
forward momentum. Also, designers could note that potential shortcomings of AI of easing
or deepening human-human collaboration and tailored technologies to best support specific
goals and tasks. Thanks for listening to the presentation and you can find more details from our
paper.

reference: Hello, my name is Silas. And my name is Tiffany. Tiffany and I are the first authors of this work, so let's jump in. Computers grading students' work is nothing new, but nowadays, deployments of AI graders have become popular, especially systems that automatically grade and give feedback for written work. This has happened on the well-known GRE, and in various states in the US. These autograders generally match humans in accuracy, and there's no denying it can save a lot of work. But just because something works well on paper doesn't mean that people will accept it. Both humans and AI make mistakes, but trust in an algorithm drops especially fast when it makes mistakes. There's fairness concerns. We have no shortage of stories about AI discrimination. And people will form folk theories of how algorithms operate and adjust their behavior to match. In education, folk theories may impact how students answer questions or even gaming attempts. Given these phenomena, the important question nowadays is less of, can AI grading be done? And more, how should it be done? The automated classroom ecosystem currently lacks insights into this crucial question. Based with this question, we studied a short-answer AI autograder. We asked students about how they thought the autograder worked and their answer construction strategies. We examined their various attitudes and would explain these attitudes. And based on our findings, we proposed guidelines for deploying imperfect AI autograders. Here's the autograder we studied. In this intro CS class, students described a block of code in plain English, and their descriptions were automatically graded. In both homeworks and exams, right and wrong submissions, exemplar answers would always appear as feedback. Students could appeal decisions that they thought were made in error. The homework allowed unlimited attempts, But exams only allowed one attempt. The grader wasn't perfect. Around 10 % of correct answers were marked wrong. And around 15 % of wrong answers were marked right. Notably in terms of raw grading accuracy, humans matched the autograder. We gathered the experiences of 71 students through surveys and interviews. We then used linear regression to find associations between student attitudes under study, and used a grounded theory approach to uncover themes in the qualitative data. Now, we will present some result highlights. First, folk theories. A majority of students thought the algorithm looked for keywords. However, only a few of them expressed details of how this matching was performed. Misalignment between folk theories and how the autograder actually worked could lead to suboptimal answer construction strategies. For example, a student reported they wrote long answers, thinking that it had a higher chance to hit more keywords, like in this contrived example. But they were not aware that the system assigned negative weights to certain words, and longer answers had more of a chance to hit those words too. Next, we examined students' perceived autograding accuracy, fairness, educational value, and satisfaction towards the autograder, all expected to be related to their acceptance of the autograder. We found that students overall overestimated the likelihood of false negatives or correct answers being graded as wrong and. and many of them had not considered the possibility of wrong answers being graded as correct, but still thought they were harmful to learning. At the same time, higher perceived false negative rates statistically predicted lower perceptions of fairness and lower satisfaction on exams. From our findings, we propose several classroom deployment guidelines. First, instructors should allow students to practice with the autograder in a low-stick setting before high-stick deployment, and prepare robust error management processes for high-stick deployments. Second, transparency could dispel harmful folk theories and improve students' attitudes, but finding the proper messaging is critical and still an open question. Third, we shouldn't focus only on minimizing false negatives to make students happier if it increases false positives, which could be harmful to learning. We need to consider both the impact on learning and students' attitudes when we make trade-offs on these error rates. In conclusion, our paper discusses guidelines on how to deploy an AI autograder. But even with our tips, you should first consider, should I deploy an AI autograder? A critical question raised in a recent scandal in the UK. Educators should carefully consider the ability and resources to address errors, algorithm aversion, fairness concerns, and more. We hope our work encourages further discussion on the deployment of AI in a manner considerate of students' needs. Thanks to our participants, NSF and Capital One for funding, and thank you for listening.

reference: Hello everyone, I'm Maggie from the MediFacts Lab of Penn State. I'm really glad to present the work on behalf of me and my co-author, Dr. Shamsunder. With the rapid diffusion of AI-driven technologies, it has become increasingly common for users to get system-generated recommendations. But this convenience comes at a price, namely users' privacy. One solution to this dilemma is for AI systems to be upfront with their users by providing the appropriate explanations for seeking and using their info. Many platforms have started to provide such explanations, and they are usually framed in a way that emphasizes potential benefits to users. For instance, on Facebook, you can see an explanation for how providing birthday information can help enhance one's user experience in the future. Similarly, YouTube explains that they need your viewing history because it can result in better recommendations. Although such explanations are very common, it is still not clear if these explanations are truly persuasive and effective in resolving the dilemma. They seem paternalistic and suggest a quip or crow, both of which would not fly in human-to-human communication. What would fly instead is an explicit request for help. So will the same holds true when AI systems talk to users about needing their personal information? As it turns out, help-seeker behavior is usually seen as a social behavior and very interpersonal in nature. According to the computers-are-social-actors paradigm, we might appreciate machines that exhibit that kind of social cues, even though seeking help might showcase machines' vulnerability and dependence on us. In addition to help-seeker cues alone, if machines provide both the help-seeker cues and help-provider cues, we might like it even more, as literature suggests that individuals are more motivated to contribute when they see the value of their contribution to not only the individual human herself, But others as well, so based on all these possibilities. we designed a 4x2 between-subject experiment among 293 Amazon MTurkers by gauging the effectiveness of four different helper cues. The AI system as a help-seeker, as a help-provider, As both help seeker and the help provider and the control condition, that is no explanations, and we mocked up a news recommender system called Mends. which was framed as an ENCOS chamber smasher that is designed to recommend news that the users will not normally see. reference: Hello, I'm Yang Shi from Intelligent Big Data Visualization Lab, Tongji University. I'll be presenting our work, a design space for animated visual narratives in data videos. Visualizations have long been used to support storytelling. For example, news organizations frequently incorporate visualizations into their journalism. So the concept of narrative visualization has emerged. Data videos is a genre of narrative visualization which combines visualization with motion graphics to tell data-driven stories. When creating data videos, designers often use animation to encode data attributes. Animation techniques in data videos are used to capture changes in visual content and geometric properties of visualizations, as well as indirectly manipulate visualizations over time. For example, this data video is well known for incorporating animation into visualization to engage the audience. In the video, the author first decodes a scatter plot by presenting its two dimensions, income as x-axis and lifespan as y-axis. The axes blink to grab the audience's attention. And a set of bubbles representing different countries gradually reveal. The author then explains the visual encoding of a single bubble. Meanwhile, the bubble glows to call attention while an annotation is added to explain which country it represents. After that, the bubbles start to move with time. During this process, the author sometimes slows down or pauses to elaborate on certain countries. As the audience is getting to understand the visual encoding, the author then speeds up the bubble movement to leave out redundant information. Likewise, we analyzed 82 high-quality data videos and identified 43 animation techniques that are frequently used in these videos. We then classified these animation techniques by their editorial layers And the narrative strategies to form a deeper understanding of animated visual narratives in data videos next. I'm going to introduce the two categorizations of animation techniques. The first categorization is about editorial layers, which refer to composable primitives of data videos. We distinguished between four different editorial layers, that is, the elements of visualization, elements added to visualization, camera, and timeline. For example, animation techniques on this layer manipulate textual or graphical elements added to visualization, such as embellishments and annotations. Examples include adding a border around a bar in a bar chart and drawing a benchmark line on a bar chart. On the other hand, we categorized animation techniques by their visual narrative strategies. Such strategies can help assemble a set of separate data facts into an expressive and memorable data-driven story. We identified eight categories of narrative strategies, that is, emphasis, suspense, comparison, cohering, ellipsis, focalization, concretization, and twist. Emphasis is one of the most supported narrative strategies in data videos. It communicates core messages by creating look-here signals with visual hierarchy. In case one, blink is added to the excess of the scatterplot to emphasize that the position of the bubbles can encode different messages. To see the full version of our design space, please check our data video explorer online. That ends my presentation. Thank you for your attention.

reference: Hi, I'm Kevin Lam from the University of Saskatchewan here to give this short talk on our paper, The Effects of System Interpretation Errors on Learning New Input Mechanisms. Written with my co-authors Carl, Madison, and Andy, this paper presents our contributions to understanding how noise and interpretation errors can affect users and their learning. People interact with computer systems through the use of an input mechanism, such as the mouse and keyboard. These input mechanisms receive real-world analog signals as input from the user that the computer must interpret and convert into a digital format that the computer can recognize and use to execute commands. E.g. the Microsoft Kinect allows users to perform in ear gestures as a form of command input. There are also devices called brain-computer interfaces that let people control their computer using signals from their brain. However, all these input mechanisms share a similar problem when it comes to interpreting an analog signal, noise. The presence of noise can obscure useful information and make it difficult for the computer system to correctly interpret the user's intended input, which may lead to interpretation errors. Interpretation errors occur when the system interprets the user's intended command incorrectly. These errors often result in one of three types, misinterpretations, where the wrong command is selected, false negatives, where the user enters an input but the computer fails to recognize the command, and false positives, where the system executes a command without the user inputting anything. Noise and interpretation errors can cause users to become more likely to make errors themselves, be less satisfied with using the input mechanism, and have reduced performance overall. We wanted to understand how interpretation errors would affect a user's process of learning to use an input mechanism. Following Fitts and Posner's stages of expertise development, users start as novices when they first use an input mechanism, and they gradually transition to becoming experts as they use and practice with the mechanism over time. We formed two hypotheses about how interpretation errors would affect learning. The first is the interference hypothesis. It suggests that interpretation errors will interfere with a user's development and reinforcement of memory pathways, leading to a longer learning curve. Our second hypothesis, the retrieval effort hypothesis, posits that when an error occurs, the extra attention and effort spent on correcting that error will actually reinforce the user's learning. To test these hypotheses, we conducted two user studies where participants were tasked with selecting items from a menu using keyboard arrow keys. We created a system that could easily differentiate between novice and expert use so that we could observe their learning process. reference: Hi everyone, my name is Martin, I'm a PhD student and a teacher for Media Informatics at the University of Regensburg and today I will give a talk about physiological and perceptual responses to athletic avatars while cycling in VR. This paper is co-authored with Florian Habler, Valentin Schwind, Paweł Woźniak, Christian Wolff and Nils Henze. We know that modern VR technology allows the user to embody avatars. Through a first-person perspective and visual motosynchrony through motion capture or other tracking technologies, we can induce a feeling of being the avatar, acting from within the avatar and accepting it as the virtual alter ego. This phenomenon is commonly known as the body ownership illusion. Since VR can render the avatar in any desired style, the user can therefore embody virtually any possible appearance. This virtual embodiment of avatars that differ from the physical self can trigger an effect known as the Proteus effect. Alluding to the versatility of the Greek god Proteus, who was said to be able to change his shape at will, the Proteus effect describes behavioral, attitudinal and perceptual changes due to the embodiment of the virtual avatar and its alien characteristics. Therefore we were wondering whether this effect can be utilized from an HCI perspective to positively affect the user in VR sports applications or immersive exergames. We have already conducted a study, which was published at CHI Play last year, where we embodied participants and avatars with different degrees of muscularity, from non-muscular to muscular. In this study, we found a systematic relationship between the avatar's muscularity and the perception of effort. We used the established Borg-RPE Scale to assess the perception of effort, and this scale was originally defined to estimate the heart rate while multiplying the measures with ten. For example, a perceived exertion of 11 should approximately match a heart rate of 110. Therefore we were wondering whether avatars can also affect physiological responses to physical effort. This time we wanted to investigate physical effort on an ergometer bike. Therefore we tried to systematically design appropriate avatars By using the two primary fitness indicators, body fat and muscularity, we increased both parameters in 33 % steps. This result, this procedure resulted in 16 female and 16 male gendered avatars. Then we ran an online survey using mTrick to evaluate the avatars with 74 participants who rated them based on the following measures, resting heart rate, heart rate speed and time. We presented renderings of the avatars, and the participants had to estimate these measures while imagining being the avatar. but then we averaged. the scores per dimension and created these heatmaps. Afterward we determined the best, worst and medium avatar resulting in a non-athletic, medium and athletic version. Now we had the avatars and were able to investigate whether an avatar's athletic appearance can really affect physiological responses to physical effort. We conducted a study in a within-subject design with 24 participants. The participants cycled following a standardized exercise protocol on an ergometer placed in our VR laboratory and we created a virtual replica and placed it in the virtual environment. They embodied avatars of their identified gender with a non-athletic, medium and athletic appearance and had the feeling of cycling in VR. We took the following measures, the heart rate, the perception of effort, the sense of presence, the body ownership and the self-perceived fitness as a manipulation check. Let's have a look at the results. We found a significant main effect of gender and body on the perceived exertion and replicated the findings from our first study. Now let's have a look At the heart rate response for both female and male participants, they had a lower. A significantly lower heart rate during the exercise while being embodied in the athletic avatar compared to the medium and non athletic avatar. Regarding the cool-down phase in the last 5 minutes, something seemed to happen so we can see that the systematic effect during the exercise did not occur during cool-down. Let's wrap up the findings and conclude this talk. We found a systematic relationship between an avatar's athletic appearance and the perception of effort. We also found that athletic avatars can decrease their heart rate response during exertion. However, we also found significant differences between the body ownership ratings. Therefore, we cannot definitely conclude that these effects are caused by the avatar's appearance or by the experienced body ownership. Now, overall, we conclude that avatars which are perceived as physically fit and athletic can decrease the perception of effort, and that psychophysiological impact of avatars may be a promising opportunity to positively affect the user by reducing the physiological exertion during the exercise, and therefore potentially. increasing exercise adherence. With this, I conclude this talk and welcome your questions.

reference: Hi, my name is Allison McDonald. Today I'm going to be talking about our research on issues with phone numbers and phone number recycling. Mobile phones have become an integral part of our daily lives, and consequently phone numbers have become a convenient and common way for businesses and services to identify us. For many of us, our phone number is connected to us across many platforms and companies. We may use our phone number for mobile messaging, in connection to our bank account, on social media, and other personal activities. But phone numbers carry privacy risks, especially when they're used in ways we don't expect. Over the last several years, there have been many different news stories about phone numbers being abused. For example, governments may use them to build networks of protesters or to physically track someone. If your phone number is recycled, that is if someone else gets it when you stop using it, the next owner may have access to your personal information and may even use that number to gain access to your other accounts. So far, these problems with phone numbers have been mostly anecdotal. With this study, we aim to comprehensively catalog what privacy, security, and access problems arise with the ubiquitous use of phone numbers and phone number recycling. To do this, we conducted a qualitative elicitation survey with open-ended responses. We first asked a broad question about annoying, weird, or disturbing experiences with phone numbers, and then followed up with some specific questions about events we expected would trigger negative experiences, like phone number recycling, loss of access to a phone number or a service, and uncomfortable experiences sharing a phone number. We received 195 responses, and I'm going to highlight some of the findings here. First, we identified five different categories of negative experience. I am going to give a few examples. Frequently, problems arise when a person loses access to their phone number, perhaps because they can't pay their bill or have moved internationally. Several participants described problems like this one, where the loss of a phone number creates cascading access issues. For example, if an email is connected to a phone number, the email becomes accessible when the phone number is inaccessible. Many people experienced phone number recycling. In some cases, participants even described getting access to significant personal data of the former owner. In this example, someone gained access to the previous owners bank transactions, Whatsapp account. and received dozens of phone calls meant for the previous owner. Sharing phone numbers could also be very personal. Participants described different situations in which they did not want to share a number, but were expected to, for example, with a delivery driver. We also identified the consequences participants said that they suffered. To give just two examples, when asked to share a number for a reason they didn't understand, participants expressed frustration or anger at companies, and many said they didn't trust the company to protect their information, leading to an erosion of trust in the company as a whole. Dealing with the various problems also had a significant emotional cost, from annoyance to fear, anxiety, and stress. Finally, we cataloged the different ways participants described changing their own behaviors to address these negative experiences and consequences. Here are some examples to give you a sense of what we found. A surprising number of participants who had a recycled phone number would go out of their way to help callers by telling them they had the wrong number, with varying levels of success. Some participants, when forced to give a phone number for a service, either could or would not, and were thus unable to sign up or participate. And finally, many participants described some level of resignation. Although they recognized that there is a cost to having their phone number shared in so many places, they felt that they had no choice. We make several recommendations. First, governments can consider reducing the rate of phone number recycling by expanding the space of available phone numbers. Companies, whenever possible, should allow for alternate ways for users to be identified, like email or username. And finally, both users and companies should opt out of Sms based multi multifactor in favor of more secure options. In conclusion, we found that phone numbers are not always a reliable way to identify people. Visual Search is about finding design examples supporting the design requirements. However, designers usually struggle to articulate their design requirements into keywords. The reason is that designers describe these requirements as images across the different design stages. So it would be more suitable to use these UI images instead of keywords as input queries for finding relative design examples. And that's the main research question we try to address in this paper. To answer the question, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 designers to gain a professional perspective into the search process in terms of different aspects. First, most designers agreed that the examples are important and are widely used within their projects. Second, designers identified difficulties which mostly relate to describing the specific UI with only text queries. Third, instead of only keywords, designers pointed that other design aspects should be considered when measuring the UI similarity, such as structure and functionality. This emphasizes the need to consider new design aspects when developing effective design searching tools. Taking these design aspects into consideration, we advanced the current research by first modeling the structure and content of the UI instead of treating it as only a pixel-based image. Second, supporting UI queries of multiple design stages. This is our proposed retrieval pipeline. It starts by using an object detection model To detect the labels and bounding boxes of the different Ui components in the input query. This will provide a structural representation of the layout. For this, we have collected and annotated a large-scale mobile UI dataset of different design stages. The system then creates a segmented image And pass it to a multi model embedding network that uses attention mechanism for retrieval. We collected our dataset because we need high-quality annotations for training the object detection, which is not currently available in the public UI datasets. Examples of these limitations are as shown in the RICO column, first, broken hierarchies. 2nd, extra space within the bounding boxes, and inconsistencies with the class label of similar objects as a result. The 1st contribution is the Vins dataset which has a total of four eight oh oh annotated Ui images across two design stages. The second contribution is the Attention-Aware Retrieval System. The image model encodes the hierarchical structure of the input segmented image By using a box attention mechanism, the label model encodes the Ui content by representing the Ui classes. The learned embeddings from the two models are concatenated for the retrieval part. More details are available in the paper. Second, we evaluate the retrieval system by calculating the precision score at top k retrieved images. So it would be more suitable to use these UI images instead of keywords as input queries for finding relative design examples. And that's the main research question we try to address in this paper. To answer the question, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 designers to gain a professional perspective into the search process in terms of different aspects. First, most designers agreed that the examples are important and are widely used within their projects. Second, designers identified difficulties which mostly relate to describing the specific UI with only text queries. Third, instead of only keywords, designers pointed that other design aspects should be considered when measuring the UI similarity, such as structure and functionality. This emphasizes the need to consider new design aspects when developing effective design searching tools. Taking these design aspects into consideration, we advanced the current research by first modeling the structure and content of the UI instead of treating it as only a pixel-based image. Second, supporting UI queries of multiple design stages. This is our proposed retrieval pipeline. It starts by using an object detection model To detect the labels and bounding boxes of the different Ui components in the input query. This will provide a structural representation of the layout. For this, we have collected and annotated a large-scale mobile UI dataset of different design stages. The system then creates a segmented image And pass it to a multi model embedding network that uses attention mechanism for retrieval. We collected our dataset because we need high-quality annotations for training the object detection, which is not currently available in the public UI datasets. Examples of these limitations are as shown in the RICO column, first, broken hierarchies. 2nd, extra space within the bounding boxes, and inconsistencies with the class label of similar objects as a result. The 1st contribution is the Vins dataset which has a total of four eight oh oh annotated Ui images across two design stages. The second contribution is the Attention-Aware Retrieval System. The image model encodes the hierarchical structure of the input segmented image By using a box attention mechanism, the label model encodes the Ui content by representing the Ui classes. The learned embeddings from the two models are concatenated for the retrieval part. More details are available in the paper. For the result, we 1st evaluate the annotations of Vins dataset with object detection overall. Vins annotations provide a 26 % increase over the mean average precision of Rico dataset annotations next. We evaluate on the complete Vins dataset across twelve classes and achieve an overall mean average precision of 76. and area under the curve of 79. Second, we evaluate the retrieval system by calculating the precision score at top k retrieved images. Overall, our model outperforms the baseline and further improves the precision rates at each value of k. Finally, we evaluate the end-to-end combined model on input queries belonging to different design categories and stages. We recruited five designers for this evaluation. These are high-fidelity queries along with the top three retrieved results. Overall, all the designers Mentioned that the retrieved results are relevant to the input queries and would provide beneficial design examples. Similarly, these are the results for Y-frame UI queries where designers were also satisfied with them. As an extra feature, the model can also be used to autocomplete Ui layouts when given partial design requirement, as shown in the figure. Thank you and if you have any questions.

reference: Hello everyone, this is Jiaming Zhang from the University of Tokyo. I will present our study, Spatial Labeling, Leveraging Spatial Layout for Improving Label Quality in Non-Expert Image Annotation. Manual image labeling is necessary for machine learning. However, it is a label-intensive process, not everyone recruits non-expert annotators to do it. Image labeling by non-experts can be very difficult, such as selecting a dog breed label to a dog image, and it may contain many errors because non-experts have insufficient domain knowledge. In this study, our goal is to reduce errors in image labeling by non-experts. We decide an image labeling interface, we call it spatial labeling. In this interface, we propose to leverage spatial layout as a temporarily working space during annotation. This is our proposed interface. The center is the image needs to be labeled, and the two sides are labels. User needs to select an appropriate label from the two-side label list to the image. Now, I will show you a demo video. In this interface, an open space is provided. User 1st spatially lays out images and the labels on the open space, placing related items together. It serves as a working space for tentative labeling. During this process, the user can build domain knowledge by observing similarity and differences among the items. After laying out the images and the labels, the user gives definitive labels to the images based on the result of spatial layout by drag-and-dropping one or more images to a label. We expect this process reduces errors in image labeling by non-experts. We run a user study to compare a traditional non-spatial layout and our proposed spatial layout interface in an image labeling task. The labeling task is to label 50 dog images by selecting an appropriate label from a 20-dog breed list. The left video shows how did the user work via the traditional labeling interface. And the right video shows how did the user work via our proposed interface. In the traditional interface, user needs to go through all the labels and try to find the best possible label to the image. However, in our spatial layout interface, user are allowed to organize concepts of labels and images on the open space before selecting a label for an image. We measure the time and error rate of the labeling task completed by the participants. The result showed that the task completion time difference was not significant between the non-spatial layout and the spatial layout labeling interface. However, the error rate in the spatial layout labeling task was significantly lower than the non-spatial layout labeling task. The main contribution from this study is that our spatial layout interface can reduce error difference in non-expert image annotation. We believe that this has presented significant insights for manual image annotation. It is because our proposed method can get better results only by tweaking user interface without increasing cost. Please read our paper for more details. Thank you.

reference: We introduce CapContact, a novel method to precisely infer the contact area between the user's finger and the surface from a single capacitive image. There are more than 3 billion smartphones in the world that use capacitive sensing for touch input. Capacitive sensors measure the proximity of close-by objects that change the electric field between the sensor lines. The resolution of these sensors is determined by their primary purpose, which is to reliably detect touch events and to discriminate adjacent touches. Therefore, a standard of around 4 mm spacing between grid lines has emerged in the industry. This pitch is insufficient, however, when fingers move too close and the resulting intensities merge. And it's cases like these where we really care about precise contact areas and not just touch locations. Of course, capacitive sensing was never designed to determine precise contact. In the HCI community, we've been at this point before, where researchers played with diffuse illumination systems. But it wasn't until the arrival of FTIR that we could work with true contact areas and distinguish touches reliably. And this is what inspired our work. With CapContact, we propose a single-image super-resolution method that estimates high-resolution contact masks from low-resolution capacitive intensities. CapContact implements a generative adversarial network that comprises a convolutional neural network with five residual blocks. These blocks are connected to three consecutive subpixel convolutional layers that upsample the image with a factor of 8. Due to the fully convolutional architecture, we can feed capacitive frames of any size into CapContact. To train our supervised method, we call it a training corpus with matched pairs of capacitive touch frames and high-resolution images of the corresponding contact areas. For this, our rig integrates FTIR into the capacitive sensor. We first mounted a transparent touch panel upside down onto the acrylic surface. The connected digitizer resolved changes in mutual capacitance at 16-bit resolution. We added a sheet of acrylic on top, illuminated with two LED strips to complete the FTIR setup. The webcam below the surface then captured the contact areas as they lit up due to the touch events. For data collection, we recruited 10 participants that performed 10 different touch gestures. In total, the full dataset has over 26,000 different pairs of synchronized frames. With the FTIR and capacitive images as input, the currently existing default implementation with a threshold produces an area that is way too large, just as expected. In contrast, Capcontact reaches a contact area size with less than 3 % difference from the actual area. Using our dataset, we also optimized a learned threshold that minimizes this error across all samples, but it still produces a much worse outcome than CapContact. In terms of discriminating adjacent contacts, the baseline often blends them, resulting in an F1 score of only 0.69, whereas CapContact achieves an F1 score of 0.93. Again, our learned threshold achieves an accuracy that is in between both. As a side effect of reconstructing contact areas, the touch input locations we can derive from CapContact are much closer to the true contact center than the center of gravity of the capacitive measurements. For full details, please see the paper. Because we're working with super-resolution, we also conducted experiments on images at just half the input resolution, so twice the pitch. And still, CapContact produced contact areas that separated touches with an F1 score that was much higher than the baseline achieved on full-resolution images. To double-check CapContact's capability to work on half-resolution sensors, we ran our network on Project Sensible, a sensor with a larger gridline pitch. Here, CapContact robustly detected contact areas even under noisy conditions, successfully rejecting false inputs and solely preserving actual touch contacts. As you can see, the threshold-based method suffers from mistouches, as well as noise due to the flexible surface. In conclusion, we have introduced the first investigation of deriving actual contact shapes from mutual capacitance sensing. Our data-driven method CapContact estimates the contact area from a single capacitive image, reliably discriminating adjacent touches and bringing input locations closer to the center of true contact, even when applied to a sensor with just half-resolution. We think that CapContact opens up many opportunities for future touch devices. For example, to reliably distinguish hover and touch, to operate a much lower-resolution sensor with higher pitches, and to produce higher touch input accuracy. You can find all materials on ziplab.org, where we have released the dataset and code.

reference: We introduce CapContact, a novel method to precisely infer the contact area between the user's finger and the surface from a single capacitive image. There are more than 3 billion smartphones in the world that use capacitive sensing for touch input. Capacitive sensors measure the proximity of close-by objects that change the electric field between the sensor lines. The resolution of these sensors is determined by their primary purpose, which is to reliably detect touch events and to discriminate adjacent touches. Therefore, a standard of around 4 mm spacing between grid lines has emerged in the industry. This pitch is insufficient, however, when fingers move too close and the resulting intensities merge. And it's cases like these where we really care about precise contact areas and not just touch locations. Of course, capacitive sensing was never designed to determine precise contact. In the HCI community, we've been at this point before, where researchers played with diffuse illumination systems. But it wasn't until the arrival of FTIR that we could work with true contact areas and distinguish touches reliably. And this is what inspired our work. With CapContact, we propose a single-image super-resolution method that estimates high-resolution contact masks from low-resolution capacitive intensities. CapContact implements a generative adversarial network that comprises a convolutional neural network with five residual blocks. These blocks are connected to three consecutive subpixel convolutional layers that upsample the image with a factor of 8. Due to the fully convolutional architecture, we can feed capacitive frames of any size into CapContact. To train our supervised method, we call it a training corpus with matched pairs of capacitive touch frames and high-resolution images of the corresponding contact areas. For this, our rig integrates FTIR into the capacitive sensor. We first mounted a transparent touch panel upside down onto the acrylic surface. The connected digitizer resolved changes in mutual capacitance at 16-bit resolution. We added a sheet of acrylic on top, illuminated with two LED strips to complete the FTIR setup. The webcam below the surface then captured the contact areas as they lit up due to the touch events. For data collection, we recruited 10 participants that performed 10 different touch gestures. In total, the full dataset has over 26,000 different pairs of synchronized frames. With the FTIR and capacitive images as input, the currently existing default implementation with a threshold produces an area that is way too large, just as expected. In contrast, Capcontact reaches a contact area size with less than 3 % difference from the actual area. Using our dataset, we also optimized a learned threshold that minimizes this error across all samples, but it still produces a much worse outcome than CapContact. In terms of discriminating adjacent contacts, the baseline often blends them, resulting in an F1 score of only 0.69, whereas CapContact achieves an F1 score of 0.93. Again, our learned threshold achieves an accuracy that is in between both. As a side effect of reconstructing contact areas, the touch input locations we can derive from CapContact are much closer to the true contact center than the center of gravity of the capacitive measurements. For full details, please see the paper. Because we're working with super-resolution, we also conducted experiments on images at just half the input resolution, so twice the pitch. And still, CapContact produced contact areas that separated touches with an F1 score that was much higher than the baseline achieved on full-resolution images. To double-check CapContact's capability to work on half-resolution sensors, we ran our network on Project Sensible, a sensor with a larger gridline pitch. Here, CapContact robustly detected contact areas even under noisy conditions, successfully rejecting false inputs and solely preserving actual touch contacts. As you can see, the threshold-based method suffers from mistouches, as well as noise due to the flexible surface. In conclusion, we have introduced the first investigation of deriving actual contact shapes from mutual capacitance sensing. Our data-driven method CapContact estimates the contact area from a single capacitive image, reliably discriminating adjacent touches and bringing input locations closer to the center of true contact, even when applied to a sensor with just half-resolution. We think that CapContact opens up many opportunities for future touch devices. For example, to reliably distinguish hover and touch, to operate a much lower-resolution sensor with higher pitches, and to produce higher touch input accuracy. You can find all materials on ziplab.org, where we have released the dataset and code.

Capacitive sensors measure the proximity of close-by objects that change the electric field between the sensor lines. The resolution of these sensors is determined by their primary purpose, which is to reliably detect touch events and to discriminate adjacent touches. Therefore, a standard of around 4 mm spacing between grid lines has emerged in the industry. This pitch is insufficient, however, when fingers move too close and the resulting intensities merge. And it's cases like these where we really care about precise contact areas and not just touch locations. Of course, capacitive sensing was never designed to determine precise contact. In the HCI community, we've been at this point before, where researchers played with diffuse illumination systems. But it wasn't until the arrival of FTIR that we could work with true contact areas and distinguish touches reliably. And this is what inspired our work. With CapContact, we propose a single-image super-resolution method that estimates high-resolution contact masks from low-resolution capacitive intensities. CapContact implements a generative adversarial network that comprises a convolutional neural network with five residual blocks. These blocks are connected to three consecutive subpixel convolutional layers that upsample the image with a factor of 8. Due to the fully convolutional architecture, we can feed capacitive frames of any size into CapContact. To train our supervised method, we call it a training corpus with matched pairs of capacitive touch frames and high-resolution images of the corresponding contact areas. For this, our rig integrates FTIR into the capacitive sensor. We first mounted a transparent touch panel upside down onto the acrylic surface. The connected digitizer resolved changes in mutual capacitance at 16-bit resolution. We added a sheet of acrylic on top, illuminated with two LED strips to complete the FTIR setup. The webcam below the surface then captured the contact areas as they lit up due to the touch events. For data collection, we recruited 10 participants that performed 10 different touch gestures. In total, the full dataset has over 26,000 different pairs of synchronized frames. With the FTIR and capacitive images as input, the currently existing default implementation with a threshold produces an area that is way too large, just as expected. In contrast, Capcontact reaches a contact area size with less than 3 % difference from the actual area. Using our dataset, we also optimized a learned threshold that minimizes this error across all samples, but it still produces a much worse outcome than CapContact. In terms of discriminating adjacent contacts, the baseline often blends them, resulting in an F1 score of only 0.69, whereas CapContact achieves an F1 score of 0.93. Again, our learned threshold achieves an accuracy that is in between both. As a side effect of reconstructing contact areas, the touch input locations we can derive from CapContact are much closer to the true contact center than the center of gravity of the capacitive measurements. For full details, please see the paper. Because we're working with super-resolution, we also conducted experiments on images at just half the input resolution, so twice the pitch. And still, CapContact produced contact areas that separated touches with an F1 score that was much higher than the baseline achieved on full-resolution images. To double-check CapContact's capability to work on half-resolution sensors, we ran our network on Project Sensible, a sensor with a larger gridline pitch. Here, CapContact robustly detected contact areas even under noisy conditions, successfully rejecting false inputs and solely preserving actual touch contacts. As you can see, the threshold-based method suffers from mistouches, as well as noise due to the flexible surface. In conclusion, we have introduced the first investigation of deriving actual contact shapes from mutual capacitance sensing. Our data-driven method CapContact estimates the contact area from a single capacitive image, reliably discriminating adjacent touches and bringing input locations closer to the center of true contact, even when applied to a sensor with just half-resolution. We think that CapContact opens up many opportunities for future touch devices. For example, to reliably distinguish hover and touch, to operate a much lower-resolution sensor with higher pitches, and to produce higher touch input accuracy. You can find all materials on ziplab.org, where we have released the dataset and code.
