reference: Hi, everyone. Thank you for listening to this talk. I'm Navina, a PhD student at the University of Washington. I'll be presenting our paper on chat-based peer support for youth living with HIV. This paper was only possible due to the work and advice of collaborators from the University of Washington, Kenyatta National Hospital, and University of Wisconsin-Madison, co-authors David, Cyrus, Brandon, Megan, Grace, Irene, Richard, and Keshet. Our work is motivated by the importance of peer support and patient-provider communication for supporting people with chronic health conditions, especially in terms of mental well-being and doing difficult tasks like adhering to medication. To make this support more widely accessible, we explore how to leverage chat apps like WhatsApp, considering their uptake for many other social, political, and commercial purposes. In looking at the use of chat apps for facilitated peer support, we attend to the complexities of online participation in the context of stigmatized illness such as HIV, and the variable access to mobile phones and internet in many underserved settings. We thus ask the following in the context of a peer support intervention for youth living in an informal settlement in Nairobi, Kenya. What is the experience of the facilitator and youth in participating in chat-based facilitated peer support for youth living with HIV? What lessons might we take away for chat-based online health communities? To provide an overview of our study design and data collection, we conducted a six-month pilot with two age groups, facilitated by David, the second author. The pilot started with an intro meeting with youth to meet in person and develop privacy norms. It ended with a closing meeting to debrief, and for youth to nominate a youth member and a health worker from a local clinic to take over facilitation. We analyzed chat records from both groups, notes from the meetings, and also post-pilot interviews with 20 youth and the facilitator. We saw a few themes around the youth's and facilitator's experience. One was the complex social dynamics of the group. The groups were diverse, with differing levels of closeness among members and differing opinions on sensitive topics and appropriate conversation. According to the facilitator, these differences were the hardest part to balance, and we described how he worked to monitor and constructively moderate conversations. Another theme was diverse patterns of participation and how they shaped the experience of the intervention. We described how factors such as intermittent access to the group, for example due to being away at boarding school or not having mobile data at the time, contributed to the work of maintaining group cohesiveness, for example effort from youth to catch up with missed content. We also discussed privacy. We described the importance of the in-person meeting and building trust, allowing youth to be sure of the person you're chatting with, as one participant said. We also discussed how agreed-upon norms such as using an app lock played out over time as youth became more comfortable with one another. Finally, we described how the group facilitated informational and emotional support, which in turn encouraged youth to reclaim aspirations they had given up on. For example, participant 36 described how upon learning about discordant couples from the group, they felt they could have a partner or children. The reason aspirations are so key in our findings is that, in youth's experience, aspirations and a steady source of support motivated them to do tasks like taking medication consistently. However, we also highlight the boundaries of aspirations as a guiding concept in design, particularly when focused on aligning with societal norms. Participant 37's quote about accepting and even reinforcing stigmatizing comments Shows how a focus on norms could even feed stigma. We outlined takeaways in three areas. One is the design of chat-based peer support and how it might support facilitators' evaluation of group dynamics and support participants in getting the most out of group content given intermittent participation. We also discussed privacy in mobile health applications, including the importance of establishing and revisiting privacy norms. We also discussed how to support broader participation we may need to go beyond norms to consider privacy in the design of the chat platform itself. Finally, in conversation with HCI for Development Scholarship on Aspirations in Design, we discuss aspirations in health and development. We describe how aspirations were successfully nurtured in this context through horizontal relationships, sustained support, and reflection and conversation around aspirations. We also discuss the limitations of aspirations when focused on the individual and how we might encourage reflection on aspirations for one's community as well. Thank you so much for listening and I'm happy to take any questions.

reference: We present the SensiAR, a workflow for authoring site-specific AR experiences for remote environments. Most AR authoring tools only allow designers to create experiences for their current environment, like adding a virtual table and chairs to an empty room. However, more and more designers need to create AR experiences for remote environments due to travel restrictions. This is challenging due to the disconnect between designers' physical context and the remote environment. For example, if designers create an AR experience for a remote living room from their office, it is often hard to navigate and locate objects. In the SensiAR, we first capture a remote environment using a LiDAR-equipped tablet. We generate the texture for the 3D scan by projecting pixels and using pyramid blending. A typical approach to remote AR authoring would be to import the scan to 3D software like Blender and add additional objects to the scene. But as you can see, current solutions do not provide an AR-like experience and users often have trouble creating. With the scan of the remote environment, the SensiAR workflow provides a tablet-based authoring interface for designers to create AR experiences at another location. Once the creation is complete, viewers can go back to the remote site and consume the created AR experience in situ. Our baseline interface simulates the experience of using in-situ AR authoring tools. In this portal mode, designers can see a 3D visualization of a captured environment even if they are physically at another location. They can walk around and place virtual objects such as a couch and move it next to the wall. They can also put a table in the middle as if they are on-site. We conducted a formative study by asking five participants to furnish an empty kitchen in a dormitory. We collected their feedback to identify challenges when they were using the baseline authoring interface. We found that in a successful system for remote AR authoring, authors should be able to freely navigate a large remote environment in a small physical space, understand the layout and appearance of the remote environment, and experience their creation as if they were using AR on-site. We need to improve the baseline system to address these issues. We incorporated a new dollhouse mode to enable free navigation in a small physical space. We incorporated a new peek mode to help designers better understand the remote environment. We keep the baseline portal mode to allow designers to experience their creation as if on-site. In the dollhouse mode, designers can transition to a bird's-eye view from the first-person view. They can keep adding objects in the dollhouse mode with a better understanding of the entire space. They can move the avatar to a corner in the room and transition to that location to examine the added virtual objects. The peek mode brings designers' viewpoint to the closest one with a captured image, so they can examine how objects look in the real environment. They can move the tablet and retrieve a series of captured images that simulate their movement. The technical problem here is to choose a frame from the captured video given the current AR camera, so that the retrieved frame most closely matches the AR view. We achieved this by minimizing the cost between the recorded view and the current AR view. We found mesh coverage to be the most robust metric to use to define the cost function. We evaluated the distancy AR workflow with a remote user study. We recruited another 10 participants and asked them to furnish the empty kitchen. They used both the basic system containing only portal mode and the full system containing all three modes. Based on ratings of the two systems, we found that dollhouse and peek modes made it significantly easier for participants to understand and navigate the remote environment. For each participant, we visualized mode usage over time for the improved system. They still spent substantial time in portal mode, highlighting the importance of being able to experience the creation as if on-site. We found that participants frequently switched between portal and dollhouse modes to understand the space and refine the design. They also tended to use peek mode towards the end to validate the AR experience with captured images. In summary, our remote AR authoring workflow allows designers to keep creating no matter where they are physically. This will also encourage remote collaboration as working remotely has become a new normal. Thank you.

reference: Hi, my name is Floyd Muller from the Exertion Games Lab. We are presenting limited control over the body as an intriguing play design resource. Our vision in the Exertion Games Lab is to experience the body as play, building on the realization that we used to play with digital content using traditional interfaces such as a keyboard, to then playing with the digital using our bodies, thanks to the Wii and the Kinect. But what we really want is to experience our bodies as digital play. And this vision led us to a desire to more deeply understand control in games, because without control, games become just stories. And as we aim to integrate the human body, we have become interested in control over the body. In particular, limited control over actions, detected by sensors in our case, that involve movement of parts of the body other than the brain. For example, it seems I have a lot of control over my hand and fingers. However, there's always some limitations, such as when I'm trying to do this. Our goal was to provide you with strategies that help you exploit limited control over the body for play design. We identified 14 strategies, which can be grouped into exploration, learning, embracement and reflection. We'll talk about the first two today. What we have done is we look back at our past games through a lens of limited control over the body. And we will use Inside Out and Balance Ninja to illustrate two strategies from the exploration and learning groupings. The strategies are not specific for each game, but we found that specific examples help illustrate them. Let us begin by showing you an excerpt of the Inside Out video that engaged with limited control over the inside of the human body. Imaging capsules are medical devices that allow us to see our interior body. However, patients often experience anxiety when swallowing medical devices. To address this, we utilized game design thinking and posed the question, what if we combine imaging capsules with digital play? We present Inside Out. Players swallow an imaging capsule and the video is displayed outside their body to be shared and interacted with. Inside Out features three types of games that let players explore how their interior body responds to bodily actions, such as eating, drinking or being physically active. Inside Out highlights the exploration strategy. In particular, we highlight the opportunity to support players in exploring the limits of control over their bodies and the different ways to reach these limits, such as by eating different foods or twisting the body, as seen in the video. Balance Ninja is concerned with limited control over one's balance to facilitate a sensation of vertigo. Vertigo has been described in game design as games that attempt to momentarily destroy the stability of perception and inflict a kind of voluptuous panic or pleasurable panic upon an otherwise lucid mind. So for example, vertigo games could include simply spinning in circles, skiing, racing fast cars and even rock climbing. With our work, we investigate how we can design digital vertigo games by taking advantage of the digital technology now available to us. To investigate this, we built Balance Ninja. Balance Ninja is a two-player balance game where players directly affect the balance of their opposing player. Firstly, players stand on a balance board and move their upper body to the left and to the right, and we measure this lean with a mobile device. Secondly, through using a technology called galvanic vestibular stimulation, or GVS for short, the game directly affects a player's sense of balance. With GVS, a small current of around 1.5 mA is applied to electrodes attached behind players' ears. The resultant effect is that the player's sense of balance is affected in the direction of the positive electrode, causing them to lean in that direction. Balance Ninja highlights learning. In particular, we recommend to provide safe environments where players can learn how to increase bodily control by going to their limits without real-world consequences, as seen in the video how players learn their maximum leaning angle. In summary, we provided strategies of how to engage with limited control over the body, which we illustrated through two examples. The strategies were grouped into exploration and learning. And this was our talk on limited control over the body, an intriguing play design resource. And here are the strategy groupings again. My name is Floyd Muller. Thank you very much.

reference: In this talk, we present an analysis of concept banners through the interaction criticism approach, with the goal of bringing together the language and conceptual landscape of HCI, design, privacy and data protection, and legal research communities in relation to the design and experience of concept banners. The language of dark patterns is increasingly used to argue across many domains of interest, including legal and design perspectives, pointing towards the limitations of policy and the need to engage in transdisciplinary scholarship across disciplinary boundaries. This paper was written over a period of almost nine months by a research team with expertise in design, EU data protection law, and web privacy measurement, using dark patterns as a connecting framework to bridge our disciplinary expertise. We sought to find a common ground while also seeking to inform disciplinary advances in each of our respective areas. Building on our diverse disciplinary expertise, we reviewed recordings from over 50 sites and extensively analyzed the design and users' means of interaction with the concept banners on these websites, building a consent task flow with four stages alongside use of Bardzell's interaction criticism approach. We used interaction criticism to explore the contributions of design scholarship, legal jurisprudence, and discussions of ethics and values from both academic and practitioner perspectives. We iteratively and reflexively built out an argument from each of four perspectives, seeking to identify salient design principles, potential social expectations or means of describing intent, and legal or policy guidance through which the consent design choices could be framed. In synthesizing perspectives from design, law, and computer science, we described a consent task flow with four different types of manipulation, which we will briefly illustrate. In the paper, we align these manipulative experiences alongside consent requirements and dark pattern strategies to illustrate tensions and opportunities in relation to law, design, user experience, and social impact. A consent wall takes the form of a dialogue or popover displayed on part of a page, but may also completely block the page, preventing any action by the user until a choice has been made. This design choice allows a user to select between acceptance and refusal. However, the concrete use of the website is blocked until a choice has been made. This design choice presents a tension between interactive separation of user activities, strategies meant to limit user interaction prior to completing the consenting process, requirements that mandate that consenting precedes use, and the various impacts of both a burden of care on the part of the designer and the freely given nature of the consent process itself. A tracking wall is an instance of a consent wall, blocking access to the website until the user makes their choice and giving the user only one option, to consent and accept any terms offered by the site, without any potential to refuse. Similar to the consent wall, this design choice increases the tension between interactive separation of user activities and the requirement to allow the user to freely give their consent. In addition, the lack of an ability to reject consent, alongside the inability to use the web resource without making this forced choice, represents an additional barrier to the user's ability to make a specific and informed decision. With reduced service, a website offers reduced functionality based on user-selected configuration and options. This design choice presents tensions along separation of access to content based on the consent choice of the user, the economic realities of producing and providing access to content, requirements for consent to be freely given with outcomes that are transparent to the user, and increasing social expectations that web content be accessible without cost or obligation. Most instances of this design choice are likely to fail, either by limiting consent choices up front, or by using manipulative language to lull the user into accepting a choice with different consequences than they may expect. Other configuration barriers manipulate the user towards accepting consent. The notion of configuration is central to the ability of the user to make an unambiguous and specific choice about how their data can be collected and used. However, so many of the visual and interactive elements relate and interact in ways that resist the ability of policy to specify allowable and non-allowable design choices using techniques such as interface interference and sneaking. As we have described, the inclusion of dark patterns and consent banners is an n-dimensional phenomenon which includes dimensions of time, interaction, design, psychology, and law, demanding a holistic analysis from many perspectives. The deeper we look into consent mechanisms and the matter of user choice, the more we understand the need to combine the perspectives of many different fields as part of a trans-disciplinary dialogue. In particular, we provide an initial framing for bi-directional design and legal argumentation, evaluating and interrogating designed experiences using the language of law and policy, while also using a user experience or user interface as a means of addressing gaps or opportunities for more precision in existing legal or policy frameworks. In conclusion, we acknowledge the support of several organizations that have funded this work, and we thank you for listening.

reference: Hi everyone, my name is Karthik and I'm a PhD student in the DGP lab at the University of Toronto. Today I'm presenting our work on task allocation for human-robot collaboration. In human-robot collaboration, humans and robots work together to achieve a common goal. One of the many challenges in HRC is determining what actions each member of the team should take, a problem known as task allocation. Prior work has proposed many solutions to task allocation. For instance, using offline or online planning methods which prescribe what the human and the robot should work on during the task. However, sometimes it is hard to pre-plan all aspects of an HRC before the task commences, and humans may want to make changes to the task allocations in an ad hoc fashion. Hence, prior work has proposed behaviors that the robot can use to facilitate ad hoc collaboration, e.g. the robot can respond to user instructions in a reactive manner, or the robot can infer allocations such as by picking up objects near its gripper in a proactive manner. We take inspiration from ad hoc Hrc and coordination behaviours exhibited by human teams, such as the notion of territoriality. and proxemics, and HCI work on designing interactions with proxemics in mind. Tabletop territoriality describes how collaborators distribute resources in a shared workspace while working on a task. Proxemic interaction states that we can exploit physical and spatial relationships with objects to enable fluent and natural interactions with them. In our work we make two contributions, a design space of novel task allocation techniques for ad hoc HRC, and a comprehensive evaluation of the design space. We propose three new explicit techniques where allocation occurs through deliberate user action, and three new implicit techniques where the robot allocates objects to itself based on simple heuristics. Our first technique is called menu, where the user can touch or point at an object to bring up an allocation menu. The second technique is called subtle relocation, through which the user can push an object towards the robot to assign it. The last technique is called fixed territories, where the tabletop is divided into territories belonging to the user, the robot, and the group. Objects change allocation based on where they're located on the table. Our first implicit technique is called distance, where the robot allocates objects based on how far away they are from its base. The. The second technique is called gaze, where user gaze triggers territories, which the robot avoids picking up objects from, And robot territories which it actively picks up objects from, and? And the last implicit technique, which is called proximity, where territories are formed when the user or the robot picks up objects from a region. Subsequently, the robot avoids picking up objects from the user's territory and only picks up objects from its own territory. We evaluated the techniques on a set of block stacking tasks, where the user manipulated yellow blocks and the robot manipulated black blocks. We studied coupled tasks, where the user and the robot had to place blocks alternatively to complete a structure, And decoupled tasks where the user and the robot could independently complete their own structures. We also studied object placement. Objects for the user and the robot could be scattered around the workspace, or they could be pre-sorted. Here are some clips from the user study. We found that implicit techniques led to faster task completion times, led to increased concurrent activity or simultaneous time spent by the user and the robot on the task, led to increased robot errors or incorrect allocations, led to an increased perception of being able to parallelize or work on the task and allocate objects simultaneously, and finally led to a reduced perception of being in control over task allocation. Based on these findings, we think that future task allocation could be improved by building implicit allocation techniques with explicit control mechanisms. For example, in the proximity technique, the user's territory is implicitly formed when they pick up objects in the region, but the user could set the territory size explicitly. Thank you very much for your attention.

In recent years, the smartphone has become a portal for managing personal health. Many people are now using mobile devices to track health metrics, access health services, and get personalized suggestions from the systems. However, scholars have raised concerns about the persuasion and nudging from technologies. They argue that persuasive technologies may undermine users' ability to reflect on their situation and decide upon appropriate action. In response to these challenges, HCI scholars have increasingly emphasized the need for customizability and flexibility in mobile health technologies. Studies have found that user customization can increase users' sense of control and support autonomy. Yet customization requires much user effort, And this can be burdensome for people with motivational and cognitive challenges, such as with those with depression and anxiety. It's unclear how this group of people interact with customizable technologies and their desired level of customizability. This study would ask, what's the optimal level and type of customizability in mental health technologies? In this research, we present the IntelliCare platform, a suite of mobile apps that help people manage their depression and anxiety symptoms. This platform includes 12 individual apps, each targeting a specific behavioral or psychological treatment strategy. The apps are highly customizable and interactive, and users can adapt the apps to their own conditions and needs. And you can find more details about this platform in our paper. We conducted interviews with 22 over 32 intellicare users to understand their experience with the platform. We asked for their feedback on a variety of things, and we were especially interested in understanding how app suggestions versus user customization were most helpful. In the interest of time, I won't go into the details, but only highlight a higher-level theme from the findings, which is the idea of human-AI collaboration, in particular the integration of system personalization with user customization. The most value valued type of customization was. Was creating to do lists and manually logging completed activities, which is basically this little app that asks you to create. Create a checklist and then check things off, so these activities were considered super intuitive, low burden and pleasurable. Our participants said that checking things off is extremely satisfying, and this could enhance that the user's sense of autonomy. and their self-competence, and also relate to their own values. According to the self-determination theory, autonomy, competence, and relatedness are three basic human and psychological needs, and can enhance well-being and satisfaction. And this has real consequences. My name is Anirudh and I'm a researcher at the University of Oxford. Together with my colleagues, Jun and Max, I've been investigating the mobile ecosystem to understand some of its privacy problems. In this video, we'll give a quick overview of what we've learned so far. The Google Play Store hosts over tens of thousands of free apps, specifically designed for children, offering great opportunities for education and connecting people around the world. However, the question is, how is all of this free? Something American Congress wondered as well. Well, how do you sustain a business model in which users don't pay for your service? Senator, we run ads. Service providers such as Google and Facebook, as well as developers, rely on targeted advertising to generate revenue. To make this possible, mobile apps collect large amounts of sensitive data through third-party libraries, posing a major risk to privacy. This can lead to concrete harms for children, such as identity theft, as well as pose risks to their reputation and opportunities as they grow older. All of this makes us wonder about the role of developers. After all, they're the ones creating the apps, and in a way, this would make them responsible. So we wanted to find out, what do developers think their responsibilities are when designing for children? And what is preventing them from creating age-appropriate apps which do not lead to long-term harms? In order to answer these questions, we decided to ask developers directly through surveys and interviews. We sought out developers by going through apps on the Google Play Store which were categorized under the family and education genres. The survey and interview included similar open-ended questions to capture developer views on data collection practices and their development methods. We received 134 survey responses and conducted 20 interviews. Audio recordings were transcribed and all qualitative data was analyzed using thematic analysis. So what did we discover? Here, we'll give a quick overview of the most important themes, with the rest being described in the full paper. Our findings show that in general, developers feel responsible for designing apps with the best interests of children in mind. As one developer puts it, the app interacts with the kid during a very sensitive period. We bear much more responsibility for the user. And the same applies to respecting children's privacy and minimizing data collection. However, developers also had several needs and goals which could only be realized through the use of certain analytics and third-party libraries. For example, the need to further understand user behaviors to improve the app. At the same time, developers expressed a want to do this in a non-harmful way, and reported to not collect personal data from users and share them with third parties. In wanting to design with the best interests of children in mind, developers faced several challenges, out of which we'll be covering the most prominent ones. Firstly, developers found it unclear what third-party libraries are doing in the background and what organizations might secretly be doing with the collected data. This made it difficult for them to navigate the libraries available on the market. As a result, developers resorted to using products from known organizations. Unsurprisingly, libraries used by Google turned out to be the most popular. Another struggle developers faced was the monetization of apps. Understandably, sustaining a viable business was one of the primary objectives for developers. After all, money makes the world go around. However, attempts to do this in an age-appropriate way, without using ads and trackers, was not easy. Firstly, paid apps which did not use any ads had a hard time competing in the competitive app marketplace, and simply did not earn enough money. Secondly, oftentimes, users themselves demanded for apps to be free by leaving bad ratings, as they often couldn't afford paying for them. And lastly, paid apps also faced the problem that clone makers would simply duplicate the app and release a free version with potentially malicious features. At the end of the day, developers had to concede that ads are a necessary evil to keep the business afloat. The question remains, however, what can we do about all of this? Unfortunately, there is no trivial solution to these problems, and we may need to rethink our current economic model. To make this possible, mobile apps collect large amounts of sensitive data through third-party libraries, posing a major risk to privacy. reference: We present Unmaking, enabling and celebrating the creative material of failure, destruction, decay, and deformation. In the 1960s, Gustav Metzger founded the autodestructive art movement as a reaction to the violence and destruction of World War II. Autodestructive art was proposed as a way for artists to create powerful controversies, bringing destruction into the public's consciousness, and allowing artists and spectators to form intimate relationships with the temporality of the art. Artists created impressive public works with acid, fire, and machines. However, Metzger recognized the limitations of the time. He called upon scientists and engineers to work alongside artists to develop technology to more fully realize his vision. Today, advances in design, human-computer interaction, and digital fabrication have enabled the creation of objects that artists of the 60s could only have imagined. Still, the dominant focus in digital fabrication has been in making. Currently, software design tools for three-dimensional modeling offer making operations, such as extrude, loft, and revolve. Resulting models can be easily made with tools such as a 3D printer. And with that, the making process is largely considered complete. We propose that unmaking, the processes of destruction and decay that occur after making, can and should be equally considered as part of the creative making process. For this to happen, we will require new fabrication strategies, software design tools, and materials. To allow practitioners to embrace unmaking in their designs, we need to enable a new set of operations. We proposed an initial set of expanded design vocabulary, such as split, bulge, sag, lean, shrink, dissolve, pit, and shed. We'll now walk through an unmaking workflow that we have developed to operationalize splitting and bulging. Unmaking can be implemented with a variety of materials and fabrication strategies. The strategy that we take as our example is to 3D print a model using conventional plastic, such as PLA, and selectively design in hidden chambers of an active material. Here we use thermally expanding microspheres, or TEMs. Upon heating, these microspheres swell like balloons. By modulating conditions such as heating temperature and time, TEMs hidden inside PLA objects create controllable unmaking effects as they expand within. To enable the design of such objects, we created a software tool that is integrated into standard CAD modeling software. Users may interactively design and visualize how they want their model to split or bulge. The tool automatically generates meshes that can be exported to standard slicing software and converted into machine g-code for 3D printing. TEMs come as a powder, so before printing, we mix TEMs with water into a slurry, which we then load into a dual extruder 3D printer alongside standard PLA filament. The object directly after printing appears to be an ordinary 3D printed PLA piece. However, when heated, the object will split or bulge as the designer specified, creating a unique artifact. This example workflow only scratches the surface of what is possible with unmaking. By combining different materials and fabrication strategies, we can design objects that have different kinds of obscured, controllable unmaking potential that is realized post-making. A designer may even build in hidden chambers of reactive materials that internally combine and trigger unmaking when an object is handled in a particular way. In addition to creating these unconventional aesthetics and new kinds of experiences with digitally fabricated objects, we believe that unmaking is also an important ally to sustainability efforts. With the workflow that we have presented, TEMs can be used to split a multicolored object into its constituent colors for easier recycling, or the technique may be used to split an object into smaller but functional parts for reuse. Moving forward, we hope that growing interest around unmaking will incentivize the development of more materials that are optimized for unmaking. We envision that these are ones that will be easily biodegradable and compostable in our own homes without specialized industrial processes. We see great potential to transform the black box processes of composting and recycling into a rich design opportunity that can be enjoyed by makers and spectators. We invite you to join us in this celebration of unmaking.

reference: Hello, in this video I'm presenting Dynamic Field of View Restriction in 360 video, aligning optical flow and visual SLAM to mitigate visually induced motion sickness. My name is Paulo Bala, I'm a PhD student from the University of Lisbon, and this work was done in collaboration with Ian Oakley from Alstom National Institute of Science and Technology, and my advisors Valentin Adizi and Nuno Nunes from the University of Lisbon. Virtual reality has resurged as a medium for work in entertainment, but key user experience issues still prevent many users from enjoying VR. One of these barriers for adoption is visually induced motion sickness, sometimes referred as simulated sickness, VR sickness, or cyber sickness. Visually induced motion sickness occurs strictly from visual stimulation, it's polysymptomatic, meaning that there's multiple symptoms, and polygenic, meaning that those symptoms manifest differently across individuals. Some techniques for symptom mitigation in VR include hardware improvements, creating vestibular responses, natural walking, and artificial locomotion interfaces. However, these techniques are not compatible with 360 video. For 360 video, techniques using visual optimization, like independent visual background and a restricted field of view, have been shown to mitigate visually induced motion sickness. It is of interest that these techniques be designed to be less obtrusive, only being applied when needed. Therefore, in this paper, we present a method using a visual SLAM, a visual simultaneous localization and mapping system, to differentiate between when the camera is static and when the camera is moving, and use this to apply visually induced motion sickness mitigation only when there is movement. We then use optical flow, a motion pattern caused by the relative motion of objects compared to the camera, of the user's peripheral vision to determine the aperture of the field of view. We extended OpenVSLAM, an open-source SLAM system for equirectangular videos, by making it compatible with videos with multiple scenes. We use visual SLAM as a way to differentiate between movement versus stationary. To test this, we manually classify the video with multiple scenes into three categories stationary in green, slow in yellow, and fast in orange. Our automatic classification of stationary and movement is generally consistent with the manual classification. We use a Gunner-Fernbach dense optical flow algorithm and group those values into a grid. During runtime, if there is movement as detected in the automatic classification, concentric rings of raycasters poll for optical flow values in the periphery of the field of view and adjust the field of view accordingly. Based on this implementation, we organize a user study comparing our dynamic field of view to two baselines unrestricted, meaning that the field of view is at 20 degrees, therefore no vignetting appears, and fixed, meaning that the field of view is at 40 degrees and vignetting is constant. We did a within-subject study with 23 participants who experienced all three conditions. We also looked at a subpopulation of this group that was more prone for motion sickness. That we adopted a mixed methods approach using self reported data like presence and the similar sickness questionnaire using semi structured interviews and using objective measures like head direction data. We highlight some of the findings. First off, looking at the dynamic field of view, there is a clear restrictive field of view restriction applied to fast intervals in orange. This is expected since those intervals have higher values of optical noise. While the dynamic field of view is also applied to slow intervals in yellow, there is more variation and those values are closer To those than when there is no restriction. Regardless of the amount of field of view restriction, users had similar patterns of viewing, exploring the scene in stationary or slow scenes and focusing on the movement direction during faster scenes. Looking at how much the head moves between readings, participants who experienced a fixed field of view had less movement than unrestricted field of view, and the values for the dynamic field of view are closer to those of unrestricted field of view. Dynamic field of view was shown to be statistically effective in reducing or maintaining scores of the similar sickness questionnaire total score and nausea when compared to the unrestricted field of view for both the full population and upper 75 percentiles of population. As expected, participants experienced unrestricted field of view reported higher values for general present and spatial presence compared to the fixed field of view. For the dynamic field of view, these values are closer to when there is no restriction. Dynamic field of view is noticeable as expected since it is the only condition where the field of view varies, but it was also mostly well accepted by participants in terms of enjoyability and comfort. From the semi structured interviews we point out some noteworthy aspects. Firstly, some participants report the dynamic field of view as distracting. We posit that this is mostly. We're referring to slow scenes where there is an instability in the field of view size that may result in the creation of more optical noise rather than masking it. Secondly, some participants report dynamic field of view as being part of the experience or for attention guidance. This also makes sense because when dramatic changes in field of view size happen, it normally is when a fast movement starts, like jumping off a canyon, so it can easily be interpreted as a cinematic choice. Overall, although noticeable, dynamic field of view was mostly well accepted by participants allowing for the exploration of stationary and slow scenes, and protecting the user from optical flow during fast scenes. In our paper, we also highlight future work like eliminating field of view instability in slow scenes that may be solved by a better distinction between fast and slow scenes, or by incorporating velocity estimation as an input. Finally, our results are promising, but further testing with different videos in longer durations is needed. This would help not only to test the efficacy of dynamic field of view restriction, but also help to generalize it to all 360 videos.

Some techniques for symptom mitigation in VR include hardware improvements, creating vestibular responses, natural walking, and artificial locomotion interfaces. However, these techniques are not compatible with 360 video. For 360 video, techniques using visual optimization, like independent visual background and a restricted field of view, have been shown to mitigate visually induced motion sickness. It is of interest that these techniques be designed to be less obtrusive, only being applied when needed. Therefore, in this paper, we present a method using a visual SLAM, a visual simultaneous localization and mapping system, to differentiate between when the camera is static and when the camera is moving, and use this to apply visually induced motion sickness mitigation only when there is movement. We then use optical flow, a motion pattern caused by the relative motion of objects compared to the camera, of the user's peripheral vision to determine the aperture of the field of view. To test this, we manually classify the video with multiple scenes into three categories stationary in green, slow in yellow, and fast in orange. Our automatic classification of stationary and movement is generally consistent with the manual classification. During runtime, if there is movement as detected in the automatic classification, concentric rings of raycasters poll for optical flow values in the periphery of the field of view and adjust the field of view accordingly. We did a within-subject study with 23 participants who experienced all three conditions. We also looked at a subpopulation of this group that was more prone for motion sickness. This also makes sense because when dramatic changes in field of view size happen, it normally is when a fast movement starts, like jumping off a canyon, so it can easily be interpreted as a cinematic choice. My name is Paulo Bala, I'm a PhD student from the University of Lisbon, and this work was done in collaboration with Ian Oakley from Alstom National Institute of Science and Technology, and my advisors Valentin Adizi and Nuno Nunes from the University of Lisbon. Virtual reality has resurged as a medium for work in entertainment, but key user experience issues still prevent many users from enjoying VR. One of these barriers for adoption is visually induced motion sickness, sometimes referred as simulated sickness, VR sickness, or cyber sickness. Visually induced motion sickness occurs strictly from visual stimulation, it's polysymptomatic, meaning that there's multiple symptoms, and polygenic, meaning that those symptoms manifest differently across individuals. Some techniques for symptom mitigation in VR include hardware improvements, creating vestibular responses, natural walking, and artificial locomotion interfaces. However, these techniques are not compatible with 360 video. For 360 video, techniques using visual optimization, like independent visual background and a restricted field of view, have been shown to mitigate visually induced motion sickness. It is of interest that these techniques be designed to be less obtrusive, only being applied when needed. Think about the leverage when only alone in Germany. 68 % of the population commutes daily by car. Although past research showed the potential of in-vehicle interventions, for example with breathing exercises, they however showed it only in controlled conditions, in a simulator or on a test track. Our study now explores the effect of in-vehicle interventions in the real world over a longer time period. What did we do? First, we carefully redesigned two established psychotherapeutic interventions for the application in the car. The first intervention was a mindfulness intervention. It was an active meditation or better guided thinking exercise that helped drivers to focus on their surroundings, the street and other traffic participants and on themselves to perception of feelings. The second intervention was a music intervention. Hereby, drivers had to collect a list of positive memories and songs linked to these memories. By listening to these songs, they should be remembered about these very beneficial and positive memories of their life. The playback of these interventions happened through a retrofitted smartphone in the car, as we can see here. The phone was always connected to the car multimedia system via Bluetooth and during a typical trip, participants received before starting to drive a notification that an intervention was selected. They could then decide to start the intervention or not while driving. They had throughout the drive always full control over the intervention. They could pause or cancel it at any time. Our target was always to ensure the safety of drivers. And as initially stated, we validated the interventions in a longitudinal field study on On open roads, hence we had ten participants that we gave each a car. which they could use with our setup for two months for all their daily driving. The results of our paper are based on the analysis of these questionnaires plus semi-structured interviews with the participants after the study. First and foremost, we found that both interventions significantly improved in the short term the effect of drivers. Mental health and well-being issues are on the rise. For example, 320 million people alone suffer worldwide from depressions. Psychotherapy and the HCI community identified this as a major problem and therefore they inspect scalable, often app-based solutions that are better integrable in people's daily life. We see another space that gained recently the interest to solve this major problem because people have plenty of time there and are in a controlled environment. It is the daily commute. Think about the leverage when only alone in Germany. 68 % of the population commutes daily by car. Although past research showed the potential of in-vehicle interventions, for example with breathing exercises, they however showed it only in controlled conditions, in a simulator or on a test track. Our study now explores the effect of in-vehicle interventions in the real world over a longer time period. What did we do? First, we carefully redesigned two established psychotherapeutic interventions for the application in the car. The first intervention was a mindfulness intervention. It was an active meditation or better guided thinking exercise that helped drivers to focus on their surroundings, the street and other traffic participants and on themselves to perception of feelings. The second intervention was a music intervention. Hereby, drivers had to collect a list of positive memories and songs linked to these memories. By listening to these songs, they should be remembered about these very beneficial and positive memories of their life. The playback of these interventions happened through a retrofitted smartphone in the car, as we can see here. The phone was always connected to the car multimedia system via Bluetooth and during a typical trip, participants received before starting to drive a notification that an intervention was selected. They could then decide to start the intervention or not while driving. They had throughout the drive always full control over the intervention. They could pause or cancel it at any time. Our target was always to ensure the safety of drivers. And as initially stated, we validated the interventions in a longitudinal field study on On open roads, hence we had ten participants that we gave each a car. which they could use with our setup for two months for all their daily driving. The naturalistic character of our study is underlined by the heat map of all trips for one of the participants that we can see here. We can see that he drove his daily commutes, but many other trips in addition, all around his region. During the time of the study, we collected the effect of the interventions by using questionnaires that were as well delivered through the smartphone. The questionnaires asked about arousal or better awakeness, tiredness and valence or happiness of the drivers. We used the effective slider before and after a trip. And After a completion of an intervention, and while still driving, we used a voice based questionnaire. The results of our paper are based on the analysis of these questionnaires plus semi-structured interviews with the participants after the study. First and foremost, we found that both interventions significantly improved in the short term the effect of drivers. Moreover, if the interventions improved the short term valence, it lasted until the end of the trip. Hence, we believe that illegal interventions can really help to improve driver well-being. However, the intervention effects differed. Whereas the music intervention was almost universally liked, the mindfulness intervention had an acceptance problem. For some participants, they just did not believe into it. Further, we see a need for variation as participants criticized that a single mindfulness exercise was too repetitive. Further, we identified promising times when to deliver interventions. Just a final note on distraction and safety. In general, we saw no major problems. Only a few participants mentioned that they had problems in very demanding situations or when they were tired of the mindfulness exercise. But in general, they could handle it well and did not feel in danger at any point. The automotive industry had in the past already the slogan, get in, get happy. We believe that our results show that in-vehicle interventions can support this claim. In-vehicle interventions can work in real-world traffic. If you need further insights into our research, I would be happy if you read our paper or if you contact me. Thank you for your attention and enjoy CHI 2021.

reference: Hello, my name is Kevin Koch and I'm happy to present our work taking mental health and well-being to the streets. We are a multidisciplinary team ranging from computer scientists to psychologists and my co-authors are Verena Tiefenbeck, Shuryu, Thomas Berger, Elgar Fleisch and Felix Wortmann. Mental health and well-being issues are on the rise. For example, 320 million people alone suffer worldwide from depressions. Psychotherapy and the HCI community identified this as a major problem and therefore they inspect scalable, often app-based solutions that are better integrable in people's daily life. We see another space that gained recently the interest to solve this major problem because people have plenty of time there and are in a controlled environment. It is the daily commute. Think about the leverage when only alone in Germany. 68 % of the population commutes daily by car. Although past research showed the potential of in-vehicle interventions, for example with breathing exercises, they however showed it only in controlled conditions, in a simulator or on a test track. Our study now explores the effect of in-vehicle interventions in the real world over a longer time period. What did we do? First, we carefully redesigned two established psychotherapeutic interventions for the application in the car. The first intervention was a mindfulness intervention. It was an active meditation or better guided thinking exercise that helped drivers to focus on their surroundings, the street and other traffic participants and on themselves to perception of feelings. The second intervention was a music intervention. Hereby, drivers had to collect a list of positive memories and songs linked to these memories. By listening to these songs, they should be remembered about these very beneficial and positive memories of their life. The playback of these interventions happened through a retrofitted smartphone in the car, as we can see here. The phone was always connected to the car multimedia system via Bluetooth and during a typical trip, participants received before starting to drive a notification that an intervention was selected. They could then decide to start the intervention or not while driving. They had throughout the drive always full control over the intervention. They could pause or cancel it at any time. Our target was always to ensure the safety of drivers. And as initially stated, we validated the interventions in a longitudinal field study on On open roads, hence we had ten participants that we gave each a car. which they could use with our setup for two months for all their daily driving. The naturalistic character of our study is underlined by the heat map of all trips for one of the participants that we can see here. We can see that he drove his daily commutes, but many other trips in addition, all around his region. During the time of the study, we collected the effect of the interventions by using questionnaires that were as well delivered through the smartphone. The questionnaires asked about arousal or better awakeness, tiredness and valence or happiness of the drivers. We used the effective slider before and after a trip. And After a completion of an intervention, and while still driving, we used a voice based questionnaire. The results of our paper are based on the analysis of these questionnaires plus semi-structured interviews with the participants after the study. First and foremost, we found that both interventions significantly improved in the short term the effect of drivers. Moreover, if the interventions improved the short term valence, it lasted until the end of the trip. Hence, we believe that illegal interventions can really help to improve driver well-being. However, the intervention effects differed. Whereas the music intervention was almost universally liked, the mindfulness intervention had an acceptance problem. For some participants, they just did not believe into it. Further, we see a need for variation as participants criticized that a single mindfulness exercise was too repetitive. Further, we identified promising times when to deliver interventions. Just a final note on distraction and safety. In general, we saw no major problems. Only a few participants mentioned that they had problems in very demanding situations or when they were tired of the mindfulness exercise. But in general, they could handle it well and did not feel in danger at any point. The automotive industry had in the past already the slogan, get in, get happy. We believe that our results show that in-vehicle interventions can support this claim. In-vehicle interventions can work in real-world traffic. If you need further insights into our research, I would be happy if you read our paper or if you contact me. Thank you for your attention and enjoy CHI 2021.

reference: Hi, everyone. My name is Haofei, and I'm excited to talk about our work on soliciting stakeholders' fairness notion in child maltreatment predictive system. I am presenting this work on behalf of my wonderful collaborators, Logan, Ruiqi, Paige, Alex, Steven, and Haiyi. With the widespread use of machine learning algorithms in various high-stake decision-making scenarios, the fairness of these algorithmic systems has drawn increasing attention. Fortunately, the machine learning community has proposed multiple approaches and criteria for fairness, which can be broadly classified into group fairness, which requires statistical property be equalized across groups, and individual fairness, which requires similar individuals be treated similarly by an algorithm. However, while these fairness criteria provide guarantees on their own, they are proposed by machine learning practitioners, and the stakeholders were not involved in the development of these criteria. Therefore, the fairness definitions may not reflect the viewpoints of these stakeholders. At the same time, these stakeholders are also the ones that will be affected by the outcomes of the algorithms. The main research questions of our study is therefore finding out which fairness definitions align with the stakeholders' viewpoints. To answer this, we developed a framework to elicit the subjective fairness notions of non-expert stakeholders. Our framework consists of two parts, an interactive interface that allows stakeholders to examine the data and audit the predictions made by the algorithms, followed by an interview protocol that probes the stakeholders' belief on fairness of the algorithms. Since fairness definitions are often complicated, the combination of an interactive interface and interview will help stakeholders visualize and understand these definitions. We use child maltreatment predictive systems as the context of our study. Each year, there are millions of child maltreatment referral cases in the US, and core screeners have to make the decisions between screen in for investigations or screen out if the cases are low-risk. Child maltreatment predictions is a high-stakes scenario, and a machine learning-based risk assessment tool was recently deployed in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania to assist with the decision-making. The algorithm is trained on past child referral cases, using features such as the age of the child and the information of the perpetrator. The algorithm predicts the risk level of each case, and core screeners make the final decisions after seeing the output from the algorithm. We conducted a study with stakeholders of the child maltreatment predictive system, which consists of four parents and eight social workers. The interviews follow our fairness elicitation framework, which I will now go over. Recall that our framework had two parts, an interactive interface and an interview protocol. The first part of our interface is the group view, which allows stakeholders to define group answer groups that they are concerned about, and compare the algorithm performance across different statistical metrics. After seeing the algorithm performance, we asked the stakeholders if the group fairness approach is appropriate for the child maltreatment situation. For example, we asked if a fair algorithm should make high-risk predictions at the same rate for victims of different races, which correspond to the notions of statistical parity. Another interface is the case-by-case view. We show stakeholders pairs of cases at a time, and stakeholders can inspect and compare detailed features of each case. This corresponds to the individual fairness notion. We first show stakeholders cases without telling them the decisions made by the algorithms, to collect their fairness notions regardless of the predictions of these outcomes, and understand the factors that they would consider when evaluating the cases. We then interview them by asking how they would prioritize the two cases for each pair, whether they should receive the same decisions, or if one of the two cases should be prioritized. Here are some highlights of our results. We found out that equalized odds was the most preferred group fairness approach among the stakeholders. One of the reasons is that equalized odds align with the existing fairness belief of the stakeholders, which is for the accuracy of the algorithm be as high as possible and as even as possible for all groups of people. At the same time, even though fairness is what stakeholders desire, they are also not willing to trade the accuracy in order to achieve that. For individual fairness, we found out that there are no unanimous agreement among stakeholders. For most situations, we see contentious opinions on how to prioritize the cases. reference: Hi, I'm Oliver, and I'll be presenting a work titled Comparison of Methods for Evaluating Complexity of Simplified Text Among Deaf and Hard of Hearing Adults at Different Literacy Levels, which was done in collaboration with my colleagues Jessica Trussell, Becca Dingman, and Matt Unerfeld. Automatic text simplification consists of computing techniques that aim to make text simpler, and there has been a lot of research into using it as a reading assistance tool for different user groups, including deaf and hard of hearing adults. Text simplification researchers typically need to evaluate if the output of their technologies is actually simpler using metrics such as comprehension questions or subjective judgments. But this evaluation can be challenging. For example, when using comprehension questions, the questions themselves may be too hard to understand. So even if the text is indeed simpler, the questions may not capture that. Another example is asking for subjective judgments that a reader with lower literacy may have a hard time providing. So the question is, can the metrics employed in prior work for evaluating simplified text be trusted to evaluate them with deaf and hard of hearing adults? So our research question in this study is, if we have texts that we know are at different levels of complexity, can a metric distinguish these different levels of complexity when evaluating those texts with deaf and hard of hearing readers? The metrics we evaluated included reading speed and comprehension questions. Now, our comprehension questions had a twist because we wrote two versions of each question that varied on their level of linguistic complexity. Each participant would only see one version of each question, which allowed us to determine whether varying the linguistic complexity of the questions themselves could affect their effectiveness. Our other metrics included participants' predictions of how well they had done on the comprehension questions and subjective judgments of readability and understandability. But how did our study work? To see if a metric can distinguish complexity levels, we first needed texts that we trusted to be at different complexity levels. So we obtained texts from Noozella, which provides different versions of the same article at different complexity levels. Participants would read one version of each article and then respond to the metrics in the previous slide. Our 54 participants also took a standardized literacy test, which allowed us to partition them into a higher literacy and lower literacy group so that we could analyze the results from each group separately. When analyzing the results from a particular metric, sometimes we would see that it was able to distinguish certain complexity levels, a difference that we knew to be true, and this would suggest this metric works to evaluate complexity. However, other times we would see no differences, which would suggest this metric would not work. We investigated six metrics in our study, but in this talk I present the results from the best two metrics only. First, the results from the low linguistic complexity comprehension questions suggest that they could distinguish between the high and low complexity conditions among the group with lower literacy. However, these questions were not able to distinguish between the text complexity levels among the higher literacy group. Now let's look at the results from the readability judgments. These were five-point Likert scale items with responses going from strongly disagree to strongly agree to the statement this text was easy to read. These were able to distinguish the high complexity condition from both the medium and the low complexity conditions among the lower literacy group, and it was also able to distinguish between the high and low complexity conditions among the higher literacy group. This was actually the only metric that was able to tell any differences between the texts with the higher literacy group. Our paper also presents the findings about whether the literacy level of participants influences their responses to these metrics. For instance, whether lower literacy participants tend to give lower overall response scores. We found that participant literacy affected responses for all of our metrics, and the paper gives more details about this. Now, this alone doesn't mean that a metric is good or bad, but it means that a researcher using one of these metrics should report the literacy levels of their participants so that the results can be compared to other studies in which participants may have differed. The key contributions from this work include methodological guidance for metrics that are effective for evaluating text complexity with different art of reading readers at different literacy levels, as well as highlighting the importance of reporting participants' literacy levels when employing the metrics evaluated in this study. There are many limitations and avenues for future work outlined in our paper, but a key avenue for future work is studying whether we can evaluate other aspects of text simplification quality, such as grammatical correctness and meaning preservation with deaf and hard of hearing adults. We thank the National Science Foundation for supporting this work, and we'll be happy to address any questions. Thank you.

reference: Hi, I'm Oliver, and I'll be presenting a work titled Comparison of Methods for Evaluating Complexity of Simplified Text Among Deaf and Hard of Hearing Adults at Different Literacy Levels, which was done in collaboration with my colleagues Jessica Trussell, Becca Dingman, and Matt Unerfeld. Automatic text simplification consists of computing techniques that aim to make text simpler, and there has been a lot of research into using it as a reading assistance tool for different user groups, including deaf and hard of hearing adults. Text simplification researchers typically need to evaluate if the output of their technologies is actually simpler using metrics such as comprehension questions or subjective judgments. But this evaluation can be challenging. For example, when using comprehension questions, the questions themselves may be too hard to understand. So even if the text is indeed simpler, the questions may not capture that. Another example is asking for subjective judgments that a reader with lower literacy may have a hard time providing. So the question is, can the metrics employed in prior work for evaluating simplified text be trusted to evaluate them with deaf and hard of hearing adults? So our research question in this study is, if we have texts that we know are at different levels of complexity, can a metric distinguish these different levels of complexity when evaluating those texts with deaf and hard of hearing readers? The metrics we evaluated included reading speed and comprehension questions. Now, our comprehension questions had a twist because we wrote two versions of each question that varied on their level of linguistic complexity. Each participant would only see one version of each question, which allowed us to determine whether varying the linguistic complexity of the questions themselves could affect their effectiveness. Our other metrics included participants' predictions of how well they had done on the comprehension questions and subjective judgments of readability and understandability. But how did our study work? To see if a metric can distinguish complexity levels, we first needed texts that we trusted to be at different complexity levels. So we obtained texts from Noozella, which provides different versions of the same article at different complexity levels. Participants would read one version of each article and then respond to the metrics in the previous slide. Our 54 participants also took a standardized literacy test, which allowed us to partition them into a higher literacy and lower literacy group so that we could analyze the results from each group separately. When analyzing the results from a particular metric, sometimes we would see that it was able to distinguish certain complexity levels, a difference that we knew to be true, and this would suggest this metric works to evaluate complexity. However, other times we would see no differences, which would suggest this metric would not work. We investigated six metrics in our study, but in this talk I present the results from the best two metrics only. First, the results from the low linguistic complexity comprehension questions suggest that they could distinguish between the high and low complexity conditions among the group with lower literacy. However, these questions were not able to distinguish between the text complexity levels among the higher literacy group. Now let's look at the results from the readability judgments. These were five-point Likert scale items with responses going from strongly disagree to strongly agree to the statement this text was easy to read. These were able to distinguish the high complexity condition from both the medium and the low complexity conditions among the lower literacy group, and it was also able to distinguish between the high and low complexity conditions among the higher literacy group. This was actually the only metric that was able to tell any differences between the texts with the higher literacy group. Our paper also presents the findings about whether the literacy level of participants influences their responses to these metrics. For instance, whether lower literacy participants tend to give lower overall response scores. We found that participant literacy affected responses for all of our metrics, and the paper gives more details about this. Now, this alone doesn't mean that a metric is good or bad, but it means that a researcher using one of these metrics should report the literacy levels of their participants so that the results can be compared to other studies in which participants may have differed. The key contributions from this work include methodological guidance for metrics that are effective for evaluating text complexity with different art of reading readers at different literacy levels, as well as highlighting the importance of reporting participants' literacy levels when employing the metrics evaluated in this study. There are many limitations and avenues for future work outlined in our paper, but a key avenue for future work is studying whether we can evaluate other aspects of text simplification quality, such as grammatical correctness and meaning preservation with deaf and hard of hearing adults. We thank the National Science Foundation for supporting this work, and we'll be happy to address any questions. Thank you.

reference: Hello, my name is Abraham Heidli. Today I will be talking about work we did looking at manipulative advertising in extended reality. Manipulative advertising is that which persuades consumers to buy a product not through logical arguments or information, but through ways that hijack consumers' buying patterns, such as appealing to consumers' emotions to override cautious deliberation, falsely associating certain traits such as power or heaviness with certain products, or lying and deception. Manipulative ads are considered bad because they can trick consumers into buying products they do not need, products they do not want, and even products that are harmful to them. They are especially concerning in extended reality. XR technologies, such as VR headsets or AR glasses, aim to enhance, augment, and replace reality. They are increasingly popular, with experts predicting that in a few years, XR will be as commonplace as smartphones today. But with this popularity comes advertising. Many firms are developing XR ads, with some viewing it as the next advertising goldmine. This is concerning when considering manipulative advertising. If ads can enhance, augment, or replace reality, how can they deceive or manipulate consumers? This was the central question of our paper. Five to ten years from now, when everyone is using XR, what will manipulative ads look like? To answer this question, we used scenario construction, a method used to create narratives or scenarios predicting how tech will be used in the future. In our case, to predict what XR manipulative advertising will look like. To construct the scenarios, we carried out a systematic analysis of XR devices, advertising, and trends in industry and research to understand where XR advertising is headed. We then asked ourselves a series of prompts to guide the construction of these scenarios. Through this process, we identified five key features of XR advertising. This led us to develop seven scenarios, which we then condensed into five key manipulative traits, through which XR advertising can be manipulative. I will now focus on one scenario, deodorant crush, and highlight its creation and what manipulative traits it exhibits. The scenario involves the following. Wei is a 17-year-old boy who wears AR glasses. The glasses scan Wei's message chats, activities on social media, and his physiological data to infer that Wei harbors a crush on classmate Jennifer. Waiting until biometric data reveals that Wei is particularly aroused, an ad appears for deodorant that is a surefire way to seduce girls. The spokesperson in the ad bears a striking resemblance to Jennifer. So how did we arrive at this scenario? We know that ads sometimes use sexualized imagery to sell products. At the same time, we observed that numerous XR devices come equipped with sensors that can measure heart rate, pupil dilation, physiological signs of arousal. If AR glasses are worn at all times, this information can be picked up at all times, and so inferences of who someone is attracted to can be measured. Lastly, with the rise in algorithmically generated ads and deepfake technologies, a spokesperson resembling the person Wei is attracted to can be made. Through the scenarios we created, we identified the various ways XR advertising can be manipulative. For this scenario, we highlight three manipulation mechanisms. First, by inducing artificial arousal in Wei, he is more likely to respond to the ad and buy the deodorant. In XR, there's the possibility that emotions are felt more strongly than non-XR ads, since XR is a more realistic immersive medium. Thus, these emotions are felt more strongly. This emotion is compounded by the hyper-personalization that XR allows. Through the various incorporated sensors, the ad was able to tell who aroused Wei, and could create an ad specifically tailored for him. Lastly, the sensors present in XR devices could tell when Wei was most vulnerable to this ad, when Wei was most aroused, or perhaps when he was saddest, or had the lowest level of self-esteem. All combined to create a highly manipulative ad. In concluding, we want to take a moment to ask ourselves what we, as an HCI research community, can do about this. Though it may seem bleak, there is a lot we can do. Most of these harms will not be realized until years down the line, and we need research to fully ascertain the harms and interventions of XR advertising. In the paper, we highlight four key research challenges. For now, we'll focus on one particularly applicable to our scenario, understanding the privacy risks of XR. Sub-questions within this challenge include asking what data can advertisers collect through XR sensors? How can this be used to harm or manipulate users? Can XR glasses tell when we are aroused, and is this an acceptable use of data? Questions like these are needed to better mitigate the harms of manipulative XR advertising. This was just one of the research challenges we identified. We encourage you to check the paper for other ones. Thank you.

the older one Crush, and highlight its creation and what manipulative traits it exhibits.

aroused, an ad appears for the odorant that is a surefire way to seduce girls. The spokesperson
in the ad bears a striking resemblance to Jennifer. So how did we arrive at this scenario?

can measure heart rate, pupil dilation, physiological signs of arousal.
