reference: Hello everyone, I am happy to present our paper, Stay Home With Me, How Do YouTubers Help With COVID-19 Loneliness? Loneliness is a severe side effect caused by COVID-19 social distancing. YouTube called on creators to join the Stay Home With Me movement by creating content that will entertain, inform, and connect with people who are socially distancing. This hashtag movement witnessed a 600 % increase in Youtube viewership. contrary to other social media platforms, YouTubers interact with viewers through parasocial relationships, the one-sided intimacy generated by conversational give-and-take. However, little is known about how parasocial relationships with YouTubers are embodied during an ongoing pandemic. To fill this knowledge gap, 1,642 videos made by creators in the United States were annotated on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Each video was annotated by three or five MTurk participants. Three research questions are addressed. First, what Stay Home With Me videos did YouTubers make and how do they relate to the COVID-19 pandemic? Second, how did Stay Home With Me videos offer social provisions? And last, how did videos with different social provisions affect viewer engagement? Grounded Theory Approach identifies nine video styles to encode Stay Home With Me videos. Artistic, Challenge, Chatting, Game, Home Life, How To, Religious, Review, and Story. To investigate how COVID-19 affects video creation, we annotate the degree to which each video mentions COVID-19. Weiss's Loneliness Theory is utilized for encoding the roles of YouTubers. Attachment is a social provision that provides a sense of safety and security. Social Integration is a provision to share interests and concerns. Reassurance of Worth emphasizes one's skills and acknowledges abilities. Reliable Alliance is a provision which the person can count on under any circumstances. Guidance is a provision through which people obtain advice and direction. Lastly, opportunity for nurturance is a provision in which the person feels responsible for another's well being. This work uses popularity, activity, and comment emotion to measure how social interaction on YouTube is affected by social provisions. Popularity is measured by view count, comment count, and like count. Activity is measured by the number of likes and comments a video received per 100 views. Comment emotion is measured by positive and negative comments. RQ1 probes what Stay Home With Me videos were created and how they relate to the pandemic. The five most common video styles are How To Video, Artistic Video, Home Life Video, Chatting Video, and Game Video. The videos did not intensively mention the pandemic. Their average rating of COVID-19 mentioning was between None and Low. Rq two finds that social integration and guidance were the most supported provisions. except for religious videos, 49 % of videos in all other styles provided social integration. Guidance was only significantly associated with How To videos. Attachment and Reassurance of Worth had a similar amount of videos. Chatting, home life, and religious videos had a significantly higher proportions, providing attachment. Artistic is the only video style positively associated with reassurance of worth. The fewest number of videos supported Opportunity for Nurturance and Reliable Alliance. Home life, chatting and religious videos had a significantly more videos with nurturance or alliance. For RQ3, videos in How To, Home Life, and Review attracted more comments by providing attachment, nurturance, or reassurance. Offering alliance and nurturance helped how to videos to gain more likes and artistic videos to gain more comments. Viewers. comments in videos that mentioned Covid-19 were more negative. Meanwhile, religious and home life videos had significantly higher positive word frequencies. In summary, stay home with me. Me YouTubers did not alarm the disaster like Twitter and Facebook. Instead, YouTubers de-escalate disaster attention and prioritize connection. Youtubers mitigate disaster loneliness by sharing entertaining content to provide social integration, teaching skills to provide guidance and showing at home activities or chatting. Stay Home With Me videos that supply attachment, nurturance, and alliance had higher overall viewer engagement. However, they were also among the least provided social provisions. We suggest that the non-disaster-focused videos can support viewers who need to relax and reduce loneliness during crises. This characteristic of YouTube should be leveraged in future designs. Viewers can find YouTubers who imitate friend, mentor, and family-like connections to mitigate loneliness. Social integration was the most prevalent social provision. People who miss mentor relationships can leverage How To videos to learn various skills and knowledge. Videos of home life activities or chatting with the audience can engender attachment and nurturance. Lastly, Youtubers should consider providing more family like provisions to increase viewers as interactions and positivity in the pair of social relationships.

reference: This is a presentation of our work, a design space for privacy choices towards meaningful privacy control in the Internet of Things. Privacy notice and choice is a predominant legal framework for data privacy protection. Privacy notices inform people about data collection and use practices. Privacy choices allow people the control over some of these data practices. However, in many real-world systems, privacy choices are difficult to find, overly simplified, and even manipulative. Recent data privacy regulations establish new requirements for privacy choices. Yet today, there is little guidance for system practitioners, including designers and developers, to implement these requirements. In our work, we introduce the notion of meaningful privacy control to characterize desirable attributes of privacy choices in addition to legal compliance. This means privacy choices not only should be effective and efficient by traditional usability standards, but also should support user awareness, accommodate a comprehensive set of privacy rights, and be presented neutrally to users. Our work promotes meaningful privacy control by conceptualizing a design space for privacy choices. Based on a technology review and a user-centered analysis, we constructed a design space for privacy choices. This is a taxonomy organized around five dimensions, namely type, functionality, timing, channel, and modality. We also identify three types of relationship between privacy notice and privacy choice. Under each dimension, we provide a list of possible design choices that practitioners can select from to design appropriate privacy choices for their systems. We also present a use case on how we leverage the design space to design a privacy choice platform for deployed Internet of Things, or IoT. This is an IoT assistant app. Currently, few deployed IoT provides privacy choices to users due to technical and usability challenges. IoT assistant fills the gap by providing a mechanism for meaningful privacy control in the IoT context. Here's how we design the IoT assistant app according to the design space. First, type. IoT assistant offers multiple types of privacy choices, Including privacy, rights, based choices to support the right to access and the right to deletion. Second, functionality. IoT assistant presents users with available privacy choices of other deployed IoT and provides timely feedback of their privacy choice statuses. Third, timing. Through a location-based discovery mechanism and customizable notifications, IoT assistant delivers context-aware, on-demand, and personalized privacy choices to users. Fourth, channel. IoT assistant delivers privacy choices of other IoT through a widely-adapted secondary channel as a mobile app. It also supports the discovery of privacy choices through a public channel using QR code. Last but not least, modality. IoT assistant uses combined modalities. It primarily delivers privacy choices visually. Also, the app's accessibility labels and notifications support auditory and haptic delivery of privacy choices. Finally, the privacy choices provided by the app are machine-readable by design. The use case is a concrete example illustrating how practitioners can take advantage of the design space for privacy choices. In summary, this paper contributes a conceptual framework and a taxonomy to characterize meaningful privacy control. The design space provides a comprehensive guide for practitioners to implement meaningful privacy choices for users. The IoT assistant app is available for download in more than 30 countries. Please give it a try. Thank you.

However, it is important for us to understand how they experience the wearable strategy for promoting long-term health. Understanding how children's and parents' experiences with wearables align and differ is particularly important, because children and parents often have different perspectives on technology use. In our work, we're aiming to understand what are children's and parents' motivation for adopting child-owned wearables in family settings, and how are children-owned wearables used by family members in everyday life. To answer these questions, we recruited and conducted a semi-structured interview with 17 families, including 19 children and 18 of their parents. We then analyzed the data in an inductive manner. Children's focus on tracking as a competitive game is partly related to commercially available wearables' method of reporting data, and relating this data to health do not fully support children. Co-use practices are mostly structured around children's motivations and promoting daily physical activity, but less towards developing children's health awareness via joint media engagement. Our funding indicates that parental mediation can support children's goal setting. Parents can teach their children about developing a balanced approach to physical activity, and to better help children in long-term health-related goals. Thank you so much.

reference: Hi, I'm Kwanggyoon Seo and I'm Jungeun Yoo are Phd students at Visual Media Lab Kaist. We are here to present our work, Virtual Camera Layout Generation using a reference video. We propose a method that generates a virtual camera layout of a 3D animation scene by following the cinematic intention of a reference video. Camera layout, consisting of framing and camera movement, is an important element of cinematography to deliver the emotion and suspense of a scene. Generally, in 3D animation pipeline, the director creates a shot list to deliver the cinematic intention. Then, the layout artist uses the shot list to position the virtual camera. While this process can be easy for professional artists, it can be problematic in case of the TV series, where the artists have to work on many shots. Also, for novice users or directors, it is difficult to position virtual camera and express the intention due to its high degree of freedom. Here is our overview. Given an input reference video, we detect the shot boundaries. Each shot is then analyzed to the camera layout within the predefined set of grammar. The user manually matches the subject and the 3d access. Then this information is stored in the form of a shot list. We calculate the virtual camera position in the Toric space, and further optimized to satisfy the visual constraint of the reference shot. Finally, the camera motion. is generated based on the information in the shot list. In this work, we focus on the camera layout analysis and virtual camera layout generation. For camera layout analysis, we use off-the-shelf 2D human pose estimation model to extract the position and the head ratio of the main subjects. Furthermore, we fine tune a pre trained Resnet 50 model to classify the framing type given on input subject. For camera movement classification, given a reference video, we first compute a dense optical flow. Yet, in order to accurately estimate the camera movement, we mask out dynamically moving object from the optical flow. Then, we separate the video into 9 regions to encode spatial information. We then construct a motion vector by making a histogram of the orientation value of the optical flow. We use these factors to train a simple three layer neural network model to predict the camera movement types. Based on the classified shot information, virtual camera layout is generated. Using the toric representation, which was introduced by the previous work, virtual camera is initially placed with respect to target characters. Then, optimization on on-screen coordinate is conducted to make the virtual camera layout closely represent the framing type of the reference. There are three cost terms for framing, and one term for preventing camera roll. First term is a visibility term, which ensures that the layout follows the framing type. Second term is a headroom term, which ensures that the layout has reasonable headroom size similar to that of the reference. Third term is a horizontal arrangement term, which ensures that on-screen horizontal arrangement is similar to that of the reference. Once the framing is determined, the camera movement is generated by interpolating the camera placements at the start and end keyframes of the shot. However, the initial placement often does not satisfy the constraint of the camera movement rules. Thus, we recalculate the position at the end frame or at keyframes in the middle so that the camera can correctly follow the conventional rules. Here are some results. These are the results generated using the same reference clip, but on different character types. It shows that our method works well with both human like characters as well as the stylized characters. We also compared our results with the camera layout generated by the previous method. While the previous method better follows the on-screen head composition, our method better follows the framing type of the reference video. To evaluate the user satisfaction on camera layout after framing optimization, we conducted a user study on 12 different shots taken with 4 different pairs of stylized characters. Layouts are generated using three different methods, Artist manual, work, our method and the previous method. The study consists of two parts. Users were 1st asked to rate how well the generated layout is with respect to the reference in five likert scale. The results show that layout generated by our method are comparable with those generated by the artist then. two alternative forced choice tests were conducted which asked users to pick one of the two results that they think is better. Users preferred our results over that of the previous method and show similar preference with artist's work. This is it for the presentation. Thank you.

reference: Hello, my name is Francisco Nunes and I'm a senior researcher at Fraunhofer Portugal Aicos. This presentation summarizes the results of the paper. Avoiding reactions outside the home challenges strategies and opportunities to enhance dining out experiences of people with food hypersensitivities. This work was motivated by the challenge of eating out with food hypersensitivities. People with these conditions face the risk of having a reaction each time they eat food that was prepared or served by other people. So when they choose where and what to eat, they may be deciding whether they will have a reaction. And while restaurants should be trained and well versed in food hypersensitivities, people often experience staff with little knowledge about their issue. In terms of technologies, we find very few support. The most relevant are restaurant recommendation platforms, but since they do not present features for these uses, they fell short on their potential. All these factors make eating out hard and motivated our study to better understand people's issues. In this work, we used semi-structured interviews. We talked with 19 participants living in Portugal about their challenge, how they managed to eat out safely, and how they learned to cope. We transcribed verbatim 19 hours of recording and analyzed them with thematic analysis. We stopped the interviews once we achieved meaning saturation, and our process was bottom-up. We uncovered 6 different practices, and today we summarize 3 of them. People often learned about restaurants before going there. They searched for recommendations from friends and family, they went to websites of the restaurant and restaurant recommendation websites, looking for the menu, critics, Everything that could help them get an indication that the restaurant was safe. Once people arrived at the restaurant, they behaved like detectives, scrutinizing everything around them. They looked at the hygiene, if the place was overall clean, that was a good sign, but if the waiters put their hands in the plates, that might be a danger for cross-contamination. Opening the menu, they read the ingredients that were there, and also they tried to guess what was not. Could the cooks have used stock cubes in the rice? Could the sauce contain shrimp? Does this dessert contain nuts? There were some of the questions on participants heads. They also talked about the lessons they had from their mothers on how food was prepared and the importance that it had. On avoiding reactions, after all these observations, participants inquired restaurant staff about their doubts, what was written, What it was not. they asked whether specific meals had the food that they were sensitive to, and one participant said to us that she needed to be very clear about the questions, she needed to ask about milk, cream, and butter, as many people did not know what contained lactose. While doing these questions, they reassured staff that they were not trying to create problems, it was not a whim, they could suffer from eating unsafe food. By the end of this discovery process, people were usually faced with very few options. The image we have on the slide is from when Arthur went to eat out with friends, and the only thing that he could have in the restaurant was a fruit salad and a juice, while his friends were having pizza and cake. And while this was insufficient for Arthur's hunger, he did not want to risk having a reaction, so there was no other option. With this study, we learned the practical and social consequences of food hypersensitivities, which complemented more medical perspectives on symptoms, treatment, and knowledge. We also learned that the self-care of food hypersensitivities resembles chronic conditions. People also need to monitor symptoms, manage reaction or treatment, they need to deal with physical and psychological consequences, perform lifestyle changes. What is very different is how much others control the aggravation of the health. Not many chronic conditions can be strongly aggravated by the actions from others. In terms of implications for our design, we would like to highlight three. First, we need to support practical knowledge development. Our participants had in-depth knowledge about their condition and what they could do, but developing this knowledge took great time and effort. We believe that technology could better support self-experimentation, learning best practices, learning how to cope, And this would be a better start for participants. A very practical implication is to include information about hybrid sensitivities and restaurant recommendation platforms. Being able to say that you are allergic to nuts that you experience X and y reaction would be a great help for other people with similar circumstances. as they are trying to understand if restaurants are safe. Finally, we believe that it's important to support restaurant staff both in training as well as in having tools that support them in catering when a customer with a specific hypersensitivity arrives to their restaurant. And with this, I conclude this presentation and I would like to thank you for the attention.

Recently, GANs have shown promise as a creativity support tool and have been used to create all kinds of interesting images. Here, I just want to quickly introduce GANs before we move on. Training a GAN involves two networks, a generator and a discriminator. The generator takes in a latent vector z and outputs the corresponding image. During training, the generator tries to fool the discriminator, while the discriminator is trained to distinguish between generated images and real images until it can no longer tell the difference. In this paper, we are interested in assessing the quality of generated outputs. For example, we want to know if it can generate photorealistic images. However, evaluating GANs is challenging, and the most common way to evaluate GAN models is still using tedious visual examination of non-interactive image galleries. So in our work, we present Gansplorer, an interactive tool for Gan exploration, that allows the user to assess capabilities and the limitations of a Gan. by browsing different images that the GAN can generate. Due to the time constraints, I would like to direct you to our CHI video for more details about our interface. Here, I will focus on how we evaluated our interface and our methods in three empirical user studies. In the first study, we showed that our interface enables users to explore a GAN. In the first study, we recruited 367 participants on Amazon Mechanical Turk and asked them to use our interface to select photorealistic images generated using an existing GAN model called BigGAN. Participants selected images from at least one of 10 BigGAN categories, for example, PoundTroll, Cobb, Butterfly. We measured how participants used our prototype to explore the GAN. The results of our first user study showed that participants were able to select over 10,000 photorealistic images by interacting with different tools in our interface. In study 2, we validated that images participants selected in study 1 were actually photorealistic. We conducted another Amazon MTurk study with 1,622 participants and asked them to select only photorealistic images from an image gallery consisting of randomly sampled images from study 1. The participants used a custom labeling tool that we developed for the study. Our results suggest that our interface could support exploration and selection of photorealistic images from GANs. However, we also noted that participants often disagreed on what makes a GAN-generated image photorealistic. So, we visually examined images that the majority of participants labeled as photorealistic and used them in our next study where we wanted to compare photorealistic images that participants selected using our tool against the image galleries generated using existing methods. However, cross-sourcing photorealistic images from a GAN is not scalable. Instead, we used a Markov chain Monte Carlo method to sample and generate 25,000 images from the posterior probability distribution of latent vector z given photorealistic images participants selected in study 1. We then compared our method with the baseline sampling methods that big GAN authors used to evaluate their model where they sampled a latent vector z from a truncated normal distribution with 4 arbitrarily selected thresholds. Using visual examination, we found that our method consistently sampled more diverse galleries of photorealistic images, which you can see on the left compared to the baselines on the right. Training a GAN involves two networks, a generator and a discriminator. The generator takes in a latent vector z and outputs the corresponding image. During training, the generator tries to fool the discriminator, while the discriminator is trained to distinguish between generated images and real images until it can no longer tell the difference. In this paper, we are interested in assessing the quality of generated outputs. For example, we want to know if it can generate photorealistic images. However, evaluating GANs is challenging, and the most common way to evaluate GAN models is still using tedious visual examination of non-interactive image galleries. So in our work, we present Gansplorer, an interactive tool for Gan exploration, that allows the user to assess capabilities and the limitations of a Gan. by browsing different images that the GAN can generate. We then use the outputs of GANsplorer to sample even more photorealistic images from the GAN, which we then organize into galleries for further visual examination. Due to the time constraints, I would like to direct you to our CHI video for more details about our interface. Here, I will focus on how we evaluated our interface and our methods in three empirical user studies. In the first study, we showed that our interface enables users to explore a GAN. In the first study, we recruited 367 participants on Amazon Mechanical Turk and asked them to use our interface to select photorealistic images generated using an existing GAN model called BigGAN. Participants selected images from at least one of 10 BigGAN categories, for example, PoundTroll, Cobb, Butterfly. We measured how participants used our prototype to explore the GAN. The results of our first user study showed that participants were able to select over 10,000 photorealistic images by interacting with different tools in our interface. In study 2, we validated that images participants selected in study 1 were actually photorealistic. We conducted another Amazon MTurk study with 1,622 participants and asked them to select only photorealistic images from an image gallery consisting of randomly sampled images from study 1. The participants used a custom labeling tool that we developed for the study. Our results suggest that our interface could support exploration and selection of photorealistic images from GANs. However, we also noted that participants often disagreed on what makes a GAN-generated image photorealistic. So, we visually examined images that the majority of participants labeled as photorealistic and used them in our next study where we wanted to compare photorealistic images that participants selected using our tool against the image galleries generated using existing methods. However, cross-sourcing photorealistic images from a GAN is not scalable. Instead, we used a Markov chain Monte Carlo method to sample and generate 25,000 images from the posterior probability distribution of latent vector z given photorealistic images participants selected in study 1. We then compared our method with the baseline sampling methods that big GAN authors used to evaluate their model where they sampled a latent vector z from a truncated normal distribution with 4 arbitrarily selected thresholds. In study 3, we recruited another 1,000 participants and asked them to select photorealistic images that occur only once in an image gallery using the same tool as in study 2. Our test found a significant main effect of methods on the number of selected images, and our pairwise test found a difference between our method and at least one baseline. Not surprisingly, our test could not find a significant effect of category. Our work will inform the design of a comprehensive interactive GAN diagnostics tool. To demo GAN Explorer, please follow the link on this slide. Thank you very much for your attention.

Due to the time constraints, I would like to direct you to our CHI video for more details about our interface. Here, I will focus on how we evaluated our interface and our methods in three empirical user studies. In the first study, we showed that our interface enables users to explore a GAN. In the first study, we recruited 367 participants on Amazon Mechanical Turk and asked them to use our interface to select photorealistic images generated using an existing GAN model called BigGAN. In study 2, we validated that images participants selected in study 1 were actually photorealistic. So, we visually examined images that the majority of participants labeled as photorealistic and used them in our next study where we wanted to compare photorealistic images that participants selected using our tool against the image galleries generated using existing methods. However, cross-sourcing photorealistic images from a GAN is not scalable. Instead, we used a Markov chain Monte Carlo method to sample and generate 25,000 images from the posterior probability distribution of latent vector z given photorealistic images participants selected in study 1. reference: Hello, welcome to the presentation of Shrinkage, 4D printing accessories that self-adapt. My name is Yang Yue, I am a current graduate student at Zhejiang University. The development of low-cost FDM 3D printing has made personal fabrication accessible. When an off-the-shelf product does not meet demands, many people redesign and remake things on their own. However, fabricating and adaptation for an existing object still requires certain skills. Measuring errors and the lack of print quality of low-cost 3D printers usually lead to size mismatch and extra iteration. To accommodate the uncertainty, a jointing mechanism will be required for secure connection, which adds further complexity to the modeling and assembly process. We address these problems by designing shrinkage to produce shrinkable attachments to fit and fasten the existing objects. It leaves enough margin of manufacturing errors and simplifies 3D modeling and assembly. The shape memory properties that shrinkage relies on can be found on common 3D printing materials, in this case PLA. In the process of 3D printing, the thermoplastic filament is first heated through the extruder at 200 degrees Celsius. It is stretched with nozzle movement and is adhered to the platform. Therefore, after 3D printing, it can be heated above 60 degrees Celsius to relax the stretched polymer chains and thus release the build-up stress to shrink along with the printing direction. The shrunk state will be maintained after cooling. Both the infill structure and the outer shell affect the overall shape retention after shrinking. Both the infill rate and the slicing layer height affect the shrinkage ratio. We recommend to use two pairs of settings To achieve shrinkage ratios of 25 % for shrinkable parts and 5 % for non shrinkable parts. The design pipeline of shrinkage is friendly to novice makers. First, roughly measure the existing object with a ruler. A 3D scanner is no longer required. Next, model the adapter. We developed a design tool in which users can input the rough size of the object, select an attachment template, set the non-shrinkable parts if needed, and as a result, they will have the model ready for printing. Then, use the common material and any common FDM 3D printer to print. Finally, assemble the print and heat up the object in 90 degrees Celsius of hot water or hot air. After cooling, the spoon can be used with new grasping gesture. Here we show a variety of adaptation examples of shrinkage. Shrinkage can change the appearance of existing objects. After heating and shrinking around the heel, the butterfly wings are strongly fixed to the high heel. Shrinkage caters to the special needs of certain populations, Such as the elderly children and patients with hand disabilities, we apply shrinkage to both zippers and the keys. to test the improved gripping performance. For daily objects that are incomplete, broken, or having parts missing, we can repair them and reuse them with shrinkage. For example, the broken curtain can be fixed by reconnecting the two ends together. We can transform wastes into shapes with new functionality. A discarded glass cup can be recycled as a mushroom-shaped pen holder. There is no adhesive involved in the joining process of shrinkage, so the parts can be easily detached through the process of heating afterwards. We can also enhance the 3D printed parts with rich material properties by embedding items such as magnet, rubber, and stone. We implanted stones at the bottom to stabilize the foam stand. In the user study, all participants successfully designed and fabricated adaptations by using our shrinkage system. Please refer to our paper for more details. I'd like to thank my co-author and all the collaborators who contributed along the way. Thanks for listening, and I hope you will try out shrinkage yourself.

reference: Most 10 to 13-year-old children are online. Given this, there is a need to improve their digital literacy skills to help them stay safe online. To help with this, many schools have included digital literacy in their curriculum, requiring teachers to educate children about various topics like privacy, security, and digital ethics. But very little is known about teachers' actual lived classroom experiences when it comes to digital literacy. And this was the goal of our research. Specifically, we were interested in exploring the types of risks that teachers witness 10 to 13-year-old children experience on digital media, the types of strategies that teachers use to mitigate these risks within their classrooms, and how prepared teachers are to actually help children. To answer our research questions, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 21 grade 4-8 teachers within Canada. We transcribed 26 hours of audio-recorded interviews and then analyzed them using a qualitative approach that was inspired by grounded theory. We organized our findings according to our three main research questions. With regards to children's risks on digital media, we found that teachers witnessed a wide range of risks, including cyberbullying, communicating with strangers online, pranks, exposure to sexual or violent content, and misinformation. In many cases, experiencing these risks caused a great amount of distress to children. For example, when describing a cyberbullying incident which made the recipient physically ill, one of our teachers explained that a group chat between two grade 6 students got to a very violent level, and the little girl was throwing up every night, and it was just very, very scary. When mitigating technology risks in the classroom, teachers described using both reactive and proactive approaches. But we found that the reactive approaches were more common. When describing a reactive strategy, one teacher explained that, I think it's kind of on a case-by-case basis, and it depends on the severity of the issue. If it's kids just being mean online, it's usually just a meet-with-the-kids kind of situation. We found that sometimes outcomes from these reactive approaches did actually lead to bigger digital literacy conversations within the classrooms. While teachers were responsible for helping children deal with Various digital digital literacy risks, they reported not having the required training. and not having access to appropriate resources, and they wanted more support from their administration. For example, when discussing teaching digital literacy, one of our teachers explained that it's self-taught, so whenever I need to do a lesson, let me see what's online. I'll take a little bit from here, a little bit from there, and then sort of morph it together to make a lesson. Our work reveals implications for teachers, schools, and parents when it comes to children's risks on digital media. For example, since teachers are expected to teach a wide spectrum of digital literacy skills, schools should provide them with the appropriate training and resources. Because most of the digital literacy risks identified by our teachers originated outside of the school, we recommend that parents should also have digital literacy conversations with their children at home. To learn more about our research, we encourage you to read our full paper or visit our website.

I'm Jennifer Peer and I'm a researcher at Google, and I'm presenting today on behalf of myself and my co-authors, Dr. Roderick Crooks from the University of California, Irvine, Dr. Morgan Currie from the University of Edinburgh, Dr. Britt Paris from Rutgers University, and Dr. Aidan Fasquetto from University of Michigan. So in our paper, we use the concept of epistemic burden as a tool for highlighting the types of research harm that can take place in participatory design research, especially when this work engages with minoritized communities and activists using a data-centered approach. We really see this as contributing to the intersection of HCI and data justice. We see this also as building on a lineage of recent excellent work in the HCI space, highlighting some of the different harms around extraction and potential challenges in really serving and equally, equitably partnering with the groups that we're intending to serve and collaborate with. Epistemic burden is a concept that really pulls together multiple related ideas around the way in which privileged groups further injustice and potential exploitation through the relationships with oppressed and marginalized community groups. There are three major outcomes that come out of epistemic burden. The first is diverting energy away from ongoing activities among community groups and minoritized communities to educate the privileged. The second is responding to stories of the oppressed with hostility. So this is not just outright hostility or explicit hostility, but also things like undue skepticism or distrust. And lastly, receiving social recognition from dedication to dismantling oppression over the channeling and funneling of that recognition to the affected groups. Our research questions for this work ask how we as academics and design researchers can avoid perpetuating the cycle of burdening community organizations through our approaches to data-centered design research. So this really entails how we can use the concept of epistemic burden to proactively help us identify the different types of harms that can take place in participatory design research agendas and how we can analyze epistemic burden to steer our approach to the least harmful, most appropriate methods. We use two case studies to answer these questions, And they serve as empirical evidence of epistemic burden at work, and put the potential of epistemic exploitation as well as an opportunity for. For experiential reflection and interpretation, so the 1st case study we investigate in our work is the Ucla Ucla Poih. Project, or Police Officer Involved Homicide Project, which was a hackathon held at UCLA to investigate gaps in official records of police data. Some of the key tensions that we saw here were that we as researchers set the agenda and assumed that data was at the center. And in retrospect, this really clashed with the distrust that we saw in community groups around the official data records and the use of data for different means. So we see this as really encapsulating the first two types of epistemic burden, so driving attention and energy and resources away for some of the ongoing work that really didn't have to do with data-centered approaches or data-centered work, and a minimizing of the actual existing distrust among those community groups around even the work of completing or helping to resolve gaps in official data records. So considering that and reflecting on that, what could we have done differently? So both community organizations and the researchers engaging in this work. And this really speaks to the, and symbolizes the 3rd type of epistemic burden, which? reference: Hi everyone, we are a group of researchers from the University of Duisburg-Essen presenting our work titled Disagree, you must be a bot, how beliefs shape Twitter profile perceptions. In this research, we wanted to know how users perceive different Twitter accounts. In particular, we wanted to know under which conditions users think an account is a social bot and when do they think it is a human account. To answer this, we rely on insights from social and cognitive psychology. In studies on motivated reasoning, researchers have found that information which is in line with prior opinions and attitudes is favoured over information that contradicts prior opinions and attitudes. This can result in an over-reliance on opinion-congruent information and rejection or suspicion against opinion-incongruent information. Hence, we hypothesize that users will perceive accounts they disagree with as more bot-like and accounts they agree with as more human. Because profiles can vary in the degree to which they seem automated, we propose that we find this bias for accounts that are ambiguous about their nature. Is an account clearly a social bot or a human? We don't expect an effect of motivated reasoning. We also assume that this process is dependent on how a user User perceives an account opinion. Incongruent accounts will be perceived as less credible accounts. and will in turn be perceived more bot-like. We ask 151 participants to view 24 mock-up profiles and ask whether they thought a profile was a social bot or a human, as well as how credible they thought the profile was. We experimentally manipulated the perceived level of botness, ranging from obvious bots over ambiguous accounts to apparent human profiles. For each profile, we created two versions, one that looked like a democrat and another one that looked like a republican account. All profiles were pre-tested concerning their appearance and their partisanship. Taken together with the three different levels of botness, we hence created six different types of Twitter profiles. We also needed to know participants' partisanship and the control variables, time spent on social media, social bot knowledge, and demographics such as age, education, and gender. We analyzed our data through repeated measure ANOVA with planned contrast. In the graph, you can see how participants perceived ambiguous profiles. Lower values indicated bot perception and higher values a more human perception. We find the hypothesized bias for accounts that are ambiguous about their nature. Indeed, opinion-congruent profiles were perceived as significantly more human than opinion-incongruent profiles. Unlike expected, we also find a bias for clearly identifiable bot and human profiles. For different profile types, we find that the effect of opinion partisanship on the profile perception is mediated by perceived credibility of the profile. The repeated measure ANOVA resulted in no main effect for the congruency, which indicates no general effect of motivated reasoning when including the control variables. However, we found that the three control variables interacted with congruency. When interpreting these results, we found that younger participants, participants who spent more time on social media and who knew more about social bots, showed a greater bias. To sum up, opinion-congruent profiles were perceived as less bot-like and opinion-incongruent profiles as more bot-like. We also found that this effect was mediated by the perceived credibility of a profile. And users who are more fluent on social media showed a greater bias. With these results in mind, we suggest that users who spend more time on social media use the term social bot as a derogative. Because the bias was more pronounced for more experienced users, we also suggest that this could be due to higher processing fluency, which has previously been connected to heuristic processing, which increases bias. We also want to point out that social bot detection tools which rely on human annotation might reproduce and amplify this bias. Thank you for your attention. For any further questions, please feel free to reach out.

reference: Hello everyone, I'm Junyoung, a Ph.D. student at KAIST. Today, I'll introduce my research, Golden Time. This is a study on digital well-being. Digital well-being is about personal well-being related to healthy use of digital technology. To promote healthy device uses, prior studies on digital well-being tried to design systems helping users regulate their devices. And among many studies on digital well-being, this study is about smartphone users' regulation. Even though smartphone itself provides many convenience to us, prior studies highlight the negative impacts on our daily life. To deal with this, there have been approaches that associate problematic phone users with a lack of time management skills. One of the representative studies from ADROC, it utilized time-boxing, one of time management techniques to manage self-interruption for digital devices. It was designed with user-driven time-boxing that can be enforced and stopped by users. Such user-driven tool offers autonomy to users, but the authors warned a lack of user engagement over time. Because user-driven time-boxing can be only started by user, so if there's no user's internal trigger or they forget to use it, it will not be used anymore. So in this study, we consider system-driven time-boxing automatically enforced by a system. By this operation, it can continuously provide triggers to users so that they can easily track users' behaviors. Under this time-boxing, we also utilize financial incentives as motivator. We consider design providing rewards for successful time-box. This approach is aligned with BJFolk behavior model. By using these two features together, we designed a system that helps users easily and continuously track users' behaviors as well as reinforce motivation for the regulation. Through this, we try to make them realize the monetary value of their phone users' time. So we called our system Golden Time. First, we explore the system design. Our system driven time boxing automatically enforces the time box every hour on the hour with the 10 min use limit. And if users use their phone, it measures their users' time in each time-box. Based on the measurement, the time-boxing determines the regulation success or failure. And the system informs the results through the notification bar so that users can easily track their behaviors. Under the time-boxing, we designed two incentive payment framing, gain and loss. In the gain frame, users get 500 golds for each successful time-box. In In the loss frame, if users fail to regulate for each time box, the same incentives are deducted. We built intervention system delivering warning message for regulation failure. In each time-box, if our accumulate user's time exceeds 9 minutes, the message is sent to the user. In this process, the message for each incentive group additionally include warnings related to incentive. We hypothesized that the loss frame would be more effective in sustaining phone regulation based on the endowment effect and loss aversion of behavioral economics. We evaluated our system through the user study. We compared how daily average of users' time was changed. In the baseline, no significant differences between three groups. But during the intervention periods, there were significant differences between the loss and other groups. We further investigate how two different incentive framings influence users' regulation over time. In the gain group, users' regulation success influence increasing the monetary value of the regulation. But when they fail in the regulation, they tend to rationalize themselves. This phenomenon results from perceiving the micro-incentive as an infinite opportunity. As a result, such experiences influence decreasing the monetary value of regulation, thereby causing devaluation over time. However, in the loss group, when they fail in the regulation, they tend to reflect their problematic users' behavior. Because through this process, they realize the cost of the behavior and wasted the time. As a result, the process influence increasing the monetary value of regulation, thereby causing devaluation over time. If you are interested in further details, please refer to our paper. Thank you for your attention.

Because user-driven time-boxing can be only started by user, so if there's no user's internal trigger or they forget to use it, it will not be used anymore. So in this study, we consider system-driven time-boxing automatically enforced by a system. By this operation, it can continuously provide triggers to users so that they can easily track users' behaviors. Under this time-boxing, we also utilize financial incentives as motivator. reference: Hello, I'm Danilo Gascas from UC San Diego and I'll be giving an overview of our work Artemis, a collaborative mixed reality system for immersive surgical telemetry. When someone suffers a traumatic physical injury, they usually require immediate medical attention. In some situations, such as a natural disaster, the right medical expertise might not be readily available. To save the patient, local surgeons rely on the help of remote experts through telemetering systems. In a typical telemetering system, the expert surgeon guides novices verbally and through video annotations. Unfortunately, telemetering forces the novice surgeon to shift focus away from the patient to the telemetering screen and then back, which sometimes leads to procedural mistakes. It also fails to incorporate the physical nature of surgery, as remote experts can't demonstrate the use of specialized trauma tools. Researchers have been addressing limitations of current telemetering systems by using mixed reality displays. Mixed reality displays are displays that sit between the user and the environment. They can show visual guidance situated on the patient, which helps, for example, in overcoming the focus shift problem we discussed before. Today, mixed reality research on telemetering is mostly focused on the novice surgeon. Remote experts still make use of regular, flat screens. This gives us a lot of opportunities to improve communication between novice and expert by also designing with the expert in mind. The literature of mixed reality in remote collaboration is rich with examples of visual affordances that can improve communication between remote parties. For example, showing representations of remote objects, virtual hands, avatars, and more. So to better understand how this rich literature applies to the domain of telemetering, we conducted a formative study. We invited four surgeons to role-play surgical procedures in a mock-up operating room. During the sessions, surgeons mentored one of our researchers on two common trauma procedures. First, side-by-side, and then by using existing mixed reality applications. The second part allowed us to understand how different affordances of existing mixed reality technology can influence their ability to mentor novice surgeons. At the end, we video-recorded the sessions and analyzed them to observe how experts mentor novices, the amount of information they need, as well as what they show to novices. We summarized our findings from the role-playing sessions into four goals that describe what expert surgeons need to better mentor novice surgeons. I recommend you to take a look at the paper for an in-depth discussion. But in a quick comparison with existing literature, Expert Goal 2 requires them to mark not only the location and length of incisions, but also their depth. With these goals in mind, we designed Artemis, a telemetering system that combines virtual reality for the expert and augmented reality for the novice. Let's go over each interface, starting with the expert's interface first. The expert interface is in virtual reality, but instead of using bulky virtual reality controllers, experts use their hands to, for example, enact the use of surgical tools. Experts can also use a customized pen to make annotations on the patient. They see the patient in 3D as a live reconstruction, and they can use this patient to show the location of anatomical head marks, as well as mark the location, length, and depth of incisions, as seen in the video. Experts have access to several camera views into the operating room. This allows them to, for example, look at a procedure from a viewpoint free of occlusions, or from a camera on the novice surgeon's head. The interface is a mini-cosurgical room, so to better understand where the novice is, the expert surgeon can see the avatar of the novice. Finally, the novice interface is simpler, as it uses augmented reality to show novices both the patient and the visual guidance at the same time. For an already overwhelmed novice surgeon, the interface is a passive display of visual information controlled by the expert surgeon. We conducted a qualitative evaluation of our system, with six novice surgeons performing a range of emergency procedures on mannequins as well as cadavers. Overall, Artemis addresses the proposed expert goals, as well as it enables them to communicate with novices in ways that are impossible to do even in real life. For example, in this video, the expert uses their hand to show a way the novice can find the incision point on a mannequin by feeling its larynx. Thank you for watching, and don't forget to read the paper for more details on the system implementation as well as on the discussion.

reference: Program synthesis is a promising technique that automatically generates programs on behalf of users. Users do not have to write any code, but only need to provide some high-level program specifications. Over the years, research has shown that program synthesis is applicable to many domains such as text transformation and the data extraction. For example, to generate a program that only matches US phone numbers, the user can add some positive and negative examples. The synthesizer will then generate a program like a record expression that matches the two positive examples and does not match the negative example. Like many machine learning models, existing synthesizers follow a black box design. As a result, there is no way to troubleshoot if a synthesizer is behaving weirdly or if there is a synthesis failure. In this work, we propose interpretable program synthesis, the first approach that opens the black box and helps the users understand the synthesis process, so users can diagnose abnormal behaviors and guide the synthesizer to recover from those behaviors. It's very challenging to directly visualize or explain the runtime behavior of a synthesizer to users, because synthesizers are quite sophisticated. Instead, we choose to visualize the explored program space, so users can understand in what direction the synthesizer is searching and where the synthesizer is wasting a lot of time. Our approach requires instrumenting a synthesizer, so it will keep logging the programs it has tried during the synthesis process. Then our approach visualizes these program candidates in three different ways. Based on the insights from the visualization, the user can provide different kinds of feedback to guide the synthesis process, such as prioritizing or eliminating a search direction. In particular, we implemented an interpretable synthesizer for record expressions. We choose the record expressions because it's widely used, it's hard to use, and it's hard to synthesize. After you add some examples and click the Start button, you can monitor the synthesis process through a live updated line chart. This line chart shows the speed and the trend of the underlying synthesis process. You can easily find out how many programs have been tried so far and how many examples have been satisfied by each program candidate. If you find something weird, like the line being zigzagging for a while, you can make an early interruption and check what's really going wrong. After each synthesis iteration, you can use different sampling strategies to inspect concrete program candidates from the explored program space. If you hover the mouse over a program candidate, the input-output examples will be highlighted in different colors. Green means the example is satisfied by the program, And the red means it's not satisfied by the program. You can also look at the search directions a synthesizer has been through. The tree visualization clusters all explore programs based on how they are derived from an empty program, step by step. The root of the tree is an empty program, and the internal nodes are partial programs derived from the empty program. By expanding the internal node, you can see how a partial program is further concretized during the synthesis process. Each branch of the tree can be viewed as a search direction. You can prioritize a search direction that looks promising to you or. or eliminate a search direction that looks unproductive. In this way, you can manually prune the search space for the synthesizer, and improve the search efficiency. We did a within-subject lab study with 18 students from Harvard SEAS. Each student finished two randomly selected tasks in two conditions. One task using the interpretable synthesizer, and the other task using the same synthesizer without interpretability support. We found that interpretable synthesis is mostly useful in challenging tasks, because the synthesizer often gets stuck on those challenging tasks, and fails to generate any program in a given time. When using a blackbox synthesizer, users can do nothing but just tweaking their examples by guesswork. But with interpretable synthesis, they can troubleshoot and figure out in which direction the synthesizer was wasting a lot of time. Then, they can prune the search space by removing the unproductive search paths. We also found that interpretability did not introduce more cognitive effort and the users perceived. much less frustration when using interpretable synthesis. Please read our full paper to find more interesting results.

reference: Videos without audio descriptions are inaccessible to people who can't see them. As stated by American Council of the Blind, popular video streaming platforms, like YouTube and Amazon Prime, have millions of uploaded videos. However, very few videos have audio descriptions, which makes the sheer amount of video content inaccessible to users who are blind or vision impaired. Therefore, we build an automatic audio description generation system. A woman is seen holding a drum set with others while others watch on the sidelines. The crowd cheers for the people. We also analyze the challenges of current video understanding research. Our system consists of three stages. First, with an input video, our system determines when to insert an audio description. This is achieved by video keyframe extraction and audio-visual consistency analysis. For each inconsistent video clip, leveraging dense video captioning algorithms, our audio description generation module figures out what activities to describe and generate several results. To yield accurate and fluent description selection from multiple generated results, we propose a description optimization module to generate the output, which is input to a text-to-speech engine for final rendering. We implemented a program to perform evaluations. We recruited 20 sighted participants and 12 blind or vision-impaired participants, and divided them into three groups. We run our study in a two-pass manner. In the first pass, we ask participants to watch or listen to original input data. We ask them to raise their hand when they think the current video needs additional descriptions to help understand the scene. In the second pass, we ask participants to watch or listen to the same data plus our automatically generated audio descriptions. Just like in the first pass, hand raise for additional information that our description does not capture. Moreover, we also ask them to raise hand and let us know if the generated description is confusing, redundant, or has grammar errors. We analyzed the results and obtained four observations. First, the additional information requests show a significant drop when participants watching or listening to the data with our generated audio descriptions. Second, according to the recorded timestamps of participants' requests and our audio description insertion time, our results that have good or partial overlaps are above 70%. This shows our audio description insertion times are close to participant demands. In terms of confusion, the generated descriptions might not convey an accurate depiction of the visual activities. Since receiving both visual and auditory information, the results of the SV group achieve much higher. The last observation is from the stark contrast between the reported redundancy between the sighted and blind users. Blind participants are generally okay with redundant and repeated audio descriptions, while sighted participants complained about excessive redundancy. For the post-study interviews, we group our findings into three topics. First, what is missing in our audio descriptions? We observed considerable diversity across sources in terms of participants' desires for the amount of content and level of detail they want in audio descriptions. And both sighted and BVI participants stated that they want to get deeper interpretations and subtle relationships beyond the audio-visual content. Second, why is our audio description not very helpful? Based on their feedback, we believe there are three main reasons. Audio descriptions do not match the video topic or title. Audio descriptions do not match the sound. And audio descriptions are not logical. They all result from the shortcomings of existing video understanding methods. We also wondered how do our automatic AD results compare with a manual AD from Netflix? In terms of insertion time, the overlaps between participants' requests and manual results are noticeably higher than those of our automatic algorithm. Regarding the description quality, very few descriptions are thought to be confusing, and rarely have redundant results or grammar errors. We have four recommendations and future directions for next-generation audio description services. We need a more context-aware prediction model to decide when to insert an audio description. We need smarter video understanding beyond just activity recognition. We need interactive levels of details for audio descriptions. We need more accurate sentence-level scene descriptions. Please refer to our paper for more details. Thanks for watching.

reference: Hi everyone, I'm Xin Yulan from Tongzhi University. Today I will be presenting our work, Understanding Narrative Linearity for Telling Expressive Time-Oriented Stories. This paper was co-authored by Xin Yulan, Xin Yue Xu, and Nan Cao from Intelligent Big Data Visualization Lab, Tongzhi University. Creating expressive narrative visualization often requires choosing a well-planned narrative order. According to narratologist Gerard Genette, every story has two orders, the natural order of the story, which is always chronological, and the order in which it is narrated. So when narrating a story, the narrative can either follow the linear order of the story events, which is chronology, or deviate from linearity, which are also called anachronies. For example, in this story, when presenting the social progress of Sweden, Hans Rosling starts from 2004, then flashbacks to 1709, and then tells chronologically until 2004 again. While evidence exists that anachronies can enhance story expressiveness in novels and films, how they can be incorporated into narrative visualization is unknown. So in this work, we examine one specific type of narrative visualization, that is time-oriented stories. So basically, time-oriented stories are stories that based on temporal data, such as the history or the Or the progression of certain things, We then ask two specific research questions. First, what are the regular patterns of manipulating narrative linearity in time-oriented stories? Second, whether different narrative order patterns help improve story expressiveness? To address these questions, first, we conducted preliminary interviews with seven experts. We identified six motivations and two challenges of manipulating narrative linearity in time-oriented stories. For example, we found that balancing the expressiveness and the comprehensibility of a story is challenging. Then we analyzed a corpus of 80 time-oriented stories and identified six most salient patterns of narrative orders, including chronology and five anachronies. This figure visualizes these six patterns. For example, traceback starts from the end of the story, then flashbacks to the beginning and tell chronologically until the end of the story. When using this pattern, the storyteller usually starts from now, asks how did we get here, and then looks back to the history to find reasons. Next, we conducted a cross-sourcing study with 221 participants to evaluate and compare the six patterns. We posed three hypotheses, including the differences in the learning outcome, user engagement, and the tension between expressiveness and comprehensibility between the six narrative order patterns. We used three time-oriented stories as stimuli. As you can see here, in this study, we presented the narrative points in a story one by one to the participants according to the narrative order they were assigned to. And here are the results. First, we did not find significant difference in recall between chronology and anachronies, or between the six patterns. Second, we found that anachronies performed better than chronology in some user engagement metrics, such as focused attention and enjoyment. Third, we found that while chronology was rated as highly comprehensible, which is represented as the y-axis, it was rated low in expressiveness by many participants, and expressiveness is represented using the x-axis. By contrast, we can see that patterns 2, 3, and 5 were rated high in both comprehensibility and expressiveness. So overall, the results indicated that anachronies have the potential to make time-oriented stories more expressive without hindering comprehensibility. Thank you very much.

reference: Hi everyone, I'm Julia Cambry and I'm excited to introduce our work on Firefox Voice, an open and extensible voice assistant built upon the web. This work was done at Mozilla in collaboration with the Consumer Voice Products team. Mozilla's mission is to ensure the internet is a global public resource, open and accessible to all. And when we think about the scope of that resource, the amount of information that's available through the web today is pretty staggering. As of 2019, there were almost 1.7 billion websites estimated to be online globally. And over the past several years, voice has emerged as an increasingly common way of interfacing with the web. Websites are beginning to offer the option to dictate search queries rather than type them. And within the context of voice assistants, recent studies have found that search and informational queries consistently rank among the most frequently used features. At the same time, however, the number of voice apps and the information that's accessible by voice assistants represents only a tiny fraction of what's available on the internet. And the number and types of voice experiences are also constrained by the fact that today's popular voice assistants are largely closed ecosystems. So the guiding question that motivated our work was this. How might we help to make more web content available by voice and to foster an open voice ecosystem? And as a first step towards that goal, we built Firefox Voice, which is an open source browser-based voice assistant. To give you a sense of how Firefox Voice works, I'll demo a few of its features with some CHI-related browsing tasks. Hey Firefox, what's the weather in Yokohama? It's 53 degrees and clear. Go to the CHI conference registration page. Play Put That There on YouTube. Hey Firefox, find my Talk Slides tab. You can find full implementation details within the paper, but to briefly unpack some of what you saw in the demo, users can initiate Firefox Voice through a toolbar icon, keyboard shortcut, or an optionally enabled Hey Firefox wake word. The wake word detection model runs locally in the browser using TensorFlow.js and was built by our collaborators at the University of Waterloo. Once Firefox Voice is activated, it listens for users' speech and sends that speech to Google's speech recognition service for transcription via a proxy server. We then take the transcription and map it to a supported intent using a simple slot filling approach. Finally, we execute the intent's corresponding action, which in some cases involves extracting and displaying an information card from Google, and in others, performs actions on the user's behalf through browser and web APIs. All of the code for Firefox Voice is open source, and we were fortunate to have a strong amount of engagement from the open source community, with 286 merged pull requests from 50 contributors, and we'd love to have others fork and build upon Firefox Voice for their own projects. Firefox Voice was the culmination of several years of research within Mozilla's consumer voice products team, with dozens of different studies that informed the final version of the system that you just saw. In the paper, we detail our iterative process of developing and deploying Firefox Voice, focusing specifically on four main studies, including formative work through a large-scale need-finding survey, and a series of user studies with early working prototypes. We also evaluated Firefox Voice once it was deployed, through system log data, and by surveying users shortly after they installed and uninstalled Firefox Voice. Between December 2019 and August 2020, Firefox Voice was installed over 30,000 times, and had a total of 12,635 all-time active users. And to hopefully pique your interest in reading the paper, I'll highlight just one example from our findings. This graph shows the number of daily active users from July 1st to August 31st, 2020, Where daily usage initially was around 30 users a day, then increased dramatically to about a thousand a day before falling and leveling off at around a hundred and 80. And that spike corresponds to a week in which Firefox Voice was featured within the new tab page on Firefox, which drove a large influx of new installs. And we see this as an illustration of some of the often unarticulated realities of real world voice assistant deployments. and in the paper, we discuss some of the implications that it suggests in terms of improving discoverability and retention. Please check out the paper and the codebase for more details, and thank you for listening.

reference: Hello, I'm Kai Lukoff, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Washington. Today I'm presenting our research on how the design of YouTube influences user sense of agency. For smartphone apps, a common business model is to capture and resell attention. This leads designers to devise features that capture as much of that attention as possible. In everyday life, people attempt to resist all kinds of temptations, such as smoking, drinking, and spending money. However, the temptation with the highest rate of failure of all is media use, which today increasingly happens in mobile apps. And of course, this high failure rate is not an accident when those mobile apps are designed to capture as much attention as possible. Concerned design practitioners and researchers have responded from within what we call the screen time paradigm. In this paradigm, the objective is to limit the time that users spend on their phone. Yet users report that these tools often indiscriminately block access to needed features, and that reducing screen time is a poor proxy for their actual goals. In this research, we instead explore how to support the user's sense of agency, that is, an individual's experience of being the initiator of their actions in the world. A lack of agency over technology use is linked to negative life impacts, such as a loss of productivity, sleep, and social relationships. A second characteristic of the screen time paradigm is that it relies upon external features that apply universally to all apps. In this research, we instead shift the focus to redesigning the internal features that might cause an app to be problematic in the first place. As a test case for this approach, we focus on YouTube, one of the most popular social media apps in the world. Our first research question asks, which existing features of the YouTube mobile app influence sense of agency? To investigate this question, we conducted a survey with 120 YouTube users from the U.S. Our survey asked, what are three things about the mobile app that lead you to feel least and most in control over how you spend your time on YouTube? This diverging bar chart shows the results. They are ordered according to which design feature was mentioned the most frequently by respondents. The features that primarily led participants to feel least in control were recommendations, ads, and autoplay. The features that primarily led participants to feel most in control were playlists, search, subscriptions, watch history, and play controls. Let's look at one example. Survey participants reported that playlists led them to feel more control. One participant wrote, I can create playlists or queue videos in advance to limit what I watch to a specific list instead of endlessly searching around for what I want. So as compared to searching around or browsing recommendations, playlists had a clear end that served as a signal for them to finish their session on YouTube. Our second research question asks, what changes to these internal features might increase sense of agency? We were particularly interested in understanding how to change features that the survey participants said sometimes made them feel more in control and sometimes made them feel less in control. To investigate this question, we conducted co-design sessions with 13 general users of the YouTube mobile app. This included an exercise in which participants sketched and explained what changes would give them greater control. Participants explained that they used Youtube in two different use cases and that they preferred different levels of control for each. When they had a specific intention in mind, such as watching a tutorial on how to solve a Rubik's cube, they wanted more control. When they did not have a specific intention in mind and they just wanted to relax or felt bored, they wanted to let YouTube take control. This leads us to our design implications. Our first design implication is to adapt the interface to the specificity of the user's intention. For example, when the user has a specific intention, the designer can present a search-first interface. On the other hand, when the user has no specific intention, the designer can present a recommendations-first interface. Switching between these two interfaces might be done either manually by the user or automatically by the system. Our second design implication is to help the user make a micro plan, which we define as a lightweight plan that guides behavior for a short time, usually just a single session of use. So, for example, the playlists feature in YouTube helped with this, but we argue that there's more designers can do here by drawing upon knowledge from the field of behavior planning. In conclusion, we encourage designers to think beyond the screen time paradigm, support greater control when users have a specific intention in mind, and help users micro plan. Thank you.

So, after projecting a set of red, green, and blue light patterns on it, you can create this colorful texture that you see right here. Then you had to go through an erase step using ultraviolet light. This is increasing the saturation of this photochromic material to 100%, so pretty much making it black again. reference: We introduce color-by-numbers, interactive structuring and vectorization of sketch imagery. Generating vector line art from rough raster sketches is a fundamental problem in computer graphics. Despite many algorithmic approaches to vectorization, the presence of The presence of noise annotation, shading and construction lines make it difficult to automatically produce desired vector output. We thus present a technique where users interactively color an automatically segmented sketch to create an intended vectorization. A user-desired stroke, whether open or closed, is conveyed by coloring the region on either side of it differently. Coloring a rough raster sketch in this fashion using traditional brush or fill coloring tools is both difficult and tedious. Our main objective is thus to structure the sketch in a manner that makes this coloring easy and efficient. Our approach has three main steps, initial color generation, interactive recoloring, and color-based simplification and vectorization. The entire process is anchored by a Delaunay complex, computed on the foreground pixels of the sketch. We also add corner pixels so as to produce a Delaunay triangulation of the entire image. We then compute an initial coloring by recursively flood-filling regions to group adjacent Delaunay triangles. Starting from the largest ungrouped seed triangle, we recursively group and color adjacent triangles as long as the edge shared between them is longer than a given threshold. This prevents color bleeding through small gaps in strokes, segmenting the sketch into an initial coloring of large compact regions. We also avoid coloring triangles with all edge lengths below the threshold, as these typically correspond to noise and gaps between adjacent sketch strokes. Users can then convey the desired vector structure by interactively recoloring the sketch. To better understand recoloring, let us first define the concepts of path flow and color flow. Given a path connecting a source triangle S and target triangle T, path flow from S to T is the length of the shortest Delaunay edge that the path crosses. Of course, there may be multiple paths between S and T, and the color flow from S to T is the maximum path flow among these paths. In other words, color flow captures an affinity for two triangles S and T to belong to the same region. In the initial coloring, every triangle in a region is assigned the color flow to it from the seed triangle for that region. Now, whenever a user clicks a triangle to be recolored, the color The color recursively spreads to adjacent triangles as long as the color flow from the clicked seed to the candidate triangle. is not smaller than its existing color flow. Recolored triangles are then updated with a new seed triangle and its associated color flow. Users can thus interactively recolor large regions of a sketch with only a few clicks. The recoloring further segments or merges regions of the sketch based on the user's choice of color. Once users are done recoloring, our approach uses these colors to simplify and vectorize the raster sketch automatically. Initially, we mark all the uncolored regions as foreground pixels. Strokes with different colors on opposite sides are then selected for vectorization, thinned to a single pixel width and structured into a connected curve network. Then, stroke segments are vectorized using adaptably fit cubic Bezier curves. Our interface begins with a rough raster image and assigns an initial coloring where automatically computed Delaunay regions are randomly and uniquely colored. This coloring can be interactively modified by adding a new color to further segment a region or by picking and dropping an existing color to merge regions. Visualizing seed triangles of existing regions can also simplify the recoloring process. Let us see a demonstration. Thank you.
