reference: Hello, CHI community. I'm Carl C. Haynes, and my advisor is Barbara J. Erickson. We're from the University of Michigan School of Information. Today, I will talk about ALPAPR, Problem Solving Efficiency and Cognitive Load for Adaptive Parsons Problems versus Writing the Equivalent Code. Introductory computing courses have a high dropout and failure rate and low diversity. Students drop out because they find learning to program frustrating and difficult. Underrepresented groups in computing are more at risk because they often have less prior programming experience. Students need a great deal of practice to acquire and retain programming knowledge. Most introductory computer programming practice requires students to write code from scratch, taking an unpredictable amount of time, and students often get stuck. We believe adaptive programming practice can reduce students' frustration, improve diversity, and provide students with effective and efficient practice. But what is adaptive programming practice? It's practice that adapts based on a student's performance. It keeps the student challenged but not frustrated. Adaptive Parsons Problems are a type of adaptive practice. These problems require learners to place mixed-up code blocks in the correct order and can include distractor blocks not needed in a correct solution. Cognitive Load Theory predicts that Parsons Problems should demand less cognitive load than requiring students to write code from scratch because they are a completion problem rather than a whole task problem. In an adaptive Parsons Problem, if the student is struggling to solve it, it can be made easier by removing a distractor, providing indentation, or combining blocks. In our system, this adaptation is triggered by clicking on the Help Me button. In contrast, write code problems, often viewed as more authentic, require programmers to create programs from scratch without any scaffolding other than unit tests to check the results. What is the effect on efficiency of solving each problem type and what is the effect on cognitive load? To answer these questions, we conducted a within-subject study in an undergraduate data-oriented programming course on Python during the winter semester of 2020. We also investigated students' attitudes about each problem type and their thought process when solving them. We conducted think-aloud observations with students in the same course to answer this question. And finally, we explored whether students understood and valued the adaptation through an end-of-course student survey. We created two different sets of problems, A and B, that were equivalent. The problem types in each set alternated between Parsons and write code problems. We collected log file data of students' interactions with each set of problems, ran Mann-Whitney U and paired t-tests, and calculated effect sizes. Participants were significantly faster at solving four of the five Parsons problems than the write code equivalent problem one has. HAS22, was not significantly faster to solve as a Parsons problem. The given solution was unusual and our findings support this claim. Please see the paper for more information. The mean self-reported cognitive load rating for each Parsons problem was lower than that of each equivalent write code problem, though the difference was significant only for two problems. However, students in the think-aloud observations all reported that Parsons problems were easier to solve than writing the equivalent code. This implies we need to find a more effective way to determine cognitive load and validate student perceptions. Some students clearly valued Parsons problems since they provide structure and help you solve the problem. In contrast, some reported it was easy to get stuck while solving write code problems. Some students were confused by the intra-problem adaptation that provided indentation and didn't find it useful when two blocks were combined that were already together. We have since modified the adaptation to no longer provide indentation and we're working on the algorithm to combine blocks. Two students who expressed a strong dislike of Parsons problems had prior programming experience. They claimed to learn more from write code problems and that Parsons problems were not beneficial. Another student liked that they had more freedom when writing code. Finally, we conducted an end-of-course survey to determine the prevalence of students' attitudes. While some students in the think aloud study reported hating Parsons problems and preferred to write code from scratch, we found only 30.4 %. of students would rather write code from scratch. Most students, 80.6%, reported finding the adaptation triggered by the Help Me button useful. However, 17.5 % reported not understanding what happened during the adaptation process, which means it can be improved. Our key takeaways are that adaptive Parsons problems are usually more efficient and require less cognitive load, prior programming experience mediates students' perceptions of adaptive Parsons problems, and improving adaptive programming practice is an iterative design process.

reference: Hi, welcome to our talk. I'm Jathan Sadowski, and this paper is also co-authored by Yolandi Stringers, Zhuying Li, Anna Shimshak, and Floyd Mueller. In this paper, we consider how recent advancements in feminist understandings of sexual consent should extend to and further inform practices of consent in HCI, particularly focusing on forms of embodied interactions with emerging technologies. Our Our paper, like the design activism work by Li and Toliver, draws on a popular consent model commonly known as Fries. developed by the US advocacy group Planned Parenthood. FRIES provides a straightforward analytical tool for considering the applicability of some of the most important elements of affirmative yes-means-yes consent for HCI, specifically that consent must be freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, and specific. We use FRIES to conceptualize the shift from a static, binary, yes-or-no model of consent towards a dynamic, ongoing, and embodied process. We supplement FRIES with concepts from erotic play practices originating in BDSM communities, which stands for bondage, domination, submission, and masochism. Drawing from these, we develop the TEAS process guidelines to provide inspiration for consensual practices in HCI. TEAS stands for Traffic Lights, Establish Ongoing Dialogue, Aftercare, Safe Words, and Explicate Soft and Hard Limits. We explore how consent is embodied and manifested in different speculative scenarios by applying TEAS to three different types of interactions. First is bodily play interactions, which involve those that place the human body in the center of the experience. For example, consider a project from the Exertion Games Lab called Inside Out, which allows users to playfully interact with the real-time video of their interior body. The player swallows an imaging capsule and wears a display embedded in their shirt in front of the body showing their gastrointestinal tract's video in real time. Such ingestible games pose a challenge for consent since it is nearly impossible to remove the sensor until the player excretes it naturally. Referring to our TEAS guidelines, bodily play interactions can make explicating hard and soft limits important. Before the interaction begins, participants should be able to discuss and establish safe boundaries around what levels of discomfort or displeasure they are willing to experience. Second is interactions with smart technologies that are designed to be constantly observing users, often with their operations being hidden. Many smart devices are now also including more active designs intended to nudge people or restrict certain choices. A smart fridge might, for example, try to incentivize people to buy healthier alternatives or report unhealthy choices to the owner's insurance provider. Referring to our TEAS guidelines, one possible approach to redesigning consent would be integrating safe words into smart devices. Just as personal voice assistants like Alexa have wake words that activate them, safe words could operate like quick commands that cause smart technology to cease collecting and sharing data or turn off its always listening mode. Effective safe words should be out of context of normal commands or requests and unlikely to be misunderstood. An example could be, hey smart fridge, aardvark. Third is intimate interactions with anthropomorphized devices and robots. Voice assistants, for example, have been criticized for responding positively or submissively to sexual solicitations and verbal abuse. Issues of sexual and HCI consent become even more entangled when considering the design and programming of intimate technologies like sex robots. Referring to our TEAS guidelines, such intimate interactions could use traffic lights in their design. Digital voice assistants or sex robots could indicate when the interaction is respectful and consensual with a green light, where the conversation is becoming disrespectful with an orange light, Or when the interaction needs to stop with a red light, which could be enforced by the device turning off for a period of time. In conclusion, in this paper we contribute a set of speculative scenarios for how affirmative sexual consent models can be put into practice in HCI by developing the TEAS process guidelines. Through this work, we show how the feminist sexual consent movement has much to offer HCI. Thank you.

reference: Welcome to the video presentation of our paper. My name is Carolyn Pang, and I'll be sharing our work on technology adoption and learning preferences for older adults. This project was a research collaboration between McGill University, the University of British Columbia, and Samsung Electronics Canada. Technology adoption among older adults has increased significantly in recent years. As a result, there exist new opportunities to explore learning preferences within this population. While older adults have increasingly adopted mainstream technologies such as smartphones over the past decade, the adoption of new generation technologies such as smartwatches and personal wearables remains low. These technologies include, among other things, health monitoring apps, which may be especially valuable for older adults. We had two research questions going into our study. First, what are the adoption priorities and challenges of older adults with regards to technologies? And second, when it comes to these technologies, what are older adults' learning needs and preferences? We set out to address these questions by examining older adults' technology experiences, both as part of their daily routines and through the lens of their personal health management practices. Our work offers insights into older adults' evolving perceptions of technologies, their ongoing learning challenges, and design opportunities for next-generation learning support. To address our research questions, we conducted a two-phase study. In the first phase, we used an online questionnaire and semi-structured interviews to better understand older adults' current technology routines. In the second phase, we reflected on prior work and findings from the first phase to develop a video prototype of a learning system called Help Kiosk 2.0 that we used as a design probe. Our video prototype featured a large 40-inch touch tabletop surface that older adults could place their devices on and receive onboarding support that would be personalized as the user progressed in their learning of the device. We also included popular learning methods identified by our participants, including access to the internet, trial-and-error feedback, step-by-step instructions in videos, and remote support through video chat and screen sharing. Once our participants had a chance to view the design probe, we followed up with a set of interviews. We asked participants to reflect on the features of the video prototype and to discuss the learning supports they felt were most useful. I'll highlight a few of the key findings next. First, we learned that technology setup and onboarding continue to be challenging for older adults. This challenge has been identified in the past, and we show that it has not improved, thus new approaches are needed. By contrast, learning preferences have shifted, such that older adults are now comfortable with more independent approaches like online searches. For example, participant 20 shares her approach for searching for help with a technology issue. I'll Google it. I'll look it up on YouTube. I mean, really, I ask questions. I go all over the place, online looking, but very often I end up with trial and error. This finding of independence is different from earlier research findings with older adults and impact the support the older adults need. We also found that older adults had mixed views when it came to new generation technologies such as smartwatches and wearables. While some were interested in learning more about them, many saw them as redundant to smartphones and perceived them as unnecessary gadgets. Take participant 16. He says, again, I get all that information from my iPhone. There's a distance monitor on it and it counts the steps as long as you keep the phone in your pocket. A smartwatch or another wearable would just be too much. These perceptions of reduced utility and redundancy are important considerations when it comes to the adoption of technologies by older adults. We also found that few participants use technologies for health monitoring due to concerns around cost and wearing additional devices. They instead relied on traditional tools to manage their personal health, such as physical calendars. This suggests the need to augment current technologies rather than providing general purpose wearables for health monitoring. Our work identified emerging design opportunities for learning supports for older adults. For example, older adults found personal support both in-person and remote to be helpful. Through our video prototype, we also saw that older adults valued the integration of various supports in one area, including easy access to the Internet, step-by-step instructions, and short video tutorials. These design opportunities are just a subset of our work that is included in our paper. We invite you to learn more about our research by downloading our full paper. Thank you for watching.

This project was a research collaboration between McGill University, the University of British Columbia, and Samsung Electronics Canada.
Technology adoption among older adults has increased significantly in recent years.
As a result, there exists new opportunities to explore learning preferences within this population.
While older adults have increasingly adopted mainstream technologies such as smartphones
over the past decade, the adoption of new generation technologies such as smartwatches
and personal wearables remains low. These technologies include, among other things,
health monitoring apps which may be especially valuable for older adults.
We had two research questions going into our study. First, what are the adoption priorities
and challenges of older adults with regards to technologies.
And second, when it comes to these technologies,
what are older adults learning needs and preferences?
We set out to address these questions
by examining older adults' technology experiences,
both as part of their daily routines
and through the lens of their personal health management
practices.
Our work offers insights into older adults
evolving perceptions of technologies.
They're ongoing learning challenges
and design opportunities for next-generation learning support.
To address our research questions,
we conducted a two-phase study.
In the first phase, we used an online questionnaire
and semi-structured interviews
to better understand older adults' current technology routines.
In the second phase, we reflected on prior work
and findings from the first phase
to develop a video prototype of a learning system
called Help Kios 2.0 that we used as a design probe.
Our video prototype featured a large 40-inch touch tabletop
surface that older adults could place their devices on
and receive onboarding support that would be personalized
as a user progressed in their learning of the device.
We also included popular learning methods identified
by our participants, including access to the internet,
trial and error feedback, step-by-step instruction
to the videos, and remote support
through video chat and screen sharing.
Once our participants had a chance to view the design probe,
We followed up with a set of interviews.
We asked participants to reflect on the features
of the video prototype and to discuss the learning supports
they felt were most useful.
I'll highlight a few of the key findings next.
First, we learned that technology setup and onboarding
continue to be challenging for older adults.
This challenge has been identified in the past,
and we showed that it has not improved
thus new approaches are needed.
By contrast, learning preferences have shifted
such that older adults are now comfortable
with more independent approaches like online searches.
For example, participant 20 shares her approach
for searching for help with the technology issue.
I'll Google it.
I'll look it up on YouTube.
I mean, really, I ask questions.
I go all over the place, online looking,
but very often I end up with trial and error.
This finding of independence is different
from earlier research findings with older adults
and impact the support the older adults need.
We also found that older adults had mixed views
when it came to new generation technologies
such as smartwatches and wearables.
While some were interested in learning more about them,
many saw them as redundant to smartphones
and perceived them as unnecessary gadgets.
Take participants 16.
He says, again, I get all that information from my iPhone.
There's a distance monitor on it
and it counts the steps as long as you keep the phone
in your pocket.
The smartwatch or another wearable would just be too much.
These perceptions of reduced utility and redundancy
are important considerations
when it comes to the adoption of technologies
by older adults.
We also found that few participants
use technologies for health monitoring
due to concerns around cost and wearing additional devices.
They instead relied on traditional tools
to manage their personal health,
such as physical calendars.
This suggests the need to augment current technologies
rather than providing general purpose wearables
for health monitoring.
Our work identified emerging design opportunities
for learning supports for older adults.
For example, older adults found personal support,
both in-person and remote to be hopeful.
Through our video prototype,
we also saw that older adults
valued at the integration of various supports in one area,
including easy access to the internet,
step-by-step instructions, and short video tutorials.
These design opportunities are just a subset of our work
that is included in our paper.
We invite you to learn more about our research
by downloading our full paper.
Thank you for watching.

At the same time, other users uninstall for the opposite reason they think interventions are too easy. Since these users have conflicting difficulty preferences, we cannot simultaneously satisfy both groups unless we adapt to users. How should behavior change systems adapt to difficulty preferences? We investigated this problem using HabitLab, a browser extension we developed that helps users reduce their time online. After installing HabitLab, users select sites they would like to reduce time on, such as Facebook, which we call goal sites. Here is an example of an easy intervention. It shows a timer in the user's Facebook feed, displaying how long they have spent on Facebook today. Here's an example of a medium intervention. It hides the Facebook feed by default. Here's an example of a hard intervention. It automatically closes the tab after 60 seconds. We used HabitLab to investigate the following research questions. First, we needed to determine whether users' difficulty preferences change over time. If they do, this means systems need to periodically ask users to check whether their preferences have changed. reference: Documentation for DIY tasks serve as codified project knowledge and help makers reach new understanding and appreciation for the artifact. Engaging in reflective processes using the documentation can be challenging when it comes to physical objects, as the documentation and the artifact exist separately. On the one hand, we have the physical object. By examining the physical object, we typically understand some of the object's qualities, such as its materials, weight, or fabrication technique. But we do not get a rationale of the decisions that went into the building of the object. On the other hand, we have their documentations. These documentations usually contain more details on the object, such as the inspiration behind it or how it was built. However, documentation on their own does not portray the full image of what the final object is. In this paper, we ask if embedding their documentation onto the object being made will promote self-reflection and whether this facilitates a deeper understanding of the object and its design process. Our assumption is that by embedding their documentation information into the object itself, we could gain in-situ access to the information, facilitating easier reflection for end-users of the documentation. From past literature, such as process products and spin, we know researchers have developed systems to embed data into the physical object to enrich the object. These projects demonstrate how this embedding can be done through different fabrication techniques and how it can create a better link of communication between the maker of the object and its end-user. However, these projects have not focused on documentation and how people might organize and share documentation information in their built objects. We conducted a preliminary study where we examined four popular examples of online documentation and interviewed and brainstormed ideas with hobbies and professional makers. From that, we gathered several design guidelines for developing a prototype system. We introduced Documented, an application that helps makers associate documentation to 3D printed objects. Let's imagine Brian. Brian teaches fabrication at a design school. To show examples of his design to his students, he used Documented to create an in-situ documentation of his mini amplifier. in their built objects. We conducted a preliminary study where we examined four popular examples
of online documentation and interviewed and brainstorm ideas with hobbies and professional
makers. From that, we gathered several design guidelines for developing a prototype system.
We introduced Documented, an application that helped makers associate documentation to 3D
printed objects. Let's imagine Brian. Brian teaches fabrication at the design school.
To show examples of his design to his students, he used Documented to create the
Institute documentation of his Mini Amplifier. He 3D printed a few copies of the Mini Amplifier
to pass around the classroom so that the students can read the documentation while exploring the
object in their hands. Step 1. Brian opened document. Where he saw that the system had four tags to
which he could attach multiple media format of files. He used the tags to organize his information
and decided to divide his documentation information based on the amplifiers models for main components.
Step 2. Brian was redirected to a thinker cat sketch where he imported the 3D model of the
amplifier and found 3D models of the 4 tags he had used previously and placed them on the model.
He has the flexibility to choose any shape or location for the tags. After positioning the tags,
Brian exported his model with the tags as an STL file and sent it to the 3D printer.

using mobile AR read about the documentation information and explore the model in their hands
to better understand the design process.

to explore a pre-built object
and the documentation materials
that we had collected about it.
We asked them to use documented in order to present
how they would document their pre-built object
using the system.

with physical tags that got embedded in the printed objects
helped people reflect on three aspects
of the process and the object.

How would they approach organization
of the documentation data
and the different categories that they would use?
Two, objects aesthetics.
Physicalization of documentation information
also requires consideration of their aesthetic
related decisions in the objects.
Three, personalization of information sharing
and appearances.
Makers prefer to separate what could be visible
to the general public from information
that should be visible to other makers.

might use our prototype in educational context
to develop and transfer knowledge.
We would also like to explore how such documentation
might be perceived by users of mass manufactured objects
in the home context.
For example, by embedding information
such as instructions to construct
and deconstruct IKEA furniture.

reference: Hello everyone, this is Hao Tian Li from HKUST. I am glad to share our paper, a Visual Analytics approach to facilitate the proctoring of online exams. Online exams have become widely used in recent years, especially during the pandemic of COVID-19. However, proctoring online exams is challenging. 1st, according to a previous study, online exams are easy to cheat, and about 29 % of the students have cheated in online exams. Furthermore, lack of face-to-face interactions lead to the low efficiency of online proctoring and makes it harder to catch cheating than conventional exams. Here are some comments collected in our interviews with teachers in a university. They all agree that it is challenging to proctor online exams. Thus, how to provide teachers with convenient, efficient, and reliable proctoring for online exams was our exploration. Existing online proctoring methods can be roughly classified into three categories. First, it is very common to employ human proctors to monitor the exam remotely. However, this method is labor-intensive and time-consuming. To improve efficiency, some fully automated methods have been proposed to apply machine learning techniques to detect cheating behaviors. However, these methods suffer from the concern on the black-box nature of machine learning models. To address the concern, semi-automated proctoring methods have also been explored to involve humans in making decisions. A common drawback of them is that they do not have a convenient method to assist teachers in exploring original data like videos. In our paper, we propose a novel viral analytics approach to facilitate online proctoring by leveraging both machine and human intelligence. We first apply machine learning techniques to help identify abnormal behaviors. Then, the suspected cases are presented to teachers by viralizations for their verification. Before we design our approach, we have conducted in-depth interviews with teachers and conclude several design requirements. The first three requirements ask us to present suspected cheating behavior in different levels of details, including student level, question level, and suspected case level. They believe that this can help them locate cheating behaviors fast. Furthermore, teachers want to achieve convenient comparison across students and questions to get rid of the effect of the question design or students' habits. Finally, exploration of raw data is also to be important for reliable decisions. To fulfill these requirements, we first design the suspected case detection module. In our approach, we collect both students' webcam video data and mouse movement data. Then, we extract abnormal behaviors of head and mouse movements from collected data. Abnormal head movements identified by machine learning models mainly reflect that the student does not look at the screen. Abnormal mouse movements can show that the student uses unauthorized materials on his computer. After detecting suspected cases, we present them to teachers with different levels of details. Student list will provide a quick overview of students at the high risk of cheating during the whole online exam. Question list will facilitate the selection of high-risk periods of each student. Behavior will present the student's detailed behaviors of head and mouse movements. Playback will make teachers able to conduct a final confirmation on students' videos and mouse movements. This is a screenshot of our entire user interface. To evaluate our method, we first explore several usage scenarios, including how we can find and verify a cheating case conveniently, and how cheating cases can be found through in-detail observation on visualized students' behaviors. Also, we conducted a user study with 16 participants who have been student teaching assistants. The user study shows our approach has better accuracy and less time cost than the current programming method used in the university. Participants also rated our system highly on the usability and visual design. Furthermore, we presented our approach to several university teachers, and they confirmed that our approach is useful and intuitive. Here are some final take-home messages. First, as an initial exploration to apply visual analytics to online proctoring, our approach utilizes the power of both machine learning and human efforts to achieve good effectiveness, efficiency, and reliability. Second, the usage of mouse movement is proved to be quite helpful in proctoring online exams. Finally, since real-time online teaching is more popular nowadays, more visual analytics methods can be explored to help teachers and students while preserving their privacy. That's the end of my presentation. For more details, visit our project page. Thanks for listening.

reference: Hi everyone, my name is Marit Bentveldse and in this video I will present our work on the technology-supported reflection inventory. Reflection is an often-addressed design goal in human-computer interaction research, and an increasing number of artifacts for reflection have been developed in recent years. These design efforts span a wide spectrum of applications, including technology that aims to encourage users to reflect on their mental health, physical activity, or just their daily life. Reflection theories highlight that reflection often does not occur automatically, but that it needs to be encouraged. Technology could offer such encouragement. An example comes from Trackly, a mobile app that helps patients with MS to manually track their symptoms, and to reflect on the collected data through visualizations. Another example is Loop, an ambient system that aims to encourage reflection on physical activity. These artifacts can potentially encourage reflection, yet it remains challenging to evaluate if and how an interactive technology helps users to reflect. In a systematic review from 2014, Baumer et al. addressed Addressed this lack of consensus regarding the evaluation of reflection support systems. Studies that used quantitative assessments rarely measured reflection, but rather focused on user experience. Qualitative evaluation approaches, on the other hand, encounter similar difficulties, such as the lack of a clear definition of reflection, and not asking users directly about reflection. This lack of proper evaluation methods makes it difficult to compare different design alternatives, which complicates future design efforts. To address this gap, we aim to create an artifact-centric instrument that enables the evaluation of technology-supported reflection, and measures the qualities of an artifact that lead to reflection. To this end, we developed the Technology-Supported Reflection Inventory, which is a skill that evaluates how an interactive system fosters personal, data-driven reflection. We began the skill formation by generating initial items for the skill. Each researcher first created items, based on related work, on their own. We then arranged a discussion session in which all the generated items were merged and discussed. The initial list of items was then subjected to two rounds of expert reviews, resulting in a final list of 58 items. We then designed an online survey consisting of these 58 items, and we recruited participants through Mechanical Turk. To ensure that participants used some form of an interactive technology that can facilitate reflection, we indicated on mTurk that participants needed to use tracking technology such as a smartwatch or a tracking app to partake in the survey. Exploratory factor analysis, item reduction, and several tests to evaluate the skill validity were performed, and this resulted in the TSRI, which is a nine-item skill consisting of three dimensions, insight, exploration, and comparison. The insight dimension describes to what extent the interactive technology offers insight to users. It evaluates if the system provides the user with insightful information and whether it inspires them to look at situations from a new perspective, or to make changes to their lives. The second dimension is exploration, and this dimension evaluates the ease and enjoyment of exploring personal data in the system. In order for users to reflect on their personal data, it should be easy for users to access and review their data. This dimension can therefore be seen as a necessary condition for reflection on personal data. And finally, the third dimension measures the social aspect of reflection-supporting interactive systems, so the extent to which users can compare themselves to others. It's often argued that current interactive technologies rarely support reflection as a social activity, but instead focus on individual cognitive processes. Yet reflection can be encouraged by conversations with others and can provide reflectors with an additional or alternative perspective. The nine items are scored on a seven-point Likert scale, and the sum of the scores indicates the extent to which an interactive system facilitates reflection. Higher scores indicate that the artifact offers more support for reflection. The TSRI can be used in the early stages of designing interactive systems for reflection. Because the scale is relatively short, it can be used for rapid feedback. Using the scale enables the evaluation and comparison of different designs for reflection, and we hope our scale will contribute to the field by enabling designers to rapidly compare prototypes or assess novel artifacts.

reference: Hi, welcome to the presentation of Let's Fretz, assisting guitar students during practice via capacitive sensing. I am Carola Maki from the University of Glasgow and this was a collaboration with Team Darmstadt from the Taylor Corporation Lab and the music school Schallkultur in Kaiserslautern, Germany. So let's start. Have you ever tried learning a musical instrument, such as the guitar? Watching someone play seems to be pretty easy, however, behind these skills are hours, weeks and years of time-consuming practice which can be frustrating at times. Beginners have limited time with teachers and experts. Because of that, they only receive limited feedback during practice, especially when they practice alone. Something that is challenging for beginners is the acquirement of perceptual mappings, so they have to map information given by musical notation to the guitar's fretboard to place the fingers correctly. Another issue during deliberate practice is the acquirement of potentially wrong movements. Those are difficult to correct later on and might even lead to health issues such as the repetitive strain injury. To assist beginners during their practice, we present Let's Frets. Let's Frets has different feedback and guidance modules. The first one is given by visual indicators that are integrated into the guitar's fretboards to guide the guitarist to finger targets. Next, we can capture finger positions on the guitar's fretboards by 3D-printed sensors. The finger positions are visualized on the guitar app and of course we can combine capacitive sensing and visual indicators. Our assistance app can also depict classical guitar notation such as fretboard diagrams and it's possible to compose exercises with it and use it for practice even if the smart functionality from the guitar is not required. To develop and evaluate Let's Frets, Frets we did the following 1st. We did an interview study with experts. Those experts were either guitar professionals or guitar teachers. We used the results from the interview study to elicit requirements. Next, we had different design integrations to realize the requirements, we tried different sensors and we found a way to integrate the sensors into the fretboard without influencing the playing too much. However, specific playing styles that require pressing from the top cannot be played with Let's Frets, but those are really advanced. When we had our first prototype, we evaluated it with a user study with 24 participants to evaluate usability and to get first-user feedback. The procedure of our study was as follows. All participants were asked to play 8 simple chords that were similar in terms of complexity. We evaluated the following 4 conditions. The first one was given by visual indicators through LED lights. The next one was the capturing module, so the capacitive sensing module, abbreviated here with CS. Next was the combination of both. And finally, we used Let's Frets functionality to depict fretboard diagrams as a baseline, because this is the traditional notation. Each participant interacted with all four of these conditions in counterbalanced order given by a Latin square, so our study was in a within-subjects design. After each condition, the participants were asked to fill in several questionnaires and after all conditions, we gave them a final questionnaire to compare the different conditions. Now let's see some results. The first ones are given in terms of effectiveness. Here we counted the number of errors that the participants made when playing the chords. As you can see here, the combination module led to the lowest number of errors. In contrast to that, the fretboard diagrams, which form the baseline, had the highest number of errors. Now let's talk about efficiency, which was the time to grip a chord successfully. Here you can see that the LEDs that aimed to guide the fingers of the guitarist were the fastest and also significantly faster than the combination module and the capacitive sensing. Capacitive sensing took longest. We think it's because the participants needed some time to familiarize them with the modules. So, we presented Let's Frets, a modular guitar practice system that aims to provide feedback and guidance for beginners. The combination module was the most promising, but have a look at the paper what else you can do with Let's Frets and how you can integrate it into other musical instruments. Thanks for your attention. Bye!

So let's start. Have you ever tried learning a musical instrument, such as the guitar? Beginners have limited time with teachers and experts. Because of that, they only receive limited feedback during practice, especially when they practice alone. Something that is challenging for beginners is the acquirement of perceptual mappings, so they have to map information given by musical notation to the guitar's fretboard to place the fingers correctly. Another issue during deliberate practice is the acquirement of potentially wrong movements. Those are difficult to correct later on and might even lead to health issues such as the repetitive strain injury. To assist beginners during their practice, we present Let's Frets. Let's Frets has different feedback and guidance modules. The first one is given by visual indicators that are integrated into the guitar's fretboards to guide the guitarist to finger targets. Next, we can capture finger positions on the guitar's fretboards by 3D-printed sensors. The finger positions are visualized on the guitar app and of course we can combine capacitive sensing and visual indicators. Our assistance app can also depict classical guitar notation such as fretboard diagrams and it's possible to compose exercises with it and use it for practice even if the smart functionality from the guitar is not required. To develop and evaluate Let's Frets, Frets we did the following 1st. We did an interview study with experts. Those experts were either guitar professionals or guitar teachers. We used the results from the interview study to elicit requirements. Next, we had different design integrations to realize the requirements, we tried different sensors and we found a way to integrate the sensors into the fretboard without influencing the playing too much. However, specific playing styles that require pressing from the top cannot be played with Let's Frets, but those are really advanced. reference: Hello everyone, I'm Youngseung Jeon, and I'm a researcher at Aju University in South Korea. In the presentation, I'm going to talk about FashionQ, an AI-driven creativity-supported tool for Facilitating ideation in the fashion design, this work is done with Seunghwan Jin, Dr. Patrick Hsu and Dr. Kyungshik Han. Being creative helps us become a better problem solver in all areas of our life and work. Creativity is important for the success of many domains such as business, education, and so on. In particular, in the fashion design field, creativity is one of the most important factors in creating a new fashion style. However, In the process of the ideation, design fixation often occurs. Design fixation is an obstacle to the successful completion of a problem. There are several attempts to apply the computer technology in designing creativity supported tools, Cst. However, there is no attempt to reflect professionals' needs, psychological operations, and AI in CST Yet, since considering these, the three factors in Cst can provide users with higher utilization and efficiency. in their creative work, we tried to reflect them in the developing CST. In this paper, we introduce FashionQ, an AI-driven creativity-supported tool for facilitating ideation in fashion design that has the following three stages. The 1st stage on the formative study we interviewed ten fashion design professionals. To obtain an understanding of the fashion design ideation phases the challenges of the each phase and potential solutions. Based on the results of the interview, we applied three cognitive operations, extending, concentrating, and blending, to support divergent and convergent thinking. The second stage is the development of FashionQ. We developed AI models that aimed to externalize three cognitive operations for divergent and convergent thinking. FashionQ has three main interactive visualizations, StyleQ, TrendQ, and MergeQ. Each visualization was developed using a single or multiple AI models. The third stage is the user study. We evaluate the effectiveness of FashionQ in supporting divergent and convergent thinking, practical usability, and ideation for the fashion design. The study results from the survey and interview demonstrate that FashionQ effectively supported the ideation process. We discussed the insights gleaned from the study, such as design implications for the development of AI-based CST. StyleQ provides cluster styles based on quantitative fashion attributes to expand the boundary of the concept of a particular style By recognizing differences in the criteria of the individual designers. A list of the fashion attributes of the fashion image the designer uploaded is displayed. Then, Styleq suggests the three styles related to the fashion images. The designer can navigate each recommended style and see the fashion image of each style. Trendq defines popularity based on the ratio of the number of the style frequencies. This helps designers construct their idea. Trendq, allows the designer to navigate the style trends. with trend forecasting and related fashion images. MergeQ is to support creation of a new combination of attributes by providing a proper combination of two selected styles of the attributes. After the designer picks one style from the trend page, the intersection fashion attribute between the two styles will be displayed in MergeQ, and the designer can check the information of the fashion runway show that is most relevant to the intersection fashion style. Our user study result from the survey and interviews demonstrate that FashionQ effectively supported the ideation process. The interesting point is that there was a demand for high customizability when setting the design directions. In other words, the designer asked for the more control over the work that is closely related to the designer's core ability. We summarize other discussion points and design applications in our paper. Please refer to our paper. Thank you.

reference: Hi, my name is Yen-Chen, today I'm presenting our WorkCodeCapture, a system that helps UI designers to efficiently communicate UI behaviors on existing websites. User interface mockups are commonly used as shared context during UI development collaboration. During communication, UI designers often use screenshots and sketches, like you see on these two Stack Overflow pages, to mockup their desired UI behaviors to ground the communication. However, sometimes interfaces can be arbitrarily complex, making them labor-intensive to sketch. Additionally, these visual references may not be available to To use in this work we ask how can we facilitate Ui designers to more effectively communicate about their Ui behaviors? in the context of the following three constraints? They are in the later stage of UI development, the UI behaviors are dynamic, and when there's no existing examples they can point to. To answer this question, we designed CodeCapture, a system that aims to help interface designers to more clearly communicate about their UI behavior issues. Let's take a look at this example. Suppose I'm developing this blog website shown on the left, and I'm thinking of adding some behaviors so that my website will look like the one on the right. To get feedback from my colleagues on this idea, I'm going to use CodeCapture to make a request. To start CodeCapture, I click this Chrome extension icon in my browser, and then I click record button to start recording the existing behavior, in my case, page scrolling. And just like normal screen recording, I will demonstrate the existing behavior on my page and use it as a base context later. Once finished, I can see three sections in CodeCapture main control panel. Let's focus on the one in the middle, which is the replay of the demonstration. Unlike screen recording, where the content is captured in, pixel, codecapture, takes snapshots of the web, geometry changes during the recording. Recording, and, when reconstructing the replay, each frame becomes a standalone website and. And CodeCapture enables users to directly manipulate the DOM element properties, like their position, or the transparency level, or even sketch new elements to add to the screen. And all those features are meant to create this prototyping environment that's almost like importing the existing behavior into it, and make each element editable so So that users don't have to waste their effort on reconstructing them from scratch and to add new behaviors on top. users can record their demonstration by directly manipulating the element. Now I'm going to show you how to do that. The 1st effect I want to add is to deem the background as the page scrolls down, and to create this mockup I 1st click the click to select the background element. element, and click the record element behavior button. And by changing the transparency level, CodeCapture records the element property changes and creates an effect as an animation. And I can adjust the slider to To set the starting and ending time of the animation with respect to when this behavior should occur, and I can replay the single animation. by clicking this replay button, or click this play all button to see the replay where the animation has been added on top of the original recording. After adding more animations, I can replay all the animations together as if they've been added to my current website. After creating these visual references, users can write their requests in the highlighted text box, and CodeCapture allows them to link part of the text to either an animation or a DOM element. When helpers read this description, they can click the hyperlink to see references either as a highlighted DOM element or a replay of an animation. We conducted two within subject studies to evaluate the accuracy and the clarity of the questions made using codecapture. We found that CodeCapture can help requesters to create questions that satisfy more required information, and also requesters spend less time on writing text to describe their questions and the length of the text description was much shorter. On the other side, helpers also find that CodeCapture can help ground the communication and reduce the navigation effort. As helper 1 said, it's like combining what email does the best with what video does the best. The key point from this project is that by enabling users to leverage existing artifacts, we help make visual communication more accurate and easy to understand, and therefore making UI development more efficient. Thank you for your time.

reference: Hi everyone, my name is Irene. I'm here today to present our work, Tabletop Games in the Age of Remote Collaboration, Design Opportunities for a Socially Connected Game Experience. In early 2020, the coronavirus disease spread rapidly and then caused a global pandemic. To prevent further spread of the virus, countries worldwide imposed social distancing rules to limit in-person gatherings. Tabletop gaming activities such as board game Night, which is a common social practice among family and then friends, is also affected. So how do people manage to move their offline tabletop gaming sessions online to stay connected with their friends and their families during the quarantine time? And what is the impact of technology usage on their game, and then social experiences to answer our research questions? we took a qualitative approach. We started with observing people in tabletop game-related online communities to learn how people adapt their offline practice to play online. We also conducted interviews with people who frequently play tabletop games remotely with their friends and their families during the quarantine time to understand the considerations behind their practice. Our data revealed three categories of themes that describe people's social and then game experiences when moving to a remote tabletop gaming setup. In this presentation, I'm going to talk about two of these insights and the design opportunities these insights revealed. When moving to a remote tabletop gaming setup, we found people often attempting to preserve the physical setup with a hybrid approach for sharing the game space. People chose a hybrid setup because they wanted to utilize their physical copies of the games or wanted to continue the game sessions they started before the quarantine time. In the hybrid setup, we found people often utilize a diverse range of physical components from sharing the entire game board and the assets to share some smaller physical game pieces. For example, in the mirrored setup, each player will have their own physical board set up and then shared. During the game, they will manipulate their board based on other players' actions as well as their own actions. Another common hybrid setup is that one player who is often referred as the game master will set up a physical board and then share with other players. Often using a phone camera mounted on a stand to capture the entire board, the player with the physical board is also in charge of Of manipulating the board, as other players verbally communicate their actions, however, in such setup. many tasks such as keeping track of different people's actions, the state of the board, and then game rules become more of the game master's responsibility rather than shared responsibility among players. As one of our participants commented, setting up and then running everything on himself can be overwhelming and make him feel like work rather than an enjoyable game experience. When people play tabletop games remotely and then interact with other people online, their attention and the engagement also change. As one participant commented, when playing online, it is more difficult to find things for his attention to grab onto and people were mostly just talking back and forth, so he would easily lose engagement with the game session. Besides, people tend to be more impatient compared to playing offline as they are more conscious with time, which makes the game session get boring easily when they perceive waiting time feels too long. To adapt to such changes, some community members suggested simplify the game rules so the game becomes easier to win to keep the game engaging when moving from offline to online play. Our findings on how people adapt their offline practice to remote play also highlights opportunities for technologies to better support people's remote game and their social experience. As physicality and the materiality plays an important role in people's tabletop game experience, we think there are opportunities in connecting shared tabletop game space and then supporting connected tangible game pieces for better game experience. And to consider for people's change of attention and engagement from offline to online play, Tabletop game platforms should also allow customization for better social experience with family and then friends, rather than focus on enforcing game rules for remote game sessions. You can read more about our other findings and discussions in our paper. Thank you for watching our presentation.

reference: Hello everyone, it is our honor to present our paper, Metamap, Supporting Visual Metaphor Ideation through Multidimensional Example-Based Exploration. The visual metaphor represents different concepts through an image by using analogy or association creatively. It is widely used in graphic design to deliver messages by fusing different objects. For example, here is a commercial ad from Nestle. It delivers the message of coffee wakes you up by associating the Nestle coffee with an alarm clock. It even strengthens the connection by fusing the two objects with the same circular shape, and also the red color. However, creating good visual metaphor is not a trivial task. First, designing visual metaphor needs additional ideation process. Such a process requires designers to be familiar with the complex associations, and also implementations of design thinking methodologies. This is a challenging for designers, and especially the amateurs without receiving professional training. Second, existing design ideation tools are insufficient in assisting designers to build concrete ideas through verbal descriptions. In this paper, we want to solve the ideation difficulties for amateur designers. To understand the process, we conducted semi-structured interviews with by-designers from various backgrounds. We asked the participants how they came up with their initial ideas, and where they got inspiration, how prototyped, and implement them. And we find all participants would iteratively go through three general steps, ideation, elements collection, and implementation. We further decomposed the ideation process, and addressed the difficulties and needs in three sub-steps, concept association, exemplar searching, and prototyping. So based on the study results, we derived the following four design requirements for our system. First, search exemplars with concept associations. The 2nd is to explore example based recommendations in diverse directions, and 3rd is to record all the ideas. and let them iteratively go through the steps and do the brainstorm. The fourth one is to keep track of all the ideas and their historical thinking path. So to fulfill the mentioned requirements, the conventional image searching process is supported by word association to inspire users to more concepts. And then, after identifying an image of interest, users can further explore the recommendation exemplars based on three-dimensional features, which is semantics, color, and shape. Users can save useful images and type comments to record their thoughts before a new brainstorming iteration. And all the saved mind maps and images record the thinking path generated by the users, for a quick recap. So here is the interface of the metamap. Metamap can provide image searching results based on automatic keyword association and also color-themed filtering. And then, exploration of the examples are shown here. And then the image from semantics, color, and shape can be stored on the canvas. And also as a support for thinking path tracking and idea recording. To evaluate the system, we use a Pinterest-like baseline. Since Pinterest is the most widely used tool to collect ideas and we need to control the differences caused by different data sources, so we implement a baseline system. And this one keeps the basic searching box, image collection, and idea recording zone. To evaluate metamap, we invite 24 amateur visual designers. Participants completed two tasks with each system to brainstorm, give feedbacks, and implement one idea draft. In the experiments, we collect all the ratings of ideas generated by them and also the outcome satisfaction, engaging level, usability, and usefulness of the two systems. After obtaining the ratings, we interview the participants to understand the reasons behind the scores. From their feedbacks, we can see the compared between the two systems. Metamap is more preferred with higher satisfaction and engagement level. Participants also highly recognize the diverse recommendation and structured thinking path tracking. To conclude this paper, we contribute a three-dimensional framework, which is semantics, color, and shape, to deconstruct and explore the visual metaphors. Also, we build an interactive system for amateur designers. Third, the user studies provides in-depth analysis of how designers gain inspiration. However, it It is just a proof of concept to explore visual metaphor ideation process, so in the future we can further improve the recommendation algorithms. The generalization and flexibility of the system and also evaluation methods, hopefully, Metamap can provide a tiny but solid steps for computers to understand and support people's creativity.

reference: Hi, I'm Navid and I'm happy to present our paper, LATTE, Use Case and Assistive Service-Driven Automated Accessibility Testing Framework for Android. 15 % of the world population have some forms of disability. Software should be accessible, especially right now, when apps are essential parts of our daily lives. Users with disability use assistive service to interact with software. For example, blind users use a screen reader such as TalkBack in Android. A screen reader announces the textual description of elements in the screen and lets users to navigate through elements by special gestures. Also, users with motor impairments use special keyboards like this one through a service called Switch Access in Android. Unfortunately, recent studies show accessibility issues are prevalent in mobile apps. Therefore, it's necessary for developers to evaluate the accessibility of their apps. Testing can be done either manually or automatically. In manual testing, given an app, a user preferably with disability, performs some use cases using assistive service and reports existing issues. This technique is accurate since the use cases are evaluated using the actual way visible users interact with the device. However, manual testing is time-consuming, impractical, and usually developers do not have access to users with a variety of disabilities. The other way of testing is through automated tools. The existing automated testing techniques such as Accessibility Scanner scans a screenshot and performs some checks on individual GUI elements according to accessibility guidelines. Automated techniques are fast and can be performed after each update of the app. However, developers either not utilize or even ignore the results. One study showed that half of the GUI templates in official Android IDE have accessibility issues. And another study showed that more than 50 % of the actual accessibility problems could not be detected by accessibility guidelines. The question is that, is it possible to have a testing technique that could benefit from both sides? We believe our approach, Latte, can be the first step toward this ideal case. Latte is automated and focuses on the main functionalities by reusing GUI test cases. Mobile developers usually write GUI test cases to test main functionalities of their apps. Also, Latte reflects the way users with disabilities interact with apps using assistive services. Here is an overview of Latte's process, which consists of three parts. First, Latte generates a use case specification from the input test case. Use case specification is a representation of the use case with accessibility-related information. Then, Latte executes the use case specification with an assistive service like TalkBack or Switch Access. Note that this is the main part that our approach differs from other techniques, as Latte actually interacts with the device using an assistive service, just like users with disabilities do. Finally, Latte produces a report that contains the accessibility failures and warnings that it finds during the execution. Accessibility warnings are steps in a use case that are accessible, however, it takes an exorbitant amount of time. Moreover, we report additional information, such as the number of actions that it takes to complete a use case and a video recording of the use case execution to make developers familiar with the struggle of users with disabilities. Now let's see how Latte works through an example. This is the launcher screen of an app. Let's say its developers want to test an important use case in this app, like registration. Here is a GUI test case that executes these functionalities. Since the test case is passed, it seems this use case is working correctly, however, only for users without disabilities. Then the developers test the app using Accessibility Scanner. It reports a several issues with elements such as low contrast and a small touch target size which do not impact a blind user. Now let's evaluate the app by Latte. Since the first step of the test case is clicking on a Qt account, Latte tries to click on it using TalkBack. When TalkBack is enabled, the background image is focused, and Latte tries to reach to the front layout, but it's impossible, because as Latte navigates the app, the background images are revolving and creates an infinite loop. This scenario is the same for Switch Access. Now let's see the effectiveness of Latte for real-world apps in our empirical evaluation. We implemented a prototype of this work for TalkBack and Switch Access in Android. We used 20 Android apps for the empirical evaluation, and for TalkBack, Latte found 39 failures where 21 of them could not be detected by Accessibility Scanner. And for Switch Access, Latte found 11 failures where none of them could be detected by Accessibility Scanner. We manually examined the failures and warnings detected by Latte and categorized them so developers can be aware of them. Due to the limited time, I encourage you to visit our website to watch video demonstrations, read our paper, or access the entire source code of Latte. Thanks for listening.

Software should be accessible, especially right now, when apps are essential parts of our daily lives. Users with disability use assistive service to interact with software. For example, blind users use a screen reader such as TalkBack in Android. A screen reader announces the textual description of elements in the screen and lets users to navigate through elements by special gestures. Also, users with motor impairments use special keyboards like this one through a service called Switch Access in Android. Unfortunately, recent studies show accessibility issues are prevalent in mobile apps. Therefore, it's necessary for developers to evaluate the accessibility of their apps. Testing can be done either manually or automatically. In manual testing, given an app, a user preferably with disability, performs some use cases using assistive service and reports existing issues. This technique is accurate since the use cases are evaluated using the actual way visible users interact with the device. However, manual testing is time-consuming, impractical, and usually developers do not have access to users with a variety of disabilities. The other way of testing is through automated tools. The existing automated testing techniques such as Accessibility Scanner scans a screenshot and performs some checks on individual GUI elements according to accessibility guidelines. Automated techniques are fast and can be performed after each update of the app. However, developers either not utilize or even ignore the results. One study showed that half of the GUI templates in official Android IDE have accessibility issues. And another study showed that more than 50 % of the actual accessibility problems could not be detected by accessibility guidelines. The question is that, is it possible to have a testing technique that could benefit from both sides? We believe our approach, Latte, can be the first step toward this ideal case. Latte is automated and focuses on the main functionalities by reusing GUI test cases. Mobile developers usually write GUI test cases to test main functionalities of their apps. Also, Latte reflects the way users with disabilities interact with apps using assistive services. Here is an overview of Latte's process, which consists of three parts. First, Latte generates a use case specification from the input test case. Use case specification is a representation of the use case with accessibility-related information. Then, Latte executes the use case specification with an assistive service like TalkBack or Switch Access. Note that this is the main part that our approach differs from other techniques, as Latte actually interacts with the device using an assistive service, just like users with disabilities do. Finally, Latte produces a report that contains the accessibility failures and warnings that it finds during the execution. Accessibility warnings are steps in a use case that are accessible, however, it takes an exorbitant amount of time. Our next contribution is the exploration of fairness challenges through the practitioners views on these toolkits gaps. We will cover the five highlighted themes. Please see the paper for the full gap analysis. The first gap is the limited accessibility of the toolkit search process. Almost all interviewees claim to use the 1st toolkit they find that meets their needs. This is problematic because of the diversity of toolkits' approaches to fairness. reference: Hello everyone, I'm Satip from the Augmented Human Lab at the University of Auckland, New Zealand. So here I am excited to present the Cloth Tiles at CHI 2021. Well, it's quite interesting that humans have evolved to a point where they can't live without wearing clothes from birth anymore. So at present, a vast number of research is focused on smart clothing, especially focused on diverse sensing mechanisms. However, the actuation dimension of clothing has been ignored most of the time. In this work, we present Cloth Tiles, a prototyping platform to fabricate customized actuators on clothing using 3D printing and shape memory alloys. Our main contribution is providing an easily customizable and versatile fabrication technique for enabling actuation on textile interfaces. Here we have used commonly available raw materials such as flexible 3D printing filaments, SMA wires, and of course, a piece of clothing. This technique basically involves two steps. First, we have to print 3D structural elements onto the piece of clothing. Secondly, we integrated an SMA wire into the 3D printed substrate. Here, we demonstrate the concept of clothing actuation using a fundamental Cloth Tiles element. Because we have the advantage of having a variable stiffness, we can easily control the thickness of the 3D printed substrates. So in return, this allows us to regulate the actuator's behavior. We propose five ways to combine the Cloth Tiles basic elements to realize different deformation types over an extended area. They are linear, perpendicular, curved, circular, and angular methods. And each aggregation method has its own unique actuation behavior as you can see here. Also, we can control the deformation forces by varying the basic element scaling properties. For example, by using widthwise scaling, we can render a more distributed force over a larger area of clothing. In the same way, using the lengthwise scaling technique, one can achieve a stronger deformation force that can increase the bending angle. As shown here, you can see how the bending angle of the basic element increases with the anchor point length. Also, with different levels of rigidity in the clothing, we can also control diverse actuation levels in terms of displacement. When it comes to the directional aspects, we propose two placements where the Cloth Actuator can be placed. Those are outside and inside of the clothing. In each placement, we identify three directions along which the Cloth Actuator can be oriented. Based on each arrangement, several properties of the Cloth Actuation can be determined, such as the bending direction, visibility to the outside, and the type of sensation. We can achieve a unique set of actuation mechanisms by combining primitive structures that I mentioned before. Figure A on the top left incorporates a linear aggregation mechanism together with a variable scaling mechanism in a longitudinal direction. This generates a more intense pulling effect from a specific point on the cloth. Also, if you look at figure B, this actuator allows clothing surface to deform as a spherical cap. To observe how users find the cloth tiles, we performed a co-design study with the support of an expert. At first, we interpreted that the users would only design functional clothing, but instead they were mostly concerned about the aesthetic aspects of the clothing. These are some cool ideas that users came up with. The first one is a face mask loosener. He had an issue with his face mask generating vapor on his spectacles when breathing. Another participant wanted to integrate a wrist compressor in his workout gloves to receive subtle notifications while doing exercises. When it comes to aesthetic designs, users came up with awesome ideas. One of the participants wanted to print a logo on his T-shirt that can visually stay. Also, another participant wanted to integrate a slight massager on her eye mask. And mainly, she wanted to retain the aesthetic aspects of that. From the user feedback, we could confirm that cloth tiles potentially can fulfill both functional as well as aesthetic aspects of clothing after user expectations. Also, we developed a set of clothing actuators to further demonstrate the potential of cloth tiles for functional and aesthetic clothing applications. And here is my amazing team behind this project. We are looking forward to future collaborations related to this project and other projects. And you can also check out our websites for more details. So, feel free to contact us for further discussions. And this is a wrap and I hope you guys enjoyed it. Thank you.

Here we have used commonly available raw materials such as flexible 3D printing filaments, SMA wires, and of course, a piece of clothing. This technique basically involves two steps. First, we have to print 3D structural elements onto the piece of clothing. Secondly, we integrated an SMA wire into the 3D printed substrate. Here, we demonstrate the concept of clothing actuation using a fundamental Cloth Tiles element. Because we have the advantage of having a variable stiffness, we can easily control the thickness of the 3D printed substrates. So in return, this allows us to regulate the actuator's behavior. We propose five ways to combine the Cloth Tiles basic elements to realize different deformation types over an extended area. They are linear, perpendicular, curved, circular, and angular methods. And each aggregation method has its own unique actuation behavior as you can see here. Also, we can control the deformation forces by varying the basic element scaling properties. For example, by using widthwise scaling, we can render a more distributed force over a larger area of clothing. In the same way, using the lengthwise scaling technique, one can achieve a stronger deformation force that can increase the bending angle. reference: Shan, a second-year Master's in HCI student at the University of Maryland and an incoming PhD student at the University of Washington, and I will be presenting our paper on Living with Uncertainty and Stigma, Self-Experimentation and Support Seeking around Polycystic Obese Syndrome. This work was done in collaboration with Rishul Sehrang, Tamir Shanmugam, and Professor Ying-King Che at the University of Maryland. PCOS, or Polycystic Obese Syndrome, is a chronic condition that causes hormonal imbalance, infertility, and irreverent menstruation in women and people with female reproductive organs. It is enigmatic in nature, that is its symptoms. causes and treatments are not well understood and vary across individuals. Hence, there is no singular cure for it either. The condition is also stigmatized by the virtue of being linked to infertility and the way it affects people's bodies and appearance, i.e. causing sudden weight changes, hair fall, acne, and facial hair, among other things. Lying at the intersection of being both an enigmatic condition with no universal cure and a women's health concern with associated stigma makes PCOS an important context to study. Moreover, it's prevalent, affecting 1 in every 10 women in the United States. But despite its prevalence, existing technologies are not tending to the diverse needs of people with PCOS. Many commercial technologies for managing and monitoring menstrual health and fertility, such as cycles, period tract, or anamapristic, are Are designed to cater to healthy individuals, often excluding people with chronic health conditions such as Pcos. Similarly, on the research side, while there is an emotional focus on women's health topics such as fertility, sexual and menstrual health, closely related chronic health conditions such as PCOS are understudied in the HCI community. Researchers in other fields have explored challenges that people with PCOS face in identifying, accepting, and managing their condition, directly motivating our work on understanding the role of technology to better support people living with the condition. Through this research, we aim to uncover people's lived experiences and challenges with PCOS, particularly their support-seeking, sense-making, and self-experimentation practices. Based on this understanding, we identify avenues for designing inclusive health technologies to better support their diverse needs. To develop a deeper understanding of different aspects that shape people's experiences with the condition, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 10 people officially diagnosed with PCOS and analyzed data on a popular PCOS-related subject forum. We found uncertainty and stigma to be key in shaping people's unique experiences with the condition. In the interest of time, I will briefly discuss one finding from each team. For more details, please see our paper. One important finding was how people often assessed and experimented with their bodies and different management techniques to find what worked best for them. We observed people assessing and experimenting with medications, birth control, food supplements, natural remedies, diets, and workout plans. They even tried to triangulate their understanding and experiment based on insights gained from experts such as doctors, based on their own body intuition, and from reading online information. Some individuals made choices and trade-offs between different management techniques, such as taking medications or incorporating lifestyle modifications to manage their PCOS, if they faced challenges in actually doing both of them or did not want to follow certain treatments. We also observed that PCOS significantly affected people's perceptions of themselves. Individuals often self-doubted their capabilities and felt afraid of being stigmatized due to physical or mental limitations in being able to perform professionally or socially as per other people's expectations. Symptoms of PCOS such as weight gain, acne, hair fall, and excessive facial hair made people feel set apart from what is considered normal, significantly impacting their self-confidence, body image, and social image. However, on the other hand, people also reported how PCOS helped them recognize their individuality and psychological gender and act upon their gender dysphoria. To sum it up, our main contributions are first providing a detailed account of people's lived experiences with PCOS, from discovery and diagnosis to living and managing the condition. Second, identifying avenues for future research and providing recommendations for design technology that can better support their diverse needs. And lastly, contextualizing our findings in light of past works on menstruation, fertility, and self-tracking to contribute to a growing body of HCI and CSCW research on designing for stigmatized topics in women's health and well-being. Thank you and to know more about our work, please make sure to read our paper.
