This work was done in collaboration with Rishul Sehrang, Tamir Shanmugam, and Professor Ying-King Che at the University of Maryland. PCOS, or Polycystic Obese Syndrome, is a chronic condition that causes hormonal imbalance, infertility, and irreverent menstruation in women and people with female reproductive organs. It is enigmatic in nature, that is its symptoms. causes and treatments are not well understood and vary across individuals. Hence, there is no singular cure for it either. The condition is also stigmatized by the virtue of being linked to infertility and the way it affects people's bodies and appearance, i.e. causing sudden weight changes, hair fall, acne, and facial hair, among other things. Lying at the intersection of being both an enigmatic condition with no universal cure and a women's health concern with associated stigma makes PCOS an important context to study. Moreover, it's prevalent, affecting 1 in every 10 women in the United States. But despite its prevalence, existing technologies are not tending to the diverse needs of people with PCOS. Many commercial technologies for managing and monitoring menstrual health and fertility, such as cycles, period tract, or anamapristic, are Are designed to cater to healthy individuals, often excluding people with chronic health conditions such as Pcos. Similarly, on the research side, while there is an emotional focus on women's health topics such as fertility, sexual and menstrual health, closely related chronic health conditions such as PCOS are understudied in the HCI community. Researchers in other fields have explored challenges that people with PCOS face in identifying, accepting, and managing their condition, directly motivating our work on understanding the role of technology to better support people living with the condition. Through this research, we aim to uncover people's lived experiences and challenges with PCOS, particularly their support-seeking, sense-making, and self-experimentation practices. Based on this understanding, we identify avenues for designing inclusive health technologies to better support their diverse needs. To develop a deeper understanding of different aspects that shape people's experiences with the condition, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 10 people officially diagnosed with PCOS and analyzed data on a popular PCOS-related subject forum. We found uncertainty and stigma to be key in shaping people's unique experiences with the condition. In the interest of time, I will briefly discuss one finding from each team. For more details, please see our paper. One important finding was how people often assessed and experimented with their bodies and different management techniques to find what worked best for them. We observed people assessing and experimenting with medications, birth control, food supplements, natural remedies, diets, and workout plans. They even tried to triangulate their understanding and experiment based on insights gained from experts such as doctors, based on their own body intuition, and from reading online information. Some individuals made choices and trade-offs between different management techniques, such as taking medications or incorporating lifestyle modifications to manage their PCOS, if they faced challenges in actually doing both of them or did not want to follow certain treatments. We also observed that PCOS significantly affected people's perceptions of themselves. Individuals often self-doubted their capabilities and felt afraid of being stigmatized due to physical or mental limitations in being able to perform professionally or socially as per other people's expectations. Symptoms of PCOS such as weight gain, acne, hair fall, and excessive facial hair made people feel set apart from what is considered normal, significantly impacting their self-confidence, body image, and social image. However, on the other hand, people also reported how PCOS helped them recognize their individuality and psychological gender and act upon their gender dysphoria. To sum it up, our main contributions are first providing a detailed account of people's lived experiences with PCOS, from discovery and diagnosis to living and managing the condition. Second, identifying avenues for future research and providing recommendations for design technology that can better support their diverse needs. And lastly, contextualizing our findings in light of past works on menstruation, fertility, and self-tracking to contribute to a growing body of HCI and CSCW research on designing for stigmatized topics in women's health and well-being. Thank you and to know more about our work, please make sure to read our paper.

Similarly, on the research side, while there is an emotional focus on women's health topics such as fertility, sexual and menstrual health, closely related chronic health conditions such as PCOS are understudied in the HCI community. Researchers in other fields have explored challenges that people with PCOS face in identifying, accepting, and managing their condition, directly motivating our work on understanding the role of technology to better support people living with the condition. Through this research, we aim to uncover people's lived experiences and challenges with PCOS, particularly their support-seeking, sense-making, and self-experimentation practices. reference: Hello, my name is Rupat Razaev. Today I would like to present a work titled Reading in VR, the effect of text presentation type and location. Virtual reality allows novel approaches for users to view, read, and interact with the text. In VR, text presentation type and location can be altered to meet users' need. For example, for better viewability, a text might tilt towards a VR user if the user is not standing in front of it. Or a user might take apart text and explore the virtual environment while reading the text in the field of view. If the available space is small, or a user needs to interact with the text and the virtual environment simultaneously, text in VR can change its presentation form to display the same amount of text in different display sizes. For this purpose, presenting text using Rapid Serial Visible Presentation, RSVP, is a promising approach. While reading with RSVP, a text is displayed sequentially, word-by-word, at a fixed location. However, it's not clear how text locations and presentation types affect the reading experience in VR. For this purpose, we conducted an explorative study. For the study, we developed a virtual exhibition where each exhibition room had a painting and a label with a textual description at the center of each of the four walls. The text labels could be displayed with two presentation types, as a paragraph or using RSVP. With a paragraph presentation type, text was displayed completely and participants could read it left to right, top to bottom. With RSVP, the text was displayed word-by-word and centered around a red pivot letter, acting as a resting point for the participants' eyes while reading. The speed of RSVP was adjusted based on each participant's regular reading speed. We used three text locations. World-fixed location, where text was displayed on the environment. Edge-fixed location, where text was attached to the environment with an edge and vertically tilted to face the user. And head-fixed location, where text was displayed on a head-up display. For the evaluation, we implemented a primary task for participants that involve common VR activities. At first, the text labels within the exhibition room were shuffled. Participants' task was to assign labels to the correct paintings. To perform the task, participants first needed to activate and read the text label and determine to which painting it belonged. Afterward, participants could switch the labels. Please refer to the paper for detailed description of the task and the implementation. Our study had two by story repeated measures designed with text presentation type and location as within-subjects variables. We had 18 participants. We measured the number of wrong switches of labels as error and the time needed to finish the task, as well as usability, perceived task load, and presence using questionnaires. Moreover, participants indicated their preference for each condition and provided qualitative feedback. The results showed that the average number of errors and the task completion time were higher with the paragraph presentation type than the RSVP. The qualitative results revealed that with the paragraph presentation type, participants didn't always read the text completely, but skimmed them to find keywords regarding the paintings. As a result, they skipped some parts of the text, which might be essential to perform the task. However, with RSVP, skimming the text was not possible. Moreover, we found that the world-fixed location increases the perceived task load and decreases user preference rating while reading with RSVP. As the task used in the study required participants to explore the virtual environment, they needed to make large attention shifts between texts in the world-fixed location and the environment. As texts were displayed entirely with the paragraph presentation type, it was easy for participants to return to the reading flow after these attention shifts and continue reading from any part of the text. However, reading with RSVP, participants had to continue reading from the world where the RSVP reading paused. In addition, we found that displaying text as a paragraph in the head-fixed location increases task load and reduces usability and user preference rating. As a single word space was needed with the RSVP presentation type, it facilitated reading while moving in the virtual environment. However, a text displayed as a paragraph in the head-fixed location partly occluded participants' field of view. Participants also indicated that they would prefer to read long and important texts as paragraphs in static environments where the reading is the primary activity. However, they will favor reading short texts using RSVP in dynamic environments where tasks require detailed attention to the environment. As the takeaway messages of the study, the results suggest that RSVP should be used for short texts displayed either in the edge-fixed or in the head-fixed location if the user needs to move within the virtual environment. Paragraph presentation type with a world-fixed or edge-fixed location should be used to display long and important texts if reading is the primary task and the movement in the virtual environment is not required. Thank you for your attention.

reference: Hello, my name is Rupat Razaev. Today I would like to present a work titled Reading in VR, the effect of text presentation type and location. For example, for better viewability, a text might tilt towards a VR user if the user is not standing in front of it. Or a user might take apart text and explore the virtual environment while reading the text in the field of view. If the available space is small, or a user needs to interact with the text and the virtual environment simultaneously, text in VR can change its presentation form to display the same amount of text in different display sizes. For this purpose, presenting text using Rapid Serial Visible Presentation, RSVP, is a promising approach. While reading with RSVP, a text is displayed sequentially, word-by-word, at a fixed location. However, it's not clear how text locations and presentation types affect the reading experience in VR. For this purpose, we conducted an explorative study. For the study, we developed a virtual exhibition where each exhibition room had a painting and a label with a textual description at the center of each of the four walls. The text labels could be displayed with two presentation types, as a paragraph or using RSVP. With a paragraph presentation type, text was displayed completely and participants could read it left to right, top to bottom. With RSVP, the text was displayed word-by-word and centered around a red pivot letter, acting as a resting point for the participants' eyes while reading. The speed of RSVP was adjusted based on each participant's regular reading speed. We used three text locations. World-fixed location, where text was displayed on the environment. Edge-fixed location, where text was attached to the environment with an edge and vertically tilted to face the user. And head-fixed location, where text was displayed on a head-up display. For the evaluation, we implemented a primary task for participants that involve common VR activities. At first, the text labels within the exhibition room were shuffled. Participants' task was to assign labels to the correct paintings. To perform the task, participants first needed to activate and read the text label and determine to which painting it belonged. Afterward, participants could switch the labels. Please refer to the paper for detailed description of the task and the implementation. Our study had two by story repeated measures designed with text presentation type and location as within-subjects variables. We had 18 participants. We measured the number of wrong switches of labels as error and the time needed to finish the task, as well as usability, perceived task load, and presence using questionnaires. Moreover, participants indicated their preference for each condition and provided qualitative feedback. The results showed that the average number of errors and the task completion time were higher with the paragraph presentation type than the RSVP. As a result, they skipped some parts of the text, which might be essential to perform the task. However, with RSVP, skimming the text was not possible. However, they will favor reading short texts using RSVP in dynamic environments where tasks require detailed attention to the environment. reference: Hi everyone, my name is Fahad Hamidi and I'm going to present our paper entitled Turning the Invisible Visible, Transdisciplinary BioArt Explorations in Human-DNA Interaction on behalf of my colleagues Lydia Astamato, Lisa Scheifele, Ryan Hammond, and Nisa Askar-Ali-Hoffman. BioArt is an art practice in which artists work with living organisms, including animal, plants, fungi, and others, for artistic and creative purposes. Some examples include ALBA, in which the artist genetically modified a rabbit to glow in the dark, and NATURE, in which the artists work with the development process of butterflies to create patterns on their wings, and a contest run by the American Society of Microbiology, in which contestants can draw on agar with colorful microorganisms. The contribution of this paper is twofold. First, we investigate the current perspectives of bioartists on working at the intersection of science and art. And also, second, we report on a first-hand account of how to creatively interact with living organisms on a molecular level through current do-it-yourself synthetic biology methods. These contributions add to the conversation at the intersection of human-computer interaction and bioart. For the first part of our paper, we interviewed six bioartists. We found that bioartists often describe their work in terms that invoke skills and epistemologies that cross disciplines towards a shared collaborative goal, a quality that we identify as transdisciplinary fluency. For example, P1 said, I wanted to develop an art piece that was in effect a biosensor, a meter of whether the genes had been synthesized. We're trying to do it in E. coli, and we're working with designing the genetic constructs to create the different steps of that pathway. Another finding was that bioartists pointed to a sense of familiarity, including through cultural symbolism and the shared quality of being alive or supporting life with the organisms that they work with. This quality contrasts with the DNA as code metaphor that sometimes is used in synthetic biology. For example, P5 said, as I told you, you're working with another living organism. You're also a living organism. Finally, We found that Bioart often requires a specialized knowledge and equipment necessitating artists to work together. with scientists to negotiate access, and that this negotiation in turn increases access to biology for diverse audiences. In the second part of the paper, we describe our experience with human DNA interaction through creating transgenic poetry-infused wine. The project revolves around the famous line of Sufi poetry by Hafez, the 14th century Persian poet, that revolves around themes of transformation and persistence through love. Hargis, namira, don que de la sande should be, ish, subtast, badgery de olam davo, memo. In this project, we first encoded the poem into Morse code and then into a viable DNA code. We then fabricated this DNA code and inserted it into a plasmid backbone. After amplifying the DNA and verifying that the resulting plasmid included the sequence with the poetry using an enzyme digest on an electrophoresis gel, we transformed the linearized DNA with living yeast cells and selected for yeast cells that contained the poetry sequence. We then grew the yeast overnight and combined it with grape juice to make transgenic wine. Raz pays homage to the resilient spirit of Persian mystic poets who use the power of metaphors and linguistic transmutations to capture vivid experiences of personal and spiritual transformation. Additionally, its engagement with the process of winemaking, which is taboo in this cultural context, parallels the ethically ambiguous practice of genetically modifying living organisms. In conclusion, we found that bioart offers exciting modes of inquiry for human-computer interaction that are inherently transdisciplinary and can be characterized as art research. Additionally, we found that interacting with living organism at a molecular level can provide insight on structures of access and power that surround our relationship with them and the environments we live in. Thank you very much. I'm happy to answer questions via email and please see the paper for more details.

People with visual impairments use fingers to scan the 2D space and use buttons to manipulate the system state. Pin displays require an interaction that consists of two phases, scanning and manipulating. The scanning phase not only takes a long time, but also requires users to scan the display using their fingers repeatedly in order to perceive changes in specific parts of the display. Therefore, multiple dynamic objects cannot be perceived simultaneously. In addition, it is difficult for users to seamlessly transition between the manipulating phase and the scanning phase. Since touch is reserved for scanning the tactile output, users are required to perform input using indirect buttons. The two-phase structure causes difficulties in interaction with multiple objects. We propose ThruHand, which uses both the palm and back side of the non-dominant hand. ThruHand users perceive tactile output using the palm, which allows them to immediately sense changes within a large area. Simultaneously, users are able to utilize the back of the hand as a touch input space. Since the non-dominant hand is used both as an input channel and an output channel, we call this design co-located input and output. We designed a 2D pin display of 12x17 pins with 10mm of spacing. We used an optical tracker for touch sensing. We conducted a user study in a total of 3 steps with 10 visually impaired users. The goal of the first experiment was to investigate the accuracy of touch interaction through the hand. In the second experiment, we tested the performance of three basic interactions. The basic interactions were then used to create several interactive applications, which were evaluated in the third experiment. Today, I will summarize the first and third experiments. For the second one, please refer to our paper. In the first experiment, we investigate how much additional error is made by performing touch inputs through the hand. The subject performed a simple task. When a pin rose to stimulate the palm, the subject touched the corresponding location of the stimulus as accurately as possible on the back of the hand. The average error was 13.2mm. This is remarkably small considering that the 2-point discrimination threshold of the palm is 10mm. Another interesting finding was that the top area, where the fingers were located, had significantly less error than the bottom area of the palm. In the third user study, we implemented and tested four interactive applications. In Shoot-Em-Up, the player manipulates an aircraft to shoot down threatening enemy planes while avoiding falling obstacles. In Whack-A-Mole, the player selects randomly appearing moles as quickly as possible. In Multiplayer Pong, two players play against each other by controlling a paddle to hit the ball to the opponent's side. In Rhythm Game, the player selects falling targets that match the rhythm or notes of a song with the right timing. After the game experience, we asked the subjects if the size of the palm was appropriate for playing games. Seven participants answered that it was large enough to play the four games. However, two participants responded that they could have better enjoyed the games if they had bigger hands. For some users with acquired visual impairments, through hand allowed them a similar experience of visual games that they played before they became visually impaired. One user said that through hand games were more enjoyable because the additional tactile output provided a richer feedback when compared to games that only used auditory output. Another user commented that through hand was better because it had more operability and gamability. One user said that through hand's rhythm game was completely different from the audio-based rhythm game that he had played before. It allowed him to concentrate on the music. My name is Donghyun Ko, and my co authors are Ji Bin Lim, Yoo jin, Lee, Jae Eun Pyeon, and our advisor is Professor Woo Hoon Lee from Kaist A. A typical 3D printed object is rigid. It is hard to modify the object after it is printed. Thermoforming is a possible solution to modify the printed object. As heating makes the printed object soft, smoothing the object's surface or even bending the object become possible. However, thermoforming is also limited due to its low thermal conductivity. Deeply and locally heating the printed object is impossible. In this research, we aim to relate this issue of thermoforming to facilitate post-print deformation. Here, we introduce a possible approach, embedding structure with high heat transference into target region for the modification. After heating these cells which are embedded into printed object, it is even possible to deform the thicker parts of the printed object. Under this approach, our primary contributions can be summarized as follows. First, we design TF cells and compound cells for enriching thermoforming. Second, we characterize TF cells to provide useful guidelines. Third, we investigated applicable thermoforming space and implemented the examples. Our research is positioned among studies of the hands-on approach to digital fabrication, embedding functional structure into 3D prints, and shape-changing through heating. Especially, we aim to enable post-print physical deformation using single material printing. Next, a specific structure called TF cells is designed to increase heat transference when embedded into 3D prints. Finally, our research target user-actuated shape-changing through heating. Prior to designing a structure, we choose hot air from a heat gun as a heat source. The design structure is called thermoformable cells, and TF cells have high heat transference in universal direction. As TF cells are built of beam arrays, it is applicable to most 3D geometries. reference: My name is Caroline Pitt, and I'll be discussing our work on Connected Learning Collapsed Contexts, examining teens' sociotechnical ecosystems through the lens of digital badges. Today's youth are more involved in the digital world than ever, but that involvement takes very specific and somewhat circumscribed forms, depending on the intended audience, creating a sharp divide between their social and academic worlds online. In our increasingly connected and surveilled world, youth have few places to call their own, causing them to jump from platform to platform and use creative measures like creating multiple accounts, for instance the Finsta phenomenon, where youth often have fake Instagram accounts. Meanwhile, researchers and practitioners constantly attempt to find ways to connect with youth, adding social media elements to academic technologies. We draw on research by Dana Boyd, Mimi Ito, Davis and Jorgensen, and others to examine the complex tension that exists between connected learning and context collapse. In this paper, we address three main research questions. One, how do youth collapse and separate their online context, particularly around professional academic versus personal social boundaries? Two, what tensions do youth navigate in their sociotechnical daily rounds, particularly surrounding identity and context collapse? And three, how might connected learning technologies such as badges be incorporated into teens' sociotechnical ecosystems in a way that supports their learning and identities while respecting their boundaries? This work takes place within a larger study on the design and implementation of digital badges at a science center in the Pacific Northwest. Using participatory design methods, we've worked to create a digital badging system drawing on connected learning that allows youth to share their accomplishments. This timeline provides some context for the case studies discussed in this work. Throughout this study, we've explored how youth science identities are complexly built and intertwined as they navigate the rich sociotechnical ecosystems of modern life. We want to understand how technologies like badges can be used to support identity development. So for the past five years, we've worked with the youth directly to design a badge system, and now we're interested in why they use these badges and why they don't after examining. in detail how to implement a badge system, see Pitt et al. 2019, we're now looking towards longer-term impacts and sustainability. Thus, to better understand how digital badges featured in youth's sociotechnical ecosystems and how they might be better incorporated and implemented, we conducted case studies with several youth from the project. After an initial interview, we observed the youth at the science center and in their neighborhoods. Then we conducted ecological momentary assessments over a period of a couple of months. Lastly, we conducted a wrap-up interview with each participant. With this data, we were able to create rich profiles of the six youth featured in the paper, learning how technology factored into their day-to-day lives. Using the research team's analytical memos and qualitative coding of the data set, we were able to draw out some themes and insights that we believe are valuable to a variety of designers, researchers, and practitioners, focusing on how to frame and implement social media for youth academic and professional development. Here are a few key findings from the study. While youth not wanting authority figures to be in their spaces is fairly well known, we discovered that youth siloed their social media profiles to a fairly extreme degree, often having multiple Instagram accounts and only using each of their social media accounts for a very specific friend group. Several participants were easily able to recount who they spoke to on which apps. There was also little use of professional social media, with academic achievements rarely being shared online. Though the participants were mostly college-bound, they did not have professional-facing social media. Relatedly, participants recounted a lot of don'ts and not a lot of dos from authority figures in regards to social media, thus no positive examples of usage for professional purposes. In addition to the rich qualitative findings, we also came up with a few design recommendations. 1st, when involving youth, bring in their the whole experience. Don't make assumptions about their lives and be aware that youth exist in complex ecologies, a more ecological perspective. Two, design for context collusion, not collision. Let youth decide where their contexts connect, creating what's referred to as context collusions. Don't cause unwanted context collapse between the personal and professional. And third, scaffold development of professional identity while allowing for personal customization. Make it easy to build professional identity online by presenting straightforward choices and lots of options for sharing where they want things to be shared. So that's all I have for right now. Thank you so much for listening, and I hope you'll check out the paper for a great deal more detail. I'd like to thank my co-authors, the NSF for funding this work, and our participants.

reference: Hello, my name is Daniel Madden, and I am pleased to be presenting research conducted in collaboration with Yuzhen Liu, Haowei Yu, Mustafa Samburak, Giovanni Troiano, and Kasper Hartfeld. Our work is titled Why Are You Playing Games? You Are a Girl, Exploring Gender Biases in Esports. We can define esports as an area of sports activities in which people develop and train mental and physical abilities in the use of information and communication technologies. Esports has become widely popular, gaining millions of viewers internationally for events like the Overwatch League Finals and League of Legends World Cup. However, if you watch many of these events, you may note that a majority of participants, if not all of the participants, are male. This disparity in participation at the highest level inspired us to examine participation within esports. Our work was inspired by two key research questions. The first being, why and how do gender biases still persist in esports? The second being, how do these biases impact overall participation? For our study, we specifically examined participation within the male and female dichotomy. We conducted a series of interviews with professional players and esports organizers among a variety of games, including CSGO, Heroes of the Storm, and League of Legends. We aimed to have an equal amount of participants between both male and female gamers and organizers conducting a total of 19 interviews. Using previous research, we developed five key questions that were used to guide the semi-structured interviews. Interviews were carried out both in person and remotely using tools such as Discord and Skype. In doing so, we developed a detailed analysis of their experiences with gender bias, identifying four key themes explained in the following slides. In the experiences of both male and female participants, stereotypes within the gaming space still persist. Female gamers are assumed to lack skill or the aggressive behavior necessary to compete at the highest level. On the other hand, male gamers are assumed to be overly aggressive and overall better at esports than female gamers. Interestingly, some participants believe this may stem from a cultural bias in which men are given opportunity and encouragement to engage in video games while women are not. In continuing with the cultural bias, many participants define games as being primarily targeted towards a male audience. This includes marketing techniques and the representation of in-game characters. Our participants noted games like Overwatch may have increased female participation because females find they are better represented in such games. Participants suggest that companies and campaigns would benefit from including women in their efforts to increase for female participation at all levels. Many of the female gamers brought up challenges they faced when gaming online. These challenges often stemmed from the previously mentioned biases and stereotypes. To avoid unwanted interactions or gender bias, our participants talked about several tactics including voice-changing software or not speaking entirely during match play. In their experience, Their mistakes and level of skill were always associated with their gender rather than their actual abilities or time spent practicing in. In order to combat these gender biases and their effects on participation, participants suggested the use of separate tournaments. It was argued that females lack the role models and mentors male gamers have. By creating separate tournaments, it allows women to compete with one another and develop their skills in a safe environment. However, both male and female agree that the goal is for all esports players to compete together regardless of gender as esports should be based on skill. Based on the experiences of our participants, we find that past HCI research and strategies may be adopted to combat the current gender biases in esports. For example, participatory design may be adapted to give voices to female gamers in a safe research environment they would otherwise lack. Additionally, many of the principles outlined in feminist HCI research may provide designers and researchers within the esports space to both identify and accommodate the different needs and experiences of female gamers. Additional practices are already being adopted to mitigate the impact of gender biases on participation. This includes a commitment to positive online interaction through organizations like AnyKey, as well as development of entire communities supporting and encouraging one another, as is the case with female legends. However, these need to work in corroboration with education and exposure among esports players to create lasting change. Moving forward, research should continue to understand the diverse experiences among various members of the community while aiming to improve upon current esports designs to create the safe environment envisioned by participants. Additionally, researchers should take the perspective of trans and queer HCI studies, as well as incorporating elements of critical race theories to further diversify and enhance inclusivity in esports studies and design.

reference: We introduce ReVisit, looking under the hood of interactive visualization studies. It is no surprise that well-designed interactions can improve the way that people use data visualizations. But how do we assess the impact that interactions have on performing visual analysis? For visualizations with few interactions, data analysts can design the study to control for the effect of each one. This can be useful in understanding how each interaction affects a user's accuracy or speed when completing a task. However, for more complex interactive visualizations, it becomes harder to control for all possible forms of interaction. Additionally, participants can use different analysis strategies, or sequence of interactions, to solve a given task. This leads to the question, how do analysis strategies impact participant performance when using interactive visualizations? To address this, we propose a new study workflow that allows researchers to better understand the effect interaction strategies have on user performance. We implement the data analysis methods in this workflow in an open-sourced, web-based tool, ReVisit. ReVisit provides support for analysis of both qualitative and quantitative results, as well as provenance visualization through event-sequence mining and playback of participant sessions. Let's take a closer look at ReVisit in action. Heather is a researcher who recently ran a user study analyzing the performance of network visualizations. Her study compares node-link diagrams to adjacency matrices for finding paths in a network. During her study design, Heather had to balance the interactions available between both node-link and matrices to not unduly favor one condition over the other. An important part of finding a path in a network is being able to identify neighboring nodes. In the node-link, this can easily be done by clicking on the node to highlight neighbors. In the adjacency matrix, Heather added an interaction that highlighted neighbors in green when a user clicks the column label. Now, she wants to be able to assess whether or not this added interaction actually helped improve performance for the adjacency matrix. Heather moves over to the ReVisit system and homepage. Here she can see a high-level overview of how her participants performed on each of her tasks, as well as the main interaction patterns used in those tasks. Hovering over the interaction patterns, She notices that users who used the column label interaction performed at point at around seven zero accuracy. Comparatively to the 60 % accuracy without. She wants to drill down into this a little bit more, so she goes over to the task analysis pane and then first groups on condition. Then she wants to group upon whether or not a user used the column label technique itself. Grouping on that and expanding the columns, she can see that users of the column label interaction technique have A 67 % accuracy compared to a 45 % accuracy for the participants who did not use the column label technique. Having validated that there exists a pretty large difference between the accuracies of individuals who use the column label and don't, she wanted to drill down into whether or not or how those individuals who don't use the column label go about solving this task for adjacency matrix. As she's interested inside of the answer that they gave as well, she goes unhides that column. and then scrolls down to look at how the individuals who didn't use the column label approach this task. As she scrolls down, she sees a fair amount of these answers of MViews. As this is an incorrect answer to the problem, she delves into the playback interaction to see how users are using this to solve the problem. Playing through each of the strategies, she sees that the users search and then select for MViews, which is located right in between Lane and Rob. Interested by this, she sees that likely what is occurring is users are looking directly in between Lane and Rob and selecting the node that exists between them that is an institution, which corresponds to MViews. This represents a conceptual misunderstanding of how edges are visualized inside of an adjacency matrix. This methodology was employed to analyze data from two published crowdsource user studies, which we present as case studies in the paper. The combined analysis of study results with the interaction patterns helped our analysts uncover novel interaction strategies, identify gaps in participant training, and measure the impact of design decisions used in the study. You can check out Revisit at this URL. Thanks for watching our video.

reference: Hello, this video is a very brief summary of the research in our paper Extended Reality Remote Research, a Survey of Drawbacks and Opportunities. I am Jack Ratcliffe, one of the co-authors of this paper, along with Francesco Suave, Professor Nick Bryan-Kinns, Dr Larissa Tokarczuk and Dr Ildar Farkhatinov. The rationale for this paper was there was a lack of literature concerning conducting remote research with XR technologies, and that evolved into this Survey of Drawbacks and Opportunities. We got 46 responses to our 30-item questionnaire, then thematically analysed the responses from these respondents and came up with six sub-themes around the drawbacks and opportunities in remote XR research. Now, we can't go into full detail about these, but we can give a brief overview of them. For full details, please read the paper. But the first of these themes was study sub-types. So we summarised the types of experiments people were running into four study sub-types. One is in-lab being vital, so that's where you have bespoke hardware or controlled conditions are very important. And on the other end of the continuum was remote vital, which is where you want to ensure that the Participant is in the wild or in their naturalistic settings when they might engage with the hardware or the exercise. Now between those there was also so in lab, preferred and remote preferred. For in-lab preferred, it was so that you wanted some kind of control, or you felt like it would be best if the researcher was there to be supportive, and remote preferred was when they really wanted to take advantage of what they speculated were the benefits of remote research, such as wider participant reach and recruitment. Which brings us to our second theme, participants. So the majority of researchers felt that participation in-lab have typically quite small recruitment sizes and that if they move to remote, they could be a lot larger. But with that came questions about balance and who were these remote participants and is it a balanced sample size? Does this have some kind of efficiency difference? Maybe it might be more efficient to run remote studies. And how do you ensure that the correct participant requisites are checked when you never actually meet these people? The third theme was data collection. A big concern about this was hardware, in that a lot of people use bespoke or rare hardware to collect data, such as ECGs or EEGs, which are not available remotely to users. Not many people have a brain scanning device at home. And typically their Vr experience is linked one that is consumer grade, such as an Oculus Quest, rather than say, an Htc with eye tracking. There were also questions about the process of data collection, how that could be stored, and also how qualitative data can be picked up from observing a participant, which is a lot more difficult when that participant is maybe doing the study asynchronously from you. The 4th theme was the experimentation questions, So things like being in a controlled environment versus not being able to interact with participants, and what that leads to? what the setting affects in the research, how hardware and software might have different problems and solutions remotely and in lab, if the setting affects the research question of the experiment, and potentially cost implications for remote and in-lab studies. The fifth theme was health and safety, which covered things like the protocols of in-lab studies and out-of-lab studies and how you can ensure health and safety measures are met, what the equipment has to be, and how support can be given both in lab and remotely. The sixth and final theme was ethics, which is we've quite well established in-lab ethical procedures, but where does the ethical response and understanding for the risk that we put remote researchers through? Is there a responsibility issue that needs to be understood? So I'm just going to present the sort of five key questions that we feel from all of these themes are still really important for the XR researcher community to answer. The first is, how can we access a large pool of remote XR participants? Because most people see this as the main game of remote XR studies. The second is, who are these potential remote XR participants and are they representative? The third is, so what extent do remote XR studies affect results compared with in-lab studies? The fourth is, what are the built-in XR data collection affordances of XR hardware and what can they help us study? How can we use the hardware that we know people have and its affordances to ensure that our experiments are useful and optimal? And finally, five, how can we lower the barrier to creating encapsulated experimental software to maximise the potential of XR research? And by encapsulated software, we mean building software where when people do remote research, it's all available, the data collection and the experimentation inside one piece of software, which can then be shared as part of the paper, part of the report, be used for reproducibility studies and even be iterated on by other researchers to enhance and develop research questions much like literature and research in the field is.

reference: Hello everyone, I'm Nianlong Li from Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Today I'm going to give a presentation of my paper, V-Mirror, Enhancing the Interaction with Occluded or Distant Objects in VR with Virtual Mirrors. Interacting with out-of-reach or occluded objects can be cumbersome in virtual reality. Although users can change their position and orientation, such as VR teleporting, to help observe and select, doing so frequently may cause loss of spatial orientation and motion sickness. In our life, it is intuitive and natural to use mirrors to observe. For example, we look in the mirror to make up, observe the rearview mirror while driving, check the teeth by the dentist with dental mirror. Therefore, we present V-Mirror, an interactive widget leveraging reflection of mirrors to observe and select distant or occluded objects in VR. To understand how to place a mirror and adjust it, we designed a formative study. We used the building blocks task, two methods for placing the mirror were tested. First is the manual approach. Participants press a button to create a mirror facing themselves. The properties of the mirror can be adjusted via the controller. Another one is the semi-automatic approach. Participants select an object center, then choose a direction to place the mirror. The system calculates the best mirror orientation, enabling the participant to see the object according to the law of reflection. Results show that seven participants preferred semi-automatic placement because it required less operations and matched their needs. Participants also said that it was cumbersome to adjust the mirror by pressing the button. Based on the feedback, we adopted the semi-automatic mirror approach and replaced the button-based interface with motion gestures. Then we conducted the second study to examine the target selection performance with mirrors at different orientations. We adopted the standard reciprocal selection test. We designed two sessions, the direct target selection and target selection with vMirror. For the target selection with vMirror, a within-subject design with three factors was used, including mirror position, target size, and target distance. Participants were the same as study 1. We measured selection time, error rates, and subjective feedback. Results show that the most efficient position to place the mirror was the inclined top. We also found that vMirror could be as efficient as direct select, even though having higher error rates. This may be because subjects appear smaller and distorted in vMirror. In the third study, we further investigated how vMirror would assist users with the navigation and target selection task in VR. The task of the game was to find a red gem in the ruins of stones and trees. We used the within-subject design with two factors, input techniques and scene range. Twelve participants were recruited. We measured the users' completion time, number of teleport, change of the orientation angle, perceived usability, and motion sickness. Results show that Teleport plus vMirror was significantly faster than Teleport and needed significantly fewer times of teleport and orientation change. Moreover, it induced significantly less motion sickness. Future work can investigate ways of using vMirror to observe partially occluded objects and compare it with other techniques. It is worth exploring automatic strategies and combine vMirror with bimanual operations to further improve user experience. Placing more than one mirror might provide additional benefits. Other shaped mirrors may enrich VR interactions than a planned mirror. In conclusion, we presented vMirror, an interactive widget using mirror to alleviate occlusion and delve issues with recasting techniques in VR. We conducted two studies that refined the design choices of vMirror and evaluated its impact on target selection. We conducted a comparative study that showed vMirror was able to significantly improve teleport technique in a VR target searching task. We believed that future work could continue to explore other types of virtual mirrors to further enhance interactions in VR. This is my report. If you have any questions, please contact my email. Thank you.

reference: Hello everyone, I'm Nianlong Li from Institute of Software, Chinese Academy of Sciences. Today I'm going to give a presentation of my paper, V-Mirror, Enhancing the Interaction with Occluded or Distant Objects in VR with Virtual Mirrors. Interacting with out-of-reach or occluded objects can be cumbersome in virtual reality. Although users can change their position and orientation, such as VR teleporting, to help observe and select, doing so frequently may cause loss of spatial orientation and motion sickness. In our life, it is intuitive and natural to use mirrors to observe. For example, we look in the mirror to make up, observe the rearview mirror while driving, check the teeth by the dentist with dental mirror. Therefore, we present V-Mirror, an interactive widget leveraging reflection of mirrors to observe and select distant or occluded objects in VR. To understand how to place a mirror and adjust it, we designed a formative study. We used the building blocks task, two methods for placing the mirror were tested. First is the manual approach. Participants press a button to create a mirror facing themselves. The properties of the mirror can be adjusted via the controller. Another one is the semi-automatic approach. Participants select an object center, then choose a direction to place the mirror. The system calculates the best mirror orientation, enabling the participant to see the object according to the law of reflection. Results show that seven participants preferred semi-automatic placement because it required less operations and matched their needs. Participants also said that it was cumbersome to adjust the mirror by pressing the button. Based on the feedback, we adopted the semi-automatic mirror approach and replaced the button-based interface with motion gestures. Then we conducted the second study to examine the target selection performance with mirrors at different orientations. We adopted the standard reciprocal selection test. We designed two sessions, the direct target selection and target selection with vMirror. For the target selection with vMirror, a within-subject design with three factors was used, including mirror position, target size, and target distance. Participants were the same as study 1. We measured selection time, error rates, and subjective feedback. Results show that the most efficient position to place the mirror was the inclined top. We also found that vMirror could be as efficient as direct select, even though having higher error rates. This may be because subjects appear smaller and distorted in vMirror. In the third study, we further investigated how vMirror would assist users with the navigation and target selection task in VR. The task of the game was to find a red gem in the ruins of stones and trees. We used the within-subject design with two factors, input techniques and scene range. Twelve participants were recruited. We measured the users' completion time, number of teleport, change of the orientation angle, perceived usability, and motion sickness. Results show that Teleport plus vMirror was significantly faster than Teleport and needed significantly fewer times of teleport and orientation change. Moreover, it induced significantly less motion sickness. Future work can investigate ways of using vMirror to observe partially occluded objects and compare it with other techniques. It is worth exploring automatic strategies and combine vMirror with bimanual operations to further improve user experience. Placing more than one mirror might provide additional benefits. Other shaped mirrors may enrich VR interactions than a planned mirror. In conclusion, we presented vMirror, an interactive widget using mirror to alleviate occlusion and delve issues with recasting techniques in VR. We conducted two studies that refined the design choices of vMirror and evaluated its impact on target selection. We conducted a comparative study that showed vMirror was able to significantly improve teleport technique in a VR target searching task. We believed that future work could continue to explore other types of virtual mirrors to further enhance interactions in VR. This is my report. If you have any questions, please contact my email. Thank you.

reference: Hi, my name is Ivan, and on behalf of all of the authors of this paper, I am delighted to present our longitudinal study of user experience of security and privacy in smart home products. Smart homes today have a dark side, which conjures up images of surveillance cameras and smart speakers that are constantly tracking, listening and watching. Previous work exploring security and privacy in smart homes has mostly consisted of surveys in-situ design evaluations and interviews. To complement this research, we proposed to better understand security and privacy behaviours in real-life contextual settings and over longer periods of time. To address the research gap, we analysed a six-month-long ethnographic study of six households living in smart homes in the UK. We collected data through interviews, observations, field notes and photographs. Our households consisted of dual-income families that are in favour of technology adoption. Households included 12 male and 10 female participants, and half our households had not used smart products before. 12 participants were working-age adults and 8 were minors. We identified three major themes through thematic analysis that I will go through briefly. From a privacy perspective, participants expressed concerns over security cameras and smart display cameras, and sometimes taped these up as a result. Similarly, concerns over tracking and microphones were also expressed. Privacy concerns were broadly and generally managed through consent preferences. However, the experience of consent management was inconsistent. Granting consent was straightforward, while withholding consent caused problems. For example, one household refused to enable web and activity tracking when setting up their smart speaker, and as a result weren't able to play music. Similarly, another household lost the use of their device's motion detection after using the built-in camera shutter. Over time, this prompted participants to revisit their preferences and grant consent for services they had originally rejected. Our results confirmed the continued existence of a well-known problem, password fatigue, which was experienced by many participants as they were required to remember additional excessive numbers of passwords in addition to their daily routine. We identified new challenges in access control management, and situations where these were not suited to the needs of the households. For instance, while family sharing features were designed into some products, they were not user-friendly and often not used. Instead, participants shared accounts instead of setting up and delegating permissions, as they found this much easier. Technology repurposing refers to the use of technology other than for its original intended use. Over time, the use of smart home devices changed. Some participants repurposed devices for parenting and entertainment, resulting in several security and privacy implications arising from these applications. For example, we identified situations where tensions arose between parents and their teenage children when the parents started reusing smart CCTV, no longer just for security, but to enforce and monitor whether the children were obeying parental rules. Our results suggest that it is the perception of effectiveness of controls that improves the experience of privacy and assurance. Smart home devices should be designed not just to give users control and choices, but to provide assurance that privacy features are effective. Our results also show that the lifecycle of consent can change over time. Users can withhold, grant, revoke, amend consent from ongoing use, new information, or repurposing. We propose that time and ongoing device use should be considerations for privacy consent management. This would move beyond a model of consent aimed largely at gaining consent during set-up. Our results indicate that smart home products were repurposed in five households, and designers should improve their understanding of audiences and contextual uses of smart home products to be able to ground and anticipate how their technologies might be repurposed and mitigate potential misuse. We conclude with three recommendations. First, we recommend that consent management needs to facilitate change over time, that the experience of withholding consent needs to be improved, and that the experience of making mistakes in consenting to data use should be more forgiving. We also recommend designers should develop knowledge of the risks and threats of repurposing and improve the transparency of sensitive features, such as being reminded when these sensitive features are enabled, or even told when they are used. Finally, we note that users are more confident in privacy controls that have physical affordances. How to improve the perception of effectiveness of privacy controls that lack physical characteristics is an important research challenge. Thank you for listening to this presentation, and if you have any questions, feel free to reach out.

This approach presents several advantages, such as extending the head-mounted display's limited field of view. This approach has been used for several use cases, However, these use cases focus mainly on other tasks, so usually navigation or 3d exploration. But the holobar offers a multilevel menu based on four grounding principles. The 1st principle is rapid activation of the menu. anytime the user needs it. To activate the holobar, the user brings the smartphone beneath the field of view and enters what we call the activation zone. In this paper, I show how design fiction can be used to analyze and reflect on ethnographic data. I call this usage design fiction memos. This paper presents a case study using design fiction memos in a project studying user experience professionals who try to engage with values and ethical issues in their work. In qualitative analysis, memo writing can help provide a step between collecting data and formal written analysis, helping the researcher reflect on and make sense of large amounts of qualitative data. Memos allow a researcher to start closely in their data, abstract away from it, then reflexively come back to their data. This paper deploys design fiction in a similar way. Design fiction is a practice of creating fictional worlds by depicting conceptual artifacts that help ask questions about configurations of that world, helping a designer think about issues such as power relationships and social values. While design fictions often come from the imagination of its designers and creators, this paper suggests creating design fictions stemming from qualitative empirical data. With design fiction memos, researchers start close to their qualitative data and move away from it by creating and exploring a fictional world inspired by that data. Then the researcher can come back to their data with new insights. Design fiction memos are meant to be created throughout the data collection and analysis process as a thinking tool, rather than being the final design outcome of a qualitative research process. I present an example using design fiction memos in a project studying the work practices of user experience professionals who advocate for addressing values and ethical issues from their positions within their companies, sometimes successfully and sometimes not. I interviewed 12 UX professionals, predominantly working at large technology companies in the US, and conducted observations at UX meetup events. While analyzing the data, I created design fiction memos that depict corporate practices. These include fictional corporate emails, interfaces of workplace software, and corporate websites and posters. And I'll briefly discuss one, the ethics work tracker. This imagined interface allows someone to track work tasks related to values and ethics. Each square represents a day, and darker squares indicate more contributions to values and ethics work. So here are Jen's details for one day, where she tracks things like attending a product meeting where she presented a set of user personas around accessibility, but then she also had to explain accessibility laws to co-workers, and she notes that she got interrupted three times by a co-worker. This design fiction helps reflect on the everyday work of surfacing values, and how this labor is often invisible and unrecognized. This design was inspired in part by a senior UX researcher who talked about creating an ethical debt tracker using bug tracking software. Tracking these issues as bugs makes values and ethical issues visible to co-workers, but perhaps as problems to be solved technically. Another senior designer discussed their uncompensated volunteer labor in furthering their company's diversity and inclusion initiatives, and they expressed frustration at having to repeatedly prompt team members to consider how product changes might create harms for end user. This participant said, quote, every single conversation is like this, where it's, oh yeah, I hadn't thought of it that way, and like, I have been telling you, end quote. The design fiction extends these accounts by creating an interface to make this type of labor more visible. The grid in the design fiction adapts a visualization used by github to track a person's technical contributions to a project, and applying that model of tracking to values advocacy work begins to raise questions about the politics and implications of making values work visible in this particular way, which can be problematic in its own right. This design helped me reflect on aspects of invisible, emotional, and gendered labor in values and ethics advocacy. Across four memos, the The paper goes into more depth discussing how the work of values and ethics advocacy by Ux professionals is not only technical. but deeply social and affected by organizational power dynamics. The paper provides several reflections on design fiction memoing, how they compare to written memos, and some guidance on creating and evaluating them. Design fiction memos can help researchers analyze and reflect on qualitative data in new ways, enable the exploration of a complex and rich set of issues in a way that resists simple design solutions, and provides a new way to circulate ethnographic accounts and stories. Thank you to many colleagues, the reviewers, and the participants for sharing their stories.

In qualitative analysis, Memo writing can help provide a step between collecting data and formal written analysis, helping the researcher reflect on and make sense of large amounts of qualitative data. Memo's allow a researcher to start closely in their data, abstract away from it, then reflexively come back to their data. This paper deploys design fiction in a similar way. Design fiction is a practice of creating fictional worlds by depicting conceptual artifacts that help ask questions about configurations of that one, helping a designer think about issues such as power relationships and social values. reference: Okay, let's talk about my paper, To Live in Their Utopia, Why Algorithmic Systems Create Absurd Outcomes. This will take about five minutes. I wrote this paper because I was looking for a theory that draws on power and governance to try to frame a useful way to think and talk about algorithmic systems. I've written about this kind of stuff before when I've talked about street -level algorithms, but that was at the level of individual cases. Street-level algorithms spoke to why AIs make the wrong calls in the moments of decision when they encounter marginal or novel cases. It didn't really answer the broader structural questions that I still felt hanging around in the air. So I wanted to try to address that. What I came up with was this framework that starts from James Scott's Seeing Like a State. He lays out how administrative states come up with a sort of bureaucratic imagination of how the world works by defining how to measure and count stuff. It's not so much the fact that bureaucracies decide how and what to count that Scott critiques. Making sense of the world by focusing on limited dimensions is something we all do. Scott talks about these abridged maps of the world we construct. Sometimes they're literally maps, as in cartographic artifacts, but even more often they're conceptual maps, ways of thinking about and making sense of the world. His critique was that sometimes bureaucracies use these abridged maps as blueprints for how the world should be, and that can become really dangerous because when you try to go from navigating the world to shaping it with a flawed map, you run into and cause all sorts of issues where reality doesn't match the bureaucratic imagination of the administrative state. In the paper, I argue that algorithmic systems commit the same kinds of harms. Machine learning systems construct a computational model of the world and then impose them on us, not just navigating the world with a shoddy map, but actively transforming it. They're shaping the world by deciding whether an applicant gets a loan, or a job, or into a good school, who we get matched up with in dating apps, whether the content we put online immediately gets flagged for review or demonetized, whether we get released on bail or held on remand until our court date, and all of their behaviors in turn shape ours so that we appear more legibly to this incredibly limited system. These systems become more actively dangerous when they go from making sense of the world to making the world make sense, when we take all of this data and tell a machine learning system to produce a model that rationalizes all of that data. The rules machine learning systems infer from the data have no underlying meaning or reason behind them. They're just patterns, without any insight into why black people are in prison at a much higher rate than white people, for instance. There's no dataset in the world that adequately conveys white supremacy or slavery or colonialism, so at best these systems generate a facsimile of a world with the shadows of history cast on the ground, skewed, flattened, and always lacking depth that only living these experiences can bring. These rules are devoid of meaning, but in the world that the AI has constructed, everything makes a kind of sense. And they punish or reward us for fitting into the model they generate. In other words, the world they construct. This is where I start borrowing from David Graeber's Utopia of Rules, where he talks about the utopia that bureaucracies enjoy by imagining a world where everything makes sense according to their rules. Whether that world even resembles the one we live in is where Graeber takes things next. He argues that bureaucracies that do absurd things but have no particular power over people have to self-correct, or be corrected, because they have no place in a world where people can freely reject or exit the bureaucracy's nonsense. But here's the thing. When an institution towers over people and they can't just leave anymore, those institutions can and do get more and more detached from the lives and needs of people. Those bureaucracies construct their own worlds where everything gets rationalized in simplified, reductive language. These worlds don't have any framework for things like race or gender or any of the aspects of our lives that meaningfully inform our experiences. Now, for those of us who can just not deal with race or gender or sexuality, we get to pass through these systems relatively unscathed. But for those of us who can't ignore these dimensions of who we are, those aspects of ourselves make us stick out. We have dimensionality to ourselves that we can't abandon, that we shouldn't have to abandon. That depth challenges the model in many ways. This is different from the conversations we have about bias in data or code. I think those things are important, but a lot of the conversations about those issues often seem to fade away once the system is out in the world. People talk about debiasing data or reviewing code before a model is trained and deployed. What I'm saying is that even if you've done everything right, if you don't pay attention to the power dynamics as they unfold and play out, the system out in the world is going to drift further and further away from reality. And that system will make escalating demands of people who have no choice but to try to appease this absurd system. I end the paper with some design recommendations, mostly falling out from the spirit of Graeber's work, which is to say that we shouldn't allow these systems to have the kind of power that allows them to derail a person's life in the first place. We should work to disempower algorithmic systems wherever we can and do it whatever we can to help people escape these systems when they feel mistreated by it. In some cases that'll mean advocating for human review mechanisms, in others it'll call for the abolition of the technology and refusal to participate in building the technology itself. reference: Hi, I'm Matthew Miller and today I'm presenting Meeting You, Seeing Me, the role of social anxiety, visual feedback, and interface layout in a get-to-know-you task via video chat. This work was done in collaboration with my amazing co-authors, Martin Deschamps and Regan Mandryk at the University of Saskatchewan. Video chat is a great tool for staying connected with friends, family, and colleagues. However, some users of video chat experience social anxiety, fears relating to being scrutinized, expressing oneself, facing rejection, or displaying anxiety to others. For these people, a video call may be a stressful experience. If someone who experiences social anxiety during video calls searches for advice online, they're likely to see advice suggesting that the preview of their own video can focus attention inward and increase anxiety. Many articles suggest turning off this preview for a better experience. In contrast to this online advice, some prior research suggests that seeing oneself on video is not such a problem for people with social anxiety. For example, one study found that adding large mirrors to face-to-face conversations did not negatively affect socially anxious individuals. In fact, seeing oneself during conversation is somewhat similar to a technique used in social anxiety treatment, known as feedback therapy. In this technique, socially anxious people watch back recordings of previous conversations, offering them a chance to identify exaggerated or untrue perceptions about how they came across. Because online advice and previous research paint two different pictures of how seeing oneself affects video chat experiences, we conducted a study comparing video chat interfaces that feature a preview of users' own video to interfaces that do not. Our study matches pairs of strangers for a get-to-know-you task. One confounding factor to the question of whether seeing oneself is harmful or helpful is the design of video chat interfaces. In some cases, a lot of the screen is dedicated to users' videos. In other cases, such as screen sharing or presentations, other content can dominate the interface. These different interfaces may affect how much attention people pay to the previews of their own video. Therefore, we tested the effects of seeing oneself in video chat in two contexts, a traditional call-focused interface and a content-focused interface. For detailed results from our study, please see our paper. For this talk, I'd like to highlight five aspects of the experience that we assessed. These are self-awareness, or how much a person focuses on themself, experienced anxiety, or the situational intensity of anxiety, use of second-person pronouns such as you, self-disclosure, and trust formation. First we'll look at a few results from the traditional call-focused interface. Our research shows that when we turn off the self-view, higher levels of social anxiety are associated with more self-awareness and greater use of second-person pronouns. Additionally, social anxiety translated into experienced anxiety at double the rate when the self-view is off. These findings suggest that turning feedback off is not helpful for people with social anxiety. In fact, it leads to a worse experience characterized by higher inward focus on anxiety and more use of words like you, which may be an attempt to shift the conversation away during a stressful situation. Looking to the other two metrics I mentioned, we see some outcomes of social anxiety in the call. For participants lower in social anxiety, our task worked as intended, advancing through more of the discussion questions we provided led to more self-disclosure and in turn to greater trust formation. But for people higher in social anxiety, we didn't see the same successful leveraging of the task. Advancing through more discussion questions did not generate more self-disclosure. And these findings were the same with or without feedback, which shows that even though feedback can be helpful for people with social anxiety, it doesn't solve everything. Briefly turning to the second interface we studied, in which the discussion questions took up most of the interface and the video call was only shown in a small bar at the top, we found somewhat different results. In this context, turning the self-view on or off did not affect outcomes such as self-awareness, experienced anxiety, or use of second-person pronouns. We also found no relationship between advancing through discussion questions and self-disclosure, even for people lower in social anxiety. For a discussion of why our findings were different in this interface, please refer to our paper. In sum, our work shows that for people experiencing social anxiety in video calls, the common advice online to turn off the preview of your own video is not helpful and can actually lead to worse experiences. This work was done in collaboration with my amazing co-authors, Martin Deschamps and Regan Mandryk at the University of Saskatchewan. If someone who experiences social anxiety during video calls searches for advice online, they're likely to see advice suggesting that the preview of their own video can focus attention inward and increase anxiety. Many articles suggest turning off this preview for a better experience. In contrast to this online advice, some prior research suggests that seeing oneself on video is not such a problem for people with social anxiety. For example, one study found that adding large mirrors to face-to-face conversations did not negatively affect socially anxious individuals.
