reference: My name is Elliot Mitchell, and I'm a PhD student at Columbia's Department of Biomedical Informatics, and I'm excited to share this research with you. The general area of focus for this work is technology to support individuals with self-management of chronic conditions, specifically type 2 diabetes. A key goal in diabetes self-management is keeping blood sugar levels within target ranges. But maintaining blood sugar levels is challenging because diet has a complex impact on blood sugar, and this relationship varies between individuals. Because of this, nutrition recommendations, including the amount of macronutrients in each meal, need to be personalized to each individual. Given these challenges, personal informatics tools that incorporate self-tracking data hold promise to reveal patterns between diet and blood sugar. However, many such tools emphasize reflection, which places the burden on individuals to analyze their data, and does not directly support action. The motivating question for this work was how to design tools that shift the focus towards directly supporting action and decision-making. To this end, we present the design of our system called Glucogoli, which analyzes an individual's self-tracking data and recommends changes to diet in the form of personalized nutrition goals. Goal setting is a common approach in health coaching and behavior change, and these goals suggest adjusting the amount of macronutrient in one's meals, for example increasing protein at breakfast to keep blood sugar from spiking later in the morning. The pipeline starts with self-tracking data, including meal logs and blood sugar readings from before and after each meal. Next, a machine learning method identifies patterns of association between macronutrient composition and change in blood sugar after meals. Identifying these patterns alone, however, is not sufficient to inform action, for someone to know what to do differently, and so one of the key innovations of our work in this approach is the incorporation of an expert system. Working with a group of diabetes educators, we designed a set of rule-based expert systems to interpret patterns identified by the machine learning algorithm and translate them into actionable recommendations for users. Finally, the expert system populates a set of natural language goal templates, which can be shared directly with users. This pipeline was incorporated into a mobile app for self-tracking. Initially, users select a generally applicable nutrition goal. Each day, users record meals and blood sugar readings, and assess whether their meals are consistent with their goal. Once users have recorded enough data, Glucogoli then starts making personalized recommendations and sends a push notification. We evaluated Glucogoli with two studies. In the first study, we examined whether users understood and could act on goal recommendations in a controlled experiment that simulated meal choices with paper cutouts of common food items. We found that users were broadly able to understand and act on the goals, but had difficulty precisely implementing them. Two-thirds of meals were consistent with the direction of the goal, but there was considerable variability in precisely meeting the goal's target amount. In the second study, we examined the experience of receiving and acting on personalized goals in a four-week deployment study with 10 individuals with type 2 diabetes. Participants were primarily female and black or Latino use had varied considerably, and 88 % received at least one. personalized goal suggestion. Next, we highlight three qualitative themes. While much prior work has focused on reflection, with Glucogoli we aimed to more directly support action. While this could have risked diminishing the advantages of reflection, we found that receiving new goals actually helped inspire deeper reflection on the behaviors that led to that recommendation. This points to a balance between supporting reflection and action, and suggests opportunities to scaffold reflection alongside action, for example by offering explanations grounded in a user's data. Second, consistent with much prior research, results highlighted the importance of personal preferences in choosing goals. Glucogoli offered broad recommendations, which users had to operationalize for specific meals. Recommender systems specialize in specific suggestions based on preferences, like recipes. These approaches are not contradictory, but complementary, and future work could explore a combined approach incorporating both health constraints and preferences. Third, as a smartphone app, Glucogoli required users to initiate most interactions, and users wanted more input into their goals and more feedback on their progress. This points to the potential of health coaching approaches, where the application can initiate interactions to offer feedback and discuss goal progress. Thank you to co-authors, funding sources, and the participants in this research, as well as fellow DBMI students. I look forward to taking your questions!

reference: My name is Ludvig Siddemark, I'm a PhD student at Lancaster University, and I'll present our research project RADII. And this work is done in collaboration with Dominic Potts, Bill Bappish and Hans Gellersen, Radii is a pop up radial interface designed to maximize expressiveness. with input from only the eyes and head, and provides discrete and continuous input and scaling to support larger future sets. And I'll present its design and results for how it supports this type of interaction. Gaze and head are attractive hands-free alternatives, as sensing is directly integrated into the HMD. Gaze is fast and effortless, while head movement is more precise for control. However, both lack an explicit selection mechanism and expose mildest touch issues, as they are always on. Hands-free interfaces have therefore remained limited in their expressiveness and control. For the design of RADII, we built on eye and head coordination insights, and RADII's core concept is to use an eye and head controlled interface for expressive, hands-free control of objects in any 3D environments. And to achieve this, RADII consists of three parts. The first part is a pop-up radial interface, and its radial structure is based on the eyes and head's capability to move in all directions when performing gaze shifts. And the pop-up nature allows on-demand control without causing clutter when not in use. The interface structure, position, and invocation depend on its context of use. Object-dependent RADII interfaces are used to manipulate specific objects, and are invoked by singling out an object in the environment. Alternatively, an object-independent RADII interface can interact with multiple objects simultaneously, or with objects that are not visible or at an uncomfortable head position. And these are invoked via a generic gesture or command. The second part is look-and-cross, a gaze-activated head-crossing technique that employs gaze-for-hover interaction and head-crossing to select the gaze-activated widget. And this is natural and efficient for the selection, as head movement naturally follows eye gaze and avoids Midas touch issues, as the head remains typically offset from gaze. Finally, combining the radial pop-up interface and look-and-cross provides a broad set of widgets available for object control. First, in addition to basic selection, RADII also supports logically connected widgets such as checkboxes and radio buttons. Second, extending look-and-cross provides continuous interaction by having the head cursor remain within the widget boundary after selection. The interaction is then active until the head cursor leaves the widget boundary, similar to holding down a button. And we can also transform the widget into a one dimensional slider along the ring arc by adding meaning to the cursor position. Finally, RADII supports scaling in three ways to support larger interfaces and increased functionality. First, nested interaction is supported by expanding the interface on outer rings. Hidden nested widgets are displayed when gazing on the parent widget that can then be selected. Second, the interface can replace widgets on a ring via toggling, and replacing widgets allow a single ring to store a large number of widgets without relying on multiple layers. Third, RADII allows fluid command composition for input of multiple parameters by placing command options on separate rings. The user then selects a command at each ring when traversing through the rings. The user may even pass over a ring without performing a selection if a command is undesirable. We developed three VR and AR applications to highlight RADII design considerations, of which you've now seen snippets of. And please refer to the paper and the accompanying video figure for full design and application details. Finally, we did a user study to see how radial properties such as menu size, widget amount, and widget direction affected look and cross-selection performance and preference. From this study, there are two key points that I'd like to highlight. One, users were able to quickly and accurately select RADII widgets. Two, it is important to consider the natural behaviors of the eyes, head, and their coordination. This includes, one, selecting a comfortable menu size for the neck. Two, consider the combination of menu size and widget amount to assure easy selection without relying on straining refined movements. And three, consider the direction of commonly used widgets as horizontal widgets were more comfortable to select. Please refer to the paper for full study details. So in conclusion, combining gaze and head for interaction extends their capabilities to allow effortless interface exploration and stable selection. reference: Hi everyone, I'm Erin Walker and I'm faculty at the University of Pittsburgh. I'm here today to present a paper authored with my former student, Shang Wang, on modeling student concept mapping processes and providing adaptive support. Concept maps are diagrams that consist of nodes, representing key concepts in a domain, and annotated links, representing relationships between nodes. When students are asked to create a concept map from one or more sources, they are required to reflect on the important concepts within a domain and make connections between different concepts as part of creating the map, and this tends to improve their understanding of the source. However, students often need support in engaging in the complex metacognitive processes required to create a concept map. Some research has explored intelligent tutoring-style support to concept mapping. This support, in the context of concept mapping, typically automatically scores a completed concept map and then provides feedback on the content of the map, and it's been shown to have some benefits for improving student understanding. However, we know that the process of concept mapping is critical to facilitating the student learning. Students learn more during concept mapping when engaging in comparative strategies where they make connections and comparisons between the concepts that they are adding to their maps. Most of the computer-based adaptive efforts to support concept mapping have focused on outcome and not on this comparative process. Therefore, our Our hypothesis is that adaptive feedback that targets both the process of concept mapping and the content of the student's current map in progress. might be most effective at improving students' comparative strategies in learning. To investigate this hypothesis, we built a system called MindDot. MindDot is an iPad app that allows students to build a concept map from a source text. It provides an integrated text and concept map view, and we've populated MindDot for these studies with a chapter on biodiversity. In MindDot, we give students combined process and content feedback. One novel feature of MindDot is that it provides adaptive feedback to students on their concept mapping via a text box connected to an image of a light bulb, which you can see in the bottom right corner of this screenshot. As students make their maps, MindDot extracts sequences of student actions and determines whether those sequences map to effective or ineffective concept mapping patterns that we've identified from our previous work. It then uses this comparison to identify positive or negative process feedback to give the student. It further compares the content of students' concept maps to an expert-authored map and uses that information to provide students with suggestions on concepts that can be added to their map. These suggestions connect to the process feedback that they had just received. For example, we've identified reading three pages in a row without modifying one's map as an ineffective pattern. In response to this, the feedback suggests the learner add a node to their content map. It then gives content feedback, suggesting possible concepts to add based on relevant concepts around that point in the book in the expert map. All told, MindDot responds to three positive patterns and seven negative patterns. To examine the potential benefits of the combined process and content feedback, we conducted a study comparing the combined feedback to process feedback alone and to no feedback. Forty-six undergraduate students participated in the study. They engaged in two different kinds of concept mapping tasks, 30 minutes of concept mapping where if they were in an adaptive support condition, they received adaptive support, and then a 10-minute transfer task in a different domain where they made a concept map without the adaptive support. For each task, we gave students pre and post-tests regarding their comprehension of key facts within that domain covered by the text. More information on the assessments is available in the paper. Some key findings from the study are that students who received combined feedback were more likely to immediately change their concept mapping process to follow the feedback. They exhibited higher frequencies of comparative strategy, such as making links between concepts on different pages or navigating back in the text to make a comparison. This was true both in the main session and in the transfer session. Students who received combined feedback also learned more in the main session than students who did not receive feedback, but this was not true in the transfer session. And unlike in our previous studies, we did not find that comparative strategies were correlated with learning across either session. To summarize, we built a system that modeled concept mapping and provided adaptive process and content support. Some conclusions we drew were that combined feedback did improve concept mapping, possibly because it was more implementable by the students than process feedback alone. However, it is possible that students went through the motions of implementing comparative strategies as a result of the support, but did not build knowledge through this process in the same ways they would have if employing comparative strategies spontaneously. Future work will investigate how adaptive support could be designed to produce meaningful changes in student cognition in addition to just changes in their strategies.

reference: Hello everyone, I will be presenting our paper that examines the effect of smartphone alerts and warnings on street crossing behavior in non-mobility impaired older and younger adults. Governmental agencies and vehicle manufacturers are exploring sophisticated vehicle technology all over the world. One such technology is Vehicle-to-Everything or Vehicle-to-X, which is technology that enables a vehicle to communicate with anything that might affect its movement. This can include communication with other vehicles. In fact, vehicle-to-vehicle communication technology is in the process of design and implementation in New York City. This can also include communication with networks, such as servers that give information about certain routes, or infrastructure, such as traffic signals, or it can include communication with pedestrians, for example to assist them in crossing decisions or display car intentions. So as technology like this advances and vehicles get smarter, there will be inevitable changes to our road networks. This is why it is important to understand how vulnerable road users like pedestrians respond to different types of information presented to them. Our work explores how vehicle-to-pedestrian communication may impact pedestrian street crossing behavior. In order to do this, we used a virtual cave environment to test ability-based phone alerts and warnings. Our cave setup consists of four walls with projectors directed to each. We used a smartphone to present ability-based permissive alerts with auditory, haptic, and visual feedback. The following video shows a person receiving a permissive alert and they cross the virtual street. We also used a smartphone to display ability-based prohibitive warnings with auditory, haptic, and visual feedback. The following video shows a person receiving a prohibitive warning and they don't cross the virtual street. Do not cross, do not. Do not cross. We define a gap as the time between two cars when a participant may have chosen to cross. Permissive alerts were given when the approaching gap was safe to cross for the participant. Prohibitive warnings were given when the approaching gap was not safe to cross for the participant. We conducted a between-subjects study with 72 younger college-age participants and 71 older participants with ages between 65 and 85. We had three conditions. reference: Hi everyone, I'm Emilie and I will present our work on CASI, Curve and Surface Sketching in Immersive Environments. First, let me give you some context about our work. Designers often go through two different steps when developing a concept. First, they explore ideas by loosely sketching on paper or with a pen tablet, or even with VR sketching. Then, they refine some of their ideas using 3D modeling software to produce surfaces suitable for rendering and rapid prototyping. In this two-step workflow, the first ideation sketches are often not reusable within the 3D modeling software, other than as visual inspiration or for manual tracing. For example, here the grey patches are created independently from the pink strokes, which are only used as a visual reference. In this context, our goal is to offer a common VR interface to perform these two steps using sketching as the prime interaction modality. So we present CASI, a VR sketching system where the user's strokes are automatically neatened as she sketches to form a clean, well-connected armature. We additionally create surface patches, lofting the sketch by trying to automatically infer where the user wants a patch to appear. We also complement automatic detection with manual control, with the option to add or delete a patch with a single click. The armature and surface patches make it possible for an artist to create a wide variety of 3D concept models by relying almost exclusively on sketching strokes as inputs. This system is composed of two separate components. First, we propose an automatic neatening scheme capable of structuring each input stroke on the fly to connect it to other strokes in the sketch, while minimally deforming the initial shape of the stroke. Secondly, we continuously analyze the armature created by the user to add surface patches to the sketch. I will provide some insight on how we do this, and you can find all the details in our paper. Neatening the input strokes is cast as an optimization problem where we set two objectives. Deform the strokes as little as possible to preserve user intent, while enforcing as many intersections as possible to get a well-connected armature. We select the appropriate subset of constraints to reach a balance of both objectives. Then we enforce those constraints on the stroke by optimizing the stroke control points. Creating the appropriate surface patches is done by maintaining a parallel graph data structure for the sketch. In this graph, the patches that we're looking for correspond to cycles, which are closed loops of nodes. So we launch local searches for relevant cycles whenever a stroke is added to the sketch or deleted. When a cycle is detected, we triangulate its boundary curve using the method of tau and colleagues. We conducted a remote user study with 12 participants, half of which were amateur or professional artists familiar with VR sketching or sculpting, and the rest were novices but all were familiar with using VR interfaces. We made them use three variants of our system. In freehand mode, users could sketch without any additional features. In armature mode, users would see their strokes neatened. And in patch mode, users would see stroke structuring and patch creation. We find that our novel features in the armature and patch systems are able to support users' creativity on par with freehand sketching. We further noticed that the automatic creation of surface patches encourages the users to create well-connected armatures. Please refer to the paper for more user feedback. To conclude, we prototyped and tested a novel interface based on sketching in VR to create both sketches and surfaces, highlighting 3D sketching as an interaction mode for 3D concept modeling. We released the code for our UnityVR application and the full dataset, from all sketches done by users during the study as well as all sketches showcased in the paper. We hope that these resources will foster exciting research in harnessing the power of 3D sketching in virtual reality. Thank you for your attention.

reference: I'm Connie Guan with the Healthcare Robotics Lab at UC San Diego. Our work explores the design of embodied technology for people with dementia and their caregivers with a community health lens. Dementia is a category of diseases characterized by progressive impairments in cognitive function, which can lead to isolation and loss of agency in people with dementia. Informal caregivers provide the majority of support, yet worldwide are overburdened by huge lack of social and financial support. Researchers across many disciplines are exploring new ways to support both populations. Current HCI research adopts a critical dementia lens, which examines dementia's social construction to understand embodied expressions of personhood via music, art, and other experiences. Meanwhile in public health, researchers consider how social determinants of health, such as racism, classism, sexism, and ableism, can impact health equity for both caregivers and people with dementia, and explore methods to address them. Our question then is, what lies at the intersection of these two approaches to dementia care? With this framing, our first research question is, how can we design sensory and embodied technologies to promote agency in people with dementia and alleviate caregiver burden? Second, how can we incorporate community health care practices into dementia technology design to advance health equity? Over a year and a half, we engaged in a three-phase research process. From our prior work, we knew that mealtimes can be very difficult, as people with dementia may need repeated reminders or assistance to eat. With this as our initial problem space, we iterated on designs and finally settled on a radio design probe intended to help during meals. It plays music to incorporate music therapy, has a robotic arm to mimic an eating motion, and resembles the familiar radio design. We used this probe in our later two stages of research to get participants to reflect on their care practice, and then envision future technology. We conducted a thematic analysis of our data, which yielded four themes, which I'll briefly introduce. The first theme was that professional caregivers structure interactions to infirm the self-agency of the person with dementia. They might ask, how do you feel about breakfast, rather than what did you eat for breakfast, to let someone with dementia express themselves without having to rely on their memory. There's an opportunity here to design interactions that are similarly tailored to reinforce the agency of the person with dementia. The second theme was that emotional well-being and task assistance are interdependent concepts. One of the hardest aspects of dementia care is supporting the emotional well-being of the person with dementia during care tasks. A person with dementia might get frustrated at being told what to do, which frustrates the caregiver, and now with two frustrated and stressed people, the care task is only harder to accomplish. Here technology could use a sensory experience like music to keep the person with dementia calm during tasks and relieve some of that burden from the caregiver. Alternatively, it could provide prompts to the caregiver to help them reorient themselves and the person with dementia back to the care task in ways that are more effective. The third theme is the importance of using non-verbal embodied cues to communicate with people with dementia. Educators teach caregivers to use action mimicry cues instead of verbal explanations, as these are better understood in late-stage dementia. For example, seeing a caregiver eating can often jumpstart their actions and help them follow along in ways that verbal prompts can't. Technology designs can employ non-verbal cues to help communicate actions with people with dementia. Finally, our participants envisioned the various roles that technology could serve to support the dynamics between the caregiver and person with dementia. For example, mediating interactions as a motivator to promote positive interactions, or as a respite provider to give caregivers a break. Technology could also support conducting specific tasks, either as a facilitator that helps people with dementia perform tasks themselves, or as an educator, for caregivers to model useful caregiving practice. There are two key takeaways from our work. First is the importance of designing technology for non-verbal embodied communication. This allows technology to adapt to changes in the brain, as language can be difficult in later stages of dementia, but sensory and embodied experiences are retained for much longer. Building this kind of community care practice into technology is one way designers can align the use of technology with the work being done in community health. Our second key takeaway is the opportunity to address health equity by designing for the community health system. We've identified three areas where technology can support the ecosystem of health workers. The first is access, which we often view in terms of how technology can help individuals access community resources. Here we can envision how technology can make community resources like art therapy or support groups available to people in their homes. The second is education and supporting caregiver educators. Perhaps educators could provide caregivers technologies to guide them during care tasks and help reduce their cognitive load. Finally, the third area is expanding the reach of the community system, where technology can expand the ability of community workers to scale their existing support programs. Ultimately, we hope our work can provide one of many starting points for future design research to draw on community health frameworks to tackle complex social issues like health equity. I'd like to thank my collaborators and sponsors and I'm happy to take questions.

reference: Hi, my name is Eunji from KAIST. Today I will talk about this topic, Secrets of Gosu, understanding physical combat skills of professional players in first-person shooters. The first-person shooter, called FPS, requires very fast reaction time to check the opponent's position, and the user has to aim the opponent accurately using their mouse. Like this, the individual's combat skills has a very huge influence on the win or loss of the game. And as you know, professional players dominate the combat skills of normal players. We call them Gosu, not only professional players, but who has a much high performance. Then how and why the Gosu perform better than the other players? Many gamers have wanted to play well, and that is why the gamers have been actively discussed in the online communities or YouTube about some tips for high performance. Even though these tips are not scientifically proved, many gamers have believed and followed the tips. In the research field, many previous studies have analyzed FPS and gamers from diverse perspectives. But many research questions were different from what actual gamers want to know. So in this study, as researchers and passionate gamers, we aimed to verify the conjectures from the online communities and analyze what makes the difference in the player's combat skill. We conducted the research in the following order. First, we organized the tips to verify. We selected conjectures from sources such as the official blogs of companies developing FPS-related software and YouTube videos with at least 100,000 to over 2 million views. We organized them into four categories, aiming, character movement, physical skills, and device and settings. Then we listed up the 15 performance metrics that can evaluate quantitatively for each tip. For example, we measured the angular velocity of mouse to find out how fast players snap their wrist when performing the flicking aim. And we measured the rotation ratio of elbow and wrist to verify the conjecture most professional players use arm aiming rather than wrist aiming. In order to collect data to measure metrics, We developed a gameplay logging system with six types of behavior or sensors, and in game data logger system we used eight motion capture cameras. eye tracker, EMG sensors, pulse sensor, keyboard, and a dual sensor mouse. For the in-game data, we logged two kinds of data, player data such as enemy's skeletal position and game events data such as player death or weapon fire events. For the user study, we recruited the participants into two groups, eight professional Fps players and eight normal players who had sufficient. FPS experience. We selected the famous FPS game CSGO for the study and used a customized map for the one-on-one match which is smaller than normal maps. Each participant played a one-on-one match for 30 minutes. As a result, we collected about 7 gigabytes of data and high-resolution gameplay video recordings. In the descriptive statistic analysis, professionals showed more effective shots per minute and shorter reaction time. Also, 6 of 13 conjectures are verified. Among them, I picked some interesting points to introduce. Please refer to our paper for other detailed results and information. First, professional players were more familiar with their mouse sensitivity so that they showed less corrective movements just before the shooting. Also, professional players tended to use more elbows than the wrists during aiming, and the rotation ratio was higher than the amateurs. Lastly, professional players' sensitivity was low and they used a larger area of the mousepad. Through these results, we revealed two interesting points about the origin of the high performance of professional players. First, we inferred that the influence of game interface could affect the combat strategies. This is because professional players' mouse sensitivity was lower, so they had to move the mouse larger to move the same distance as the other player who used the high sensitivity. Second, we deduced that the high performance of professional players may be due to their innate cognitive ability, because professional players showed lower reaction time in our study. So, this is end of our presentations and thank you for listening.

reference: Hi, my name is Susan Lechholtz, and today I'll be sharing our work on EvalMe, which is a system with a tangible interface designed to help students and instructors evaluate and reflect on learning experiences together. So this work was carried out together with my co-authors Frederick Broody, Nikolaj Marquardt, and Yvonne Rogers at University College London and the University of Edinburgh. So asking students to reflect on their learning experience and their understanding of pedagogical content is a really important part of the learning process, but methods of eliciting reflection that are most widely adopted, like surveys and post-tests, can miss important aspects of the learning experience, and this is because students can forget how they felt or what they learned at specific points in time. At the same time, with these methods, students are not often given the opportunity to discuss together with their peers how their experience and understanding changed throughout a learning session. So the key questions we sought to answer in this research were, might there be alternative approaches that are both lightweight and enjoyable to use, and which can support more in-depth individual reflection and shared reflection among students? And if so, If so, what are the practical and pragmatic considerations of using them in real learning environments? So to address these questions, we chose to adopt a. research through design approach, which had four stages. First, we conceptualized an evaluation system with a tangible interface within our team of academics. Second, we co-designed the system with two different groups of expert educational workshop leaders. Third, we co-developed eval.me, and fourth, we used it in three educational workshop settings for 12-14 year old students, and these workshops were run by our co-design partners, with eval.me used as their evaluation method. So we described the first two stages of our process at length in the paper, and these led to a number of important findings about practical and pragmatic considerations of using an in-situ evaluation tool in learning environments, so for example, insights into what types of questions to ask students and how often, as well as how to introduce a novel evaluation tool while keeping the students' and instructors' focus on the learning content. And and I would encourage you to look at the paper for those insights, but for the rest of the talk I'll focus on our development of Eval, Me, and our findings from the workshops. So at its core, eval.me comprises a tangible interface, which we call the eval.me sender, and a desktop application. The eval.me sender is passed around the classroom at different points during the learning session, and students use it to input their answers to three different questions, which are decided on by a teacher. Students input their responses to the questions through turning a rotary encoder, and lighting up corresponding LED lights on an LED ring. The design allows for asking for responses to questions or statements that ask for a level of agreement, for example, I'm having fun, as well as multiple-choice questions. The sender can work with or without requiring students to authenticate their identity through personal RFID tags, And once satisfied, the students submit their answer and then pass the sender on to the next student. And when they do so, that their submitted data is immediately wirelessly transmitted to the desktop application. The form factor of the eval.me sender was designed so that students could hide their responses from others, or also to make them visible to those around them, and the aim of this was to encourage them to congregate around the tangible interface and discuss their answers to the questions together when submitting responses. So on the desktop app, instructors manage the question sets, and this is also where the children's aggregate responses to the questions over time are visualized. For example, looking at the yellow bar charts in the image here, we see how the student's responses to the statement, I have a strong understanding of this topic, changed each time the device was passed around throughout the learning session. The application is designed to enable these visualizations to also be displayed back to the students on a large screen, in order to also facilitate group discussion at the end of the learning session. We also found that when eval.me was passed around, its physical presence provided a place around which the students could congregate, and this in turn prompted the students to talk about what responses they had selected and why. So this kind of physical presence made the process of evaluation a shared, connected activity that the students could choose to complete together. So in sum, our paper explores the value and pragmatic considerations of using new technologies for supporting gathering and discussing reflective data in real learning environments, and we hope you give it a read for more information. So asking students to reflect on their learning experience and their understanding of pedagogical content is a really important part of the learning process, but methods of eliciting reflection that are most widely adopted, like surveys and post-tests, can miss important aspects of the learning experience, and this is because students can forget how they felt or what they learned at specific points in time. At the same time, with these methods, students are not often given the opportunity to discuss together with their peers how their experience and understanding changed throughout a learning session. So the key questions we sought to answer in this research were, might there be alternative approaches that are both lightweight and enjoyable to use, and which can support more in-depth individual reflection and shared reflection among students? And if so, If so, what are the practical and pragmatic considerations of using them in real learning environments? So to address these questions, we chose to adopt a. research through design approach, which had four stages. First, we conceptualized an evaluation system with a tangible interface within our team of academics. Second, we co-designed the system with two different groups of expert educational workshop leaders. Third, we co-developed eval.me, and fourth, we used it in three educational workshop settings for 12-14 year old students, and these workshops were run by our co-design partners, with eval.me used as their evaluation method. So we described the first two stages of our process at length in the paper, and these led to a number of important findings about practical and pragmatic considerations of using an in-situ evaluation tool in learning environments, so for example, insights into what types of questions to ask students and how often, as well as how to introduce a novel evaluation tool while keeping the students' and instructors' focus on the learning content. And and I would encourage you to look at the paper for those insights, but for the rest of the talk I'll focus on our development of Eval, Me, and our findings from the workshops. So at its core, eval.me comprises a tangible interface, which we call the eval.me sender, and a desktop application. The eval.me sender is passed around the classroom at different points during the learning session, and students use it to input their answers to three different questions, which are decided on by a teacher. Students input their responses to the questions through turning a rotary encoder, and lighting up corresponding LED lights on an LED ring. The design allows for asking for responses to questions or statements that ask for a level of agreement, for example, I'm having fun, as well as multiple-choice questions. The sender can work with or without requiring students to authenticate their identity through personal RFID tags, And once satisfied, the students submit their answer and then pass the sender on to the next student. And when they do so, that their submitted data is immediately wirelessly transmitted to the desktop application. The form factor of the eval.me sender was designed so that students could hide their responses from others, or also to make them visible to those around them, and the aim of this was to encourage them to congregate around the tangible interface and discuss their answers to the questions together when submitting responses. So on the desktop app, instructors manage the question sets, and this is also where the children's aggregate responses to the questions over time are visualized. For example, looking at the yellow bar charts in the image here, we see how the student's responses to the statement, I have a strong understanding of this topic, changed each time the device was passed around throughout the learning session. The application is designed to enable these visualizations to also be displayed back to the students on a large screen, in order to also facilitate group discussion at the end of the learning session. So we used eval.me in three educational workshops, which were all between 2 and 5 hours long, and all included 12 to 14-year-old students. All workshops were led by our Co design partners, and the Co design partners led both the learning content and developed the questions to be used with the Eval Me. Related, and the questions that they developed, related to learning outcomes, the students' level of engagement and the students' perceptions of the learning content, so just to highlight a few. key findings, we found that the students spent a lot of time reflecting on their responses to the questions and hesitating before submitting their responses. And our observations of how the students interacted with the eval.me sender really compellingly showed how its physical form factor transformed the task of entering data input into one that was more embodied and evocative than, for example, answering questions on paper might be. We also found that when eval.me was passed around, its physical presence provided a place around which the students could congregate, and this in turn prompted the students to talk about what responses they had selected and why. So this kind of physical presence made the process of evaluation a shared, connected activity that the students could choose to complete together. So in terms of the data that was collected, the data was perceived to be really valuable by the instructors, especially for informing their pedagogical practice, But getting the children to reflect on their aggregate responses as visualized through the bar charts that we we created was quite tricky and based on our work. more work is required to understand how to scaffold students' interpretations of how their aggregate learning and experiences evolve over time. So in sum, our paper explores the value and pragmatic considerations of using new technologies for supporting gathering and discussing reflective data in real learning environments, and we hope you give it a read for more information. Thanks for listening.

reference: Hello everyone, I am Deepalia Neja and today I am going to present our work on understanding conversational and expressive style in a multimodal embodied conversational agent. Embodied conversational agents are interactive virtual characters that combine facial expressions, speech and gestures to enable face-to-face communication with the users. Most of these agents have relied upon scripted dialogue or prescribed intents that had to be pre-trained, limiting the opportunities for less-constrained interactions. While the state-of-the-art embodied conversational agents have proven useful in limited domains, none of them have been developed with an eye towards open-ended conversations across a wide variety of domains or for general productivity tasks. Style matching has numerous benefits that help interpersonal interactions proceed more smoothly and efficiently. For understanding human conversational style, Debra Tannen categorizes conversational style into High Consideration and High Involvement. The High Consideration style emphasizes consideration, independence, and is characterized by longer pauses, whereas High Involvement style emphasizes interpersonal involvement, understanding, and is characterized by faster but shorter pauses between conversational turns. This brings us to our first research question. Can we design an embodied agent that is capable of relatively open-ended conversations and automatically align its response to the style of the user? We present CIVA, Socially Intelligent Virtual Agent, an expressive, embodied conversational agent that can recognize human behavior during open-ended conversations and automatically align its response to the style of the user. In our work, we combine both the conversational and the expressive style of the user to generate agents' style-aligned behavior. The design of CIVA is truly multimodal, allowing for capture of audiovisual features and synthesis of engaging face-to-face conversations with a human. Here we show an overview of CIVA's architecture. We built components to sense and analyze the audio signal from the user for conversational style matching and generating the lip-sync, performing text sentiment analysis for extracting the contextual information, and sensing and analyzing the user's video feed for expressive style matching. Finally, the outputs from both audio and video pipelines are composited together to synthesize CIVA's conversational and expressive style-aligned behavior. CIVA performs style matching based on the user's interaction style during the conversation using the listed style variables. Our second research question is, do people connect better with a style-aligned agent that uses matching as opposed to one that does not? To investigate the effect of conversational and expressive style matching on users' perception of the system, we conducted a user study with 30 participants comparing two interaction conditions, participants interacting with CIVA with style matching, the experimental condition, and others interacting with CIVA with no style matching, the control condition. Our results show that the participants rated the style-matching condition to be statistically significantly more reflective of their emotions compared to the control condition. The results also showed that the participants perceived CIVA to exhibit more convincing non-verbal behavior for the style-matching condition compared to the control condition in a statistically significant manner. Our next research question is, how style-matching influences the perception of the agent? For evaluating agents' impressions, we found significant interaction for perception of animacy. High-involved conversational style groups found the style-matching more lively and natural, whereas high-considerate conversational style participants paid more attention to the verbal communication and perceived the control condition to be more natural. Now we show an interaction demo from a user study where the participant is performing one of the tasks. What do you do for fun? I love to just hang out and talk to people. What do you like to do? I like to play some video games. Since I have no hands, all I can play is my games. Are there any games you like to play? Ever? Have you ever played war games? Yes, I have played a few games of war games. We presented an embodied conversational agent that is capable of longer conversations with a user, examined how multimodal conversational and expressive style-matching influences a user's perception of the emotional behavior and connection with the agent, and demonstrated how style-matching influences the perception of the agent. We found that the agent was considered more animate by people than by the user. We found that the agent was considered more animate by people who preferred interpersonal involvement and less animate by people who preferred independence. Thank you.

reference: Hello everyone. Welcome to my presentation on VirtualCHI 2021. I am Tarzin. Today I will present our work on effective interfaces for student-driven revision sessions for argumentative writing. We present the design and evaluation of a web-based intelligent writing assistant called ArgRewrite that helps students recognize their divisions of argumentative essays. It helps students revise their essay by showing them where and what kinds of revisions they are making. The goal is to help students write better papers. We conducted a lab-based Wizard of Oz study with university students. Students write an essay at home based on provided reading material and then after a few days revise the essay based on expert feedback on the argumentative elements of the essay. To understand how our revision assistant can best support students, we have implemented four versions of our system with differences in unit span of revision analysis and the level of feedback provided. Students revise their draft too using one of the ArgRewrite conditions and finally submit a survey about their experience with the interface. Now I will describe the interface first and then show how we evaluated using the survey and student essay revision. To start with the interface, students need to upload their original and revised drafts to the server, although in our study the one in charge of data collection did this part. The system processes the drafts and shows an overview of the student's revision process from draft 1 to draft 2. The ArgRewrite categorizes the revisions made between draft 1 and draft 2 and shows a revision distribution. It also compares the revisions with a revision map where the left column shows draft 1 and the right column shows draft 2. Each small tile represents a sentence in the essay. Students can also click on the sentence or small tiles on the revision map to see individual revisions. After observing their previous revision effort, students process to further revise their essay and create draft 3. As mentioned before, we have tested four versions of the ArgRewrite interface. Condition A where we did not provide any revision categorization or feedback. This is used as a control condition. Condition B with binary revision categorization at sentence level. Condition C with sentence-level revision categorization with six content and three surface-level revision categories. And finally, Condition D with detailed revision categorization like Condition C but at the sub-sentence level. To evaluate our research hypothesis that more detailed feedback is more helpful, we conducted experiments to answer the following research questions. First, we asked do students perceive the ArgRewrite to be clear and easy to use? From the perceived ease-of-use survey questions, ANOVA shows conditions A, B, C, and D are increasingly more difficult to use where A is significantly easier than D. Then we asked do students find the ArgRewrite helpful for their writing? Perceived usefulness and usage behavior survey questions shows C is significantly more helpful or C is significantly more useful than A and B and D is more useful than A. Overall, we can say that detailed feedback is more useful than no feedback or binary feedback which supports our hypothesis. Then we asked is ArgRewrite beneficial for student essay improvement? Students' normalized essay score gain shows that Condition C gained significantly more than Condition A. Students in B also gained more than Condition A A, but students in D did not gain much compared to B and C. From this result, we can say students found detailed sentence level revision feedback to be more effective compared to no revision feedback at all. Finally, we asked is there any difference in students' revision behavior based on ArgRewrite conditions? In A and B, we observed significantly more surface revisions and fewer content revisions when revising using the system compared to revising without ArgRewrite system. But distribution of types of revision is not significantly different in Condition C and D. In conclusion, our findings are consistently showed that Feedback on detailed revision categorization categorization is perceived more helpful than no feedback. However, we observed an inverse relationship between the granularity of the feedback and the usability of the system. We believe we still need to conduct more experiments. Thank you for attending my talk. Please let me know if you have any questions.

reference: Hi everyone, my name is Woosuk Seo, and I'm a PhD student at the University of Michigan. Today, I'm going to present our study about designing technology to support effective child patient-provided communication based on healthcare providers' communication strategies. In the pediatric care context, having effective communication with a child patient is challenging for healthcare providers. Existing communication guidelines and training for providers often focus on general communication skills for interacting with child patients, and have less concentration on providers' unique challenges to have effective communication with child patients who have different personalities, preferences, and needs. Also, poor communication hinders providers from accurately assessing child patients' symptoms. As a result, healthcare providers have to frequently develop their own communication skills to interact with children effectively. Analyzing In these challenges, we conducted a qualitative study that focused on the following research questions. 1st, what are the key elements of effective communication that providers value? when they interact with child patients? Second, how do providers strategically interact with child patients to accomplish effective communication during clinic visits? Third, how can technology support healthcare providers' communication strategic development? To answer these questions, we conducted 12 field observation sessions and 10 semi-structured interviews with healthcare providers at an urban children's hospital. Based on the collected data, we found four communication strategies. The first strategy is building rapport with children. For instance, providers in our study explained what they would do to the children before their actions, such as having physical exam Or giving giving injections. In this way children know what to expect for the medical procedures. and consider providers as someone trustful and build rapport with them. The second strategy is developing children's familiarity with care settings and luteinizing clinical procedures. Children who meet the same care team members have the same order of treatment procedures and communicate in the same method as their last visit. This structured hospital care process would allow children to be more familiar with care settings and clinical procedures. The third strategy is respecting and adopting children's communication preferences. For instance, a provider in our study met a child who refused to talk to the care team. So the provider asked the patient to the stuffed dog that the child brought. Then the child began to answer the for the dog, reflecting his own preferences and needs. The last strategy is delegating small decisions and inviting children to conversations. Providers directly ask children about which arm they prefer to have injections, or where they want to sit during consultations. Such small decisions are not essential to the treatment decisions, But relevant enough to allow the children to feel sense to fill a sense of control during clinic visits. Based on these four strategies, we found three elements of effective communication that providers value in the pediatric care context. Transparency, respect, abstentions, and empowerment. Transparency refers to providing transparent information about clinicians and their actions rather than simply providing access to the detailed medical information. Respect and abstentions indicates adopting each child's specific language and communication styles. Empowerment means helping children to confer over their care at their perceptual level. To promote providers' strategies for accomplishing these three elements, We present for the following design considerations for technology Among these three, I would like to introduce the 1st consideration. facilitating patients' familiarity with providers and the care setting. An example for this consideration is a mobile application that collects patients' information such as their favorite character, foods, activity, and personal interests. Then it shares the information with the providers after having patients' consent. For the patient, the app can provide brief heads-up about the care team members and treatment procedures before talking to the provider. So the app promotes rapport building by providing transparent information to the child patients. And I would like to thank my wonderful co-authors listed here, and thank you everyone for watching.

reference: Our motivations for this work stem from our interest in the mind, body practice of meditation. The regular practice of meditation has shown benefits for mental and physical well-being, for instance, improving emotion regulation skills through the development of interoceptive awareness, which is fully attending to bodily sensations and letting those guide your experience. Most HCI technologies for meditation aim to support an inwards focus towards bodily sensations for that reason. In most cases, the main focus of attention, however, is taken away from the body, as a common approach is mapping brain activity data and meditation states into visual and aural interfaces. For instance, meditation states are usually represented on a vertical axis, with being mindful generally represented as high, for example in position or pitch, and mind-wandering as low. However, the design of such mappings of bodily experiences for meditation has been limitedly described. The framework and concepts presented in the paper draw from the bodies of work of phenomenology as well as on linguistic analysis of metaphors. We focused on the main metaphors used in traditional meditation to describe the different states, as well as the bodily sensations associated with them. This theory allowed us to develop the framework, which is also informed by a review of meditation technologies in HCI. We looked at the metaphors used in these systems and how they were conveyed in different creative mappings of brain activity data. We have developed and revised the framework through an exploratory study comparing two distinct feedback modalities, aural with Muse and thermal with a warm mind prototype, for metaphor-based mappings of three key meditation states, being mindful, mind-wandering, and the changes between them. For the aural modality, in our study, we have purposively chosen Muse, an increasingly popular commercial brain activity application providing nature-inspired soundscapes in real time to map and guide one's meditation experience. For the thermal modality, we designed and implemented the warm mind prototype, which is made up of four heat pads attached to the skin, from the chest to the belly, as you can see in the image. Drawing from our previous study, exploring the bodily sensations associated with each meditation state and how these can inform the design of more holistic meditation technologies, we explored the creation of movement and warmth metaphors on the upper body with heat, following a somaesthetic design approach. This exploration was key to designing the thermal patterns for meditation, as this is a novel material and modality of feedback for meditation technologies. The mapping of warm mind's own bodily haptic feedback differs from Muse's aural feedback in three important ways. First, warm mind targets bodily internal senses by recreating bodily sensations as identified in our previous work. Second, it provides discrete feedback with patterns that activate when a change of state is sensed. And finally, the mapping is more abstract and ambiguous as it uses warmth and movement-based metaphors on the upper body, a key body part for meditation as we identified also in our previous study. The patterns are composed of four six-second actuations of one or more heat pads at a time, see the orange blobs in the image, with a four-second break after each to convey the movement metaphors by allowing the heat to dissipate between actuations. These findings inform the development of our proposed framework which has three main design intentions that should be considered when designing meditation systems. Rich to subtle sensory stimulation, continuous to discrete feedback of meditation states, and familiar to ambiguous metaphorical mapping. For instance, we found that rich stimulus, continuous feedback, and familiar metaphorical mapping such as Muse's soundscape Support discoverability of meta meditation states, but hinder attention regulation as it was too cognitively demanding. In contrast, the subtle stimulation, discrete feedback, and ambiguous metaphorical mappings of warm mind supported attention regulation, but the rather vague feedback was more difficult to understand. This may be a good trade-off as it prevented self-judgmental attitude which Muse reinforced and goes against meditation principles. We argue that this framework informed by our empirical findings, phenomenology, and embodied metaphors of meditation can inform the design of new technologies for meditation mapping bodily experience onto interface modality and content. We also propose the concept of interoceptive interaction which allows to facilitate paying attention to bodily sensations by tapping on the interoceptive awareness sense as the feedback provided is perceived as coming from the body instead of, and despite, being provided by an external interface. We illustrate this concept with a warm mind prototype in which the body acts as the input and the output interface by sensing the brain activity and actuating on an on-body interface using warmth-based feedback patterns to guide the experience which was perceived by most participants as part of their bodily experience. And these patterns have been designed based on contemporary theory of metaphors in meditation. Thank you.

reference: Our motivations for this work stem from our interest in the mind, body practice of meditation. The regular practice of meditation has shown benefits for mental and physical well-being, for instance, improving emotion regulation skills through the development of interoceptive awareness, which is fully attending to bodily sensations and letting those guide your experience. Most HCI technologies for meditation aim to support an inwards focus towards bodily sensations for that reason. In most cases, the main focus of attention, however, is taken away from the body, as a common approach is mapping brain activity data and meditation states into visual and aural interfaces. For instance, meditation states are usually represented on a vertical axis, with being mindful generally represented as high, for example in position or pitch, and mind-wandering as low. However, the design of such mappings of bodily experiences for meditation has been limitedly described. The framework and concepts presented in the paper draw from the bodies of work of phenomenology as well as on linguistic analysis of metaphors. We focused on the main metaphors used in traditional meditation to describe the different states, as well as the bodily sensations associated with them. This theory allowed us to develop the framework, which is also informed by a review of meditation technologies in HCI. We looked at the metaphors used in these systems and how they were conveyed in different creative mappings of brain activity data. We have developed and revised the framework through an exploratory study comparing two distinct feedback modalities, aural with Muse and thermal with a warm mind prototype, for metaphor-based mappings of three key meditation states, being mindful, mind-wandering, and the changes between them. For the aural modality, in our study, we have purposively chosen Muse, an increasingly popular commercial brain activity application providing nature-inspired soundscapes in real time to map and guide one's meditation experience. For the thermal modality, we designed and implemented the warm mind prototype, which is made up of four heat pads attached to the skin, from the chest to the belly, as you can see in the image. Drawing from our previous study, exploring the bodily sensations associated with each meditation state and how these can inform the design of more holistic meditation technologies, we explored the creation of movement and warmth metaphors on the upper body with heat, following a somaesthetic design approach. This exploration was key to designing the thermal patterns for meditation, as this is a novel material and modality of feedback for meditation technologies. The mapping of warm mind's own bodily haptic feedback differs from Muse's aural feedback in three important ways. First, warm mind targets bodily internal senses by recreating bodily sensations as identified in our previous work. Second, it provides discrete feedback with patterns that activate when a change of state is sensed. And finally, the mapping is more abstract and ambiguous as it uses warmth and movement-based metaphors on the upper body, a key body part for meditation as we identified also in our previous study. The patterns are composed of four six-second actuations of one or more heat pads at a time, see the orange blobs in the image, with a four-second break after each to convey the movement metaphors by allowing the heat to dissipate between actuations. These findings inform the development of our proposed framework which has three main design intentions that should be considered when designing meditation systems. Rich to subtle sensory stimulation, continuous to discrete feedback of meditation states, and familiar to ambiguous metaphorical mapping. For instance, we found that rich stimulus, continuous feedback, and familiar metaphorical mapping such as Muse's soundscape Support discoverability of meta meditation states, but hinder attention regulation as it was too cognitively demanding. In contrast, the subtle stimulation, discrete feedback, and ambiguous metaphorical mappings of warm mind supported attention regulation, but the rather vague feedback was more difficult to understand. This may be a good trade-off as it prevented self-judgmental attitude which Muse reinforced and goes against meditation principles. We argue that this framework informed by our empirical findings, phenomenology, and embodied metaphors of meditation can inform the design of new technologies for meditation mapping bodily experience onto interface modality and content. We also propose the concept of interoceptive interaction which allows to facilitate paying attention to bodily sensations by tapping on the interoceptive awareness sense as the feedback provided is perceived as coming from the body instead of, and despite, being provided by an external interface. We illustrate this concept with a warm mind prototype in which the body acts as the input and the output interface by sensing the brain activity and actuating on an on-body interface using warmth-based feedback patterns to guide the experience which was perceived by most participants as part of their bodily experience. And these patterns have been designed based on contemporary theory of metaphors in meditation. Thank you.

This work was done with Lindsay Popovsky from Harvey Mudd College and Tom Mitchell and Brian Myers from Carnegie Mellon. What we did in this work, on a very high-level summary, is a technique for embedding the semantics of GUI screens into a vector space so that screens that are semantically similar to each other can be closer to each other in this space. Screen2Vec is a part of a larger project called Sugilite, which is an interactive task learning agent we have been working on in the past four years that can learn tasks and the task-relevant concepts interactively in a variety of domains from end-users through a combination of natural language instructions and demonstrations on existing third-party mobile apps. An important research contribution of Sugilite is that it features a new mixed-initiative multi-model GUI grounded approach where the agent sits in between the user and the GUIs. This approach leverages existing app GUIs as a medium for the user to communicate with the agent. The user demonstrates doing the task on GUIs while explaining the task in natural language with references to the GUIs. The main motivation of the Screen2Vec project for us was to enable the agent to learn more generalizable and more robust task knowledge from users by having a better representation of the semantics of the GUI screens. You can learn more about the entire Sugilite project if you look up our previous papers. We figured that with the available data, we can construct a user-agnostic model of app GUI screens and interactions. The representations we've done with knowledge learned from user instructions in Sugilite are mostly symbolic so far, but we see an opportunity in moving into a neural network. So as a first step towards this direction, we developed Screen2Vec, which is a self-supervised approach for embedding the text contents, the visual layout, the app context, and the design patterns of each app GUI screen into a vector space so that screens that are semantically similar to each other can be closer in the space, which is useful for representing the task at a higher level of app structure. The approach we used for training the model is conceptually similar to word embedding methods such as Word2Vec, GloVe, or Elmo, but we designed the model structure to reflect the structure and the different types of information in GUI screens and components. There are two levels for the model. The first level, shown in the light gray shade, encodes individual GUI components within a screen, and the second level encodes GUI screens. Both models are trained in a continuous back-or-forwards, or SABAL, prediction task. We used a dataset named Ricoh in training our model. Ricoh contains interaction traces of users interacting with over 66,000 screens from 9,000 apps. Each trace contains a sequence of app GUI screens, as shown on the slide. Let's first look at the first level of the model. In the first level, the SABAL task predicts each of the GUI components using the context of other components near it on the same screen. For example, for the screen on the right, let's say we want to predict the text view item, hot drinks, using its nearby items. So this is similar to how you train a word2vec model using a SABAL task, as shown on the left, where you have a sliding window and try to predict each target word in a sequence using the other words around it. Then, in the second level, we used a similar SABAL task on a sequence of screens from the user interaction trace. reference: Hi, I'm Monica, and today I'm presenting Assessing the Impact of Automated Suggestions on Decision Making, joint work with colleagues in MIT CSAIL. Automated decision aid can accelerate often tedious tasks across domains. But if users misplace trust in or cede agency to the decision aid, things can go awry. And due to the ever-growing presence of automated decision aid, we build on past work to ask, how does domain expertise mediate the influence of decision aid? In particular, we're interested in this question in a task with a complex decision space, where we can use objective measures of trust in agency instead of relying on user perception. And then finally, we want to do so over an extended period of use so we can factor in users' fatigue. We investigate via a user study over a clinical text annotation task that's a perfect sandbox for these questions. In the task, the user is presented with a sentence from a clinical text and asked first to identify instances of clinical jargon in that text, and then disambiguate those instances and map them to a term in a structured ontology with over 400,000 concepts. To conduct the study, we developed an annotation platform with built-in decision aid. The decision aid included label recommendations, which appeared when users highlighted a term as well as pre-filled suggestions, which contained a box with both a span and a label and can be accepted in a single click. We then analyzed, how does this decision aid influence our domain experts and impact their agency? In our study, we had 18 clinicians from nine institutions, and novelties of our study included the fact that we jointly studied agency, what to label, and trust, how to label, using objective measures based off of their interactions with the platform. We had a large label space, and we had about eight hours of annotation per user. We conducted the study in two stages, which I now detail. In the first stage, we look at label recommendations. We have three user modes with full recommendations, no recommendations, and artificially weakened recommendations. We analyze accuracy, speed, and search behavior, particularly where recommendations are inaccurate, so 1st, we ask how does user behavior shift? We find that users with full recommendations created more annotations than those without any, and they did so in much less time, as you can see in the graph on the right. Next, we ask, do users search when needed, or do they misplace trust when recommendations do not surface the correct answer? And on those examples where the underlying recommendation algorithm truly fails, they do search most of the time, 83 %. And they perform equivalently, and you can see in the plot on the right. there's no significant differences in performance across the three modes. However, they perform much worse when they expect the correct answer to be surfaced, and it is not. They only search 73 % of the time. You can see the drop in performance on the right, and this indicates that it's important for users to develop proper intuition of model behavior in. In the 2nd stage we look at pre filled suggestions. We have four modes with a control as well as suggestions with various settings. In addition to the prior metrics, we also look at additional annotation behavior. Do they annotate those spans that were not indicated by pre-filled suggestions? We first see if users react appropriately to the suggestions, and they do most of the time. They accept almost all of the correct labels and spans. When the label is incorrect, they only accept it 17 % of the time. And when a span is incorrect, they show slightly less agency accepting it 33 % of the time. However, overall, they tend to have higher performance than users without pre-filled suggestions. Interestingly, there was large user variability in the accepting of incorrect labels and spans, and this was not correlated with their prior task performance. We also found that providing label confidence made no discernible difference. Now, if we look at these new annotations that they had to create and label by hand, we found that they experienced a loss of agency compared to their prior performance, as well as the control group, and this was significant. Interestingly, this loss of agency went unnoticed by users, who noted in their exit interviews that they thought they were more thorough than before. So our takeaways are first, our domain experts properly modulate trust and mediate model errors if they have the correct mental models. Second, users lost agency without noticing, making it very important to use objective measures for user behavior. And finally, we believe that both user interfaces and machine learning systems should adapt to account for this loss of agency. Thank you.
