reference: Welcome, my name is Svetlana Abramova. In this video, I will summarize a study carried out in collaboration with colleagues from the University of British Columbia in Canada and Innsbruck in Austria. With the price of Bitcoin rising tenfold in the past 12 months, we are facing a new wave of mainstream adoption of cryptoassets. Once a tight-knit circle of computer geeks, the global population of cryptoasset users has grown substantially. Recent estimates suggest more than 100 million of unique investors. However, many users have trouble keeping private keys secure. Users forget or lose these strings of bits which grant access to digital funds. Some estimates state that more Bitcoins have been lost in the past 10 years than will be created in the next 100 years. Our work is an empirical study of security behaviors, risk perceptions, and experiences of cryptoasset users. It addresses two fundamental questions. Who are cryptoasset users? How do they handle cryptographic private keys? Recall that the security of cryptoassets rests on one's ability to keep a private key secret. To answer these questions, we had to overcome two roadblocks. Cryptoasset users are hard to reach, and more importantly, they are very heterogeneous. To address the former, we used both broad and deep sampling to recruit almost 400 cryptoasset users as participants. To deal with their heterogeneity, we applied cluster analysis to identify groups of individuals who share similar attitudes towards risk and security. We ran the cluster analysis on five psychometric constructs adopted from behavioral theories. The scatterplot suggests a solution with three clusters of users. We decided to call them cypherpunks, rookies, and hotless. Let me introduce you to the representative user persona of each cluster. Cypherpunks are technically-versed enthusiasts, like Bitcoin's early adopters. They are mostly male in the age group of 25 to 44 years and with more than three years of experience of cryptoasset use. Rookies, our second cluster, are casual users who joined the cryptoasset market more recently, perhaps because of fear of missing out on an investment opportunity. This cluster is more diverse, with a higher fraction of female and elderly investors. Finally, hotless are middle-aged and high-net-worth traders who started to use cryptoassets three or four years ago primarily out of financial motives. Besides the crypto market, they report being active on conventional stock exchanges as well. Note that we didn't start with the idea of finding these user personas. By contrast, we were surprised that the data on the psychometric constructs alone offered an interpretation that's in line with media reports and common sense. As we shall see, these personas differ in behaviors of interest. This is why we believe that future research can adopt this procedure to better understand this heterogeneous population. In the rest of this talk, I will focus on security behavior. Interestingly, almost 30 of hotless had already fallen victim to key thefts, Compared to three point 15 % for cypherpunks and rookies, this explains why Hotless are highly concerned about security risks. and willing to undertake protection measures. When it comes to the control of private keys, almost half of rookies are willing to share keys with another party, for example, a trusted person or exchange, whereas cypherpunks and hotless prefer to manage their keys themselves. If we look at the wallet types used, we see a clear preference among all the clusters. The most popular are software, mobile and hardware wallets, with almost 80 % of respondents reporting to use them. When it comes to the main reason for choosing a wallet, cypherpunks look at security, whereas rookies consider the convenience of making transactions. We have seen that the population of cryptoasset users can cluster into distinct groups, and these groups differ in levels of user expertise, risk concerns, and protection efficacy. These differences suggest that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to the design of digital wallets. Virtual asset service providers should therefore consider offering more personalized services. For example, wallet developers may profile their clients, like we did, and offer knowledgeable users some advanced features, such as setting a custom transaction fee. Personalization could also go beyond the interface alone and could be applied to more effective training, knowledge transfer, or risk communication. As our results show, cypherpunks and hodlers are experienced users, while rookies need much more support in managing private keys. And overall, managing cryptoasset keys leads to a fundamental trade-off between security and convenience. To stash bits under your mattress, akin a bundle of cash, or to trust a third party to guard your cryptoassets.

reference: Hello, I'm Deepika from the University IIIT Delhi, India. This study comes out from a deployment work that was conducted in 2019 in India with the collaboration of Anindya Swachh and our research is supported by Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation. Our study focuses on improving the training and learning opportunities of community health workers in India, who are known as ASHAs, by investigating alternative mobile-based solutions. We identified the training needs of the health worker through a large-scale deployment of a mobile-based training tool for the training of 500 ASHAs. The tool is low-cost and overcomes the constraints of low literacy and lack of access to computer and smartphones by ASHAs by using interactive voice response, such that trainers can conduct audio-based online training sessions. The ASHAs just need to have access to basic phones through which they connect to these audio conference calls, where they listen to audio material, Interact with the peers, and in fact, with experts by giving touch tone inputs. In a period of six months, 500 ASHAs were trained on the six topics of home-based postnatal care in 20 batches, Which means one one batch had a size of around 20 to 25 Ashas. Total 01:44 sessions were conducted. From these sessions, we collected 1178 question and answer exchanges between the expert and the ASHAs, which we analyzed to understand the information seeking of the ASHAs and their gaps in knowledge. We then mapped the ASHAs' questions with the reference material they are provided and finally interviewed 48 ASHAs to understand their rationale of information seeking, their training experiences and expectations. Our analysis of the questions found 75 % of these to show gaps in the basic knowledge to deal with the field cases. We understand this by developing a detailed distribution of the topics and severity of the health problems. We arrived at three areas which need attention. First is improving knowledge on routine care and problems for which community typically do not consult experts and rather approach ASHAs as a first point of contact. An important aspect to address these that was highlighted in the queries was related to the cultural associations that contains various kinds of beliefs and practices and because of the lack of knowledge, ASHAs showed difficulty in using their cultural competence and helping the fellow community members. The other two themes were on danger sign and breastfeeding support. On mapping the questions with the reference material, we found the coverage to be low. Only 22 % of the questions could be answered. 15 % were partially answered, and 16 % could not be answered at all. We found basically three gaps with respect to the coverage, presentation and accessibility. First is the material is comprehensive, however, it is inadequate to answer what ASHAs are currently seeking for their community needs. And second, the material is present in form of lessons and chapter forms, whereas from the deployment, we found that ASHAs require content in form of Q&A format, which they can easily use by searching the topic of their queries and field pieces. And third requirement that was highlighted by the ASHAs in the interview is the access to material in form of audiovisual material, which Which they can use in the fields on on demand basis, e.g. while interacting with their clients during the home visits. A key challenge that our deployment faced was related to the poor cellular connectivity. 86 % of the participants. faced at least one call drop in every session. That means they had to reconnect to the sessions and miss portions of their sessions. Voice quality issue was frequently reported by many of the ASHAs and ASHAs navigated these challenges by adjusting the locations from where they attended these sessions. Finally, in conclusion, we draw four implications from our study. We need to improve the design of reference material in terms of coverage of the common questions ASHAs ask, which also represent the unmet needs of their communities and enable ASHAs to effectively use this material. Second is mobile learning platforms fit into the context in which ASHAs work and are and have good scope for providing learning opportunities on continued basis. Third is interactive voice response is powerful in terms of reachability and overcoming the constraints, however, poses barriers in user experience that we face in form of call drops. Finally, in order to improve the knowledge and skills of ASHAs, we need to work on basics and focus on problem solving and constant skills. Thank you very much. I'm happy to take the questions.

reference: Welcome to the virtual presentation of FlexTruss, a computational threading method for multi-material, multi-form, and multi-use prototyping. I am Zhaojie Li. I will be presenting our team from International Design Institute of Zhejiang University. Conventional 3D printing models with like pla or Abs are difficult to shape change physically. FlexTruss is designed to make flexible prototype with 3D printers and assemble by threading. As it combines linear material, it expands possibilities of physical properties and provides new HCI methods. By recent works, a hot topic of fabrication is to enable users to receive continuous feedback. Compared to existing methods, we adapt advantages of low-fidelity fabrication, interactive fabrication, and construction kits for quick prototyping. Our parametric design tool creates instructive and sensible design by allowing users to on-demand modify with the final artifacts. Let's take Stanford Bunny as an example to introduce our workflow. Firstly, virtual model is imported and simplified. The density can be adjusted. Truss-shaped nodes will then be generated on every point of it. An Euler path visits every nodes would link them together. Then we 3D print these nodes with any conventional printers. The threading process needs a while, but the label on nodes would help users to finish it. We can see the final FlexTruss Bunny is deformable for any on-demand shape changing. Besides the type of nodes on Bunny, we develop more modifiable type semi-flexible for compromising objects, and moreover fully flexible. In addition, we also made fully fixed type as a solid truss without threading. For example, replacing the nodes on Bunny's ear with fully flexible nodes. The modification gives the ears a softer touch that allows deformation in more angles. More wiring and threading material can be integrated with FlexTruss, including wire, elastic rope, and even optical fiber. For flexible type of nodes, we can largely shorten the manufacture time by replacing pipe with other material, such as acrylic, PLA, or soft rubber. In theory, Flextruss can achieve any simplified shape from digital model. We tested the multiple fundamental geometries to demonstrate the feasibility. Then, I will show some applications to indicate what we can really do with FlexTruss. The FlexTruss workflow enable designers to create on-demand fashion piece. Video shows it as an example of multi-use handbag. Users can reshape the handbag as functionally needed, for telephone, or book, or other stuff. Threading with elastic rope, we demonstrate a wearable device design. We complete the prototype by reconstructing a waistband with 40 nodes. The artifacts can be worn by users with different waist size and deform according to the action. We also made an arm band with semi-flexible nodes, embedding an optical fiber. This prototype can give a real-time feedback on wearer's gesture. We adopt SLA printing to explore the minimum size of FlexTruss. We complete a flexible ring by reconstructing it with 10 tiny nodes. Video shows that the FlexTruss jewelry can be stretched and worn without breakage. Our final application is an enclosing consisting of three segments. A crop top can be extended into hip-length vest, moreover, be further extended as a dress. In conclusion, shape changing, physical property changing, and the media embedding features. enable our design tool generate multi-material, multi-form, and multi-use applications. We look forward to extending our method into future sustainable fabrication. Thank you for watching.

reference: Hello all, my name is Daniel Madden, and I am pleased to present my work, Constant Pressure of Having to Perform, exploring player health concern in esports, done under the supervision of Casper Hartfeld. Before beginning, I'd like to thank the Chi conference for the opportunity to present today, and for the honorable mention to understand the our examination of esports. we use the following definition, the umbrella term for organized competitive digital gaming that has taken on the aesthetics of professional sports. Within this definition, we can understand that competitions, routines, and training regimens of these players reflect traditional sports. Because of this, we began to ask the following question, what are the major health concerns in esports? To answer this question, we conducted a two-part investigative study. Part one was a series of semi-structured interviews carried out with professional esports players to develop an understanding of the key health concerns and experiences in esports. The information gathered was then used in part two of the study, a survey administered to a wider esports audience of players. For part one of the study, 10 esports professionals were interviewed. The participants included eight male and two female gamers with an average age of 25.8 years and 4.67 average years of competitive experience. These participants competed in a variety of games, including Starcraft 2, NHL 2K, and League of Legends. The interview questions were divided into four main categories. The first three, daily routine, physical health, and psychological wellness, were developed based on previous literature. The fourth area of investigation, support, was added during the interview process as players continued to mention a lack of official resources. Instead, they relied on friends, family, and other networks for mental and emotional support. The thematic analysis of the interviews resulted in the first draft of our health in esports model. As the image shows, each theme can be broken down into sub-themes frequently mentioned during the interviews. This model reflects the biggest concerns in health identified by the players. However, the model does not show how such concerns may relate to one another. We developed a survey administered through various online communities to begin understanding how factors in the model related to one another. The themes in the survey were consistent with the themes used in the interview process. Because of the concerns of the participants in the interviews, special attention was given to psychological wellness. Previously verified instruments were used to determine levels of overall mental wellness and perceived stress, while additional Likert scales were used to determine the relationship different support networks may have on negatively or positively impacting a player's overall mental wellness. In terms of physical pain, responses were consistent with previous studies. Wrist pain, back pain, and general eye fatigue were among the most common injuries players experienced. Examining mental health, 40 participants experienced symptoms of depression or anxiety related to esports participation. However, only one considered seeking professional support. This may be because of a lack of support options provided in current esports communities. Among survey participants, the highest perception of support came from the team members, not from professional resources. We used the data gathered in the survey to carry out a correlation analysis to begin understanding how the identified health factors affect one another. Stress is a major focus in the model, as all interview participants and survey participants reported stress. While the cause of their stress differed, all players felt the negative impacts, especially from stress they afflicted upon themselves. Additionally, we begin to see how various members of the community and a player's support network may positively or negatively impact stress and mental well-being. While the results show both physical and mental health needs improvement in esports, the player's primary concern is on their mental health. Almost all players experience stress due to their involvement in esports, leading many to experience symptoms of anxiety, depression, and burnout. Despite this, players had little to no resources to manage their mental health in the organizations they participated in. Adapting social-emotional learning and mindfulness practices for esports may provide players and members of the community with tools and knowledge to mitigate the stress and other factors negatively impacting their mental health. Community education may also be used to aid player support networks, such as friends and family, to understand their impact on players. The HCI community may begin to develop new designs for esports viewership, tournaments, and online play to create greater human connection and experience that is, quote, virtual and isolating.

Before beginning, I'd like to thank the Chi conference for the opportunity to present today, and for the honorable mention to understand the our examination of esports. we use the following definition, the umbrella term for organized competitive digital gaming that has taken on the aesthetics of professional sports. Within this definition, we can understand that competitions, routines, and training regimens of these players reflect traditional sports. Because of this, we began to ask the following question, what are the major health concerns in esports? To answer this question, we conducted a two-part investigative study. Part one was a series of semi-structured interviews carried out with professional esports players to develop an understanding of the key health concerns and experiences in esports. The information gathered was then used in part two of the study, a survey administered to a wider esports audience of players. For part one of the study, 10 esports professionals were interviewed. The participants included eight male and two female gamers with an average age of 25.8 years and 4.67 average years of competitive experience. These participants competed in a variety of games, including Starcraft 2, NHL 2K, and League of Legends. The interview questions were divided into four main categories. The first three, daily routine, physical health, and psychological wellness, were developed based on previous literature. The fourth area of investigation, support, was added during the interview process as players continued to mention a lack of official resources. Instead, they relied on friends, family, and other networks for mental and emotional support. The thematic analysis of the interviews resulted in the first draft of our health in esports model. As the image shows, each theme can be broken down into sub-themes frequently mentioned during the interviews. This model reflects the biggest concerns in health identified by the players. However, the model does not show how such concerns may relate to one another. We developed a survey administered through various online communities to begin understanding how factors in the model related to one another. The themes in the survey were consistent with the themes used in the interview process. Because of the concerns of the participants in the interviews, special attention was given to psychological wellness. Previously verified instruments were used to determine levels of overall mental wellness and perceived stress, while additional Likert scales were used to determine the relationship different support networks may have on negatively or positively impacting a player's overall mental wellness. In terms of physical pain, responses were consistent with previous studies. Wrist pain, back pain, and general eye fatigue were among the most common injuries players experienced. Examining mental health, 40 participants experienced symptoms of depression or anxiety related to esports participation. However, only one considered seeking professional support. This may be because of a lack of support options provided in current esports communities. Among survey participants, the highest perception of support came from the team members, not from professional resources. We used the data gathered in the survey to carry out a correlation analysis to begin understanding how the identified health factors affect one another. Stress is a major focus in the model, as all interview participants and survey participants reported stress. While the cause of their stress differed, all players felt the negative impacts, especially from stress they afflicted upon themselves. Additionally, we begin to see how various members of the community and a player's support network may positively or negatively impact stress and mental well-being. While the results show both physical and mental health needs improvement in esports, the player's primary concern is on their mental health. Almost all players experience stress due to their involvement in esports, leading many to experience symptoms of anxiety, depression, and burnout. Despite this, players had little to no resources to manage their mental health in the organizations they participated in. Adapting social-emotional learning and mindfulness practices for esports may provide players and members of the community with tools and knowledge to mitigate the stress and other factors negatively impacting their mental health. Community education may also be used to aid player support networks, such as friends and family, to understand their impact on players. The HCI community may begin to develop new designs for esports viewership, tournaments, and online play to create greater human connection and experience that is, quote, virtual and isolating.

reference: Hello, my name is Kresen Djikol and I'm a PhD student at the University of Bath. In this video, I'll be presenting our paper titled Effects of Emotion and Agency on Presence in Virtual Reality. Arguably, one of the most important characteristics of virtual reality is its ability to induce higher levels of presence compared to other conventional forms of media such as 2D screens. Significant advancements have been made in what concerns the technical aspects of VR over the last three decades, and yet, research has remained inconclusive on how presence is affected by human-related factors such as emotion and agency. Even more so, it is unknown whether emotion and agency interact in the presence creation process. Additionally, we were interested in whether the valence of emotions elicited by the virtual environment will result in different presence levels. We thus had two design factors which we named Emotion V and Agency V, respectively, and several subjective factors which were Intensity, which is the intensity of the dominant emotion in each environment, Subjective Agency, which was the degree to which participants felt they controlled the virtual environment, and the third one was Presence. Our hypotheses for the study were as follows. 1. The intensity of the dominant emotion in each virtual environment will correlate positively with presence. 2. Presence will be significantly higher in environments where participants have agency. And 3. Agency will moderate the effect of emotion on presence. Here we adopt a novel design to investigate the effects of both emotions and agency on presence by testing virtual environments inducing either happiness or fear with or without user agency. We employed a between-participants design and in total we recruited 121 participants. In the non-agency condition, users could only observe a friendly dog as seen in the video. In the happy condition with agency, users could interact with the dog via a laser pointer. The dog reacted to the laser pointer so as to create a feeling of agency. The fear scenario occurred in the exact same park environment at night and instead of the friendly dog there was a creature which would attack the participant. In the non-agency condition, users could not defend themselves while in the agency one they could use a flashlight to fend off the creature thus creating the feeling of agency. Results showed that the dominant emotion induced by a virtual environment is positively correlated with presence. Thus, in the happiness conditions it was the level of felt happiness which predicted presence and the felt level of fear predicted presence in the two fear conditions. We can thus accept the first hypothesis. For the second hypothesis, we found that presence was higher in the condition which facilitated agency only in the fear scenario. The same was not found for the happiness conditions, therefore we could only partially accept the second hypothesis. The explanation for this effect could be the special status of fear amongst all other emotions as it benefits from cognitive and perceptual priority which stems from its evolutionary role in survival functions. If the creature we used in the fear condition did in fact trigger a fight or flight response, this could have made agency all the more important for defense and thus made it more salient to participants. It can be thus said that agency does in fact moderate the effect of emotion on presence which validates our third hypothesis. Last but not least, our data allowed us to build a structural equation model or SEM which shows us how our two design variables namely emotionV and agencyV seen on the left of the graph impact emotion intensity and reported subjective agency directly. As expected, emotionV and agencyV also interact and this results in further impact on felt emotions and agency. Finally, the observed dissociation between emotion and presence is also reflected in the SEM in that the regression coefficient for the effect of agency on presence is much higher compared to that of intensity. This suggests that emotional intensity is able to predict presence in VR but to a lesser extent than agency is. Furthermore, our model gives VR designers a tool to predict the effects of their design choices and thereby optimize designing for presence. Ultimately, it becomes apparent from the SEM that controlling only emotions or only agency in VR cannot suffice for ensuring presence. Instead, the interrelations between emotion and agency and their influence on presence mean that VR designers need to prioritize agency in the right circumstances while designing the V to elicit high levels of emotions. Thank you very much for listening from me and my co-authors.

reference: Hi, my name is Maggie Hughes, and today I'll be presenting Keeper, a synchronous online conversation environment informed by in-person facilitation practices. This project was completed by myself and Deb Roy, and we are at the Center for Constructive Communication at the MIT Media Lab. Keeper's design is informed by a circle process. Circle process is a facilitation style in which a facilitator or circle keeper gathers a group. They leverage tools such as talking pieces to facilitate turn-takings and enable deep and vulnerable sharing, and facilitators use different mechanisms such as a centerpiece and the prompts they design To invite participants to share stories from their personal experiences, foster connection with the group and ground to one another in that community and its values. Circle today is used often within the restorative and transformative justice movements that are in response to traditional punitive justice and mass incarceration in the U.S. Circle originates with Indigenous groups in North America and continues to be practiced by these people today, and is a foundation of many other conversation facilitation styles. For time, this is a highly truncated explanation of the history, structure, and importance of circle and restorative transformative justice. For further information, we recommend you learn from the organizations referenced here, and while such practices have proven to be effective in enhancing empathetic, community-oriented, meaningful communication, rarely do we see interfaces designed informed by that knowledge. With this in mind, we ask how we might design a virtual environment informed by circle practice and knowledge of circle practitioners. And if we design that environment, might it foster an experience closer to that desired and circle than a traditional virtual call environment might? To answer this question, we first embarked on an ethnographic study and became trained in the practice. We then designed a tool informed by the practice and iterated and evaluated that design. And today we'll discuss the latter two points. Informed by this question, we identified high social presence, tone, and ease of communication to be structural components of circle that are not bound by the facilitator themselves, but could be bound by the environment. It is an important foundation for this project that we did not intend to replace the facilitator or to execute circle automatically, but rather to leverage the knowledge from the field of HCI and create a container informed by the practice of circle. To begin by breaking down social presence, we wanted to break the traditional Zoom grid of a video call and a conference call online. We also removed video as a component and explored the possibility that audio-only calls with abstract avatars could enable a more vulnerable and inviting conversation space. We then explored how folks might be supported and with their avatars and sitting in a circle and. We explored how making that physical act of dragging and dropping the talking piece to your avatar could mimic the passing of a talking piece. We explored social presence as well through the use of light glowing within the avatars. And we grounded the tone in blues and violet hues to create a calming presence throughout the environment. All animations are calibrated to a slow, calm breathing rate, and we implemented features such as a cue, a raised hand to facilitate ease of turn taking. Further, we introduced a tool to signal a flag or a harm, as well as positive affirmation. Altogether, the platform offers a space to show visible guidelines, the cue, and questions that are offered. And the facilitator is shown through a darker avatar. We evaluate this study in three parts. First, a qualitative analysis with 72 participants, followed by a randomized controlled trial with 100 participants, and closing with a semi-structured set of interviews with eight expert facilitators. From the qualitative study, they highlighted that the social anxiety from waiting to speak in awkward silences was nearly completely eliminated. The tool allowed them to listen actively. Participants highlighted that they felt close to the participants, though they could not see an image of the others. And many emphasized that this enabled the conversation to go smoother than it might in other video calls. From the randomized control trial, we see a significant increase in sense of ease and tone from the control to full treatment. We identify that specifically within tone, participants felt increased feeling of relaxation and calm, and increased willingness to be vulnerable and listen actively. Further, participants felt more connected to others, they felt the participants' presence further, and a specialness within the conversation, more than they did when in a traditional audio call. Finally, through expert interviews, it became clear that facilitators saw that this was clearly a conscious space, and an intentional space. That Keeper did fill an identified need through introducing things such as the talking pieces and sitting in a circle, and that the space felt human, though it was abstract. However, a clear tension and critique arose for it can be hard for facilitators to facilitate without being able to see the faces of participants, especially in moments of tension. In next steps, we are exploring how memory and data might influence the quality of conversations by making hidden dynamics more visible. This notably breaks from the clear inspiration from circle practice, yet could be valuable in making clear power dynamics and other inequalities that might exist within a conversation. As we close, we'd like to thank Dana Cunningham, Marshall Ganz, and Belen Saldías for their contributions to this work, especially Belen Saldías, who built the foundation of Keeper, and we'd like to acknowledge the restorative justice for Oakland youth, Unity Circles, and Suffolk Center for Restorative Justice, who enabled this project to happen based off of their teaching and wisdom. Thank you.

reference: Good day, everyone. My name is Joshua Manzana, and I am presenting our paper entitled Using Boolean Satisfiability Solvers to Help Reduce Cognitive Load and Improve Decision Making when Creating Common Academic Schedules. Our paper focuses on student scheduling, which is defined as assigning students to sections of each course such that they have no schedule conflicts. Many universities employ a method wherein they let the students pick their own courses and create their own schedules. This entails students having to pick from a list of courses and creating their own schedules. This usually leaves them having to deal with picking from a lot of courses and also coordinating it with a lot of peers. This leads to mental stress and high cognitive load, which then impairs their decision making and makes them create poor quality schedules. The related literature around this problem shows that scheduling tends to be a complex task due to the constraints involved. And due to this complexity, the quality of the final decision, and in this case the schedule, is more likely to be stifled. And bad schedules can affect the grade and performance as well as the motivation of a student. Constraint satisfiability has been proposed as a technique That can be used to solve the student's scheduling problem. An example of such technique is the usage of a satisfiability solver. which has been used in course scheduling, employee timetabling, and tournament scheduling. There is an opportunity to integrate a SAT solver in a semi-automated system to tackle the problem of student scheduling. There have been minimal studies in tackling the student scheduling problem, especially with a SAT solver. So our research questions are as follows. First, what impact does the use of a SAT solver-based system have on the decision making process in schedule creation? Next is what impact does the use of a SAT solver-based system have on the cognitive load of users? To answer our research questions, we have the following methodology. First, we do need finding to identify the preferences and the necessary design goals needed. Next, we design the system and configure the SAT solver. And next, we evaluate our proposed system to existing methods. For our need finding, we were able to gather 54 respondents. And from these 54, we were able to interview 16 respondents who had unique and unexpected answers. To further understand, we got another set of 5 respondents for contextual inquiry. From this, we were able to create our preference taxonomy, which is used as a basis for a SAT solver. And we had the following design goals, which is first, to improve efficiency, to reduce stress, and to minimize mental load. And thus, our system was designed with these design goals in mind. To evaluate our system, we recruited 7 friend groups with 2-4 participants each, for a total of 42 participants. These participants were separated in control group, which were allowed to use any method or system they want, and the experimental group, which used the proposed system. They were tasked to create their schedule individually and to coordinate with others. To measure the different aspects in schedule making, we used multiple metrics for each aspect to ensure that we correctly capture each aspect. For our results, we found that students experienced less difficulty when using our proposed system. This can be seen in subjective mental effort questionnaire and the Nasa Tla. It is interesting to note that students in the experimental group found that they experienced less physical demand than the those in the control group, even though the task in general is not really physically demanding. We also found that students were able to decide faster and create their schedules faster. We saw that students experienced slight confusion with the first group task, and this was attributed to the lack of feedback and confusion with how some of the automated features were used. We also found that students experienced less stress. For the user experience, we found that in general, in most aspects in the user experience questionnaire, the proposed system had good and excellent scores, with the exception for perspicuity, which is just above average, which can be attributed to the aforementioned confusion. When asked to pick between schedules created by the control group and the experimental group, we found that students favored schedules created using the proposed system, which is the experimental group. In general, students were also more satisfied and think that their method was more efficient when using the proposed system. For design recommendations, when creating a user-centric semi-automated system for creating personal schedules, we provide the following recommendation. Is to first provide informative feedback with semi-automation, this due to the fact that feedback reduces the likelihood of perceived ambiguity and confusion with automated results, and also aids with decision making. Next, is to visualize and contextualize content through the use of visualizations such as a calendar or weekly view with color highlights, as these can simplify the task of deciding a common schedule. Next, is to always strike a balance between automation and autonomy, as too much automation often leads to the user getting confused and actually harms their decision making and their efficiency. For future work, we would like to explore more collaborative features, to benchmark against other automation algorithms, and to explore course timetabling in tandem with a semi-automated student scheduling system. That is all. Thank you for listening.

reference: Hi, I'm Fiona Bell, and let's talk self-destaining textiles. Traditionally, stains are unintentional and unwanted, resulting in a strong desire to reduce the stain, whereas dyes are intentional and wanted, having a rich history in textile design. So, what if we can de-stain textiles? In this work, we see stains as a mark we can interactively de-stain to create aesthetic patterns rather than seeing stains as something negative. We thus introduce self-destaining textiles, which are interactive textiles that degrade organic stains using light. Our self-de-staining textile works by applying a photocatalytic coating to the surface of the textile that, when exposed to light, degrades stains. We use a colorometer instrument to measure color intensity, and we calculate the stain degradation based on those measurements. We call these self -de-staining textiles because all of the components for stain degradation are embedded within the textile itself. Creating a self-de-staining textile takes five steps coating, staining, LED integration, programming the textile, and light exposure. We start by coating cotton with silver-doped titanium dioxide nanoparticles, which degrade stains when exposed to light. We first explored three methods of coating the cotton with nanoparticles painting, spraying, and immersing. Painting yielded the best results over spraying and immersing. We then coated a double-woven cotton textile with pockets designed to hold LEDs. After the coating cured, we stained our textile with coffee, a common unintentional stain. We then embedded programmable LEDs by placing them inside the textile's pockets. To make this decision, we explored three possible embedding options the LED on top of the textile, the LED within a cut hole, and the LED underneath the textile. Our measurements indicated that embedding the LED underneath the textile provided the best light intensity for de-staining. We then wired the LEDs to an Arduino board and programmed them to show our de-staining design. As you can see, we experimented with a cross and a square LED pattern. Lastly, we triggered our self-de-staining textile by exposing it to light. The intensity of the light and exposure duration played key roles in self-de-staining, with the color of the stain degrading more over time and faster at higher light intensities. After 24 hours of LED exposure, our self-de-staining textile degraded our desired pattern. We further explored passive interactions and controlled interactions that the user can have with the self-de-staining textiles. For passive interactions, we used laser-cut stencils to create a set of photograms that reveal patterns through passive sun exposure over 24 hours. In this perspective, we used the stained textile as our empty canvas, light as our paint, and stencils as our paintbrushes. We also created a hair tie that self-de-stains when passively exposed to sunlight, revealing patterns unique to the user's experiences, movements, and environments, allowing them to encode the memory of a special day into a tangible object. For controlled interactions, we experimented with embedding LEDs into a woven swatch. We also created a station where we can place the self-de-staining textile on top of a programmed LED matrix. We used this station to pattern a phone case. To obtain a new design, the user can simply re-stain, reprogram, and re-expose the textile. In conclusion, we developed self-de-staining textiles that interactively degrade stains to create aesthetic patterns. Thank you all for listening. I want to give a huge shout out to all my co-authors, and I am now happy to take questions.

reference: Hello, everyone. Welcome to the presentation on player AI interaction, what neural network games reveal about AI as play. My name is Jennifer Villareale, a PhD student at Drexel University. Literature on human AI interaction is among one of the fastest growing fields in the CHI community. With few exceptions, most recent literature focuses on productivity related domains. However, one overlooked area is the context of play. The history of AI has long been associated with games. Video games have often been the test bed to try new AI algorithms and use the user interaction they afford. Therefore, games offer a rich domain to understand and explore new ideas in human AI interaction. In this work, we study the interaction in neural network based games. With this, we propose the new research area of player AI interaction. In our paper, we showcase how the concept of play can expand the current discussions around human AI interaction and point out new opportunities for AI infused products in general. We chose to use neural network games because they provide insights into some of the most pressing open problems in human AI interaction, such as the low interpretability of the machine learning models. These are the methods we used. Through the first systematic review in this domain, we collected a data set of 38 games wherein players can interact with the neural network as part of the core gameplay loop. Then, using this data set, we used grounded theory to develop a framework for how players interact with the neural networks and how much its existence is foregrounded in the user interface. To compare player AI interaction to the broader discussion in other AI products, we also adapted existing guidelines for human AI interaction and used them to evaluate our games. Our analysis found four interaction metaphors that provide familiar structures for players to interact with the AI. Apprentice, competitor, designer, and teammate. For example, the game AI Evolution uses neural network as teammate metaphor, where the player interacts with the neural network as a colleague. The focus of the gameplay is a collaborative cycle between the player and the neural network where they both work together towards a shared goal. Players are able to build hilarious looking neural network creatures and they're able to construct their brain and avatar structure in order to train them to compete in a race. This is a new kind of interaction we typically don't see outside of games yet. Playful interaction that motivates players to try different kinds of AI configurations. We also found that there is a range of how much games highlight the use of neural networks in their user interface. This visualization represents the design space of player AI interaction based on these three dimensions. Each dot on this outer ring represents one of the 38 games. This diagram helps us identify under explore areas. For example, we noticed that all games that adopted neural network as apprentice interaction used online learning for player agency, such that the player may play with or control the training of the neural network. This interaction leads to a variety of neural network behaviors, whereas most other metaphors use offline learning for more predictable player experience. We compared the compliance with these guidelines across the characteristics of our framework. Most notably, we found that neural network as apprentice games comply well with the guidelines, particularly with regards to providing global controls to the user and learning actively from the user behavior. For games where neural network is represented as a competitor, the compliance with the design guidelines are very low because the guidelines are not created for the cases where AI is an adversary. However, an increasing number of AI infused products would fall into this category. We also compared the design guideline compliance of neural network games with reported outcomes of AI infused products by Amershi et al to see what key similarities and differences exist. We find that like other AI infused products, neural network games struggle to make the limitations of the AI known to the user during the initial interaction. However, games do this intentionally as the point is to learn the limitations through play. Neural network games generally perform better in enabling the user to provide feedback indicating their preferences during regular interaction. They are also better in allowing the user to globally customize what the AI system monitors and how it behaves. For game designers, UX designers, and HCI researchers interested in human AI interaction, one of our key takeaways is that reframing AI as play offers a useful design approach. AI as play can offer a new design space where users can tinker, explore, and experiment with AI. With that, we would like to thank NSF and DFF for supporting this work and the anonymous reviewers for providing their comments. Thank you for joining our presentation. If you have any comments, feel free to reach out via Twitter or email.

Today, I am going to talk to you about my project Vid2Dop, which utilizes millimeter-wave Doppler radar for privacy-preserving human activity recognition. This work was done with my collaborators Yuexiang, Mayank Goyal, and Chris Harrison. Millimeter-wave Doppler radar is a new and promising sensing approach for human activity recognition, offering signal richness approaching that of microphones and cameras, but without many of the privacy-invading downsides. This is because unlike images and audio, which can tell you what the person looks like or the contents of their speech, the millimeter-wave radar sensor returns a radial velocity across a distance map. This has made it very popular for ranging and pedestrian detection-based tasks for autonomous driving. For example, the signal on the right here shows that something 4 meters away from the camera is moving at 0.7 meters per second in the direction of the sensor. For the purpose of activity recognition, we want to characterize and identify these motion profiles and one of the best ways to do so is to train a supervised deep learning model. So what is Discover? Discover is an app launched by Facebook under its philanthropic arm to provide limited internet access for free in countries in the Global South. Prior work has both lauded Facebook's previous free internet initiative and criticized it for violating net neutrality and privacy. We wanted to enrich this discussion by analyzing how Discover, the new initiative, situates users in economic and political relationships. To do this, we used document theory, a framework which was developed in documentation studies and has been adapted for HCI. Our approach frames internet access via Discover as a specific configuration of costs and benefits rather than just as distributing a good. In line with this, we pursue the following research questions guided by document theory's structure. Who is involved in rendering and organizing the websites as they are viewed on Discover? What is used to render the websites? How are websites organized and made visible on Discover? And how do the rendered websites look on Discover? With the help of research associates based in the Philippines, we systematically collected screenshots of the Discover app and cataloged the so-called popular websites that were made prominent in the app's homepage. Our analysis of the categorization reveals that rather than being a neutral portal for free internet, Facebook's categorization and display choices perpetuate the dominance of sites from the U.S. and also promote harmful malware, which are considered popular due to having many redirects. We further attempted to accomplish tasks on the most popular sites on Discover. Many of the sites were actually unusable due to the way that Discover is set up to save data By automatically stripping stripping most images, videos and other data intensive features of websites. Discover effectively redesigns packages and sells internet access in smaller forms like digital sachets. At a smaller scale, we urge engineers and technologists implicated in technology companies colonizing actions to mobilize in solidarity with those affected by the products they design and create, and hold their employers accountable for the ethical standards that they claim to follow. Thank you for listening to our talk and we hope you'll read our paper.

reference: Deep neural networks, or DNNs, are found in many modern applications because of their powerful ability to learn from high-dimensional data, like images and natural language. In order to use neural nets for custom applications, they must be trained and tuned, a process which can be challenging to debug. One significant challenge of this process is that errors are often silent. For example, a model can have random chance accuracy during evaluation, meaning it hasn't learned any patterns from the data. In cases like this, there are no messages that directly inform the user what errors led to this condition. Models can also produce unexpected output during training, which can be hard for non-experts to interpret, such as when loss values increase rather than decrease, or when NANDs appear in the output. While experts can use tools like TensorBoard to inspect the behavior of their models, non-experts often think of DNNs as black boxes, and lack strong mental models to interpret their results. In our work, we identify three critical gulfs of the DNN debugging process, mapping from symptoms to their root causes, choosing a strategy to address the underlying problem, and mapping from the strategy to a concrete code implementation. We introduce Umlaut, a Python library and a Web application which supports users through these gulfs in the Dnn debugging process. Umlaut runs automated checks of a deep learning program's structure and behavior, and guides users through explanation-driven error messages, which are tightly coupled with visualizations and code. Let's take a look at an example of Umlaut in action. Here is a typical program for an image classifier written in the Keras framework. The model we create classifies 10 kinds of images, such as cars, airplanes, dogs, and birds. The program defines a model, and trains it on the CIFAR-10 dataset for 10 epochs. After training, we see our model isn't able to learn any meaningful patterns from the data. Our 10 % accuracy is the same as random chance. Let's attach an umlaut client to see what's going on. Running the program again, we see Umlaut emits error messages to the command line. Let's open its web interface to understand what these are. The Umlaut interface shows us a timeline of raised errors on top, error messages on the right, and standard visualizations of model loss and accuracy on the left. This critical error is telling us a softmax calculation is missing before the model's loss function. The error explains the underlying theory, suggests potential solutions, and includes a code snippet to implement a suggested fix, an additional argument to pass into our Keras loss function class. Let's make the change Umlaut suggests to add a softmax calculation. Now our model seems to be learning well. However, Umlaut is warning us that the model seems to be overfitting on the training data. To see if this error represents a trend, we click it, which annotates the plots and the timeline. Let's do what Umlaut suggests and add dropout to our model, a well-established technique in the literature to reduce overfitting. With dropout added, the overfitting warning is now gone, and our loss is going down smoothly. There's only one error left, indicating we forgot to normalize our data. Umlaut includes the program context during runtime, telling us the model received an input of 255, which is outside the typical range from minus one to one. Let's make the change and run umlaut again. Our model now achieves a 76 % test set accuracy, and umlaut shows no errors. A satisfying result. In the Umlaut interface, error messages are linked to annotated visualizations of model loss and accuracy, helping users recognize symptoms and map them to their root causes. Umlaut error messages help users choose a strategy to address the underlying problem with explanations of their theory and program context. To map from strategy to a concrete code implementation, Umlaut errors include code recipes, link to stack overflow and documentation, and references back to the source code. In order to run heuristic checks, the Umlaut client monitors several components of the deep learning program runtime. Static checks, such as checking for activation functions, are run on the model graph and source code before training begins. Dynamic checks, such as checking for overfitting, are run during training. In addition to static data, they capture model input and output in training metrics. When a heuristic check fails, it populates an error with a relevant program context. This data is logged by an API request to an Umlaut server, which renders the web interface. To evaluate Umlaut, we conducted a within-subject study with 15 participants. Their task was to debug two image classification programs with different sets of three bugs introduced. Participants were asked to find and fix all the bugs in these programs, alternating with and without Umlaut in counterbalanced conditions. When using Umlaut, participants found and fixed significantly more bugs in each program. Please look at our paper for details. In summary, we created the Umlaut system, which helps users find and fix errors in their deep neural networks. Umlaut helps users overcome critical gulfs in the deep learning debugging process by linking explanation-driven error messages, annotated visualizations, and code in the same interface. We believe Umlaut presents many opportunities for future work in supporting users throughout the process of developing, debugging, and deploying deep neural networks.

reference: Hi everyone, I'm Sharifa Sultana from Cornell University. Today I will present our paper Munmochan, a tool to combat online sexual harassment over Facebook Messenger. reference: Hello, I'm Fanny, and I'm a research scientist at SNAP. I'm presenting Significant Audit, Understanding the Role of Biosignals in Communication. It's well known that remote communication is challenging. Over technology, you just don't get the social cues we need to establish social connection. I'm sure all of us have experienced this during the pandemic, where we've had to rely heavily on text or video calls, even now during this conference. In all these channels, it can be hard to get a sense of someone without proper access to cues like their facial expressions or their gestures. In my research, I'm exploring new opportunities to address this through expressive biosignals, the use of sense physiological data, such as our heart rate, as a new kind of social cue. Today's world has a number of devices with sensors that record data like heart rate, and even share them with other people, like the Fitbit and the Apple Watch. Several prior works show that sharing this type of data can be a playful way to express your emotions and let people know what you're up to, but. But while these works show that expressive biosignals have the potential to affect the way we communicate and connect with others, they haven't quite clarified what those effects are. That was the goal of this research, investigating the role of expressive biosignals in communication through two versions of an app called Significant Otter, one with biosignal sensing off and one with it on. We investigated how shifting between these two versions might, one, affect our communication, and two, our feelings of connection with each other. Significant Otter is an Apple Watch app for couples that's available on the App Store, so you can feel free to download and check it out. We've had over 60,000 app installations since our release, and we've been featured on the App Store, Apple Retail Stores, and Product Hunt. To use Significant Otter, you can view the app on your watch using the crown on the top right to scroll and see a set of otter emotion animations sensed from heart rate. For example, if your heart rate is high, you might see both an excited and an angry otter. In the sensing off version, you'd see a set of random otters. After selecting the one you want, you can tap to send it to your Significant Other, who will then get a notification on the watch that they can tap to view the otter animation you sent, after which they can scroll through their own otters and tap on it to react. We ran a one-month study deploying Significant Otter with 20 couples. During the study, participants used the sensing off version for the first two weeks before switching the sensing on for the last two weeks. We collected data throughout the study through interviews and daily surveys on participants usage. Based on our qualitative analysis of their responses, We found opportunities for biosignals to function as enhanced emojis with sensing off. the otters were essentially in a shorter emoji or sticker keyboard. similar to those on existing apps. One of the challenges of emojis, though, is that they're known to have multiple possible meanings. We also saw this in our study, where people were confused about what their partner's otter meant. Sensing on actually mitigated these issues and enhanced communication, where people could more easily send their state back by data. Since it was tied to their biosignals, the otter simply represented their emotions, which we found also helped couples become more open and honest with each other about their true emotions. Overall, three-fourths of participants preferred the sensing on version for this reason. Future work could explore extending these benefits into existing communication platforms, such as integrating biosignals into existing stickers or emojis with badges to indicate that they reflect the body's state. At the same time, we saw tensions between people and our system. Significant otter is a form of AI-mediated communication in which messages are supplied by an AI system. The app suggested your otter's emotion based on your heart rate, which some people blindly trusted while others were more skeptical based on their lay understanding of emotions or confidence in knowing themselves. This led to concerns that people didn't have agency over their own feelings or they weren't putting in effort to reflect on how they were actually feeling versus just sending what the system told them. Future work should explore these tensions further and build systems that better collaborate with users based on their subjective understanding of their own emotions. To summarize, we evaluated the role of biosignals in communication by By exploring people's perceptions of shifting between a sensing on and off version of significant otter. In terms of communication, we found that sensing on with biosignals helped people more easily keep in touch with each other's emotional state, backed by data. This depended on people's perceptions of the system's accuracy, though. We also found that biosignals helped build feelings of connection through authenticity where people became more compelled to share their actual emotions with each other though with some questions around agency over those emotions. Thank you very much for watching.

So I doubt I need to remind anybody, but due to COVID-19, we've been living in various states of quarantine for about a year. And this has led to surges in mental health issues but has also led to a surge in video gameplay, and a great deal of existing work has shown that games can help people cope with unpleasant or stressful situations, but for obvious reasons, this has never been explored in a quarantine context. So that led us to a research question which was how have people used games to cope with the COVID-19 quarantine? To answer this question, we chose a two-step qualitative methodology. In the first step, we conducted a thematic analysis of approximately 2,000 Twitter posts. This resulted in 12 themes that were then used to author a 12-question open-answer survey. This survey was distributed on Facebook and it received 130 responses. We performed a thematic analysis of these responses, and the result was 15 themes organized into four categories. The first category contains five themes related to how people used games to maintain mental well-being, which are listed on the slide. The italicized themes are those that we found were not present or are only partially present in previous work, and you can see an example quote that this category applies to on the right, where this participant speaks about how they were using games to handle their anxiety and depression, which were worse because of the quarantine. Some of the interesting findings in this theme category include people feeling a connection through games that allowed them to stave off loneliness, not only because they played with other people, but also because they felt a strong interpersonal connection with non-player characters, even in single-player games. The second category contains five themes related to how people used games to connect with others. Again, the italicized theme is one that was not entirely present in previous work. And on the right, we have an example quote from this category where the participant talks about using games to feel like they're still a part of their brother and sister's lives, even if they can't be there in person. Some interesting findings in this category were the importance that participants placed on using games to remain a part of loved ones' lives, as illustrated by the example quote, but also that a great deal of people also discussed using games to connect with people who were not necessarily family or close friends, such as co-workers and classmates, just to feel a connection with them. We also found that some participants who had picked up or increased their gaming during quarantine had turned to social media to find people to play with since they were not part of an established group already. The third category contains three themes related to how people used games to substitute reality, all of which we did not see in previous work. On the right is an example where the participant discusses how they built their summer cam and animal crossing, since they couldn't be there in person because of the quarantine. So this category is interesting because there is a history of events and recreations being done in game, most notably, funerals are held in MMOs when a known player passes away, But what is different is that all of these themes emerged from a prominent response pattern indicating that these substitutions were happening not because of any kind of established in-game community, which often informs the previous examples of such events, but because it was impossible to access or realize real world versions of any of this. The final category contains two themes, which are related to how people used quarantine as an opportunity to create games, both in the sense that they were learning game design, also in the sense that they were game-refying every day activities like chores. On the right is an example where the participant discusses using their extra free time to learn how to make games, and these themes are a bit different from the rest as they're not strictly about how people are using games, but it was interesting to see that people were using as quarantine as an opportunity to create games. We note several contributions and implications of this work. First, the study confirms that the findings of previous work persist even in a context of something as extreme as a quarantine. Second, we note the discovery of new behaviors, such as people using games as a surrogate or substitute for reality, that we believe may be unique to the extreme isolation brought on by quarantine. Third, we argue that this presents a foundation for understanding the impact of games on isolation-related stress, which paves the way for many avenues of future work, especially since isolation-related stress, even to these extremes, can occur outside of a quarantine context. Finally, we argue that this provides insight into the value of games in human lives, which can be used to motivate a great deal of future work. That concludes our presentation and we cannot take any questions, thank you.

reference: Hello, my name is Kimain Tang, and I'm a PhD student from KU Leuven, Belgium. Today I'm going to present a work on the role of technology to support breastfeeding that is a part of my PhD research. This work was done together with my co-authors, Catherine Gerling, Luc Kurtz, and Kata Spiel. Breastfeeding brings many benefits for parents and children, although the process is often challenging. The adherence to the recommended breastfeeding practices is determined by many factors such as the ability to breastfeed, and the intention to breastfeed, just to name a few. Many attempts to leverage technology to tackle barriers to breastfeeding have been made. For example, there are many systems that provide breastfeeding education, and systems that support breastfeeding at a pragmatic level. There is a body of HCI research in breastfeeding and parenthood, however there is no structured understanding of technology use in this space. In our work, we investigated the role and the potential of technology that support breastfeeding through a two-step inquiry guided by the integrated behavioral model. We sought to answer our research question, what is parent-anticipated or lived experience of breastfeeding, and what are the implications for the role of technology to support breastfeeding. What are parents' general perspectives on technology to support breastfeeding? How do they align with their preferences and needs across the feeding journey? In the first phase of our work, we interviewed 12 participants about their lived and anticipated experience of feeding a child, and their perspective toward technology in this space. In the second phase, we then built upon the findings from the interview study and conducted an online survey study on breastfeeding and technology, which we received 175 responses. Analysis of the interviews and the survey responses shows that the lived breastfeeding experience is more complex than anticipated, and is entwined with practical and emotional challenges along the feeding journey. Parents' breastfeeding practice is heavily influenced by the society and the environment. We set an expectation on how and when parents should feed their child. Technology in this space needs to embrace and adequately reflect the complexity of the lived breastfeeding experience. For postnatal technology, the system needs to provide flexible support throughout the feeding journey, and there is also a potential for technology that targets the wider society. Concerning parents' perspective toward technology, participants were cautiously optimistic about the potential of technology in supporting breastfeeding, with many of them already engaged with technology-based breastfeeding support. However, we recognize participants' skepticism about the potential of technology in providing practical support, and there is also concern about the credibility of the information provided. More generally, our work offers two points of reflection for technology that supports breastfeeding. The first concerns the relevance of the lived experience in technology design. Our data illustrates the complexity and the emotional conflict of the lived breastfeeding experience, which requires parents to be resilient to these highly individual challenges. However, breastfeeding technologies developed by the research community make little reference to the lived experience. This risks presenting only the factual information rather than painting a complete multidimensional picture of the experience, and is a missed opportunity because technology could support parents in becoming resilient infant feeders. We speculate that the system in this space could come in form of mobile apps that are easily accessible for people who don't have any hand to spare, but we also want to highlight that these systems can only supplement problem solving, and that human support remains vital, particularly in the early stage of breastfeeding. Secondly, our work highlights the impact of social and environmental factors on the feeding practice. While in many interventions, the burden to follow with breastfeeding is placed on parents. We argue that technology to support breastfeeding needs to engage a wider audience, and has to cast breastfeeding as a collective effort that includes partners, family and friends, but also the wider society. For example, technology could leverage simulations to convey breastfeeding parents' need to stakeholders such as policy makers and architects, so that they can reflect on how they shape the environment that breastfeeding parents find themselves in. There is also potential for technology designed to normalize breastfeeding at the societal level. This entails technology that raises awareness about the feeding process, and the right to breastfeed in public. We hope that our work will inspire further research in this area, and we invite you to read our full paper for additional and more nuanced research insights. Thank you very much.

reference: In this study, we examine sources and patterns of gender bias in research participant populations. This research was conducted at the University of British Columbia. Gender bias in data can have serious consequences for people with underrepresented gender identities. E.g. previous research shows women are approximately 50 % more likely to sustain injury in the event of a car accident. which is attributed to a lack of consideration of women's data in safety system design. Leaving non-binary identities out of design and training data for computer vision systems leads to creating gender recognition systems which misgender people. In HCI, study participants are the primary source of research data. Gender bias in these participants can lead to theories, systems, and design guidelines that marginalize or harm underrepresented individuals. Previous surveys of HCI research participants have shown a gender disparity in the HCI participant samples. As these studies focused on evaluation methods and sample sizes rather than gender, further data is needed for a gender-specific data-driven analysis to verify the extent of these patterns of bias. We tackle these issues by exploring the following questions. How are women and non-binary individuals represented or underrepresented as participants in HCI research? What are the variables that are associated with the gender demographics of HCI research participants? How can we systematically collect gender data from published research for a data-driven analysis? We conducted this study in two phases, interviewing 13 researchers to identify variables connected to gender bias in research participants, then collecting participant data from published HCI research for a quantitative analysis to identify trends of gender bias across all the years of CHI. From our interviews, we identified three key variables, participant recruitment methods, the research area of the study, and the year the study was published. We then created a data schema to codify participant gender and related variables and used it to structure data collected from 1,142 randomly selected papers from CHI 1981 to CHI 2020. From our data, we identified several important patterns. While we are starting to see some reporting of gender beyond men and women, non-binary participants are practically invisible. Looking closer, it seems likely that non-binary identities are not being included in demographic surveys. Our next few findings focus on the comparative representation of men and women. To analyze this comparison, we developed a ratio metric called distance from even representation of men and women, DER for short. A DER of zero means equal numbers of men and women participated in the research. Negative one means there were men participating but no women, and one means there were women but no men. When examining the comparative representation of men and women, we find that the underrepresentation of women is persistent. The average DER of negative 0.15 that the median hovers around is equivalent to 10 men for every 7 women. This is the same ratio of men to women that previous literature found in 2014. When looking at effects of participant recruitment, we find that the impact of recruiting sources on participant demographics can change over time. For example, Amazon's Mechanical Turk as a recruiting source appears to be becoming more biased in favor of men. Finally, we found that research topics that have a more even representation of men and women tended to be about social interaction, whereas topics that are more prone to a bias in favor of men tended to be about physical interaction. This analysis has identified several weak spots in participant gender practices in HCI research. Our data shows that recruiting practices can introduce gender bias into participant populations, and certain research areas are more prone to bias than others. We therefore recommend these research areas to re-evaluate their recruiting methods. Comprehensive data is necessary for being able to conduct a gender-inclusive analysis of representation, and the invisibility of non-binary participants in our data suggests that non-binary identities are not being included in data collection. To combat this issue, we recommend researchers to follow current guidelines to collect gender demographics in a way that is compatible with complex gender. As a final note, we would like to stress the iterative nature of this work. The co-authors are interested in carrying it forwards, and we welcome suggestions for future directions. Our dataset has been made publicly available, and we encourage further analysis and discussion.

Leaving non-binary identities out of design and training data for computer vision systems leads to creating gender recognition systems which misgender people. In HCI, study participants are the primary source of research data. Gender bias in these participants can lead to theories, systems, and design guidelines that marginalize or harm underrepresented individuals. Previous surveys of HCI research participants have shown a gender disparity in the HCI participant samples. As these studies focused on evaluation methods and sample sizes rather than gender, further data is needed for a gender-specific data-driven analysis to verify the extent of these patterns of bias. What are the variables that are associated with the gender demographics of HCI research participants? How can we systematically collect gender data from published research for a data-driven analysis? Looking closer, it seems likely that non-binary identities are not being included in demographic surveys. Our next few findings focus on the comparative representation of men and women. To analyze this comparison, we developed a ratio metric called distance from even representation of men and women, DER for short. For example, Amazon's Mechanical Turk as a recruiting source appears to be becoming more biased in favor of men. To combat this issue, we recommend researchers to follow current guidelines to collect gender demographics in a way that is compatible with complex gender. As a final note, we would like to stress the iterative nature of this work. The co-authors are interested in carrying it forwards, and we welcome suggestions for future directions.
