reference: Dear fellow scholars, my name is Jan Ole Rixen and I'm a research associate with the Institute for Media Informatics of the University of Ulm, Germany. Today I want to talk to you about our work on exploring future AR devices and how their capability to influence our visual perception of the world around us might impact our interpersonal communications. For this reason, please imagine a future AR device looking like ordinary prescription glasses but having seen understanding and capability to opaquely display on the full field of view. Possessing such a device, we can now overlay reality and visually shape it the way we want. Today we are often talking about the acceptance of AR devices themselves but leave aside the acceptance and the impact of what the devices will do into our daily lives. We therefore want to explore how augmented visual alterations are influencing our social interactions in before the technological feasibilities arise and therefore keep the discussion about what should be done one step ahead. To explore this topic, we need a simple, understandable yet universal reason for carrying out visual alterations. These in turn cannot be based on aesthetic preferences alone, which of course would vary between participants in a potential study. We found this reason in the so-called color and context theory. In summary, it says that we are not only perceiving color aesthetically, but that perceiving color alone can trigger subconscious reactions in certain situations. As an example, our subconscious mind knows that when people get angry their blood circulation is raised and they appear more red, but in turn it cannot differentiate if the person is red in the face or if they are just wearing a red shirt, and our subconscious mind readies us for conflict in an equal way. Over the course of a day we face a multitude of situations and in most of them we perceive color. As our future AR device possesses seen understanding and can overlay reality, it can now help us by overlaying colors that trigger effects that we deem as negative, while changing color to induce positive ones. It could therefore recolor a goalkeeper's red jersey to raise our chance of scoring in a football or, as you might know, its soccer match. On the contrary, we could recolor our own to make us feel more dominant and more vengeful. At this point I want to empathize that we do not argue for or against color alterations in augmented reality. We in turn, develop the concept as an explainable reason for executing visual alterations that are new, not purely aesthetical. We therefore use this concept to get insight into people's feelings about the thought of visually altering themselves or another person, or in turn being altered by someone else. In an online social acceptability study with 64 participants, we used this concept as a carrier to explore how either of the conversational partners felt when the device wearer, their opposite or objects disconnected from them, are visually altered in the wearer's view only, and how it is influenced by their relationship to each other. We also explored which parts of their body the participants felt comfortable with altered for both persons. For time purpose we only present some of the results, please refer to our paper for the full insight. For example, we found a self-stigma against alterations when being with a closed person, where the person not wearing the AR device and therefore not perceiving the visual alterations was more comfortable with the thought of being altered than the wearer with altering them. Generally, we propose that you could stand towards visual alterations in two ways. On one hand, if you possess a private display that only you can see, for others there should make no difference from you just imagining it. Limiting the possibility to perceive the world the way we want it to be could be regarded as censorship. Contrary, visually altering someone could be regarded as a strong intrusion into a person's self-determination, as they can no longer decide how they want to appear to others on a visual level. This is what a participant in our study stated. As a woman, I'm very uncomfortable with the idea that augmented reality might change something about my body. In this study, it's just a color, but what if technology could be used to change the appearance of parts of my body without my consent? I think that would absolutely happen in the real world and I would be not okay with it. No matter which strain of thought you might entertain, we can agree on one thing. With our work, we took a first peek into how visual alterations might impact social interactions, but the topic needs a bigger discussion that should be held before the technological availability arises. Thank you for your attention.

reference: Hello, I am Emad Jangoudai from Aalto University. I will be presenting a design approach that translates paper mock-ups into digital models during the initial design stages of architecture. I will elaborate on our methodology and the design process. Then, I will talk about the highlights of the study and its future implications. Paper folding is a quick and effective manual technique for modeling three-dimensional volumes. The soft and flexible nature of the paper has made it a suitable material for free-form exploration. We study curved folding as a test case to combine physical and digital workflows in the early design processes. Compared to polyhedral surfaces, curved folded paper surfaces can provide rich and tractable designs for computer-aided design applications. We focus on two issues. The first one is converting simple mock-ups to complex digital models. The second one is about facilitating intuitive non-linear explorations. We adopted a research-through-design approach and a material engagement framework to support spatial explorations by mixing digital and non-digital tools. By using a research-through-design approach, we aim to present our findings with concrete examples. Our design process consists of physical paper folding, 3D scanning, digital simulation, and plywood prototyping. The design process started by deforming the physical form of a single sheet of paper through three scoring and folding strategies. Applying these strategies returned a total of 42 curved folded designs. We shortlisted five rigid and volumetrically complex models for digital translation. We assessed the rigidity and the volumetric characteristics through paper prototypes, photographs, and the observation notes taken during each folding test. Next, the 3D scanning method was used to transfer paper models into the digital software. Using a scanner to input physical geometry offers an alternative conception for digital processes where the user can employ any object or material to interface with the computer. We utilized a structured light scanner with a rotary table configuration to generate high-definition 3D models. The rotary table allowed 360 degrees tracing while the camera captured forms with the projected background grid. Linking paper mock-ups with digital tools facilitated a feedback platform in which physical data can be fed and tested digitally. In the next stage, 3D geometries obtained from the scanning process were fed into the digital design software for simulation and optimization. We used RhinoSera software with Grasshopper and Kuramba plugins. The software displays problematic areas with gradient blue and red colors on the model. We observed that an increased number of curved creases returned more unstable surfaces. To test this finding, we examined optimized digital concepts with tangible prototypes. The prototyping test focused on two models that have the least and the most number of curved creases. We utilized a laser cutting technique on flexible plywood sheets. The laser-cut plywoods were bent physically by applying heat on their surfaces to achieve desired shapes. Attaining stable geometries with large surfaces required significant heat application and physical support. In contrast, thinner curved folds were easier to manage and manipulate into organic forms. We explored existing conventions in architecture to understand how physical and digital design techniques can facilitate a feedback-oriented approach. Manual paper folding tests have shown that mock-ups are practical for formulating complex design ideas without extensive digital software knowledge. Using paper as a medium to explore curved folded surfaces establishes a tangible design environment beyond mouse and keyboard-based interactions and graphical user interfaces. We believe that the feedback-oriented approach would contribute to real-time fabrication methods for bridging the gap between physical and digital design platforms. Furthermore, exploring tactile manipulation of scanned paper models with immersive technologies such as mixed reality and virtual reality could enable intuitive 3D explorations. Thank you for listening.

reference: Hello, I'm Zhilan Zhou, and today I will introduce our work, Modeling and Leveraging Analytic Focus during Exploratory Visual Analysis. This is a joint work with Ximing Wen, Yue Wang and David Gotts at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. In many real-world problems, analysts deal with information found in large and heterogeneous data sources. For instance, in social science, these sources include structured census data, unstructured social media posts, and large-scale social networks. In the healthcare domain, relevant data sources include electronic health records, biomedical literature, and so on. Traditionally, structured data are often managed by relational databases and visual analytic tools, while unstructured tests are managed by searching engines and natural language processing tools. This separation of tools of structured and unstructured data management presents a big challenge when a data analyst tries to explore and synthesize information across data sources. The disconnect between tools means that the analyst has to take notes of her own focus in one data and transfer it to another data. In an exploratory task, the analyst will inevitably go back and forth between data sources many times. The manual transfer of the analytic focus can become a tedious burden and prone to errors. Our research goal in this vision is to computationally model a user's ever-changing analytic focus during exploratory visual analysis. In further-front user interactions, if an accurate model can be obtained, it can be used as inputs in other tools to get new information in real-time. This requires a unified representation of the analytic focus. Our proposed approach has been prototyped within a pre-existing visualization system in the medical domain. The prototype implementation leverages this focus model capability to capture all user interactions and continuously search PubMed abstracts for documents relevant to the user's focus. These relevant abstracts are displayed to users to contextualize the current visualization and to suggest the new opportunities for future exploratory analysis. Our prototype implementation is based on Cadence, a pre-existing open-source visual analytics platform designed to allow users to discover patterns in structured time-sequenced event data, such as EHR. The Cadence platform includes a coordinated set of interactive visualizations. Here we introduce two components that worked closely with our prototype. The milestone-based timeline visualization in the middle that allows users to filter based on temporal constructs between events. And the coordinated scatter plus focus plot on the right that allows users to quickly identify new event types to incorporate into the timeline to help separate patients with different outcomes. Our focus model is essentially comprised of a list of concepts with corresponding important scores, A. A concept here refers to a meaningful data attribute in the modern domain, like attributes of data records in a structured database schema, for example, a disease term. In the visual analytics process, each concept is usually associated with one or more user actions such as selection, filtering, or aggregation criteria. Here the plot shows how the action involving a concept will affect the important score of the concept. At t1, the important score rises to a value that is determined by the action time, and then it decays gradually until other actions at t2 increase its important score again. Finally, the focus model is comprised of a list of concepts with corresponding dynamic important scores over time. We then leverage the focus model as a representation of the user's information need and use it to retrieve relevant documents from a full-text index of permet abstracts. To evaluate the accuracy of the model and the user interest in our general approach, we conduct a user study using our prototype. The participants are assigned a task exploring medical conditions given certain outcomes. They are asked to describe their current analysis every 6 minutes and we then show them our computed focus model and ask them to compare the model to their own descriptions. Overall, our focus model achieves high accuracy and participants provide positive feedback on the helpfulness of the focus model and abstract previews. Here comes to the conclusion. So we present a formal model and algorithm to capture analytic focus in exploratory visual analysis. We do contextualizing visualized data patterns by surfacing articles relevant to current focus. Our prototype application in medical data analysis showed both the focus model and retrieved articles are helpful in an exploratory task. More details can be found in our paper. Thank you.

On behalf of my co-authors Marc-Abdell Assis, Lukas Mecke, Alia Saad, Jonas Auder, Uwe Grunefeld, Florian Alt and Stefan Schneegers, I will present to you our work with the title Understanding User Identification in Virtual Reality through Behavior Biometrics and the Effect of Body Normalization. Applications for virtual reality often require to know their user's identity. This is necessary as it allows the application to personalize the experience by loading or setting personal preferences or granting access to personal information. Current approaches to identify users employ authentication schemes such as pins or passwords that are entered through handheld controllers and a virtual keyboard. Previous work has shown that these traditional forms of authentication are vulnerable to observation from a bystander who can easily spy on the hand gesture of the immersed VR user. Also, traditional authentication schemes that are currently widely used need yet another password to be remembered and interrupt the VR experience throughout their password prompt. In our work, we alternatively employ behavioral biometrics in combination with two task-based scenarios to identify the users of our VR application. Our scenarios mimic common VR activities such as bowling and archery and are probably only two of many possible examples. Users interact naturally with the scenarios and transparently in the background, the spatial data of the handheld controllers and the head-mounted display are captured by an identification system. The captured data is highly individual and it allows to determine the identity of the user through a deep learning classifier. At this point, it is important to note that these bowling or archery scenarios are not intended as a drop-in replacement for a password prompt. Instead, they enable an implicit interaction with an identification scheme where users behave naturally with the task but provide the required spatial data for the identification scheme on the fly. We moreover seek to better understand the role of behavioral biometrics in user identification and especially the connection to physiologic biometrics within them. A movement that intends to solve a task is first of course a form of behavior thus falls into behavioral biometrics. But the capabilities to move are also partly defined by for example the length of one's arms which means that physiology also plays a role. Virtual reality gives us the chance to explore this relationship as we try to eliminate the influence of physiologic biometrics by imposing a body normalization in VR. To do so, we impose a height normalization where each user has the same virtual height of 168 cm. Shorter or taller persons subsequently have their virtual height reduced or enlarged to match this exact value. We proceed in the same fashion with the arms of each user which is set to a span of 70 cm measured from the front of the head to the hand. A combination of both is also possible where both the arms and the height is normalized. We evaluated our approach in a lab-based user study using a repeated measures design. The study took place in two sessions where each session was conducted on a different day. Our independent variables were first scenario with two levels bowling vs. archery and second type of normalization with four levels following a counterbalance design. We acquired 16 participants and tested them for both activities for 12 repetitions per body normalization on a standard Oculus Quest device. Afterwards, we created multiple feature sets and trained recurrent neural networks and multi-layer perceptrons with the data obtained from the first day of the study. We validated the models exclusively with data from the second day. Each validation was performed per activity and per type of normalization So that only data of the same kind was compared in total, we find a validation accuracy of up to 90 % for archery and 68 % for the bowling activity. We also found several significant increases in the identification rate that were imposed by the body normalizations where especially height normalization had a large impact. We also tested the acquired scores in the activities if the body normalization had any effect on performance and could not find significant differences there. Further, we asked the participants if they felt any change and only two participants mentioned this on their own during bowling and another two during archery. More participants realized the changes once we asked more detail, but only less than half of them realized the changes at all. To conclude, the data that can easily be collected with a standard off-the-shelf HMD is suitable for identification and contains highly specific information. When utilizing deep learning, data normalization is a best practice. A body normalization can further increase this effect and boost the identification accuracy significantly. Moreover, we have not seen a significant difference in user performance imposed by the body normalizations, which could be perceived only by less than half of our participants. Thank you for your attention.

Current approaches to identify users employ authentication schemes such as pins or passwords that are entered through handheld controllers and a virtual keyboard. Previous work has shown that these traditional forms of authentication are vulnerable to observation from a bystander who can easily spy on the hand gesture of the immersed VR user. Also, traditional authentication schemes that are currently widely used need yet another password to be remembered and interrupt the VR experience throughout their password prompt. In our work, we alternatively employ behavioral biometrics in combination with two task-based scenarios to identify the users of our VR application. Our scenarios mimic common VR activities such as bowling and archery and are probably only two of many possible examples. Users interact naturally with the scenarios and transparently in the background, the spatial data of the handheld controllers and the head-mounted display are captured by an identification system. The captured data is highly individual and it allows to determine the identity of the user through a deep learning classifier. At this point, it is important to note that these bowling or archery scenarios are not intended as a drop-in replacement for a password prompt. Instead, they enable an implicit interaction with an identification scheme where users behave naturally with the task but provide the required spatial data for the identification scheme on the fly. We moreover seek to better understand the role of behavioral biometrics in user identification and especially the connection to physiologic biometrics within them. A movement that intends to solve a task is first of course a form of behavior thus falls into behavioral biometrics. But the capabilities to move are also partly defined by for example the length of one's arms which means that physiology also plays a role. Virtual reality gives us the chance to explore this relationship as we try to eliminate the influence of physiologic biometrics by imposing a body normalization in VR. To do so, we impose a height normalization where each user has the same virtual height of 168 cm. Shorter or taller persons subsequently have their virtual height reduced or enlarged to match this exact value. We proceed in the same fashion with the arms of each user which is set to a span of 70 cm measured from the front of the head to the hand. A combination of both is also possible where both the arms and the height is normalized. We evaluated our approach in a lab-based user study using a repeated measures design. The study took place in two sessions where each session was conducted on a different day. Our independent variables were first scenario with two levels bowling vs. archery and second type of normalization with four levels following a counterbalance design. We acquired 16 participants and tested them for both activities for 12 repetitions per body normalization on a standard Oculus Quest device. Afterwards, we created multiple feature sets and trained recurrent neural networks and multi-layer perceptrons with the data obtained from the first day of the study. We validated the models exclusively with data from the second day. Each validation was performed per activity and per type of normalization So that only data of the same kind was compared in total, we find a validation accuracy of up to 90 % for archery and 68 % for the bowling activity. We also found several significant increases in the identification rate that were imposed by the body normalizations where especially height normalization had a large impact. We also tested the acquired scores in the activities if the body normalization had any effect on performance and could not find significant differences there. Further, we asked the participants if they felt any change and only two participants mentioned this on their own during bowling and another two during archery. More participants realized the changes once we asked more detail, but only less than half of them realized the changes at all. When utilizing deep learning, data normalization is a best practice. A body normalization can further increase this effect and boost the identification accuracy significantly. Moreover, we have not seen a significant difference in user performance imposed by the body normalizations, which could be perceived only by less than half of our participants. reference: Hello, my name is Daisuke Uryu, project lecturer at the Information Somatics Lab in the University of Tokyo. I'd like to introduce our research called Generating the Presence of Remote Moners, a Case Study of Funeral Webcasting in Japan. In the middle of June 2020, we had a sudden opportunity to webcast a funeral, connecting a funeral hall with believed relatives who were unable to attend in person. We were given this opportunity because our lab had a strong connection with the widow of the deceased. The deceased was a man named Takashi, who passed away at age 74. He was the second youngest of eight siblings. Only his two sisters were able to physically attend the funeral. The others decided not to join due to the risk of COVID-19 and their decreasing physical strength. Throughout this webcasting, we endeavored to transfer the presence of the siblings to the funeral hall. In particular, we aimed to allow them to feel as if they are really attending the funeral, holding farewell rituals, talking to the deceased and giving him farewell messages, and more generally, really existing in the same place and time with the other attendees. On the technical side, we prepared our original telepresence system, consisting of a 360 camera, microphone and speakers. We placed three of these modules in the hall. We envisioned that the remote attendees would virtually stand at circuited points in the hall. Unfortunately, however, our system did not work well when they were needed most. In addition, we found that neither the funeral hall nor the remote attendees' houses had the high-speed internet connection necessary to support 360-degree video streaming. As a result, the performance of our system was worse than Zoom on iPhones, not only in terms of image and sound quality, also in terms of mobility. Hence, the siblings remotely attending the funeral used our system at first, but ended up using Zoom almost all the time by the end of the funeral rites. From here, I'd like to explain what the siblings actually experienced during the funeral. A typical Japanese funeral takes two days. At the beginning of the first day, they were interested in and focused on information which is generally important at Japanese funerals. After the first day's rite, the widow, Takako, showed the deceased Takashi's face to the siblings via Zoom and thanked them. At the end of the second day, before that deceased departed for the crematorium, all physical attendees filled Takashi's casket with flowers. At this point, I held an iPhone close to the deceased's face with the speaker on to allow Takashi's older brother to say his farewells as physical attendees listened. In this case study, we, the authors, participated in funeral as Remote Funeral Conductors, RFCs, desk workers in charge of webcasts and telepresence at funerals. An RFC has to not only understand the technical aspects of webcasting and how to generate remote presences, but also know the sequences and manner of funerals and perform as mourners while conducting webcasting. In fact, we did so-called incentive rituals along with the other attendees because we were interpreted as being mourners in addition to being technical staff. Lastly, I'd like to share some implications for designers who are looking to produce funeral webcasts. The first is interactivity. We must design a way of exchanging a sense of presence between the physical and remote attendees. The second is cinematography. We must understand what to focus and capture at funerals. The third is that we must remember Remote Funeral Conductors. While this is still a developing role, designers should carefully consider the role they play when they produce funeral webcasts. Finally, the fourth is cultural differences. In this research, we reported a case in Japan. However, the role RFC plays and the factors important for generating a sense of presence may differ in different cultures. More work is required to discuss how valuable funeral webcasting could be provided all over the world. That's all. Thank you for listening.

reference: Hello, everyone. My name is Huawei Tu. Today I'm going to talk about my work, Distractor Effects on Crossing-Based Interactions. Crossing is an important paradigm for mouse input, stylus input, and direct finger touch. Unlike classic point-and-click interactions, the basic element of crossing interactions is to draw a stroke through the boundary of a target to trigger an action at frequency in the demo. Crossing-based interface is a visual-spatial-dependent gesture interface. Targets provide visual stimuli so that users can comprehend spatial information to cross the target. Let's take a look at the example on the right. Users draw a gesture to cross some menu items to trigger actions. The gesture itself doesn't carry much information. The expressiveness of crossing interactions doesn't rely on the stroke gesture. It depends on graphical targets that the stroke gesture crosses on the interface. In realistic interaction scenarios, intended targets are often surrounded by distractors. Selecting these targets is a typical task on crossing-based interfaces. The images show crossing-based interactions with distractors for checkboxes, radio buttons, dialog boxes, and menus in a goal-crossing framework. For example, when crossing item A in the checkbox, item B could be a distractor. Existing fundamental studies of user performance in crossing tasks generally didn't consider the presence of distractors around targets. Therefore, we conducted the first study to investigate distractor effects on crossing-based interaction. This study focuses on typical crossing-based interfaces with items aligned horizontally or vertically. We adopted six representative target-distractor spatial layouts in our experiment. We also developed six quantitative models for these layouts. First, let's take a look at direction-constrained crossing. This is a layout without distractors. Two vertical targets are each crossed from left to right. We used this layout as a baseline. We can see the distractors placed on the left of the target, on the right of the target, and also on the left and right of the target. Here we can see for amplitude-constrained crossing, which is to cross two horizontal targets with downward strokes. We consider the layout without distractors, distractors placed above the target, below the target, and also above and below the target. We conducted an experiment to investigate the effects of distractors on crossing-based interaction. The independent variables were target-distractor spatial layouts, target distance, target and distractor width, And spacing between targets and distractors. the dependent variables were completion time and the error rates. We found that the presence of distractors slowed down crossing interactions without significantly affecting target crossing accuracy. When target-distractor spacing increased to 7.25 mm, its effect on selection time would become insignificant. When spacing is smaller than 11.27 mm, crossing tasks with distractor interference can be regarded as pointing tasks, or a combination of pointing and crossing tasks. Regarding model fitting, compared to Fitts' law, our proposed models yielded better fits with the experiment data in all six layouts, with R-squared always greater than 0.95. Also, our models had smaller AIC than Fitts' law. Such results confirmed the advantage of our proposed models. In this study, we carried out the first investigation into distractor effects on crossing-based interactions. We developed six models for six crossing tasks with distractor interference. We also provided a set of general guidelines and practical suggestions. That's the end of my presentation. Thank you.

This is a joint work with Zui Gu and was advised by Jeffrey Tolsky at Cornell. Exploratory visual analysis platforms are key in data science, guiding users to deeper insights into the data with user-friendly visualization and summarization elements. Commercial tools such as Tableau and C2Data provide both analysis and data warehousing functions. Data analysis can be done through programming too. For example, one can easily use plotting libraries in Python to visualize desired data. However, beginners largely rely on commercial tools, which are not customized to their needs, and they must learn how to write plotting codes for more complex analysis. Worse, beginners have a high risk of losing track of what has been done and what's next when they are analyzing a large volume of data. Experts too, perhaps as a result of messy notebooks, they can lose track of what they've been doing as well. Imagine a data analyst is analyzing a IMDB dataset, exploring the relationship between actors, directors, and producers. One common approach a data analyst might take is to decompose the final task from the top to the down, such that they can start with some simple sub-goals and gradually achieve the goals. And ultimately, they will be able to answer the original question. This creates a tree-like structure in the analysis. On the other hand, EVA systems do not have exposure to this goal-oriented task decomposition. Instead, systems collect event log data or chronological sequences of time-step data and interface activities. Here is an example. In the event log E1, we have the data transformation information, where users set the year constraint to filter the data and visualize the selected data points through histograms. If EVA systems were to have access to users' goals and task direction, then they might offer better support and intervention. For example, they could provide users with next steps or present a summary of their exploration afterwards. But first, the question is how do we map the users' goal-directed structure to the log sequences the software gathers without promoting them? In our work, we propose a technique for segmenting analysis logs. We call that Tessera. Tessera estimates the similarity of two log events using data, cognitive, and temporal features in order to create blocks of goal-directed activity. For direct distance, we compare the intersected data points and focused attributes between two event logs with respect to the union of data points and focused attributes. For status distance, we measure the distributional similarities between data populations. This memory window dramatically reduces the computational cost, and also perhaps better aligns with the user's working memory and limited attentional resources. reference: With Oxfam Australia, we implemented the concept of programmable donations by trialling Smart Donations, a platform built on a private Ethereum blockchain that enables people to donate money to certain causes in response to real-world events. They could donate when an earthquake is detected, or when a petition receives signatures. They could donate when a cyclone forms, or when the temperature exceeds a monthly record, or whenever an activist tweets about refugees. The data comes directly from respected sources. For instance, earthquake insurance pulls data from the US Geological Survey that monitors international seismic events. Donors can choose a pre-set plan or customise a contract. They can set thresholds for seismic events, specify a region of the world, set one-off or recurring donations, set a time limit. If the conditions that the donor sets are not met by the time the contract expires, funds are returned to them. We trialled Smart Donations for eight weeks, with 86 participants, mostly in Australia, who set up contracts to be triggered at different thresholds and frequencies and over different durations. We collected analytics of their app usage, surveyed them before and afterwards, and interviewed 15 at the end. In this paper, we focus on participants' experiences of temporality. The inflexibility enforced by the contract prompts or intensifies emotional and moral ambiguities when donations do or do not result. When donations were made, users felt gratified and then guilty by the success of their contract design. When inactive contracts expire, users felt disappointed, then remorseful or relieved, and then frustrated or excited to set up another contract. But programming a Smart Donation does not simply mediate if a donation is made, but when it is made. Users are notified when the criteria they set are reached. For instance, for an earthquake contract, This user was 1st notified on the 29 September when an earthquake was detected in Mexico at 1021 Australia time. Participants had several distinct experiences of temporality while engaging with the app. An instant awareness of events and release of funds contributed to a sense of agency. Participants felt an immediacy in the tie between their donations to humanitarian crises and data about phenomena that caused them. This made them feel involved in emergency response. For some, the sense of involvement in causes was ongoing, and they suggested different ways that Smart Donations might map their donations to unfolding conditions and keep them aware of ongoing circumstances. Some differentiated between slow and rapid onset crises and said Smart Donations might sustain users' involvement in long-term change. reference: Hello everyone, and welcome to our paper talk on VisX Machina, an analysis of trust in human versus algorithmically generated visualization recommendations. My name is Rachel Zaron, and I'm Aspa Singhal, and we are currently master's students at the University of Maryland. This is joint work with Dr. Leilani Battle and Dr. Michael Correll. In this talk, we aim to provide a brief overview of our work, so without further ado, let's get started. Visualization recommendation systems are increasingly popular in both academic and industry visualization tools, such as Voyager's Related Views, Tableau's Show Me, and Power BI's Quick Insights panel. Given that visualization design can be a time-consuming and complex process, these systems attempt to help analysts by automatically generating expressive and informative visualizations. Despite the prevalence of these systems, it is unclear whether users use or even trust these features. Extensive work has explored user trust in algorithmic decision-making systems, and generally users trust human recommendations or decisions more than algorithmic ones, though some exceptions have been noted. However, it is unclear whether these insights translate to the realm of automated visualization recommendation systems. That leads us to our primary research question. How do existing preferences for human versus algorithmic recommendations affect perceptions of visualization recommendation quality? We focused our research on exploring how existing beliefs impact the ways that users assess visualization recommendations, especially in terms of relevance and utility. Our experimental setup was as follows. We recruited 114 participants from Prolific, a crowdsourcing website, to complete a survey. This survey first asked participants about their prior preferences for human or algorithmic recommendations. Then, participants were asked to evaluate two sets of recommendation panels. Lastly, participants had to choose a panel and to explain their rationale. Here is an example of the two recommendation panels shown to participants. One panel, on the left, is labeled as human-curated and the other as algorithmically generated. In reality, both were created by the authors. We created relevance metrics for panels based on the top five attributes of interest gathered in a pilot study, and then used those metrics to create panels of varying relevance. Now that we've covered the motivations and the experimental design, let's move on to the results. We first wanted to evaluate how prior preference related to subsequent choice. To demonstrate, let's say that this is our sample. When we solicited participant priors, we found that approximately 60 % preferred human recommendations. 10 % preferred algorithmic recommendations and the rest had no preference. However, when participants had to choose between panels that were labeled as human or algorithmically generated, we found that participants were split evenly between human or algorithmic panels. This suggests that prior preferences were not indicative of subsequent panel choice, which goes against our intuition. So, what were some of the reasons for this mismatch? We did a qualitative analysis of participants' free-text explanations of their decision-making process and found that most participants seemed to make their decision based on information that they thought was important, such as relevant attributes and relationships between attributes. We found two prominent information-forging strategies amongst participants, whom we named All-Rounders and Seekers. All-Rounders seemed to value panels based on the quality of the panel as a whole. For example, this could be the number of insightful visualizations. On the On the other hand, seekers seemed to hone in on the presence of a specific visualization or visualizations. That said, around a fifth of participants seemed to value the source of the panel when making their decisions. In these cases, participants often referenced common beliefs such as the notion of a human touch or that algorithms are more accurate than people. To conclude our presentation, let's discuss some of our takeaways. First, we found that prior preferences were not predictive of visualization recommendation choice. Instead, most users chose panels in a data-driven way, based on the attributes or relationships that they found to be most important. As a result, we suggest that designers should consider tailoring recommendations to the different information-forging strategies of users. We also found that the labeling of a visualization panel as human-curated or algorithmically-generated was influential to some participants, so we suggest that designers could address this through incorporating explanations into their recommendations. Thank you for listening to our presentation, and we're happy to answer questions now. We've provided our contact information and a link to our paper for further reading.

reference: Hello everyone, I am Leslie Wöhler from the Computer Graphics Lab at TU Braunschweig and I am happy to present our work towards understanding perceptual differences between genuine and face swap videos. First, let's look at face swap videos. For these videos, the face of an actor is replaced with the face of another person while keeping the movements and facial expressions of the original actor. As can be seen from the example, the quality of state-of-the-art face swaps is high and they can be unobtrusive or even undetectable for viewers. This offers great possibilities for creative scenarios but also leads to problematic situations where face swaps are used as a tool to create defamatory video material. Therefore, the detection of face swap videos is an important topic. Current methods to detect face swaps are based on image analysis systems and rely on the detection of specific artifacts. Different from these methods, humans are inherently very sensitive to faces and excel at facial recognition tasks. In our work, we aim to gain knowledge on the perception of face swap videos and investigate which features or artifacts are important for humans to recognize the forgeries. These insights can be used to improve detectors. We conducted three experiments to investigate the perception of face swap videos. These focused on eye tracking, the effect of video lengths on the detection accuracy and the conveyed emotions in face swap videos. First, we investigate eye tracking as it can be used to assess artifacts and could easily be integrated to face swap detection frameworks. In our experiment, participants freely watched face swaps and genuine videos with a duration of 60 seconds, where we recorded their eye movements. In this experiment, we investigate which facial areas attract the gaze of viewers. Our hypothesis was that especially artifacts like unnatural eye movements or overlapping facial contours would influence gaze. To better assess the impact of the artifacts, we used face swaps of high and low quality. Furthermore, we wondered whether participants would notice the face swaps without being informed about them beforehand. Therefore, we asked participants to freely report their impressions of video quality and artifacts. The results show a significant difference in gaze between genuine and face swap videos. In high-quality face swaps, fixations are more prominent on the nose and mouth than on the eyes. This indicates that eye tracking data could be used in pipelines to detect face swap videos. We also found that artifacts are not generally more salient if they are reported by participants. Especially artifacts on the facial contours biased the fixation behavior for low-quality face swaps, even though they were reported less often than artifacts on the eyes. Based on the three answers, we find that participants notice artifacts like blur or contour artifacts, but usually attribute them to bad video-quality and compression. In the first experiment, we used video durations of 60 seconds to give participants enough time to explore the video. In the second experiment, we wanted to assess whether the video length has an impact on the detection accuracy of participants. Here, participants were informed about the concept of face swapping before the experiment and for each video had to decide whether it was a face swap or a genuine person. We found no significant differences between the conditions. This may indicate that participants are able to quickly decide whether a video is genuine or not. Additionally, we found that participants were only able to detect around 25 % of face swaps. This shows that state-of-the-art face swap videos are convincing, even when participants know about the method beforehand. As our first two experiments generally showed that face swap videos are convincing, we decided to look into whether they are also able to present the same emotions and expressions as the original videos. For With this, we used short clips showing isolated emotions and expressions. Using these stimuli, we investigate whether the participants can correctly label the emotions in the videos. Additionally, the participants rank the sincerity and intensity of the displayed emotions on a Likert scale. Our results show that participants rate the emotions and face swaps similar to real videos. We did, however, find significant differences in the recognition of disgust. Further, disgust, cluelessness, disagree and thinking were rated differently for intensity and sincerity. This indicates that face swaps are overall able to convey the intended emotions and expressions, making them even more powerful. In our work, we found that participants are able to recognize artifacts in state-of-the-art face swaps, but only seldomly attribute them to manipulations. Furthermore, we investigated eye-tracking patterns and found significant differences in fixation behavior, which could be used to detect face swaps. reference: I'm Richmond Wong, a postdoc at the UC Berkeley Center for Long-Term Cybersecurity. And I'm Tanya Nguyen, a PhD student at the UC Berkeley School of Information. Our paper introduces Timelines, an accessible, low-barrier-to-entry design activity that facilitators can use to help participants think about technologies, social values, and ethics. The activity primarily uses the creation of news headlines and social media posts to create and explore possible worlds. The design activity is motivated by the problem that researchers, industry practitioners, and educators are increasingly looking for new ways to help their colleagues notice and discuss social values and ethical concerns as relevant to their technical practice. We were inspired by multiple approaches to values and design, including values and ethics advocates, value-sensitive design, design fiction, and scenario planning. We also conducted background interviews with UX professionals who act as values and ethics advocates, and they expressed a need for tools to help educate their colleagues about the relevance of values to their work. While a lot of existing work focuses on creating values interventions within the design process, we design timelines to be an activity that can occur outside the design process. A skilled facilitator, like a values advocate or educator, can use it to engage their colleagues. We designed timelines to be lightweight in terms of materials, using things like a whiteboard, index cards, and sticky notes. We used an iterative approach where we play-tested multiple versions in different settings. We'll quickly walk through the activity steps. First, participants choose or are provided a technical artifact and a social context that they will be exploring. Second, participants generate a range of direct and indirect stakeholders, drawing on value-sensitive design. This is done early on, as we found that this works as a good brainstorming warm-up activity. Third, participants generate a range of news headlines depicting how the artifact gets adopted, appropriated, and contested in multiple ways. Fourth, participants group their headlines into chains that create different stories, drawing on design fiction practices. They place these on what we call the timeline's triangle. Inspired by the futures cone, the present is represented at the narrow point on the left, while multiple futures are suggested as the triangle broadens. This temporal aspect helps participants think about secondary and tertiary effects of their artifact, and consider multiple ways in which the artifact might get adopted and appropriated. Fifth, participants return to their stakeholders from earlier. Participants create social media posts from the perspectives of different stakeholders experiencing the events depicted in the headlines. This then leads to a general group discussion. We'll briefly mention a couple important reflections, and the paper provides a more detailed discussion. Using familiar forms like news headlines and social media posts are ways to make the design activity approachable to a broad range of people. The activity's seeming simplicity is intentional to try to allow timelines to be used in a range of settings, such as classrooms, workshops, research groups, or product teams. However, the activity also foregrounds several important ways of thinking about values and ethics. We highlight to participants that seemingly divergent or conflicting stories of adoption and use that they create can actually happen in the same world and at the same time, reflecting that the same technologies in real life can be used in multiple and unintended ways. We also try to steer people away from creating completely dystopian or utopian worlds by having them create stories involving both positive and negative headlines. The focus here is on more complex and sometimes conflicting experiences that can arise in everyday use of technologies. The news headlines depict changes that happen at scale, helping explore possible worlds at a macro level, while the social media posts are rooted in more micro-level, everyday-situated experiences. Together, this reflects how the experience of values and ethics is affected both by broad, shared, large-scale infrastructures, as well as by local situated conditions. We also note that timelines is partial as a design intervention. Our experience facilitating timelines leads us to recognize the importance of the facilitator in helping prompt participants to reflect. Timelines is designed to be used in situations where there is a skilled facilitator. While the paper is based on our experiences facilitating the activity, future work might investigate how others might facilitate it. Thank you to our colleagues, the reviewers, and our participants. You can find activity resources, facilitation guides, and the paper at tinyurl.com.

reference: Hello everybody, my name is Melissa Rogerson and I'm presenting this research on behalf of my co-authors Lucy Sparrow and Martin Gibbs. When we think about tabletop gaming and tabletop games, we typically think about these very situated material practices. There's lots of paper, there are physical screens, there's co-location around a table and there are dice and miniatures and hand-drawn maps and probably a good collection of wooden cubes. But increasingly we're seeing digital tools coming into this space that are used not only to support this play, but to enact it. Today I'm going to talk to you about hybrid digital board games, which are part of this shift in how the boundaries of traditional tabletop gaming are being expanded by a whole range of digital tools. This work is supported by GameInLab, an industry-funded not-for-profit organisation dedicated to supporting research into tabletop games. And this research really started with board games like this, The Lord of the Rings Journeys in Middle Earth, which used digital tools as a necessary part of the tabletop game experience. This game incorporates an app which controls what goes out on the board, so what the map looks like, what creatures live there, and it also takes on the role of the various evil forces that the players need to defeat. And looking at these games brought us to this definition of hybrid digital board games, which reflects that these games are a compound artefact that necessarily combines a physical and a digital element. They're not one or the other, so it's a form of material hybridity rather than hybridity of genre or of story. And we wanted to understand how digital tools contribute to this material hybridity. To understand this space, we started with an exploratory online survey, collecting examples of hybrid digital board games and stories about people's experiences with them. And then I interviewed 18 people working in the board game industry. And this wasn't, you know, your friend down the road who's designed a new Monopoly knockoff. These are people who are very influential and respected in both the hobbyist community and who've had really significant commercial success as well. We started to hold some critical play sessions where we would play a game and then reflect on how it was using digital tools, but they were interrupted by COVID, although we did manage to play some at our homes during lockdown. And lastly, we used card sorting techniques, affinity mapping techniques to group and sort our ideas and to test those groupings. Building on all of that data, we developed a model where we conceptualise 41 different functions that digital technology performs in hybrid digital board games. This is the overall view of the model. And in our paper, we describe each of these and we give examples of where the function is used in commercial games. Here you can see the eight top level domains that we identified, timing, randomising, housekeeping, informing, storytelling, remembering, calculating and teaching. And here's a breakdown of the timing domain, for example. So it's about counting down time, but also about tracking and limiting the time available to the players and initiating and coordinating events. So you can see there's really quite a diversity of functions that we've identified, but also a really strong logic that holds each domain together. And our paper goes into each of these in detail with examples of games that use the features. So for example, the board game XCOM keeps track of time, but also prompts players when it's time for different roles to take an action. The housekeeping domain is about choosing and tracking components and configurations, including players. So in the search for planet X, for example, the game selects or generates a solar system which includes particular objects in particular hidden locations that the players need to deduce. And of course, our paper doesn't contain exhaustive lists of all the games that use these functions, but rather illustrative examples to assist people to understand what those functions are useful for. The model is really a contribution. in itself. It sets up a language and a structure for discussing these different tools. It's. It's valuable for us as researchers, but it's also really valuable for people who are working in this novel design space. And we've had some fantastic feedback from the people we've shared it with so far. So we're confident that the value extends beyond academia to board game and even digital game designers. Thank you so much for your time. I'm really happy to take any questions either here or offline.

reference: Hello everyone, I'm Dajun Deng from Zhejiang University. In this work, we propose a framework for interactive data annotation of racket sports videos. Racket sports, such as tennis, table tennis, and badminton, have similar hierarchical game structures. These sports are popular all over the world, attracting the focus of millions of data analysts and sports fans. For data analysis, optical tracking systems, such as HotEye, can provide precise trajectory data. However, they are expensive and only deployed in a limited number of top games. For most data analysts and sports fans, a popular choice is broadcast video, which covers different games and supports historical data analysis. More importantly, they are accessible to the public. In recent years, more and more computer vision models have been used to automatically acquire data from videos. However, automatic data acquisition might fail in some cases, when there are occlusions or blurring. In addition, the acquisition of some information may require expert knowledge, such as technique and tactic. Therefore, to acquire clean and correct data, we have to introduce human efforts and annotate the data with human-computer interaction. To obtain general requirements on the data, we conducted an expert interview and a survey for general sports fans. For the experts, we collected their analytical tasks and relevant data in their own domains. For the sports fans, we summarized the tasks they are interested in when watching game videos. Based on the interview and the survey, we proposed our interactive annotation methodology, Event Anchor. For the object-level data, we used computer vision models to automatically extract the data from the videos. Based on the object-level data, we derived the event-level data, and further annotated contest-level data through interactions. In this work, we implement a prototype of Event Anchor for table tennis to verify the usability of the framework. We extract the object-level data, such as score, scene, ball, and player pose with computer vision models. Then, we obtain events by estimating the moment of score changing, scene changing, the ball hitting and ball bouncing. For the contextual information, we designed two customized hotboxes for interactive data annotation. Here is our interaction design for anchor calibration. Video will stop at the anchor, and users can control the timeline with a calibration box, and revise the spatial position of the anchor by clicking on the screen. We recruited eight table tennis fans to annotate when and where the ball hit the table. From the results, we discovered that ETT is significantly better than the baseline in task time and temporal error, but has a slightly larger spatial error than the baseline. For contest addition, the hotbox supports annotating categorical data. The data can be organized in multiple levels to improve efficiency we. We recruited eight table tennis analysts to find the rallies where ETT used the tactic of serve and attack and won the rally. The results show that ETT is significantly better than the baseline in task time, but ETT only has slightly higher precision and similar record compared to the baseline. In conclusion, we proposed EventAnchor, a multiple-level video data annotation framework for rapid sports. EventAnchor is scalable, which supports low-level and high-level data annotation for sports fans and data analysis. In addition, it is cheap and accessible compared to optical tracking systems. Thank you for listening.

reference: When we think of dance in its most basic form, we think of it as a way of artistic expression through body movement. However, when we think of technology in dance, the image is less clear than, for instance, the use of technology in painting or in music. The reason is that the tool of expression in dance, which is the abstract movement of the human body, cannot be simply captured in digital formats without losing its essence. Intrigued by this unique challenge, we conducted a systematic review on the literature of dance and choreography in HCI for the past two decades. My name is Qiu Shizhou, and I will present an overview of our findings on behalf of my co-authors. In this review, we discuss the literature from two perspectives. First, 1st, we focus on the body as the instrument of artistic expression in dance. and look at how technology contributed to the recognition and analysis of the expressive qualities in dance movement. Then, we look at how technology has influenced the practice of dance-making in existing case studies. So, what is the body in the context of dance? From an HCI perspective, the dancer's body is a physical interface that can be accessed and extended through technology. We can read the bodily signals through physiological sensors to directly control multimedia stage effects and to provide context for further augmentation of the performance. We can also write to the body through its underlying sensory neural system to alter the felt experience of the dancer. Physical costumes can change the dancer's perception of their own bodies and redefine the possibility of movement. A similar effect can be achieved with visual and acoustic effects, which influence the dancer's lived experience on stage. Recognizing and analyzing the expressive movement qualities has been another direction of the research in dance. Learning from existing frameworks for categorizing movement qualities, such as the Laban Movement Analysis, previous works have attempted to automatically detect movement qualities and convert them to visual output and to help with choreographic training and education. Equipped with advanced technologies such as motion tracking and machine learning, HCI dance researchers are still faced with a major challenge of quantifying the kinesthetic creativity, the felt experience of the dancers, and expressive movement qualities, channeled through the embodied perception from the choreographers to the audience. As a result, previous works have employed alternative approaches to the body and its abstract movement apart from the direct bodily sensing and motion capturing. One of the promising trends of those approaches is the use of virtual and physical agents to accompany the dancers' performance while forming new bodily relationships on stage. For instance, neural networks have been used to create virtual body extensions that react to different features in the movement of the dancers. Robotic agents have also been explored extensively, including drones that respond to specific types of movement from human dancers, and autonomous agents that collaboratively improvise with the human dancers. The other perspective in our review is to look at how technology has influenced the creative process of dance in practice. Those works include novel tools for choreographers, such as the sketching interfaces that help reflect abstract choreographic ideas, and recording and annotating tools used across the development process of a dance project. The common conclusion from those works is that the creative process of dance is highly complex and idiosyncratic, and the introduction of technology may produce unexpected impact. For instance, while choreographic tools with online user interface makes communication between choreographers and dancers more easily accessible, they also cause disturbance in the creative process, due to the change of context from face-to-face rehearsals to the online text communications. Overall, the challenges and opportunities reflected in the field of dance during the past 20 years contributed a wealth of knowledge that benefit broader HCI research in the context of creativity support and beyond. The focus on the lived experience of the body and the attention to the diverse and specific cultural context in dance embody the characteristics of what we call the third wave shift of HCI. The unique offerings in HCI dance research, such as the bodily improvisation with robotic agents, and the attempts to reflect abstract movement qualities using computational tools, provoke future works in HCI to rethink the relationships between human experience and technology. Thank you for watching, and we invite you to read the paper for more details.

reference: Hi, I'm Janet Johnson, a PhD student at UC San Diego, and I'll be giving you a brief overview on our paper that focuses on referencing in collaborative mixed reality. Mixed reality is a spatial medium that allows physical and digital objects to coexist and interact with one another. It is especially suited to enable remote guidance for physical tasks, and that's the collaboration setting we focus on in this paper. This is where you have a remote helper guiding a local worker through manipulating objects in the real world. If we break down this example, the reference has two parts. The first part is where the person initiating the reference specifies what is being referred to, and the second part specifies where the referenced object is and serves to help others understand the reference. More efficient forms of referencing, like diaxes, where one word conveys both what and where, Also require the person initiating the reference to know where the object is, and so spatial information, or an awareness of spatial relationships in the task space. Is fundamental to the helper's ability to direct attention to an object. Now mixed reality is a technology that is inherently aware of the environment it's in. And so in our paper we conduct a factorial design experiment to study and discuss two specific opportunities that it presents to make referencing easier. The first one is to explicitly provide helpers with relevant spatial information. For this, we built a 2D map for helpers that represents the different objects and the worker in the task space. We also created a list interface as the version with no spatial information. The presence or absence of spatial information became our within-subjects factor in the experiment and answered whether 2D representations of spatial information will be enough to support referencing. The second opportunity mixed reality provides is to automatically guide workers to referenced objects. Here you can see object 2 is highlighted for the worker when the helper clicks on it. We built a HoloLens application that used visual cues to dynamically direct the worker's attention towards objects in the task space when they were referenced. And the presence or absence of mixed reality guidance became our between-subjects factor and helped us understand whether it could enhance performance or reduce the effort required for remote guidance. Now, given that the helper's need for spatial information is primarily used to direct workers' attention to objects, one of the questions we had was if helpers still needed this spatial information when mixed reality guidance is present. Our mixed factorial experiment also helps answer this by understanding how the presence of mixed reality guidance impacts the need for spatial information. We had 40 participants complete a simple task that isolated referencing. Workers wore a Microsoft HoloLens and helpers guided them using either the map or the list in addition to a first-person view. On whether explicitly providing spatial information works, the answer is yes. It decreased task load and allowed helpers to make richer references. And notably, it made it significantly easier to use spatial diaxis despite it being a cognitively expensive process in remote collaboration settings. Mixed reality guidance, on the other hand, decreased task load and increased task performance and the use of diactic pronouns. Something we did not expect was that it also allowed for alternate forms of acknowledgement and task parallelization. As per our last question, mixed reality guidance did indeed impact how much spatial information helpers needed and often made spatial information superfluous. An example impact of this is in the crossover interaction you see here for performance, where in the absence of mixed reality guidance, the map was more effective and in its presence, the list was more effective. You will find in-depth explanations and more information about the impact and affordances of spatial information and guidance across a variety of measures in our paper. Mixed reality is already used in domains where expertise is distributed, from car repairs and factory maintenance to surgery. We expect the findings in our paper to help build more optimized remote guidance systems. More specifically, in helping workers understand references, mixed reality guidance is a way to partially offload the referential process to the system and lower the overall communication effort. The paper further outlines what types of tasks and settings could benefit from this. While features like immersive 3D reconstructions can theoretically make referencing as easy as it is in face-to-face collaborations, they limit access to remote experts in very specific environments. Both the methods outlined in the paper allow for experts to provide rich guidance using everyday devices too. Designers and developers also have more freedom to choose the technology that best suits the physical tasks they support. And overall, this makes expertise which is often scarce, a more scalable and accessible resource. thank you.

reference: We present Patchprov, supporting improvisational design practices for modern quilting. The modern quilting movement has changed the process of making quilts and their appearance. One technique, improvisational quilting, often results in colorful, bold geometric designs that can look like some modern paintings. Improvisation is a well-known technique in music and acting, and much of the prior work on improv in the HCI community emphasizes supporting brainstorming or the performing arts. In improv quilting, spontaneity is important, but the process does not have the urgency of live performance. This means that a system to support it does not necessarily require real-time responsiveness and must account for longer-term reflection. We wanted to know if we could design a system to support this improvisational design approach. Whereas the process of making a traditional quilt involves following a mostly linear process, improv quilting is more iterative. Quilters start with some design inspiration and then cycle through design, cutting fabrics, and sewing the final piece. From reading several popular books on improv quilting, we identified key properties of the technique and its challenges. These challenges include getting started, getting stuck, costly experimentation, and recording process. We set out to design a system, Patchprov, to address these challenges. Our system needs to assist the user with starting a design, help users avoid indecision, promote reflection, and capture the overall approach or process by which a design is produced. To use Patchprov, a quilter starts by cutting fabric, working directly in the usual medium. They then load the piece to create the digital representation in Patchprov automatically. They can then use this digital representation to cut and lay out pieces digitally without having to waste precious fabrics. They can then add pieces to the design. Note that as they make changes digitally, items are getting added to the to-do list, which keeps track of this experimentation. Then, as the user cuts and sews real fabrics, they can check off these items on the to-do list to make sure that what they see in Patchprov matches what they see in their sewing studio. And they can see how their design looks repeated by adjusting the rows and columns in the layout guides. As you may have noticed, the user is taking steps in both the digital and physical environments, and this can cause the two representations to become out of sync. First, as we just saw, the user may update the digital representation without cutting or sewing any real fabric. To keep track of these digital changes, we use what we call a process graph. For more information on our approach, please see our paper. Second, in cases where the user gets out of sync in the physical world, they can just load the new pieces into the system to replace any pieces that are out of date. To evaluate Patchprov, we invited four quilters to create a quilt block in a two-hour remote study. They were required to upload at least one photo, but were otherwise free to choose their workflow. Here are the blocks that they designed. We found that Patchprov helped quilters with many of the key challenges identified in improv quilting, particularly low-cost experimentation, with one participant noting, I've gotten stuck with the pieces that I've made in the past, being scared to try anything because I only have this much fabric and I don't want to cut it up. So being able to take a picture of that fabric would definitely help bridge that artist's block when I'm not quite sure how to proceed and your materials are limited. Quilters also appreciated abstracting away some material and construction constraints to focus on the visual design. And based on these insights from designing Patchprov, we think that there are some questions to consider when looking to support improvisation. How tied the digital and physical representations need to be, and how much of an active role the tools should play in the design process, likely depend on the creation time and physical scale of the finished artifact. We chose to take a lightweight approach, providing relatively few design suggestions, but there are likely other domains in which a more active approach may work well. We have shown the possibility of supporting improvisational design for quilting, and we hope that our project will encourage future work on supporting improvisation in quilting and beyond. Thank you for watching our talk.

reference: Hi, I'm Franziska Tachner from TU Wien and today I'm presenting our paper Unaccompanying Youth and Mental Health Technologies, a social-ecological approach to understanding and designing. Unaccompanying youth are young asylum seekers and refugees who are unaccompanied by other relatives. They struggle in accessing appropriate mental health resources in spite of their high need for mental health support. Research increasingly shows technology can support accessing and engaging with mental health services. However, there is a lack of understanding of how to design technological mental health support specifically for refugee and displaced communities such as unaccompanied migrant youth. We investigated how to design technology-driven interventions to integrate as mental health resources in unaccompanied migrant youth's everyday life. We conducted two series of co-design workshops with in total 12 unaccompanied migrant youth in Austria. As part of this study, we were particularly interested in how different socio-ecological systems support or hinder the unaccompanied migrant youth's usage of mental health technologies. According to a theory on socio-ecological resilience promotion, a well-working interplay of different socio-ecological systems is important for successful mental health promotion. In In our study, we identified different socio ecological systems that interplay with unaccompanied migrant youth's usage of the mental health technologies. We identified that the macrosystem, namely legal policies, influences all systems negatively. We also identified different types of microsystems. We grouped them into the everyday living situation, namely other unaccompanied migrant youth at their accommodations, social contacts who are not physically close and with whom the participants stay in contact via their mobile phones, and persons of trust, such as volunteers acting as mentors and anonymous online support contacts. We also learned that chronic systemic developments, such as changes in the way the social support structure and personal developments over time, influences the experience of using these mental health technologies. The interplay of different systems in the microsystem, the everyday living situation, is exemplary for the different interplays in this context. Here, the macrosystem, namely policies and asylum system, influences the social and physical factors of this microsystem. The macrosystem determines unhealthy daily routines of unaccompanied migrant youth, assigns accommodations where youth live with other unaccompanied migrant youth who have similar unhealthy daily structures, and where every resident lacks technical infrastructure and space to engage with the mental health technologies. In these accommodations, the physical factors, such as lack of private space, and the social factors, such as social perception and the pressure by peers, ties into each other. Participants expressed concerns that engaging in mental health interventions or changing routines could be perceived negatively by their peers and that their everyday social contacts might gain access to their mobile phones and private notes in their mental health applications. We argue for the pivotal need for accounting for the macrosystem's influence when designing mental health technologies for this population, as this influence fundamentally impacts all other systems. The technological interventions need to tailor the timing, the content and means of delivery to fit with the social and physical factors of the current microsystem and be designed for trade-offs. The youth need to be able to use the mental health technologies even if the social and physical factors of the microsystem are restrictive. Mental health technologies need to support the youth in managing the different influences and roles of the different microsystems, for instance, by supporting accessing and exchanging with different types of persons of trust and managing competing tensions caused through social media apps through which unaccompanied migrant youth stay in contact with physically distant social contacts. We also need to design mental health technologies to be adaptable to ongoing changes and be adaptable to be able to move with the unaccompanied migrant youth. We cannot design technologies for mental health of unaccompanied migrant youth without supporting ways of acknowledging and countering unjust macrosystem factors. We need to explore how these technological solutions could make activist groups more proximal within unaccompanied migrant youth's microsystem to advocate for change. We need to design towards societal transformation that would enable a more socially just macrosystem that in turn contributes to a facilitative environment in which unaccompanied migrant youth can apply mental health technologies as resources. Thank you for your attention. You find more information about the research methods, the interplay between systems and unaccompanied migrant youth's usage of mental health technologies and detailed design suggestions in the paper. And please do not hesitate to contact us if you have any questions or comments.
