reference: Hello, welcome to this talk about our paper, learning to automate chart layout configurations using crowdsourced paired comparison. My name is Aoyu Wu, and this is a joint work from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and Microsoft Research. Our motivation, existing charting software or libraries such as Excel and VegaLite, often use predefined heuristics to generate styles of charts, which are often suboptimal. People need to repeatedly adjust different style parameters, which, however, is time-consuming and challenging, especially for those without design backgrounds. To address this problem, we aim to provide a machine learning approach to automate chart configurations by learning from human feedback. This requires collecting training dataset consisting of charts and human-given scores. However, humans often find it difficult to give an accurate score, and the scoring skills among different participants can be different, that constrains the reliability of the resulting dataset. To address this problem, we ask participants to compare two charts and choose the one that they prefer. Comparison is relatively easier than scoring a single chart. To be more specific, we generate training dataset through crowdsourced paired comparison. First, we generate comparison pairs, which are charts encoding the same data but with different parameters. Then, we ask participants to choose a better one from a pair, And if all participants agree with each other, we mark the better chart as a positive and the other as negative. There is also a desk reject step where we mark charts violating a set of design rules as the negative in a pair. Thirdly, we train a machine learning model to learn human preference from paired comparison data. And finally, we propose two sampling strategies to improve the efficiency, and the details can be found in our paper. Here comes a machine learning model, which is a semi-structure that consists of two identical scoring networks working on the pair. The goal is to predict a higher score for the positive chart in the pair than the negative one. We evaluate our machine learning approach on two datasets collected from two experiments. In the first experiment, we have three parameters of a bar chart, and in the second experiment we extend the parameter to six. The results show that our method outperforms the baseline approach rank SVM and And handcrafted matrix for layout quantities such as whitespace and scale, that said. handcrafted matrix are insufficient in capturing human preference. With the machine learning model, now we could recommend chart configurations. In two user studies, we show that our method can at least achieve human-level performance and outperform the default styles in Excel and Vega-Lite and outperform the random configurations. We reflect on our implications. First, do not trust the default values. Psychological studies show that the default effect that human can blindly trust the default values. However, default values are made to be acceptable but not best for all cases. Also, we discuss how to improve aesthetic quality of visualizations from a data-driven perspective which is relatively under-researched in visualization recommendation system. Besides, we note the debate over what is beautiful is good. Aesthetic chart layout configurations might have negative influence over the perception that warrants future research. For more details, please refer to our paper and all of our source code is made public in this GitHub.

Advances in generative machine learning techniques, such as GANs, introduce a new way to create media. These networks are trained on large data sets to generate new data samples that possibly could have been drawn from the original data set. Though GANs are complex technical algorithms, they have real-world implications for younger students. reference: Hi, my name is Daniel. I have a question for you. What have you done to help others in difficult times? And why did you help? In our paper Sharing Heartbeats, we explore the lived experience of volunteers during the pandemic. We investigate motivations of citizen scientists in times of crisis, and provide recommendations for future crisis informatics and citizen science projects. To control and mitigate the spread of the coronavirus, many countries developed digital tools. One of them, the Corona Datenspende app, was released by the Robert Koch Institute, the German public health institute, in early April 2020. The app lets citizen scientists share data from fitness trackers and smartwatches. By analyzing heart rate and physical activity on a large scale, the goal is to predict COVID-19 hotspots. It has been promoted through government authorities and public Public Broadcasting news, as of September 2020, more than half a million people downloaded the app. and registered a wearable device. To find out what motivates people, we analyzed 464 reviews from the Apple App Store and the Google Play Store. Additionally, we conducted 10 interviews with 6 female and 4 male users. Based on our analysis, we created a model of interaction with the app. It revealed that after having decided to use the app, both positive and negative emotions were evoked. They led to either reassessing the motivations or reassessing the app, resulting in two outcomes. Either dropouts, that means people removed the app or stopped donating, or continued use. And this continued use or persistence was of special interest for us. It originated from collective motives, as highlighted by a review in the App Store that says the users had not thought they would share such intimate details, but now want to help statisticians to understand their data, which protects family members at risk and friends. We noticed that users tried to serve a greater good, showed social responsibility and that they were really supporting this cause. Those collective motives made the citizen scientists overcome technical difficulties, for example when they waited for app updates that supported their devices. This became apparent when users updated their reviews. Other contributors provided help to peers in their reviews, for example referring to the FAQs on the app website, transforming the review section into a platform for peer support. So how can we use our results to make future citizen science apps better? First, we recommend that users need to be made aware of the societal relevance of the project. In the case of the Corona Datenspende app, this has been highlighted through the authority of the Robert Koch Institute and news reports. Second, users should receive fine-grained information about the value of their donated data. The app did not inform users about which exact data they were sharing and how it was contributing to the mitigation efforts. Third, we propose that volunteers take the role of community managers to address some of the communication shortcomings in the project. Thank you for your attention.

reference: Hello everyone, my name is Dylan Gaines from Michigan Technological University, and I will be presenting our work Enhancing the Composition Task in Text Entry Studies, Eliciting Difficult Text and Improving Error Rate Calculation. It is common for studies evaluating text entry interfaces to use tasks where users transcribe short and memorable phrases. However, this task is artificial and not necessarily representative of the way a user might use an interface in the real world. Short phrases are too simple and may not exercise error correction or prevention features. Long phrases can be difficult for participants to remember, and showing a phrase to a participant while they are entering text can cause their attention to shift between the interface and the referenced text, which would not occur in a real-world task. Additionally, language is constantly changing with slang and proper names, which creates the need for composition tasks in which the participants invent their own messages to type. An added bonus is that composition tasks can be conducted in any language. In our paper, we show that users can modulate the difficulty of their compositions based on simple instructions, and that their more difficult compositions exercise more error-corrective interface features. We also confront the problem that compositions lack a definitive reference text, which is needed to calculate error rate. We compare three different methods of obtaining this reference text. In our first study, we provided simple instructions in two counterbalanced conditions. In the easy condition, we asked participants to invent a message, choose a message that would likely have no autocorrect errors if typed on a mobile device. In the hard condition, we asked participants to invent a message, choose a message that would likely have one or more autocorrect errors if typed on a mobile device. Both instructions also informed participants that they could tap and hold to lock in characters, which was one of the error prevention features of our interface. Doing this would prevent the probabilistic decoder from changing or deleting that particular letter in the autocorrect process. Some example participant compositions in the easy condition included, the leaves are already falling here, and finally done with the easy one. In the hard condition, some examples included, the USS Zimbald is a new class of destroyer, and the Taj Mahal is amazing. The results from study 1 showed that phrases composed in the hard condition took longer, were typed slower, and utilized the lock letter feature more often. Each of these graphs depicts the difference between conditions on one of four metrics. Starting on the left, we found that hard compositions had a higher and more variable task time than the easy compositions. Moving to the second graph, we discovered similar distributions of entry rates, but significantly lower for hard compositions. Next, we found a drastically higher use of the lock letter feature in hard compositions, coupled with barely any use in easy compositions. In the final graph, we can see the error rate was slightly higher in hard compositions, but this difference was not significant. Study 2 used similar instructions as in study 1, but this time they were mixed together instead of in distinct conditions. We found similar results to the previous study. Additionally, the hard compositions in this study had a higher out-of-vocabulary rate, a higher error rate, and more use of the error prevention features than the easy compositions. The error prevention features in this study consisted of the same lock letter feature as the previous study, but also word suggestion slots, one of which contained the literal characters that the user had typed, essentially locking all characters. More details are provided in our paper. In these two studies, we also compared three different ways of obtaining the participants' reference text. In study 1, we asked participants to type their compositions on a laptop after they finished entering each one on our interface. We then corrected obvious typographical mistakes in the reference texts after the study. In study 2, we asked participants to dictate their intended text to the experimenter once they finished typing it on our interface, clarifying any difficult-to-spell words. For both of these studies, we also used crowdsourcing to try to generate participants' intended text from their final inputs. Our crowdsourcing procedure was based on previous work from two of our authors, and more details can be found in the original paper. Ultimately, we found that there were trade-offs between each method. The crowdsourced method required no further participant action, while the laptop method required the most. However, we found that in both studies, the crowdsourced method underestimated the error rate compared to using the participant-provided references. The final trade-off is that the crowdsourcing dictated methods are easier to use in a wide variety of situations, while the laptop method is not as easy for eyes-free or virtual reality situations where the participant may not be able to see the laptop. To recap, we showed that people can modulate the difficulty of their compositions based on simple instructions. This can be used to evaluate novel interface error correction features. We also showed the differences and trade-offs between three different methods for obtaining users' intended composition text. Thank you very much for your time, and we would also like to thank Google, the National Science Foundation, and the Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council for supporting this work.

Long phrases can be difficult for participants to remember, and showing a phrase to a participant while they are entering text can cause their attention to shift between the interface and the referenced text, which would not occur in a real-world task. Additionally, language is constantly changing with slang and proper names, which creates the need for composition tasks in which the participants invent their own messages to type. An added bonus is that composition tasks can be conducted in any language. In the hard condition, we asked participants to invent a message, choose a message that would likely have one or more autocorrect errors if typed on a mobile device. Both instructions also informed participants that they could tap and hold to lock in characters, which was one of the error prevention features of our interface. Doing this would prevent the probabilistic decoder from changing or deleting that particular letter in the autocorrect process. Some example participant compositions in the easy condition included, the leaves are already falling here, and finally done with the easy one. In the hard condition, some examples included, the USS Zimbald is a new class of destroyer, and the Taj Mahal is amazing. Starting on the left, we found that hard compositions had a higher and more variable task time than the easy compositions. Moving to the second graph, we discovered similar distributions of entry rates, but significantly lower for hard compositions. Next, we found a drastically higher use of the lock letter feature in hard compositions, coupled with barely any use in easy compositions. In the final graph, we can see the error rate was slightly higher in hard compositions, but this difference was not significant. reference: Hi everyone, my name is Kathrin Gerling and together with my co-author Katja Spiel I carried out a theoretical examination of the accessibility of virtual reality for physically disabled people. In our paper, we argue that ableist assumptions about human bodies underpin the design of the current generation of VR systems. More concretely, we leverage disability studies, most importantly the theory of the minority body by Barnes. This is a postmodern theory of disability that defines being disabled as simply something that makes you a minority or a way of having a minority body that can, depending on the situation, be either something that is good, neutral or something that is bad. We also work with Campbell's concept of the corporeal standard which describes a non-disabled supposedly ideal human body that most of us don't have. We combine these theories with surrogate body theory by Foss which originates from film studies and postulates that viewers lend the effective expressiveness of their body to the film and intersubjectively embody the so-called surrogate body. We previously applied surrogate body theory to entertainment technology to analyze its key elements including aspects such as the physical distance between players and hardware that is, how closely the player's body is intertwined with it and the type of actions that can be lent to the game, meaning the actions that the player is expected to perform. In the context of the work presented here, the combination of these theoretical perspectives allows us to systematically review the different layers of VR systems with respect to access for disabled people. Our results show that the design of the current generation of VR prioritizes non-disabled people with respect to bodily involvement and the shape that interaction paradigms take. For example, many wheelchair users would find bodily involvement of the legs or the trunk unsuitable, people who interact with one arm would not appreciate the expectation of VR systems that users involve two arms, and individuals who experience pain might find it difficult to involve their body over longer periods of time. While these examples may seem obvious and there are of course more nuanced examples of how physical disability is difficult to reconcile with bodily involvement expected by VR, our examples do illustrate the extent to which the normative assumptions about how human bodies will be able to support interaction are ingrained in VR technology. We also observe a lack of consideration for the integration of assistive devices or the need of people to engage with VR in a variety of environments. For example, holding two controllers may not be suitable if a person also uses a cane, interacting with the controllers may not be possible while propelling a manual wheelchair, and the headset may not comfortably fit with the layout of the headrest of a powered wheelchair. All of these elements contribute to increased physical distance between the body and the hardware, either because actual physical distance is temporarily increased, for example when placing controllers in one's lap to propel a wheelchair, or because the union between body and surrogate body is interrupted by uncomfortable, overly present hardware. Hence, our analysis suggests that VR, in its current shape, does not attend to the experiences of people with physical disability. For most dimensions of the surrogate body, physical disability results in what Barnes would call a local BAD, limiting the accessibility of the current generation of consumer VR technology. We therefore conclude that the current design of VR technology propagates the corporeal standard and needs to be regarded as a technology with underlying ableist assumptions that diminish the experiences of disabled people. Moving ahead, we suggest to focus on design strategies that appreciate the diversity of bodies as a starting point for design. This would allow us to shift from a paradigm of making accessible for to the perspective of creating for, and thereby we would have the opportunity to account for disabled people from the very start of system development. More generally, this means that we need to take our responsibility as technology developers and HCI researchers. Too often, we seem to be surprised by the inaccessibility of body-centric technology, for example when we observe it in evaluations, when we should have been able to reflect on accessibility issues at the very beginning of the design process. Thank you very much, and please read our full paper for a more detailed and nuanced analysis and presentation of our findings.

reference: Hello, my name is Brittany Johnson, and today I'll be presenting our paper titled Exploring Approaches to Data Literacy through a Critical Race Theory Perspective. Thank you so much for joining me. In this paper, we describe and analyze a workshop developed for a work training program called DataWorks. In this workshop, data workers chose a topic of their interest, source and process data on that topic and used that data to create presentations. Drawn from discourses of data literacy, epistemic agency and lived experience, and critical race theory, we analyzed the workshop's activities and outcomes. Through this analysis, three themes emerge. The tensions between epistemic agency and the context of work, encountering the ordinariness of racism through data work, and understanding the personal as communal and intersectional. Finally, critical race theory also prompts us to consider the very notions of data literacy that undergird our workshop activities. From this analysis, we offer a series of suggestions for approaching designing data literacy activities taking into account critical race theory. During this presentation, I will cover the sections outlined in this overview. The background, context, methodology, research questions, key findings, implications, and acknowledgements. Beginning with the background of our work, we have recognized how the consideration of race and racism within technology is growing, and HCI researchers are beginning to become more attuned to the issues of race in their work. However, the increased engagement with race has also prompted researchers to examine how this engagement occurs and how race is embedded in technology through critical race theory, also known as CRT. We also use CRT and its tenets as a way to frame our reflections on what it means to support equitable computing and data practices in the context of everyday work. The context of this research is DataWorks, a A workplace training program housed within a university where people from historically minoritized and underrepresented communities are employed. and learn basic data skills such as cleaning, formatting, and labeling datasets. This approach draws from other training programs that aim to increase individual data skills such as boot camps and virtual courses. However, our program differs in its design to specifically engage underserved communities in data work through an authentic work environment instead of through formal coursework. Through DataWorks, we aim to foster unique approaches to data literacy and data work. The methodology we leveraged for our research involved ethnographic methods and participatory design workshops. We used data collected through audio, video, and photographs, as well as semi-structured interviews and focus groups to conduct our qualitative analysis. This analysis was conducted by four of the authors who read the transcriptions and watched videos to identify themes and patterns. These themes and patterns were refined by the research team through several discussions. The PD workshops developed were scaffolded into a four-step process to guide each activity. These four steps included, one, specify a problem, two, find applicable data, three, analyze and organize this data so that it can be shared with a broader audience, and four, communicate this data to other people. The conception of these workshops were to examine two key research questions in more detail. These questions ask, how do the data workers develop and practice data skills while addressing a problem of interest to them, and how does the lived experiences of the data workers impact the data work they engage in? Out of the key findings that emerged from our analysis, one of these findings present the tensions between epistemic agency, critical data literacy, and the work context. Our hypothesis was that the data workers would develop their own personal approaches to data work, but we did not find evidence of this in our findings, nor did we find that the data workers brought their critical perspectives to the data they gathered. However, we argue that this is not the fault of the data workers and should not be interpreted as a lack of engagement with the data process or the exploration of the data. Instead, if the data workers were empowered to be skeptical of the process and develop critical perspectives of data, then epistemic agency would have been demonstrated. This directs us to the implications we present in our work, one of which is the need to critically engage the context of work. K through twelve education programs and community engagement events are contexts that are often already critical. However, the context of work involves paradynamics and cultural context and is uncritical in itself. CRT prompts us to examine our own liberal biases that may cause us to expect the data workers to develop a critical perspective to data or the data process in the context of work. If we want to pursue critical data literacy in the context of work, then the context of work must itself be approached as an environment and process open to critique and refiguration. Thank you so much for joining me during this presentation. We'd like to extend our sincere thanks to those who have provided generous support for our work and feedback on our paper. It's not like you.

reference: Nearly 100 Martin County residents making it known they do not support a recently passed mask mandate in the county. But don't try to make me wear a mask. The order requiring people to wear masks in businesses and in outside spaces where social distancing is impossible. Controversial understandings of the coronavirus pandemic have turned data visualizations into a battleground. Coronavirus skeptics and anti mask protesters throughout the country have campaigned against a major public health measures. arguing that the pandemic that affects a few should not impinge on the liberties of a majority to go about life as usual. And while many researchers in computer science and public health seek better forms of data and scientific literacy in order to redress the problem, what does a data-driven approach to understanding the pandemic really mean? For some, this breakthrough moment for data visualization explains the popularity of line charts comparing infection rates across countries or COVID data dashboards that show how the pandemic is unfolding in individual counties. But do the data show that the pandemic is exaggerated and that the crisis is over? Unlike the liberal media, numbers don't lie. It's critical, you know what, that we look at these numbers with a clear lens. From 2009 to 2010, nearly 61 million Americans got swine flu. Beyond that fact, we still don't have the numbers. We need to fully understand what's happening around us. To look at some of these charts I'd love to. What's compelling about the rhetoric here is the emphasis on following the numbers, where people might use the same data from the CDC and WHO, and yet draw radically different conclusions. How does this work in practice, and how did we get here? To start answering this question, we combined tools in computational social science and digital ethnography to get a sense for how information circulates. First, we took a bird's eye view by studying half a million tweets and 41,000 visualizations computationally. We then combined that with digital ethnography so that we could identify the phenomena in a more granular fashion. But let's be concrete here. When it came to the computational social science, we first collected all tweets mentioning some combination of the words COVID and data, and if they included an image. Then we created a network of Twitter users and classified the communities using the Louvain method. Concurrently, we classified all of the images that were associated with these tweets using a computer vision model to ask, what kinds of data visualizations do different groups use? Do anti-mask groups tend to use 3D bar charts compared to the New York Times graphics section? We also conducted a digital ethnography using an iterative process. We collected posts where people talk about COVID-related data, then posts where people do their own COVID-related data analysis, then their angry posts where people who hate masks talk about science and data. And we ultimately asked, what does follow the data mean for anti-mask communities? As we followed these different communities, we began to slowly discern different modes of interpreting data. In our ethnographic study of anti-maskers, we show how their discussions exemplify a fundamental epistemological rift about how knowledge about the pandemic should be made, interpreted, and shared. While previous literature and visualization in science communication has emphasized the need for data and media literacy as a way to combat misinformation, this study finds that anti-mask groups practice a form of data literacy in spades. Indeed, these groups often use orthodox scientific methods to make unorthodox arguments. Data visualizations are not a neutral window onto an observer-independent reality. During a pandemic, they're an arena of political struggle. In these discussions, we find that anti-maskers think carefully about the grammar of graphics by decomposing visualizations into layered components, and you can explore these different dynamics in the interactive piece that accompanies this article. Data is not a neutral substrate that can be used for good or ill, and anti-maskers often reveal themselves to be more sophisticated in their understanding of how scientific knowledge is socially constructed than their ideological adversaries. Put differently, there's no such thing as dispassionate or objective data analysis. Instead, there are stories, stories shaped by cultural logics and animated by personal experience. This story is about how a public health crisis, refracted through seemingly objective numbers and data visualizations, is part of a broader battleground about scientific epistemology and democracy in modern American life.

reference: Hello, I'm Inha Cha, a master's student in the Department of Industrial Design at KAIST. Today we're going to present our recent work exploring the use of a voice-based conversational agent to To empower adolescents with autism spectrum disorder a few years back, a mother of a 13 year old son with autism. reported that her son, Goose, fell in love with Siri by expressing his emotions and searching for information related to his specific interests. We consider that people with autism have characteristics such as obsession with particular interests, repeated behaviors, and difficulty in social interaction. Inspired by this story, we set out to explore how the VCAs could serve as an empowering accessibility technology for autistic adolescents in navigating their daily lives and personal characteristics. We choose a participatory design approach by actively involving adolescents with autism as design partners. We investigated the life experience of using VCAs in labs. During a two-week study, the participants navigated various aspects of VCAs in their daily lives and shared their experiences with researchers in the workshops. The first workshop was to allow participants clearly to understand VCA functions and plan how to use them through multiple discussions with researchers. The second workshop was to let them develop their own strategies for using certain functions of VCAs to fit their own context. The last workshop was to make them discuss their expectations toward VCAs based on their experience. Our scaffolded and activity-based approach enabled participants to identify VCA's role by themselves and develop their own strategies for using appropriating its functions. We found five opportunities and possibilities of Vcas in autistic adolescents' daily lives. a Vca. VCA can help autistic adolescents think about which part of themselves they want to improve upon, like promoting self-care skills, regulating negative emotions, and practicing conversation skills. Here we introduce a couple of these in detail. Like the good example in the introduction, one of our participants soothed his stressful emotions and figured out how to express his feelings by conversing with the agent. Like him, other participants also wanted to share their personal stories with VCAs. They said it is because the VCA is a machine with human-like features such as giving supportive words, honorable conversational attitude, and a calm voice tone. Using VCAs allowed our participants to improve on their inaccurate pronunciation. For example, during the first three days, Tom repeatedly had difficulty activating the agent because of his pronunciation, even if he tried many times. However, after much practice throughout the study, he thought his pronunciation got better enough to activate the agent right away. Interestingly, the participants took advantage of the fortune-telling function and accepted general advice on attitude or motivational messages from VCAs. Adolescents with autism often have emotional conflicts with their caregivers or therapists, which makes their communication difficult. We found VCAs could provide advice on behalf of caregivers or therapists, reducing their burden and conflict. So our findings suggest that VCAs could be engaging, empowering, and emancipating tools that support autistic adolescents by addressing their needs, personalities, and expectations. Unlike many prior works, VCAs can actually promote self-expressions and self-empowerment rather than accommodate the technology. Finally, we propose design implications to promote positive experiences using VCAs in the daily lives of autistic adolescents. Our design implications include providing initial moments and scapegoated approaches to developing strategies for using VCAs, personalizing conversational styles and experiences, and designing system guidance to handle improper user requests or behaviors. reference: Hi there, I'm presenting our study into human-nature relations in urban gardens, explorations with camera traps. The authors of this study live in a city with a fairly large amount of wildlife. We have possums that visit our yards and roofs, a multitude of birds, insects and reptiles, bats that fly across the city at dusk, as well as those urban icons, rats and other rodents. But looking at this Google Earth shot of Brisbane, you can see that despite some large patches of habitat, a great deal is fractured across parks and private gardens. William Odom, back in the 80s, spoke about the tyranny of small decisions, or the ways in which unregulated everyday decisions can accumulate catastrophically. I'd like to also think the opposite is true, and that by better understanding what people want to know about their gardens, we can help shape decision-making that will lead to better human-nature relations. Now what better way to find out things than to plan a camera in your backyard? There are many inexpensive cameras on the market, as well as DIY options. Most commercial cameras produce still images and video with audio, and are triggered by infrared sensors or can be scheduled. So in short, we gave commercial scout cameras to people who had gardens, and some interest in learning about them, to better understand how do people use these, and what are they interested in? And from that, what does it indicate about new technologies we might design to improve human-nature relations in cities? We had 10 adult participants, and of these, four families with children. Each participant filled in a diary, and was asked to take part in an interview at the end. We found that people were producing hundreds of unsatisfying images, like the one on the right, and that the labour of editing and experimentation to produce something rewarding, such as an answered question, or a memorable image, required sustained engagement through the learning curve. So how can we design for sustained engagement with nature sensing? While we have many ideas, we believe that some of the most fruitful involve linking sensing to other practices of care, such as gardening, time with children, or keeping a diary. Secondly, we learned that the kind of media that was produced influenced understanding of animal lives. In particular, video with audio provided a sense of mystery, and clues as to lives lived just out of view. These observations, made in real life and matched with digital media, led to contemplation of animal relationships with other animals, the environment, and people. And these thoughts were typically being discussed in households, rather than online with the wider public. So we asked, how can we design for these relationships? We suggest that by making local nature data part of a home life, we build kinship with local animals, and an appreciation of their needs. We also found value in focusing on children's experience of sensing technology, and the possibility of making it more accessible and engaging to them. Finally, it was not our intention to learn if cameras made people care more about the wildlife in their garden, but we learned something about care regardless. Human-nature relations were informed by pre-existing interest and knowledge of ecosystems. Cameras added information that informed both care and garden management decisions. A hard line was drawn between care for native or cute animals and rats. Rat shame was prevalent. What is most encouraging Is that new questions and interest and some care about wild animal lives arose through enhanced observation so? Lastly, can we design technologies that increase curiosity in more than human lives. We noted the disparate interest in shots where animals appeared to be staring into the camera, and suggest that the gaze itself could be useful, for example, by reconstructing animal viewpoints. In summary, we find further value in designing technologies for smaller and localized nature cultures, such as private gardens and households, even neighborhoods, as well as in exploring other viewpoints, especially those of children and animals. In particular, sharing nature data within families can seed interest and care for nature in future generations. Thank you.

Today, We are going to present our technique, Keech, combining the keyboard with a touch screen for rapid command selection on toolbars. Desktop applications frequently use drop-down menus, toolbars, and ribbons. This results in an object-to-command transition cost, and it breaks the interaction flow. Previous work on reducing object-to-command transition costs can be separated in three categories. Keyboard shortcuts, optimized menu techniques, and augmented desktop environments. But these solutions cannot fully replace toolbars and their advantages, such as supporting large numbers of commands, having a constant spatial layout, dismissing the need to memorize gestures, or requiring an environment upgrade. In addition, the computer marketplace has seen the appearance of laptops integrating a secondary touch screen, where the touch screen can either be located at the top or bottom of the keyboard. To overcome the limitations of previous work and reduce object-to-command transition costs, we decided to export this concept to desktop computers by positioning a smartphone below the keyboard. In this work we propose Keech a novel solution to select items on simple or multi level toolbars. It is based on the combination of the keyboard with the touch screen affixed to it. With our solution, users select commands on a toolbar displayed on the touch screen through gestures combining key presses and screen touches. In a preliminary study, we determined the size of the reachable areas on the touch screen below the keyboard While interacting with both devices simultaneously, in fact, we found that most of the surface of 5.8 " touch screen. placed below a keyboard can be comfortably thumb-rubbed while holding the control key. Using these results, we designed three interaction techniques. For simple toolbars, we designed a direct pointing technique that we call keych touch, and an indirect pointing technique that we call keych magnet. For comfortably reaching four targets, we evaluated simple toolbar keytch techniques and compared them to the traditional mouse. We found that for simple toolbars, average selection time with the mouse and keych magnet were 40 % greater than with keych touch. Accuracy rates were above 98 % for Keech Touch and the mouse, but lower for Keech magnet. We therefore dismissed the indirect pointing technique from the two-level toolbar techniques. The Mouse and Keech Touch achieved the equivalent of good as an Sqs score, while Ktm scored an Ok. These results stayed true for toolbars containing up to 16 items. We evaluated the two-level toolbars techniques and compared them to the mouse. We found that average selection time with the mouse were 30 % greater than with keytch techniques. All techniques had an accuracy rate above 96 %, and the mouse and Keech Touch achieved the equivalent of good as an Sus score. While Keech Key scored an OK. And all results stayed true for toolbars containing 20, 40, and 60 items. These studies are also validated through two follow-up more ecological user studies presented in the paper. To conclude, And this work we presented Keech, and we established through four user studies that introduces the object to command transition cast. For the future, we are planning to study Keech with both hands and with more complex toolbars. Finally, to illustrate our approach, we adapted Microsoft Word's ribbon to two versions of Keytch. containing respectively 20 and 40 items per tab. In extreme cases, this was presented as a moral absolute, that inaction was wrong and action was right. They believed that anyone critiquing actions and slowing things down was obstructionist and immoral. Alternatively, safety-focused communities tended to focus on the risks of medical making. reference: Hi there, I'm Junnan Yu from the University of Colorado Boulder, and I'm presenting our paper titled Parental Mediation for Young Children's Use of Educational Media, a case study with Computational Toys and Kids on behalf of my co-authors, Andra, Devorah, and Rick Ross Roque. Young people today consume lots of media like video games and the internet, which can bring some benefits and also pose certain challenges. Parents perform various strategies to maximize the benefits and minimize the negative impact of media use, which are framed as parental mediation theory. This theory includes restrictive mediation, active mediation, and co-using or co-viewing. As the landscape of media is expanding rapidly, new parental mediation practices are emerging. Therefore, it is necessary to keep exploring parental mediation practices so that future media design can better support productive parent-child interactions. In this paper, we explore parental mediation practices in the context of educational media and aim to expand the parental mediation theory. We ask how do parents mediate young children's use of educational media? We situate our research in the context of coding kits. Coding kits are toys and apps that are designed to teach children computational thinking and coding skills. We performed semi-structured interviews with 18 parents who obtained coding kits for their young children at home. Through thematic analysis, we summarized three high-level parental mediation categories, including creative mediation where parents provide support for children's creating and learning with media, preparative mediation where parents explore and prepare media for children's engagement, and administrative mediation where parents administer and regulate children's media use. We identified six creative mediation patterns, including collaborating by participating in children's play, providing encouragement for children's projects, providing scaffold to direct children's play into meaningful directions, respecting children's play ideas, solving problems children encounter during a play, and teaching children how to use the kit and coding skills. Preparative mediation includes exploring media and setting up media, such as investigating new media that can benefit children's education and setting up devices for children. In administrative mediation, parents control children's media access, especially with screen-based coding kits, setting rules for children's interaction with coding kits, and keeping an eye on children's play. We further examined how parents' mediation patterns distribute across physical, virtual, and hybrid kits. A key finding is that parents reported less access control but more scaffolding, problem solving, and teaching with physical kits than screen-based kits. Importantly, different from consumption-oriented media like TV, Internet, and video games, parents mainly perform supportive practices with coding kits because of the kits' educational benefits. Through our findings, the parental mediation theory does not well capture parents' efforts in preparing the media and helping children to learn from the media. As such, our work expands the parental mediation theory into the context of educational media. Joint media engagement is a frequently cited framework within HCI to describe shared media experiences. However, JME does not examine the behind-the-scenes work like exploring, preparing, and administering media use. Therefore, we propose to expand JME to include all aspects of involvement in shared media experiences. Finally, we highlight some implications for designing educational media that support parental involvement. First, we suggest including space and resources to support both parents as co-creators in children's independent play. Second, we suggest giving more priority to physicality in design because physicality can invite more parental participation. Third, we suggest including approaches that better support parents as audiences, like commenting on children's projects and providing encouragement in person and remotely. Lastly, we suggest including the features that support parents to better scaffold a children's learning. such as activity prompts that are associated with different learning goals. This is a brief overview of our paper. For more details, please refer to the paper. Thank you for listening.

We ask how do parents mediate young children's use of educational media? We situate our research in the context of coding kits. Through thematic analysis, we summarized three high-level parental mediation categories, including creative mediation where parents provide support for children's creating and learning with media, preparative mediation where parents explore and prepare media for children's engagement, and administrative mediation where parents administer and regulate children's media use. Preparative mediation includes exploring media and setting up media, such as investigating new media that can benefit children's education and setting up devices for children. reference: Hello, I'm Advait, and on behalf of my co-authors, I'll be presenting our work Solofinger. This is a joint work between Saarland University and the University of Copenhagen. Often times, our hands hold a wide variety of objects and manipulate them based on the plant activity. However, gestural input techniques while holding objects are prone to false activations due to grip adjustment, natural finger movements, and various object manipulations. A recognizer might misinterpret these as input, leading to false activations. In this work, our goal is to avoid false activation for digital input while holding or manipulating everyday objects. Inspiring prior work in this direction Has been has mainly focused on holding smartphones, and for smartwatches with delimiting gestures such as flipping or pressing. However, these gesture designs would not generalize to everyday objects, for instance while holding a coffee cup or using the ear pump. In contrast to these device-specific delimiter gestures, which by the way would interrupt the primary activity if you are holding an object, our approach uses easy and rapid-to-perform single-finger movements that are compatible with a wide range of everyday objects. More importantly, it is resilient to false activations. We used our observation and built two key assumptions that finger either remains static or multiple fingers move concurrently during everyday hand-object actions. And this creates a sweet spot for single-finger movements that are unique and not present during everyday hand-object actions. We call this concept as solo-finger, a robust and easy gestural input technique to avoid false activation while holding objects. We confirmed our two assumptions by contributing peak-score metric, which quantifies how strongly a single-finger moves with respect to other fingers. In the graph, you may see that peak-score for daily hand-object actions is extremely low compared to solo-finger gestures. The ease of single-finger movement makes our concept generalizable on diverse graph types and objects. Thanks to the dexterity of our fingers, multiple gesture variations can be created. For example, a designer can create this exact gesture while sharing a photo and swipe left for rejecting calls. We performed a series of data-driven analysis to validate our concept, which you may find in the paper. To give you a brief idea, we used an existing dataset and compared it to our collected dataset of solo-finger gestures. Our extensive dataset collected using Optitrack is available to the research community. We performed our concept validation with 36 everyday hand-object actions, representing a diverse set such as pouring wine, reading a letter, writing, and many more. Through a simple thresholding technique, we found no false activation for 23 actions in the large dataset of everyday hand-object actions. We discussed the actions wherein false activations occurred with more details in the paper. And later, we show a more sophisticated classifier that can eliminate false activation on such actions. Now let's move on to the deployment of our concept. While our concept can be realized using various sensing techniques, like objects augmented with high-resolution sensors, IMUs, or radar-based approaches, views are commercially available in PR Club. We collected a second dataset with hand-object actions and solo-finger gestures. We used this dataset and trained a multiclass classifier using Random Forest. We included 7 gesture variations and hand-object actions. If the held object is known, we achieved an accuracy of 89 % with no false activations. and if the object is not known. The accuracy is 86 %, and the false activation rate still remains low to around 2 %. To summarize, we presented a novel concept that uses only one finger for gesture input while holding everyday objects. Through a series of analyses, we show our concept is resilient to false activation. And ultimately we used the commercially available hardware and trained a multiclass classifier to show seven gesture variations can be detected. with very low false activation. Thank you.

reference: Hi, everyone. I'm Alexandra To, and today I'm presenting Reducing Uncertainty and Offering Comfort, Designing Technology for Coping with Interpersonal Racism. This is a participatory design study that uses interactive fiction to facilitate conversation and generative ideation around racism and technology. This study is a part of the Larger CARE Project, which stands for Coping After Racist Experiences. So I do want to provide that content warning that the project deals with racism, and it looks at how we might design technology that prioritizes the well-being and coping of individuals who deal with racism on a regular basis. As larger context, in the project we use critical race theory, which tells us that racism is an ordinary, everyday occurrence. And even though modern racism can be subtle and even unintended, experiencing racism on a regular basis is incredibly harmful to mental, emotional, and physical well-being. And in some previous work on the project, we identified some specific challenges that HCI and design might address in this space. Namely, that social support seeking is one of the best ways of coping with interpersonal racism because it allows for connection and meaning making. However, people of color justifiably do not feel that popularly available tools for connection are made for them. Often the risk is too high or the labor involved is too great to seek that necessary support. So this informs an agenda for participatory design that can center the needs of people of color. We ran six workshops with 26 people who identified as having experienced racism. And before joining us in the workshop, we asked participants to read through an interactive fiction in a vignette study as a primer for our design space. Interactive fiction vignette studies are extraordinarily powerful for helping us understand how people respond emotionally to socially complex and sensitive situations, while also providing quite a bit of agency in how a person might interact with the story. So we developed this interactive vignette in Twine. And in the narrative, we wrote, you take on the role of Sam, a college student who experiences a racial microaggression. In the narrative vignette, you get to make choices about what Sam says, feels, and does. And at a research lab networking event in the story, a visiting professor says three back-to-back racial microaggressions to Sam. After completing the story at home on their own, participants answer some survey questions, interpreting the experience, and then later join us in the lab in groups to engage in a co-design workshop. In the workshop, participants who are often strangers work together to recall the narrative and reconstruct it together. They analyze it for needs, pain points, and opportunities, and they role play some scenarios where they might want to seek social support in similar situations. They storyboard and develop ideas for technologies that might better support themselves or Sam in similar situations in the future. And the method we developed here using interactive fiction embodies values of community based participatory research. We prioritize the comfort and safety of our participants, center their insights and experiences, and position them as collaborators and experts in this work. Safety mechanisms were a really important part of this and a big part of the paper, and you can read more about that there. In the end, participants produced a wide range of interesting technologies, both near and far future. There's a few on the screen, including a smartwatch button for racism, an augmented reality device that allows you to see a person's history of making racist remarks, and a smart speaker that's a little friend that reassures you and helps you talk about your experiences with racism. We conducted a thematic analysis of participants' recall of the story, their own analysis of it, and their design proposals. And this ultimately produced, among other things, themes for technology that might prioritize coping with racism. And these themes reveal that our participants have complicated relationships with the ways that technology specifically can support them. The paper presents new methods for helping facilitate conversations and speculative design around sensitive subjects. And in the workshop, participants also shared complex and sophisticated understandings of modern technology. Finally, the paper produces considerations in designing technology that empowers coping with interpersonal racism. However, it's important to note that the design fictions proposed here are not solutions to be implemented. They are what is known as naive, fragile fictions. So the work is more in the vein of research through design. This helps us uncover characteristics of socio-technical tools for support, rather than generating immediately viable design ideas. And in our future work, we synthesized and evaluated these ideas in context. This work is supported by a great number of student research assistants, colleagues, and mentors. And you can find more detail about the designs in our participants' own words, as well as our methods in the paper.

reference: Hi, my name is Mateen. I'm a PhD student in the Design Lab at UC San Diego. This video is a preview on our paper about understanding the interaction gaps in online classrooms. If you participated at a university lecture in 2020, this is most likely what you experienced. In your class, most students did not share videos during lecture, and everyone stayed muted, except only one person, who most often happened to be the instructor. As depicted by one instructor, teaching at a synchronous online classroom felt like talking into a void. This feeling was attributed to the lack of students' video and audio feeds during class. These social cues can help instructors read their classroom and adjust their teaching pace. To understand classroom perspectives, we conducted interviews with instructors and survey studies with students at UC San Diego shortly after the COVID outbreak prompted the shift to all-remote instruction. Given the two perspectives, we present recommendations for instructors and designers. Overall, our paper presents four recommendations. First, we offer a design recommendation, facilitating flexible distribution of students' visual data. Let's take the example of a classroom with one instructor and three students. As demonstrated in this figure, when each participant decides to share their video, they share it with everyone else. What if students could be flexible in what they share and how they share it? For instance, students can choose to share their videos only with their instructors and close friends. This can help students feel more comfortable with sharing videos. Also, students can choose to broadcast less invasive forms of social cues, such as facial expressions and nods, instead of their videos. This recommendation comes from considering both students' and instructors' perspectives in the interview and survey studies. Our survey responses revealed that 80 % of students were reluctant to share their videos when asked why. 44 % expressed discomfort with displaying appearances when attending classes remotely. 27 % of students believed that sharing videos served no purpose and avoided doing so. And 23 % attributed their decision to the consensus among peers. Our interview suggested the need for simple visual information, such as students' confusion signals, that can help instructors with teaching. One of the instructors who taught a 92 % undergraduate classroom at the time of the interview. alluded to the benefit of aggregated and simplified representation of students' video feeds. This instructor believed that students' attention was the only signal they needed to be able to manage the pace and content of the lecture. Our next recommendation is for instructors to facilitate more opportunities for students in formal interactions. We recommend two interventions for enhancing students' social interactions. Simply adding virtual hall times immediately before and after lecture can help students bond with their peers and instructor. In co-located settings, this is similar to how students interact with each other as they arrive at their lecture halls or ask informal questions from their instructors right after class ends. Another intervention for boosting students' sense of community is empowering students to control their interactions and engage in smaller groups as desired. Hall time and individual control are 2 out of 10 characteristics of co-located interactions that our survey responses support. In the survey, students pointed out the benefits of after-lecture time, when they used to have informal exchanges with their instructor. Here, the student mourned the lack of opportunity to discuss their major after class. Another significant challenge of online lectures was the lack of interactions between students, which inhibited deeper peer interactions and contributed to a broken sense of community. For example, one student highlighted the struggles of making friendships, Given the lost opportunity of creating informal interactions, we, we presented two of the needs and recommendations that emerged from our study. The other two needs highlight the benefits of chat to provide a less polarized classroom and instructors' need for aggregating and presenting real-time social cues. For more details, please visit our paper. Thank you!

reference: Hello, everyone. My name is Sai. I'm a PhD student at the Human-Computer Interaction Institute at Carnegie Mellon University. Today I'll be talking about our project, From Tactile to Naptile, Opportunities and Challenges with Multimodal Feedback for Guiding Surfaces during Non-Visual Navigation. Today, there are many technologies that support non-visual navigation, but despite this proliferation, tactile sense remains an important cue to support non-visual navigation. However, there are several challenges with relying on only tactile feedback. First, cues are discreet. Second, implementation is often inconsistent and leads to dangerous situations. Third, tactile surfaces are prone to crosstalk from the environment, from mud, snow, etc. Finally, tactile surfaces inherently lack geographic orientation during wayfinding, i.e. the ability to determine position relative to the destination, topography, or distance in an unfamiliar area. So one key question we wanted to answer with this project was how can we best design tactile guidance surfaces with multimodal feedback to overcome these challenges? To understand the challenges better, we conducted a mixed-methods investigation involving a survey of 67 blind and visually impaired travelers and 10 orientation and mobility experts along with public transit authorities. From our survey results, we learned that most travelers have often encountered blister or truncated dome-style of tactile surfaces but have very minimally encountered or did not even understand the meaning of other types of tactile surfaces, which are often used to convey roadway hazards, cycleways, etc. Our interview results indicate that the travelers tend to not just rely on textures alone. For instance, many travelers reported that there can be a lot of ambiguity in the placement and also the contextual meaning that the textures conveyed. Interviewees also reported that tactile surfaces played a crucial role in providing alerts and alignment support, thereby increasing the efficiency of travel while navigating in high-traffic destinations. There are many priorities to support multimodal feedback. Here are a few. Our participants indicated that audio feedback was important, and many participants even extracted and relied on natural audio feedback from the environment. While interviewees highlighted the need for additional feedback, they wanted to have the ability to control when and how they received this additional feedback. They illustrated many situations where too much feedback can be overwhelming. Finally, participants also suggested that tactile surfaces need to be visually designed in a way that they don't seek unwanted attention and leading to social issues. Interviews also revealed many practical considerations that our tiles need to support. First, travelers wanted the tactile surfaces to be easier to discover, and they wanted them to assist in learning the meaning that they conveyed. Second, our participants highlighted that many situations where the context around the surfaces changed. In particular, they emphasized that texture surfaces may need to be moved if they are used for pop-up events like poster sessions at conferences, or if bus stops are redistributed. We present our main design recommendation, that is the adoption of low-cost rapid prototyping technologies such as 3D printing that can reduce the cost and complexity while lowering barriers for prototyping and encouraging new texture exploration. Multimodal feedback with Sensing should support customizability, discoverability, and learnability of new and existing textures. Finally, there should be software support for consistent installation, deployment, and resource planning. In the future, we are very excited about this work, and we are actively working along with our partners towards deploying and evaluating our multimodal tactile surfaces in real-world settings. We would like to encourage a safer and a diverse set of participants as well. especially from the Deaf and DeafBlind community who rely even more on tactile feedback and might benefit from increased consistencies in texture. With that, I would like to thank you for your attention, and I am open to questions. I would like to encourage you to also look into our paper for more details and analysis.

reference: Hi, my name is Hana. My co-author Yijun and I will be presenting our research on conveying privacy choices with icons and link text. Our past work has found that using privacy choices is kind of like a scavenger hunt. They're difficult to find, they're spread out across services, and websites offer inconsistent options. The new California consumer privacy Act requires that companies provide choices related to the sale of personal information and has a provision related to a. to an opt-out button or logo. We embarked on a study to help identify an icon as well as accompanying text description, which we'll refer to as link text, to help consumers actually take advantage of their new opt-out rights. We designed 11 icons related to three concepts, Choice, opting out and do not sell my personal info in support of the Ccpa, We. We evaluated these icons as well as one proposed by the Digital Advertising Alliance with participants recruited from Amazon Mechanical Turk. We showed participants one icon at random, half of participants saw the icon without any context, and the other half saw it with the link text, do not sell my personal information. We then showed participants all 12 icons and asked them to select which icon best represented privacy choices and do not sell choices. Based on our initial results, we refined five icons and conducted another evaluation on MTurk. We found that the stylized toggle icon generated the fewest misconceptions, while the one proposed by the DAA was commonly misinterpreted as a play or informational button. The slash dollar icon communicated concepts related to money when displayed without a link text, but was participants' preferred icon for representing do not sell. Since our icon study showed the importance of link text, we next evaluated 16 link texts using a similar protocol and selected five for further evaluation. After identifying promising icons and link texts, we evaluated their combinations, including a link text without an icon and an icon without a link text. We randomly assigned 1,468 MTurk participants to one of 23 icon-link text combinations. The icon and link text were placed in a fictitious shoe retailer's website to mimic a real-world scenario. We found that participants' interpretations were primarily influenced by link text rather than by icons, and some of the icons continued to convey misconceptions. The privacy options link text paired with stylized toggle best conveyed privacy choices, and the CCPA link text best conveyed do not sell choices. We shared our results with the California Office of Attorney General, or OAG. After receiving our results, the OAG announced an icon that's similar to our stylized toggle but with important differences. Particularly, the OAG's icon was red and strongly resembled an actual toggle button. We then ran a follow-up study to compare our stylized toggle icon with the OAG's icon. Each icon was tested in both red and blue. Indeed, we found that stylized toggle better conveyed do not sell choices than the OAG's icon and led to fewer misconceptions. Our research provides design implications by showing that privacy icons should aim to represent familiar and straightforward concepts like choice. This is evidenced by the stylized toggle's success over other candidates. Additionally, icons, especially new icons, need link text to aid comprehension, as our research shows that link text significantly impacted how an icon was interpreted. Our work has also directly influenced public policymaking. Our evaluation of the OAG's icon shows that even small changes could make a big difference in how users interpret an icon. We show that it's important, but also feasible, to integrate user testing into policymaking to ensure more usable controls for consumers in privacy and possibly other contexts. In March 2021, the OAG announced the approval of amendments to the CCPA, recommending our stylized toggle as an optional privacy options icon for conveying do not sell choices and potentially other types of privacy settings. Follow the links here if you'd like to check out our series of papers or download the privacy options icon. Thank you.

reference: Thank you for attending this presentation. I'm Gyeori Yoon, a Ph.D. student from POSTECH of Korea. Our study is improving viewing experiences of first-person shooter gameplays with automatically generate motion effects. Many people, including me, really love playing games and even watching the games like esports. Then, have you ever imagined that watching esports in a 4D cinema with motion effects? It would be very fun and immersive. In this work, we combine viewing gameplay and 4D technology using motion effects. Thanks to 4D technology, we can enjoy multimedia with various sensory feedback. For example, we can feel motion, olfaction, wind, and the like. We focused on motion effects, the major feedback of 4D applications. However, manual design of motion effects is very difficult and expensive. So, Lee proposed an automatic motion synthesis algorithm previously. In that study, they made motion commands by estimating camera motion, movements of a salient object on a screen, and impulsive sounds like collision or explosion where you can feel vibratory motion effects. We wanted to apply this idea to viewing experiences of first-person shooter gameplay. Why did we choose the FPS game? When watching a first-person view video, you may feel like being the main character of the video. Also, there are two major actions that players can take. First, moving their characters, and the second, firing the weapons. So, we expected that it would be very immersive when we emphasize on these two major actions. From the previous work, we could use the camera motion effect for the characters' movements and the impulsive sound motion effects for gunfire. By the way, we had to improve some points of the algorithms for esports applications. First, it was very slow to compute the camera movements, but must be faster for esports broadcasting. Also, impulsive sound motion effects are not suitable for viewing FPS gameplay because we wanted to detect a specific gunfire sound, not general impulsive sound. Moreover, let's imagine that you're shooting a gun. You may feel strong reaction force, but vibration cannot express that kind of force. We needed to make it better. In our system, for FPS gameplay videos, we estimated camera motion using images and detected the moments of gunfire using sounds. From this information, we computed proper motion effects for characters' movement and gunfire, then combined them. For the character movement motion, we followed the same procedure as Lee et al.'s algorithm. But the main bottlenecks were an optical flow estimation and RANSAC in camera movement estimation. So, we solved it using a faster optical flow algorithm and modifying RANSAC parameters. After that, we transformed camera movements to motion commands using washout filters. For more detail, please check the paper. For gunfire motion, we chose DNN for the gunfire detector, a simple deep learning model, and made a dataset containing two classes for that. Our model showed the hit rate over 90 and the first alarm under 20%. Then, we decided to present the basic motion profile for every gunfire, which mimics the strong reaction force using the pitch axis. To not exceed the pitch limitation, some portion of the remaining pitch value was added. In addition, for enjoyable experiences, we provided raw motion with the same basic profile but with a random range. Finally, we did a user study with 24 participants. We wanted to compare four motion conditions, none, motion effects for characteristic movements, gunfire, and the sum of the previous two. We asked eight questions about overall user experiences and motion effect qualities. As a result, we found that the motion condition combining character movement and gunfire showed the best scores of immersion, harmony, and preference. Thank you for your listening and please check our paper.

reference: Hello, welcome to our talk on exploring a makeup support system for transgender passing based on automatic gender recognition. I'm Toby, and I'm a first year PhD student at the University of Tokyo. I work on VR and AR interactive systems mostly. Before we go into our work, we need to introduce a couple of things to provide more context of what we did. Passing in this context refers to the ability of transgender people to be perceived as the gender they want to identify as this. This is by no means saying that all transgender people want to pass, but many do. Many companies provide commercial solutions to identify gender of faces in images and videos. They usually provide either a binary label, male or female, or a confidence score. Recently, a growing critical body of research brought attention to the numerous issues transgender community face with the adoption of current automatic gender recognition system, AGRs. However, we noticed that publication around these issues mostly come from a few specific countries, such as the US. In contrast, we want to explore how such technology could potentially be appropriate to support transgender practice and needs, especially in non-Western contexts like Japan. Our contribution lies in the ethnography that we did prior to the work, and an automatic system that suggests make-up for passing. And finally, qualitative interviews we conduct with potential users of our system. To do this, we conduct a three-year-long digital ethnography that revealed that make-up is a common practice for many transgender people to express themselves and to help them pass. However, there are differences between cisgender-focused make-up style and transgender-focused make-up style. More importantly, many transgender people face obstacles when learning make-up. Based on these findings, we designed FlyingColor, a virtual make-up assistant that uses automatic gender recognition to help people pass better. It has a few main features. First, it's very similar to those commercial camera filter apps that you already have in your phone. It supports an array of virtual cosmetic products, such as eye shadow, cheek color, etc. It also provides a feature which we call make-up feedback. Make-up feedback is an AGL-based numerical feedback that tells you whether and how much the current make-up system helps you pass. Currently, the user can select the goal of passing as either male or female. Finally, we offer a recommendation system that automatically identifies the optimal make-up combinations. After pressing the recommend button, the system proposes 5 sets of cosmetic combinations that the user can preview by pressing the buttons. We use this machine learning generated phase to illustrate our make-up feedback. Let's say this person wants to pass as female. The make-up feedback to the input image always starts from zero, as we are not trying to determine whether this person passed or not. And as we apply more make-up to the image, it can either go positive or negative depending on whether the make-up makes the image look more masculine or feminine. With this system, we wanted to ask the question that whether AGL can be subverted for the transgender community. We recruited 15 participants via a local gender development clinic. All the participants want to pass at various degrees. The interview lasts for 2 hours. We first interview participants about their make-up habits and experience with AGL system, if any. Participants then test our system and we interview them about their experience with it. Result from the study shows that AGL-based system can potentially be leveraged as a tool to support people who wish to pass. As an automatic system, AGL provides some advantage for our participants as it can be completely confidential, consistent, and support what we call blameability. Some participants felt that they can disregard the feedback when they don't agree with it, while it is much harder to disregard feedback from other people. Having a score instead of a binary prediction also highlights the fact that gender is inherently a non-binary concept And it allows people to have a better sense of progress and expectation Some of our participants are. are also interested in goals outside passing, such as wanting to practice make-up of a particular style. We could also easily extend this tool to assist people who want to explore make-up that explicitly do not conform with traditional gender norm. Thank you.
