reference: Hi everyone, my name is Ryan Kelly and I'm a researcher at the University of Melbourne. Today I'm going to be talking about some research on the ways that students use digital technologies to alleviate homesickness. Homesickness refers to the distress that people experience when they feel separated from their home. Research shows that 94 % of students experience homesickness at least once, and that it can be a very distracting feeling. Those who feel strongly homesick can experience depressed mood, impaired concentration, and are much more likely to drop out of university. Homesickness has also become relevant due to the COVID-19 pandemic, which has left many students unable to return home on a regular basis. This means that much of the contact students have with their home is through things like video chat and social media. However, the role of these tools in dealing with homesickness is not well understood. In this study, we wanted to understand students' existing practices around the use of technology so that we could identify opportunities for new designs for people who are homesick. With this aim in mind, the main question we wanted to answer was how do students use digital technologies to alleviate homesickness? To explore this question, we recruited 50 students who were living in Melbourne, Australia. The students were from a range of cultures, and all of them had moved away from home to attend university. In the study, each person completed a questionnaire and an in-depth interview held over Zoom. 12 of the participants also completed a diary for four weeks, which involved writing about daily uses of technology and how this helped deal with homesickness. Now, as a qualitative study, there's a lot of detail in the findings, so here I'm just going to focus on two of the main ideas from this paper. The first thing we found was that technologies are used to connect with a lot more than just people. It's worth noting that the students did talk extensively about connecting with friends, family, and even their pets through things like video chat and instant messaging. These technologies were helpful because they allowed students to acquire social contact and find support from others in times of distress. But technologies were used to feel connected with many other things from home as well. As an example, the students frequently talked about connecting with food and culture when they felt homesick. Many described craving the food from their homeland and missed the experience of eating with others. To replicate this feeling, the participants used platforms like YouTube to watch others eating the same food. This somehow helped to satisfy their cravings. Other participants discussed the importance of music and valued the way that platforms like Spotify give on-demand access to rare songs from their home. Listening to music helped people to feel a sense of homeliness and reminded them of where they had come from. There were also cases where music and videos were used for emotion regulation, which involves using technology to change how one is feeling. Another way technologies were used was for a connection with places. Again, this stresses that missing home is not just about people. One participant talked about using a live stream video to virtually visit her hometown in North Macedonia. This gave her a sense of presence and a feeling of actually being there at the remote site. Ideas around presence also emerged during discussions of social technologies like online games, which were mentioned as particularly helpful for alleviating homesickness. Some examples mentioned in this study included League of Legends and Animal Crossing. In these cases, it wasn't just the experience of playing the game that made people feel better, but rather the sense of being together with others in virtual space. The participants said that this created the same kind of vibe they experienced at home. It gave a sense of being connected to others, even though they were physically separated. The second main finding of this study was that technologies sometimes made homesickness worse. The students discussed problems such as heightened emotional labour, frequent exposure to homesickness triggers, and the feeling that technologies sometimes increased the sense of distance from home. Based on these experiences, the students shared various ideas for new designs. One example was for a system that could create stronger co-presence with people and places. The participants used words like holograms or teleporting to describe what this would be like, hinting at the possible use of virtual reality to connect with home. They also wondered whether technology could allow them to experience food and culture, such as through stimulation of taste, touch, and smell. These ideas suggest that research on the production of digital flavours could be usefully applied to the problem of homesickness. Overall, this research suggests that students use a wide range of technologies to deal with homesickness, and that some of these may help to bridge the sense of psychological distance from home. A challenge for HCI researchers lies in designing technologies that provide a meaningful experience of connection, without increasing the sense of being away. That's all from me, thanks very much for your attention.

of cultures and all of them had moved away from home to attend university. In the study,
each person completed a questionnaire and an in-depth interview held a resume.

about daily uses of technology and how this helped to deal with homesickness.

to focus on two of the main ideas from this paper. The first thing we found was that technologies
are used to connect with a lot more than just people. It's worth noting that the students did
talk extensively about connecting with friends, family, and even their pets through things like
video chat and instant messaging. These technologies were helpful because they allowed students to
to acquire social contact and find support from others
in times of distress.

with many other things from home as well.

about connecting with food and culture
when they felt homesick.

and missed the experience of eating with others.

like YouTube to watch others eating the same food.

reference: My name is Jayesh Tulani and I'll be presenting our work on locimotion, a training interface to learn a strong random password. in a single training session. For high-value secrets such as master passwords and sysadmin accounts, passwords must be strong and should not be written down, but this places an incredible burden on users to both generate and remember a strong secret. LociMotion is a training interface that helps users memorize 12-character random passwords based on the method of LociMemory technique. Loci motion has a 99 % recall success rate after one day, and unlike the space repetition technique. in which users need up to 2 weeks of training to learn a password, it works in a single training session. The LociMotion training interface is made up of two components, a dynamically generated video clip, and a cup and ball game. Based on the method of LociMemory technique, the video clip contains a virtual tour of a house where we pick 12 key locations, or loci, in and around the house. Each of the loci is tied to a specific letter of the password. We selected 26 common objects that visually represent the 26 letters of the English alphabet. Depending on the generated random password, Twelve of these objects would appear at the 12th loci of a virtual house, e.g. given this randomly generated password. a ball for B would appear above the mailbox before entering the house, a violin for V would appear at the front lawn, And so on, the other component of locimotion is a cup and ball game where the user is trying to catch a falling ball. by moving the cup under it. Instead of using the arrow keys to move the cup left and right, the user must instead type a specific chunk of the password to move the cup under the ball before it hits the ground. The game screen is divided into four columns, each column representing a three-letter chunk of the password. For this randomly generated password, the first column is associated with the chunk ABC, the second with the chunk DEF, and so on. The game has eight levels, including two levels that serve as a mental break for the user from the memorization process. The science behind locaemotion's long term memory training is based on a combination of declarative memory. such as the ability to recall locations or addresses, and procedural memory, which is responsible for acquiring motor skills, such as riding a bicycle or playing a musical instrument. The video clip triggers declarative memory by using the method of LociMemory technique, helping participants to consciously remember the associated objects in the order of the landmarks. The cup and ball game, on the other hand, leverages procedural memory acquired through repetition, practice, and motor coordination. We conducted two user studies to evaluate the effectiveness of LociMotion. In the first study, we examined the effectiveness of LociMotion to help users learn a 12-character random password and recall it seven days later, compared to a control condition in which the users were left to their own devices to try to remember the 12 random characters. We conducted a user study on Mechanical Turk With 300 participants over two sessions, a learning session on day one and a recall session on day. Day eight, 86 % of the participants in the locimotion condition logged in successfully within five attempts. Compared to just 42 % of participants in the control condition, participants using locimotion needed 19 min and 22 s. to learn these strong passwords, as compared to 11 minutes and 54 seconds for the control. The additional time and effort that users put into LociMotion training Paid off in much higher recall rates In the 2nd user study, we aim to evaluate the effectiveness of loci motion training interface. over a long period of time. To do this, we conducted a user study on Mechanical Turk with 200 participants who learned the password on day 1 and did recall testing on days 2, 5, and 19. We observed a recall rate of 99 % on day two, 96 % on day five, and 81 % on day 19. Locimotion also received a score of 74 on the system usability scale, which is considered above average overall. These results indicate that locimotion with its combination of the method of loci and procedural memory training, can help users memorize secure. high-value authentication secrets such as master passwords, enterprise or admin account passwords.

reference: Hi, my name is Chengcheng Zhang. I will present the research patterns for representing knowledge graphs to communicate situational knowledge of service robots. This work is done in collaboration with my co authors Zixuan, Wang Chaoran, Chen, yi, dai, lyumanshan Ye. And Xiaohua Sun. Service robots need to not only utilize but also communicate their situational knowledge of the working environment. Knowledge graphs, or KGs, are commonly used to represent such knowledge in robots. Recent research focused on designing KG interfaces for expert users. This helps experts to understand the internal state of the robot and program new tasks. However, how to design an understandable interface for non-expert users remains to be explored. To this end, we aim to discover patterns that naturally arise when ordinary people try to visually communicate the knowledge of a robot using cards on a canvas. We describe the process of discovering and formalizing these patterns. Then, we derive design recommendations by prototyping and Wizard-of-Oz testing. We began by creating comic strips to represent stories of knowledge communication between a human and a robot. We took care to depict the scenario in a way that does not hint at how the knowledge is presented to avoid influencing the study outcome. We then designed hexagonal cards to represent pieces of robotic knowledge. The hexagonal design allows for versatile arrangement and efficient use of space. The color code of the cards corresponds to common types of situational knowledge, which is summarized from a literature search. The content of the cards is filled in according to each scenario. The 12 participants of the study had no prior knowledge of KGs or robotics. We presented them with scenario comics and asked them to play the role of the robot. They arranged the cards and drew on a canvas in a way they think is most understandable and clear. Then, they narrated the canvas using a rectangular frame meant to represent the limit of the robot screen. Shown here is a time-lapse of the entire process. To extract common patterns from the final canvases, we developed a five-step process that consists of iterative coding and verification. The coding is done in two levels, one for local smaller patterns or low-level patterns, one for the overall structure of the canvas or high-level patterns. We use diagrams to formalize them to arrive at the final pattern library. The low-level patterns or components provide various ways of grouping knowledge elements to communicate short pieces of information, like using affinity to group similar knowledge or using location on the canvas to indicate where events happened within the room. The high-level patterns or modules are ways to combine and organize components to tell a more complex story. For example, participants may nest many smaller patterns within a larger flowchart pattern to show the robot's reasoning and knowledge used while carrying out a task. Our co-researchers not involved in the analysis designed a set of knowledge communication interfaces for lab service robot using the pattern library. We then tested the interface using Wizard-of-Oz techniques on a TAMI robot. During the process, we found that an advantage of using the patterns is that they can be directly translated to graph database queries. Meanwhile, designers can design interfaces without detailed knowledge of the KG structure. Overall, the 10 participants of the testing responded positively regarding the interface. Interviews with them highlighted several design recommendations. Technical language in the ontology can confuse users, so it's better to use user-friendly language when presenting KG data. Loops in the KG structure and a large number of similar elements also confuse users when browsing the interface. The classification tree pattern can help ease this problem, but at the expense of increasing interface depth. Browsing KG using the entity and relevant information pattern is easier than browsing by ontology, but a preview of the neighborhood might be needed to support this interaction. If you wish to learn more, please refer to our paper for more details. The cards, dataset, photos, and code we used are available on the project GitHub. Thank you very much for your attention and interest, and we wish you a great day. Bye!

reference: Video games afford a range of different experiences, with some having a profound emotional impact on their players. In recent years, interest in these experiences has grown in HCI games research. However, this research does not account for how game designers should cater for such experiences, and so, we presently lack an understanding of how designers of such games approach and perceive their work. Understanding designers' professional practices is essential to developing theories and tools that support the design and evaluation of games with rich emotional content. In this work, we set out to explore three questions. What do designers of emotionally impactful games focus on? What challenges do they encounter in their work? And to what extent does existing HCI games work align with their practices? This knowledge may help identify and eventually bridge the gap between research and practice, and steer the field towards the more impactful play experience research. To address these questions, we interviewed 14 indie game industry professionals who had worked on commercially released games known for their emotional impact. We selected titles from a diverse pool of styles and genres, and we also aimed to include perspectives from a diverse sample of participants. The first major theme we identified revolves around the design vision. Designers first and foremost wanted their games to impact players on a personal level. Typically, they had a clear vision for the emotional experiences they intended to evoke. To achieve this, some designers started off by mapping out the emotional flow of each level or created a spreadsheet with specific emotions and their intensities that the players were expected to feel at different points in the game. In some cases, designers wanted to afford experiences that leave the player with something to think about, without actually specifying what something may be. The designers also noted that they appreciate when players report experiences other than the ones originally intended by them. To allow players to create unique personal experiences, designers took a range of different approaches. For instance, providing a purposefully vague ending could encourage players to arrive at their own interpretation about what happens in the game. The next theme is about creating room for experience. It refers to setting the stage for the intended experiences, and different approaches for doing that. Creating room for experience sometimes meant providing plenty of space within the game for the players to play around with each other, without being marched through a story that they have no control over. Others created room for players by letting them piece together information by themselves and build up conflicts in their head rather than being explicitly presented with it in the game. Another approach was to deliberately remove or lower the gameplay difficulty to allow players to focus on their internal thoughts and feelings, without being distracted by the gameplay aspects that were considered less important. That said, players actively experiencing the game first-hand was seen essential for the experience to be impactful, to enhance the felt emotions, and to encourage empathy. The third theme is about experiential fine-tuning, which refers to the involvement of players in the different stages of the game creation process. Player experience plays a significant role in the development of emotionally impactful games, with the designers shaping and attending to the intended experiences throughout the whole process. When testing parts of the game early on, the designers mainly focused on evaluating if the players understood what was happening in the game, with less focus on evaluating the emotional involvement of players, which was instead done closer to the completion of the game. Designers typically gathered these insights from players through interviews and observations, although evaluation of emotional experiences was not always perceived as straightforward. For instance, emotional reactions like fear were seen as easy to test for, but other experiences like how mysterious something seems to the player were seen as much more challenging to assess. Emotional fine-tuning was particularly difficult when no similar games existed to compare to, and to give comfort as to what would be considered the right balance. The interviews we conducted allowed us to gain a better understanding of the intentions of designers of emotionally impactful games and the challenges they encounter in their work. But more importantly, we revealed an existing gap between player experience research and practice, particularly with regards to the mismatch between the focus on how specific emotions are created in player experience literature and the designers' vision of leaving experiences and interpretations to the players. This opens up new avenues for future work that can help narrow this gap down. We list these in our paper. One such suggestion is to explore the role of interpretive and fictional agency and interpretive challenge in shaping players' unique interpretations of games.

reference: On behalf of my co authors Marianne Graves Petersen from Aarhus University and Stijn Ossevoort from Eindhoven University, I present our paper entitled Expressivity in Interaction. A framework for design, my name is Miguel Bruns and I work at the Department of industrial Design at Eindhoven University of Technology. Our work is particularly inspired by artificial intelligence, emerging materials and shape-changing interfaces. Expressivity, expression, expressive behavior or expressiveness are reoccurring terms in HCI and design research. And while many researchers emphasize that interaction should be expressive, there is little agreement on what the term denotes. To give a few examples, Felitsia and Betabby discuss how expressive interactions support the development of a relationship between a user and a system. And Wensveen and colleagues refer to expression as a system's reaction with a diversity of dynamic qualities reflecting the expression of a user's action. Finally, task, guarded colleagues define expressivity as the way in which people can convey thoughts or feelings. Towards a system using multiple multimodal and nuanced approaches, depending on their competences, these different perspectives. Are summarized in this figure, showing the interaction qualities from a human artifact and social cultural perspective. and illustrate the cacophony surrounding the term. Expressivity has also been prominently used in the design rationales of various research-through-design projects, which can serve as a theory nexus. E.g. the alarm clock by Stephen Wensveen enables humans to express their emotions towards a system, Planck's. By Anna Vargada shows the expressive qualities of a computational composite, and finally the Aai lamp designed by Philip Ross. is illustrative for expressive interaction, supporting both the expression of emotions through human behavior, as well as expressive behavior of the lamp. We built on the perspective framework of Philip Ross, which provides four perspectives of engagement, namely sensory-motor activity, dynamic form, social activity and value, in relation to human behavior and artifact behavior. Based on an analysis of various research-through-design cases, the following terms emerged in relation to these perspectives, Emotion, Freedom of Action, Ambiguity and Subtlety, Skill Development, Temporal Form, Multimodal Feedback, Action Perception Loops and Societal Context. To confirm these terms, we conducted a systematic literature review, Yielding 29 design cases describing expressivity and interaction from these 29 design cases, we extracted the author's descriptions. of their design rationales, as illustrated in the example of Dancing with Drones. The quotes were categorized by two of the authors Based on the terms found in our 1st review, which confirmed that all qualities had been used to a certain extent to describe the expressivity and interaction. Based on our findings, we proposed this framework for exclusivity and interaction. Expressivity and interaction is achieved by supporting emotional expressivity and freedom of interaction, and through temporal form of the artifact. The action perception loops between human and artifact can have multimodal qualities and allow for subtlety and ambiguity. Through the interaction between human and artifact, a skill can be developed. The framework was presented in a master course at industrial design. And used to design a self, robotic shape changing interface.

reference: Hello everyone, I am Yang Li, a Ph.D. researcher from Kochi University of Technology, Japan. Today we will talk about text revision designs in VR environments. During the virtualization process of daily office work into VR, we found plenty of scenarios where need effective and useful typing methods. Based on voice-to-text and AI-assisted techniques, users can enter typo-free text quickly into VR applications. In real-life scenarios, we also need to change the entered text to express precise or proper intention. That brings us to the question, for virtual reality scenarios, how do current VR typing methods handle text revision? To To answer this question, we 1st did a thorough review on Vr typing papers in last 20 years. We found that researchers mainly put attention on boosting typing speed and accuracy in VR via proposing novel methods. For text revision, however, it is seldom mentioned. Ironically, some solutions didn't include backspace and or cursor control into their designs. To fill this gap and to make the initial step to explore text revision solutions in VR, we include cursor control and backspace into our consideration. As shown in this slide, for cursor control, we get two options, discrete and continuous, into our design. Similarly, for backspace, we also set character level and word level as two alternatives. Based on these two tools and their options, we turn them into a design space as shown on the right. Every cell of the design space represents a combinational use of backspace and cursor control method. To further validate the design space, we implemented four text revision techniques with the virtual keyboard and handheld controllers. In detail, we used the click and swipe behavior on the physical button or on the touchpad to realize different backspace granularities and cursor control methods. We designed a within-subjects experiment with 16 participants to evaluate their text revision performance with four techniques. We also put different types of targets for participants to revise. Every participant needs to revise totally 120 targets with four proposed techniques. Overall, results showed that the combination of word level backspace and continuous cursor control got the better performance than other techniques in terms of correction time, operation per character, the number of using backspace and cursor control, and user preference. In detail, continuous cursor control leads to less operation number to revise a target. For targets far from the end of the sentence, techniques with continuous cursor control can significantly reduce the workload to finish the revision. Continuous cursor control can reduce efforts to manipulate the character, especially for far targets. However, it should be noted that participants have to focus on the fast-moving characters to stop the character to the intended place. Word level backspace contributes to the less use of backspace during revision, whereas it may also be a double-edged sword to bring potential cascade efforts for recovery to participants if they misdelete more words. To conclude, we first reviewed the lack of text revision in current VR typing designs. Then we proposed a design space and text revision techniques in VR. Results of our user study also serve as guidelines for future designers. For future work, we will conduct mass-scale usability study for deeper understanding users' text revision behaviors in VR environments. Based on current results, we will also include AI-assisted techniques and propose novel tools and procedures to enhance users' text revision performance in VR. Thanks for your attention and please check our paper for more details.

reference: Hi, my name is Evan Strasnick, and this talk is titled Coupling Simulation and Hardware for Interactive Circuit Debugging. Simulation is a powerful tool in the design of analog circuits, and most often we use it before building out real components in a prototype or a Pcb. We do this to verify a schematic design. However, simulation also has the potential to aid as a debugging tool when working with that physical hardware. Specifically, it can help the designer to compare their measurements to theoretical expected behaviors to identify where errors may first arise. They also offer a way for the designer to quickly explore alternatives without modifying the hardware, so that they can reveal how changes to the design improve the behavior. But there are also challenges in making comparisons between the simulation and the physical circuit. When the designer adjusts the hardware and measures a response to some input, they have to perform that same change in the simulation, capture the input they observed, and import it into the simulation. Similarly, when the designer explores alternatives quickly in simulation and wants to compare back to the hardware, they would need to manually rework that physical circuit for each case explored. So we address these challenges in a tool called SimPoint. SimPoint tightly couples the designer's physical circuit with its simulated counterpart to facilitate debugging. SimPoint is built on the infrastructure of Pinpoint, a PCB debugging tool we introduced at CHI in 2019. Pinpoint generates for the designer a custom jig board that interfaces their PCB to testing hardware, allowing the user to perform their debugging operations in a software interface as opposed to manipulating the hardware. Simpoint uses new testing hardware capable of modifying physical components within the circuit and routing external components in their place. SimPoint's software then also manages the simulation of the user's circuit, represented as a SPICE netlist. At the highest level, the first thing that SimPoint enables is comparing live measurements from the hardware with the expected behavior as predicted by the simulation. As an example, imagine you have this very simple RC filter circuit, which attenuates high-frequency noise. Suppose we have a fault and the capacitor's value is outside of tolerance. When we hook up the circuit to an input, here a sine wave shown in red, we can see that the output, in cyan, is attenuated. But is this filter working correctly according to the parameters of our design? With one command, SimPoint takes measurements across the full circuit and juxtaposes them in an interactive plot with the responses to the same live input as predicted by the simulation. So we can see here how our physical circuit's output, that's shown in purple, differs from the simulation, shown in light blue. SimPoint also makes it easier for me to make changes to my physical circuit and its inputs, and when I do so, the simulation updates in parallel so that I can continue to compare behaviors. For example, it can programmatically substitute a physical component on the board with a different component from an external bank. As an example of that, here I can use this modify resistor command to change R1 in my physical circuit to a different resistor value, and as I do so, we can see the circuit update in real time. When we repeat that comparison, we see that the simulation has updated as well. So this ability to modify the hardware helps us to mirror on the hardware the explorations that we typically perform in simulation. For example, SimPoint gives us automated tools to directly investigate how these alternative circuit parameters affect behavior. So here we can ask how the amplitude of our output varies with the value of the resistor. And with one command, SimPoint rapidly samples different values of that resistor, measures the responses, and plots those results, here in green, alongside the simulation in red, at those values. And we can see that the output varies inversely with the resistance in both cases, but with a different coefficient because of that incorrect capacitance in the circuit. So please check out the paper for many other features of SimPoint, such as summarizing high-level patterns across the circuit, automatically detecting relationships that may indicate error, and a specification language for authoring tests on high-level behaviors. The paper also includes demonstrations to show how these capabilities can be used in context to solve a variety of real-world bugs on different types of circuits. And thank you very much.

reference: Hello, I'm Florian Jesche from the University of Siegen in Germany and I'm presenting our study about the comparison of different types of augmented reality visualizations for instructions on behalf of my co-authors Sven Hoffmann, Thomas Ludwig and Volker Wulf. In the past 20 years there were several studies which used augmented reality to support maintenance and manual assembly tasks. In these studies, the augmented reality instructions were often compared to instructions on paper or different augmented reality systems like handheld devices or head-mounted displays were compared to each other. The results regarding the key performance indicators like task completion time, error rate and mental effort are not consistent, but augmented reality is often seen as a very promising technology for such problems. However, the actual design of augmented reality instructions or more precisely the holograms is not very well studied and there is no study which investigates the influence of different visualization types for augmented reality instructions in complex machine setup tasks. In our study, we are comparing four different augmented reality visualization types for setting up an industrial bending machine using the Microsoft HoloLens. The first visualization type includes concrete 3D models from CAD data to show where and how to mount different parts on the machine, as you can see here on the right side. The second visualization type only includes abstract elements like arrows and boxes to indicate where to mount the parts on the machine, as we can see here on the left side. In the other two visualization types, we are using the same holograms, but we add videos for each step in the instruction. Furthermore, we use a paper-based instruction as a baseline. The study was carried out as a between-subjects study with each 10 participants for the augmented reality conditions and 8 participants for the paper-based line. We measured the time for setting up the machine, counted the arrows, and asked the participants about the mental effort during the task by filling out the RSME and NASA-TLX questionnaire. Furthermore, we collected data about the user experience and usability of the augmented reality applications using the user experience questionnaire and the system usability scale. We also video recorded the sessions and conducted a closing interview with the participants for qualitative feedback on the applications. We performed a statistical analysis of variance on the data with the following results. The participants with the paper instruction completed the task the fastest, followed by the two augmented reality instructions with the abstract visualizations. Both visualizations with the concrete holograms were the slowest, but there are no significant differences in the task completion time between the different visualization types. The different visualization types lead to significant different error rates. Participants with the concrete holograms with additional videos made only 1.7 from 11 possible errors on average. The abstract holograms with additional videos and the paper instruction performed well, too. Participants using these visualization types made 2 errors on average. The most errors occurred with the augmented reality visualization with only the abstract holograms with 3.9 errors on average. This number is significantly higher than for the conditions with videos and the paper-based instruction. We can also notice a similar effect for the mental effort. The mental effort was the lowest for the paper-based instruction, followed by the two conditions with videos. The visualization type with only abstract holograms lead to the highest mental effort. Summarizing our findings. Videos cause no significant longer task completion time and different visualization types have no impact on the task completion time. The concrete visualization with videos promotes a correct execution and is beneficial for the mental effort. Furthermore, the videos have a high positive effect on abstract visualizations and they should always be considered when creating augmented reality instructions. The videos have given the participants confidence in their actions. The augmented reality applications were rated as novel and helpful and no major usability flaws were noted by the participants. For the whole results, please read our paper. Thank you.

reference: Hey, I'm Katie Cunningham. I'm excited to talk to you about purpose-first programming. A growing number of people are studying computing toward a wide variety of goals, but we teach programming to everyone in largely the same way. This approach causes particular problems for conversational programmers. Conversational programmers want to learn programming so they can talk with others about technology, but they don't plan to program themselves. Conversational programmers could be project managers, designers, or entrepreneurs. Conversational programmers often feel that they don't benefit from typical resources, like online tutorials and formal courses. These approaches prioritize syntax and semantics, while conversational programmers want high-level knowledge about how programming is used to solve real problems. Since typical programming instruction focuses on a deep understanding of how coding structures operate, it can take a long time before novices work on authentic tasks that they might see in a workplace. Designing for conversational programmers is hard because they have seemingly conflicting goals. They want high-level knowledge about programming gained in a short time frame, but they also want to understand authentic tasks, which are often complex. Our approach, Purpose-First Programming, achieves both goals by focusing on domain-specific code patterns. This focus on patterns makes the application of what students are learning very clear. Added technical support allows learners to understand and use these patterns quickly. To develop a proof-of-concept, Purpose-First Programming system, we identified five common patterns of web-scraping code that use the BeautifulSoup Python library. We identified these patterns from code on GitHub and validated the authenticity and coverage of the patterns with two experts. Drawing inspiration from the literature on programming plans, each pattern is annotated with the goal it achieves overall, sub-goals within the pattern, and information about where and how the pattern should be changed. We built a brief curriculum that supported learners' ability to recognize, understand, combine, and tailor these patterns. reference: Freelance work as we know it is changing as a result of digital platforms that connect highly skilled professionals with clients. Not only is remote work growing in popularity, but you can now easily commission a talented graphics designer in Kenya to edit your photos, pay a programmer in Colombia to build your website, or even pay an editor in the UK to proofread your academic paper. As research on platform-mediated work is growing, there is still little work looking at the implications for freelancers. Therefore, we set out to understand freelancers' points of views on such platforms. To gather unfiltered, original experiences of doing online freelancing, we qualitatively analysed 528 posts and 7,499 comments from four freelancing subforums on Reddit. Our data points to three main themes that intersect freelance work with online freelancing platforms precarity, control, and networks. By exposing how freelancers perceive platform-mediated work, we provide evidence to support future directions for designing freelancing platforms that are more worker-centred. Freelance work comes with associated precarity and financial pressures, as frequently mentioned in posts. The biggest thing I did poorly when transitioning to freelance was being naive about how damn hard it is to find new clients, and I paid for it big time with months of close calls like not being able to pay rent. Platforms were recognised as a beneficial source of work and experience for those freelancers starting as self-employed. I started on Upwork with zero freelance experience while in college, and now I'm basically an intermediate freelancer. A common reason mentioned for becoming freelancers is to feel in control when, where, and how one works. However, we found freelancers also vocalised their frustrations about how platform elements actually reduced autonomy over one's work, while still bearing the same risks and uncertainty of freelancing. Putting other people in the driver's seat of your career is usually called being employed. So why lose the control while also having no benefits, no job security, no legal rights? You're completely right. Handing over your career to Upwork is like having a boss but also being a freelancer. The worst of both worlds. Whether deliberately or not, platforms control freelancers' earning potential through rating scores and discretion over account termination. I have no problem with suspending my account, but I got paid just before the suspension and I have no access to that money. They'll back the money without giving me details of the violation. In my opinion, Upwork's clients have the upper hand. I feel like a bad rating hurts freelancers much more than clients. We found that freelancers see client relationships as equal partnerships that enable power to negotiate work arrangements and push back against abusive practices. One of the nice things about freelance work is that it's more of a business-to-business kind of relationship than the master-subordinate relationship you usually see with employment. Cultivating networks of clients is also true for freelancing platforms, but platforms were seen to gatekeep and constrain these client-freelancer relationships. Platforms do everything in their power to erect a wall between you and your clients because this is how they make their profit. They will ban your ass in a heartbeat if you try and circumvent this wall. By strictly controlling the client relationship, they own you and your business because you can't leave unless you start over from scratch. Ultimately, while platforms can be seen as a good starting point, they were not viewed as sustainable career options and might actually push freelancers away. While platforms are helpful, you're running a business, so you should learn how to find clients on your own. To sum up, we found that while platforms can mitigate some of freelancers' precarity, they also introduce new forms of worker control and erode work autonomy. These findings point to the need to construct fairer futures of freelance knowledge work. We must envision futures where freelancers have control over their client relationships, reputation and abilities to nurture their freelance career. To do so, we argue that platforms should embrace new worker-centred design directions.

reference: I'm Teresa O'Leary. I'm a personal health informatics PhD student at Northeastern University. Today I'll be presenting our work examining the intersections of race, religion, and community technologies, a photovoice study. Historically, black churches have been integral in addressing race-based health inequities, although little work has examined to what extent technology can support such efforts. Addressing this gap, we engaged two churches, churches A and B, in a four-year research project. Our long-term project goal is to design an mHealth intervention with church members to address health disparities in their communities. Over the course of the first year, church members joined us for numerous design activities. Today, I'll focus on photovoice. We examined these intersections as we explored how technology can promote well-being in churches with historically black memberships. Our findings helped to answer these questions. Today, we'll focus on how can we characterize the intricacies of racial identity in community organizations, and how can we design for multicultural communities? Our work provides a case study of how HCI can use an assets-based approach to study race in a community context. We acknowledge that systems of power reinforce racial inequity in the research process by not engaging BIPOC participants as equal partners. In an attempt to disrupt this power imbalance, we used a photo elicitation technique called photovoice. Photovoice is a flexible participant-led methodology where participants use camera to explore matters of personal relevance. First, we facilitated an affinity diagram activity where participants explored the intersections of race, religion, health, and technology as it relates to their church community. And next, members took one to two photos based off of the clusters they created. And in a follow-up focus group, they returned to view these photos. Participants ended in group dialogue where they discussed how the concept of race should impact technology design in each of their church communities. We analyzed photos, worksheets, and interviews using grounded theory. Traditional models used to understand black religious participation have focused on a limited set of characteristics. Instead, using an assets-based approach, church members dispelled monolithic perceptions of the black church. To demonstrate how distinctions between these organizations drive the need for more nuanced technology designs, I'll present the following findings, comparing church missions and exploring adaptations to change. We found that each church's mission suggested unique directions for design. First, much of church A's mission focuses on nurturing the spiritual growth of their congregation by engaging members in fellowship activities. This mission is exemplified by photos participants selected, highlighting the need for designing technology to connect church members around spiritual matters. Whereas church B's mission and members described a commitment to societal issues. This photo is one of many ministries that address social inequities. As a result, church B's members were interested in using technology to support social justice activities. Both communities continually adapt to change, which in turn impacts their feelings about technology integration. For example, church B has had success rapidly growing their membership. In this photo, church members juxtaposed the connection they feel when in person to technology integrated into their worship hall. They lamented that streaming options come at a cost of fellowship. Future work should explore how hybrid technology solutions can support a sense of connectedness in growing communities. Now, church A is focused on engaging younger members to grow their church. Church members posited that technology may be an answer. However, church A is housed in a historic building. We see how church legacies, like preserving a historic building, sits in direct tension with technology integration. Thus, there's a need for design methods that could help church communities move toward a consensus on the role of technology in their church. reference: In this paper, we studied older and younger adults' privacy decision-makings and found that older adults are more likely to make their decisions based on privacy calculus. According to Census Bureau, older adults are individuals who are at least 65 years old. By 2030, 12 % of the world's population will be older adults. Older adults may need more care compared to others. For example, they may need emotional care to prevent being isolated from the society. Or they may need medical attention, and maybe someone to remind them to take their pills in the morning. There is a good news. Technology can help with many of these. For emotional care, there are social apps that can help older adults keep in touch with their loved ones. For medical care, there are apps which help older adults schedule their medicine consumption or remotely access to health practitioners. But if technology can be significantly beneficial for older adults, then why older adults' tech usage is much below other populations? Some people argue that older adults fell behind past pace of technology and are just not tech-savvy. We believe that this is not really the case. Instead, we believe this is technology's fault. Technology is not tailored to older adults and is not designed to be older adult-friendly. Older adults' perspective is usually not being involved in designing stages of technology products while they are a different population compared to younger adults. Psychology research shows that older adults have a different thinking mechanism compared to younger adults. Older adults follow a model-based way of thinking, which is more of a goal-driven and economic decision-making style, while younger adults follow a model-free way of thinking, for which future rewards are less pronounced and is more of a heuristic approach. In this work, we study privacy decision-making process of older adults. Privacy concern is among top three reasons for older adults not using technology. Our research question is how privacy decision-making process for older adults is different than younger adults. To address this research question, we used two theoretical frameworks. Privacy calculus, which argues that privacy decisions are rational and that individuals make a trade-off between the risks and benefits of disclosure when making the decision. And a heuristic account, which argues that privacy decisions are not fully rational. To study older and younger adults' privacy decisions, we designed a financial recommendation app. The app claimed to give suggestions for users relating to their financial situations. For example, provide suggestions to increase their credit score and generate loan recommendations. The app claimed that users can increase the quality of recommendations by disclosing more data such as their credit score and yearly income. In addition to measuring disclosure behavior, we also measured participants' perceptions of the sensitivity level of each of the data and the extent to which they think disclosing the data could improve the quality of recommendations. We also measured participants' trust to the app. Here is our result. One of the predictors of disclosure behavior is data sensitivity. Both younger and older adults were less likely to disclose sensitive data. The other predictor of disclosure was recommendation quality. However, this is only a predictor for older adults. When older adults believe disclosing their data will improve the recommendation quality, they will be more likely to disclose it. While younger adults' disclosure decision is merely based on the sensitivity level of the data, older adults' decision is closer to privacy calculus, which is based on a trade-off between the sensitivity and the benefits. Furthermore, trust predicted recommendation quality. Those who trust the app more believe that they will receive better recommendations by disclosing their data. For younger adults, trust was also a predictor of data sensitivity. When younger adults trust the app more, they believe that their data is less sensitive. This may be counterintuitive as sensitivity of a data is an inherent aspect of the data and it sounds like a heuristic decision making. We found that older adults make a better trade-off in their privacy decisions compared to younger adults. Our work refutes the deficit-based narrative against older adults' technology use and shows that they can even do better in privacy calculus. We discussed some practical suggestions in the paper. For example, apps should clearly communicate the risks and benefits of a product, especially when having older adult audience. reference: Hello everyone, my name is Tong Xue and I am a 4th year PhD student at Beijing Institute of Technology in Beijing, China. This is a presentation video of our CHI 2021 work, titled RCEA360VR, Real-Time Continuous Emotion Annotations in 360VR Videos for Collecting Precise Viewport-Dependent Ground Truth Labels. This is a collaboration work with my co-authors in CWI and TODAFT. Watching 360 videos using HMD can provide interactive and immersive VR experience. Whether the goal is to induce emotion or track and recognize emotion with the VR, it is important to collect accurate and precise ground truth emotion labels. However, unlike 2D videos, by allowing users to freely rotate their heads and construct their own viewing experience, we can no longer be sure users' annotations pertain to that specific scene at any given point in time. In general, emotion data collection takes place by post-stimuli self-reports, like self-assessment mannequin. However, such self-reports are temporarily imprecise, since one can experience multiple emotions while watching video content. Moreover, collecting emotion in VR can be time-consuming, demand cognitive thought, and even break the sense of presence and the immersive. To minimize such workload and distraction, we designed two joystick-based continuous emotion annotation techniques, HoloLight and DotSize, in our prior work. The color of the visualization represents which quadrant they are annotating, and the transparency of size means emotion intensity. In this work, we first present and evaluate the usability of RCEA360 VR system. Our experiment is conducted in a controlled indoor environment with 32 participants using both HoloLight and DotSize. They viewed 8 360 video clips through an HTC Vive Pro iHMD, and they were instructed to annotate emotion states by moving the joystick head into one of the four quadrants. A helper function was embedded for easy lookup. Besides head movement, annotation data, and physiological signals through empathic E4 bands, participants were also asked to report their overall emotions using a WizenVR time-rating scale and fill in SSQ, IPQ, and NASA TLX questionnaires. Through our controlled usability evaluation, we found no significant differences between HoloLight and DotSize concerning motion thickness, presence, or helper function usage amount. For mental workload, we don't find significant differences neither from NASA TLX nor physiological methods among HoloLight, DotSize, and the WizenVR time ratings. Together, our findings indicate HoloLight and DotSize don't result in high thickness workloads nor break presence. Then we verified the reliability of our continuous annotations. The mean valence and rozo ratings for HoloLight and DotSize are in line with ratings from original data set, as well as our WizenVR time ratings. Also, they are rated similarly across HoloLight and DotSize. To ensure our continuous annotations are effective for building precise ground-truth labels, we developed a segment-level viewport-dependent annotation fusing method. We first calculated time delays and did continuous annotation time alignment by DTW. Then we ran hierarchical clustering to cluster users based on similarities in their viewport behavior. Lastly, we conducted frame-level and segment-level fusing approaches to robustly fuse multiple viewport-dependent annotations. These fusing results provide temporal details into the peaks, valleys, and trends of users' experience, which enable a more fundamental temporal lens to understand emotion states and specific sense of an immersive 360-viewing experience. Thank you for watching this video. All our code is open-source and can be obtained by scanning QR codes or visiting GitHub. If you have any questions or want to know more details about our RCEA360VR work, please feel free to contact us.

reference: My name is Vasiliki Tsaknaki. I'm an assistant professor at the It University of Copenhagen in Denmark. And I will present the work I did together with my colleagues Kelsey Colton, Pavel Karposevich and Pedro Sanchez at Kth Royal Institute of Technology. in Stockholm, Sweden. In this paper we report on a collaboration between a singer, Kelsey, and interaction designers exploring, through soma design methods, how non-habitual breathing patterns can be sensed through muscle movement occurring on the torso And how to capture the nuanced somatic experience of breathing through sensing technologies? In the context of our research, non habitual breathing refers to the process of the familiarizing one's breathing. Through Soma design methods, but also how, but also to how, somatic experiences of breathing cannot always be mapped to breathing patterns that biosensors. are most often designed to capture. We present a detailed articulation of an autobiographical soma design exploration focused on sensing technologies for capturing biodata from breathing, including the adaptations we made to all the self-sensors, a wearable strain sensor and an electromyography sensor, EMG. These explorations resulted in the Breathing Shell prototype, designed firstly for capturing the wearer's breathing in the muscles showing on the top right, and secondly for giving the sensation of tangibility of the act of breathing. This is experienced as shape-change actuation evoked through custom-made sensor-actuator pillows placed on top of the muscles that contract and retract while breathing. We contribute with two implications for designing with biosensors from a soma design perspective through a process that prioritizes diverse felt experiences when working with sensing mechanisms. The first is to engage with biosensors through reflecting on the somatic experience of being sensed, in tandem with the data captured, and the second to use actuation for deepening one's understanding of how the soma relates to or with a biosensor when engaged in complex bodily functions. For a period that lasted about five months, we engaged in an autobiographical design process of exploring sensing non-habitual breathing through soma design. We worked closely with a somatic connoisseur, in this context, the author Kelsey, and we practiced three non habitual breathing exercises led by her. With the intent of the familiarizing this bodily function, the exercises helped us to become attentive to the act of breathing. and to imagine and explore new ways of using sensors to interact with it. They can be found as supplementary material to our paper in ACM. From the explorations with the sensors, we became curious about how the tangibility of sensors, experienced as pressure applied against the skin, could create a tactile somatic experience of being sensed. In order to explore this further, we developed a new type of shape-change sensor-actuator mechanism for this context, seen in the figures. We programmed each pillow to deflate when pressure is applied on it, and inflate when there is no pressure applied to its surface. Thus we created a mirrored effect of the degree of inhalation exhalation to the shape change material. The breathing shell has five shape change pillows and evokes two distinct experiences, Total interaction integration and total disruption. The first refers to how the responsiveness of the pillows added to the somatic experience of feeling like a body within a body when wearing the shell. The second, as articulated by Kelsey, refers to the sensation of being trapped within her own body or within someone else's body as the pillows inflate to their maximum volume. The design implications we offer can help designers working in the space to achieve a match between what bodies experience when being sensed, how different bodily areas such as muscles participate in a bodily function, and what sensors are able to capture in relation to the felt experience of being sensed. To conclude, our research opens a design space on working with biosensing technologies from a somatic, first-person perspective that can expand from breathing to other bodily functions. Our implications lay the groundwork for others to delve deeper into the space and explore further how to design for the somatic impact of being sensed. Thank you for listening. Please read our full paper and we are looking forward to your comments, feedback and questions.

reference: Hi, my name is Shen Mei. I'm a fourth year PhD student in computer science at WPI. Today, I will present the results of the findings regarding the effects of local latencies on competitive first-person shooter game players. It's a common knowledge that the decrease in latency helps game players, and the local latency is an important type of latency. It's the time between the mouse clicking and the rendering on the screen. Now, if we upgrade the system to a high-end gaming system, there would be shorter local latency. The question is, how much does the upgrade help competitive first-person shooter players? Talking about affecting gamers, the first aspect would be performance. This would affect your ranking in the game. We have two metrics for performance, and they are weapon accuracy and in-game score. We also want to know how the lower local latency helps player feelings, And the player feeling is represented by the quality of experience. To understand the impact of local latency on gamers, we designed a user study. The game for the study was CSGO. We customized the game, so the game mode is deathmatch-free for all, and the goal for the players is to kill as many as they can. We have log files to record all the game data. Different types of systems cause different local latencies. The latency for gaming system are mainly in a range of zero to 100 milliseconds, and normal pieces are like 100 to 200 milliseconds. Consoles and TVs would have latencies even higher. The local latency of the gaming system used in the study was measured at 25ms. There are five shuffled latency values added to the game rounds. and they are 0, 25, 50, 75, and 100ms. The game flow was self-contained. All the users need to do was to double-click on the only button on the desktop, and the flow will be loaded automatically. We have another script to clean the system in case the game or the computer crashed. After each round of the game, players answer 4 questions about their experience and feelings. After completing all the games, players fill out a demographic questionnaire. A total number of 43 users were recruited, And they are all experienced Csgo players with over 01:00 in the game. Here are some of our results. The graph on the left denotes accuracy versus latency. The x-axis is latency in milliseconds, and the y-axis on the right is accuracy, and the y-axis on the left is the accuracy improvement compared to the 125ms condition. The rectangles are the mean values Bounded by 95 % confidence intervals, the dashed line denotes the linear regression. For the mean values, the regression fits the data well. with r-square high at 0.95, and a significant p-value. We can learn that accuracy decreases linearly with local latency in a low range. And a decrease in local latency by 100ms Improves accuracy percent by eight. The graph on the right is for score. The axis and points are as in the left graph. but the data is for score instead of accuracy. The linear regression fits the data well with r-square high at 0.98, and a very low p-value. We can learn that score also decreases linearly with local latency in a low range. And a decrease in local latency by 100ms improves score by 12 points. For reference, Twelve points means six more kills in Cs. Go for an overall measure of Qe, We. We compute the mean ratings by weighting all the questions equally in this. in this graph, the X axis is local latency. and the y-axis is rating. The linear regression fits the mean values well with r-square high at 0.96, and a significant Significant P value, same as performance, Qe, also decreases linearly with local latency. And a decrease in latency by 100ms improves QE by 1.5 out of 5. Thanks for your attention on the work.

reference: Hello, everyone. I'm Arthi Asrani, and I'm excited to discuss our work examining the use of online platforms for employment. A survey of U.S. job seekers. The Internet is now pivotal for those seeking employment. However, it is unclear which online resources are key to employment, how job seekers take advantage of them, and how these resources and strategies relate to positive outcomes. We conducted an online cross-sectional survey of 768 job seekers in the United States, where we investigated which online platforms, specific job search phases, behaviors, and strategies job seekers used in their job search. We included 10 popular platforms that we categorized as career-oriented, such as company websites, Indeed, Career Builder, job-related Q&A sites, and LinkedIn, and non-career-oriented social media platforms, such as Facebook, Facebook Groups, Twitter, Instagram, and YouTube. We analyzed how the use of these platforms was associated with employment and perceived social support. We then examined whether these results correlated with demographic factors, such as race, gender, income, educational status, and geographic location. We found that most job seekers used all 10 of the online platforms in their job search that we proposed and others. Perhaps unsurprisingly, individuals with higher income and education used these platforms more frequently. However, Indeed was not significantly correlated with any demographic variables. This suggests that the platform was used broadly across demographic groups. Our work suggests that inequality could be amplified when digital employment platforms are designed and marketed to specific job seekers, especially professionals or white-collar workers. Companies, practitioners, and designers could change their marketing and design strategies to include lower-wage job seekers or blue-collar workers. For instance, Indeed and its marketing aims to be inclusive while LinkedIn targets professional job seekers. While we found that these platforms were beneficial for information seeking, we found opportunities for more active job search behaviors, such as getting advice, getting referrals, and seeking training. These behaviors were used less frequently and are, as past research suggests, beneficial for job seekers who experience marginalization. Our third research question sought to understand whether adopting different job search strategies online was associated with different outcomes. Exploratory and focus strategies were positively associated with the increase in the odds of getting callbacks, and these were two strategies that higher income job seekers were more likely to employ. The use of Q&A sites and company websites were significantly associated with exploratory strategies, those that involve exploring multiple employment options and collecting information from multiple sources. Our work highlights that typical employment sites like Indeed and LinkedIn might not be as effective as Q&A platforms. We found Q&A platforms to be used for more exploratory strategies, which surprisingly were used predominantly by higher income populations. A qualitative examination is needed to further understand specific barriers that might prevent low-income job seekers from using these platforms in an exploratory way. Could sites that promote more exploratory job search strategies benefit a more diverse set of job seekers? We conjecture that Q&A sites could be better designed to address the needs of low-income job seekers. Mobilizing offline social networks is a common job search strategy and essential to finding employment. Thus, we aim to address our final question, how does one's perceived social support correlate with their use of these platforms for employment? Our findings suggest that the use of non-career oriented social media platforms is associated with reductions in perceived social support, while the use of Indeed is associated with a marginal increase in perceived social support. Our findings also reveal a positive association between lower income job seekers' use of non-career oriented social media and their perceived social support. It's possible that those who already have a strong offline network were less likely to find social media a useful source of social support, or that social media could be an opportunity to foster social connections for lower income individuals, especially those who don't have strong social connections offline. Going forward, researchers should investigate how social platforms could influence job seekers' perceived social support, especially for lower income individuals. Thank you, and this work was funded by the NSF.

reference: Hi everyone, I'm Ariful Islamonic. I'm a first year PhD student at the University of Manitoba, and I'm happy to present our paper, Data-Centric Explanations, Explaining Training Data of Machine Learning Systems to Promote Transparency. Machine learning algorithms are used in a range of automated systems we use in our life. Most of these systems are data-driven, which means that they work based on the data they have, which is necessarily the training data of the system. However, the challenge with this approach is that someone has to pick this training data, and owing to the limitations of resources and availability, sometimes these data are not accurate and they are not representative of the population who might be using the system. This leads to several performance issues and biases that we see with existing machine learning systems. For example, most face recognition softwares seem to perform poorly for people of color. Now, one explanation to this is that the system has been trained with images of mostly white faces, which are not representative of the population. Now, despite the importance of training data, for a number of stakeholders, the training data and the training process is a complete black box. They don't have any information on it. To provide transparency into this training process, in our work, we present training dataset information to potential end-users of the system, and then we study how this information might impact their perception of machine learning systems. Now, we presented this information through an explanation prototype, where the goal of the prototype was to communicate important information on training data, including how the data was collected and what data was used in the system. We grouped information about training data into five categories, where for every category, we provided some overview information. Within each category, we presented the information in a Q&A-based approach so that the reader can easily focus on the information that they're particularly interested in. On the right, you can see the questions and answers for the demographics category, where the prototype in particular is displaying the gender distribution of the training instances. We evaluated our prototype in a user study, where the goal of the study was to explore how this explanation impacts users' trust and fairness perception of machine learning systems. We conducted the study with 27 participants, where we explicitly recruited participants with a range of expertise. Participants interacted with a number of explanations from example systems, where we varied the stakes of the system, ranging from low to high stakes, and also the quality and the balance of the training data presented into these explanations. We used questionnaires and semi-structured interviews to collect data from our participants. Our study data shows that these explanations are positively received by participants, and they have a positive impact on end-users' trust and fairness perception of the systems. Participants talked about how they trust the system more because they have seen this explanation and they feel that they know more about the system. Among all the information presented, participants found the demographic information to be the most useful, and they talked about how it helped them to identify any potential biases in the system. For example, This participant mentioned that since 90 % of the data were from male, they can easily conclude that the system would perform better for men. Additionally, we saw some interesting insights that machine learning experts might be underestimating the capabilities of general users of machine learning systems. Some expert participants in our study seemed to think that these explanations would be too difficult for people without any computer science or machine learning background. However, we did not see any evidence of our non-expert participants finding this information difficult to understand. To summarize our contribution, we designed data-centric explanations that communicate training dataset information to end-users of the system with the goal of increasing system transparency. We also presented study findings that show that these explanations have the potential to inform participants' judgment of trust and fairness in machine learning systems. Going forward, it would be important to explore how we can evaluate these explanations in the context of real-world systems, and in doing so, we can better understand how this type of transparency might impact users' interaction with machine learning systems. We hope that our work would motivate other researchers to work with different aspects of data-centric explanations. Thank you everyone for your attention.

reference: I'm Sonia Hashim. And I'm Jingyi Li. Today we're presenting work with Jennifer Jacobs on what visual artists can teach us about software development. Software is closely integrated with art production, but developing software for artists is challenging. By analyzing how artists use and develop software, we identified opportunities for end-user software development to map to creativity support tools. We interviewed 13 professional artists. We then analyzed interview data to surface themes such as why artists choose to build software and how software development shaped their practice. We focused on expert practitioners and visual artists across diverse domains, such as painting and interaction design. Artists were motivated to build software for multiple reasons. Artists built software for functional applications, like adding interactivity to artwork. Artists also use software for creative growth, such as coding their own interfaces to support specific forms of exploration or creative constraint. Lastly, artists develop software to establish technical authority when working with other artists or software developers. Next, we share some implications of our findings for HCI systems researchers. For instance, creativity support tools that prioritize black-box automation and high-level abstractions can prevent artists from developing unique processes and outcomes. There's a trend in creativity support tool research to build tools for novices. To lower barriers to entry, many systems rely on automating processes and abstracting data to generate artwork. However, we found artists value granular control over the ways their materials are used, their data, and the ways they are transformed through processes to develop bespoke and sophisticated outcomes. That's one example. Molly, an artist, used a vinyl cutter to cut parts for a sculpture. The out-of-the-box software was incompatible with her designs based on line drawings. In order to cut her designs and maintain their stylistic integrity, Molly wrote her own cutting algorithm that could handle intersections and interpret Bezier curves with thickness. She needed to write her own algorithm to reflect 1. her technical understanding of the vinyl cutter functionality and 2. her need to transform her line drawings into a format aligned with that functionality while retaining the intended stylistic quality. Another theme of our research highlighted the ways artists who rely primarily on digital tools frequently switch back and forth between physical and digital materials throughout their processes. For example, Ben alternated between painting on a tablet where it was easier to pick and preview colors and painting with oil paints where the materiality of the paint that could not be replicated in software mattered for the final look. Michael used digital fabrication techniques to think through different physical representations of a vector graphic he made, saying, I can extrude this, I can laser cut it 15 times and laminate it, I'm going to find opportunities past the computer. Due to these flexible workflows, we see opportunities for designing digital software that accommodate manual input and physical materials. These systems could support nonlinear workflows such that the output of any single stage can be the input of another. For example, in contrast to the usual linear digital fabrication workflow, we can imagine a software environment where a single interface lets artists author graphics, modify manual input parameters, and program CNC machine behavior. While our previous two takeaways provided guidelines for system design and engineering, we now discuss the larger socio-technical context of end-user programming for artists. From our interviews, we have seen many examples of how and why artists are creating their own software. Artists have a deep domain knowledge of their craft, choose tools based on their constraints, and feel a constant need to innovate. Chris described how there's this weird race to find the new edges of the new box every time a software update is pushed out, constantly finding the new aesthetics, or what are the aesthetics that everyone is sort of working in, but that you need to push just beyond. As the goal of end-user programming research is to also enable users to push beyond what current tools allow, we argue that visual artists who treat this pushing beyond as an integral part of their practice are ideal technical collaborators. Their experiences adapting software to meet their needs can inform the design of low-level domain-specific program representations, and their understanding of creative communities can help researchers grow interdisciplinary communities who extend software use in diverse ways. However, collaborations are a two-way street. We also advocate for HCI researchers to consider as potential contributions the kinds of achievements that are valued in an art career, such as making polished artifacts with systems over time and releasing technologies back to the creative communities. We hope that these forms of community engagement strengthen the depth of systems research and increase the impact it has outside the academy. Thanks for watching our presentation. We hope you'll read the paper and reach out. Thank you.

Some designers have produced visualizations that elicit user beliefs. E.g. a New York Times visualization allows users to sketch their beliefs and compare it with the empirical data. When researchers tested those, they found that people recall data better if they were asked to predict it first.
