reference: Hi, I'm the first author, Zhang Enzhang. The work I'm going to present today is I got some free time investigating text execution and text effort metrics in mobile cross-sourcing tasks conducted by MUI Lab, and my advisor is Yongru Zhang. Nowadays, many researchers or companies try to use people's idle attention to attend the data they need to optimize their services by sending notifications to users. This includes when people are listening to music, going to class, or waiting in line. However, some might find it annoying to be prompted with notifications when they are busy. Therefore, our research goal is to find out what is the good time for people to do mobile cross-sourcing tasks, and how these people will choose tasks. Previous research has explored how contextual factors may affect the timing of interruption. Contextual factors include what users are currently doing, users' emotions, and the relevancy of the content. For example, Petrovic et al. found that people who are more focused on what they are currently doing are less available to be interrupted. As for mobile cross-sourcing, Kim et al. designed Hit or Wait, which allocates cross-sourcing tasks and notifies contributors based on their mobility patterns. Currently, there is no research that explores how breakpoints affect whether users will do the mobile cross-sourcing tasks and how they will choose the tasks under different situations. We divided the measurement and classification into two aspects. The first is the activity situation, and the second is mobile cross-sourcing tasks. We classify the activity situation according to three kinds of activities. Preceding activity, current activity, succeeding activity. These activities also have different characteristics. Activity complexity, perceived mental and physical efforts, and require attention. Based on the three kinds of activities, we divided the situation into five different types. When there is a long span of free time, either or not, preceding by or succeeding by an activity, between two activities, and in the middle of an activity. We also measure the mobile cross-sourcing tasks based on task types. Complexity, perceived mental and physical efforts, and require attention. In addition to those attributes, we measure how many clicks users made and the time they spent on the task. Next, we are going to discuss methods. We use a mixed approach method to collect contextual data. We've created a context collecting app that focuses on detecting two target apps, Google Cross-Source and Google Local Guides. We recruited 30 people and limited the process to six weeks. When participants begin performing mobile cross-sourcing tasks, the app will detect their activity and start to log data, such as their location or transportation mode. After the participants finish the mobile cross-sourcing tasks, an ASM questionnaire will be sent to them. Users will be asked several context-related questions, such as whether they have completed mobile cross-sourcing tasks and what activity they were doing before they performed mobile cross-sourcing tasks. Every two weeks, we conducted a semi -structured interview asking them context-related open questions when they performed mobile cross-sourcing tasks. Our results indicate that people tend to be more proactive at transitions between tasks. When users perform tasks between activities, the execution outcomes comprise around 55%, which is greater than the other kinds of breakpoint situations. Surprisingly, people are less proactive in a long span of free time. Some users even reported that when I was not doing anything, I wanted to get some sleep or just veg out. Overall, 30 participants performed 17 distinct types of mobile cross-sourcing tasks. The participants' choice of tasks also differed across different activity situations. We found that it is because participants found certain kinds of tasks are more suitable to do in certain situations. For more detail, please read our paper.

reference: Hi, everyone today, I'm going to talk about Adapttutor, an adaptive tutoring system for machine tasks in augmented reality. Modern industry shows an increasing demand for flexible and self-configuring production. This poses challenges for training workers to rapidly master new machine operations and workflows, or simply called machine tasks. Augmented reality has been widely adopted in machine task tutoring systems. Some tutoring elements have been proven effective and welcomed by end-users, such as text, animated components, and avatars. Although these AR tutoring systems have the benefit of spatial and contextual visualization, they are not adaptive to a learner's real-time behavior and prior knowledge. As a result, the learning is less effective than using a human tutor. To improve the learning outcome, we turn to the area of intelligent tutoring, in which many approaches have been proposed to adapt the tutoring content. In general, Researchers have considered diverse source of adaptation, such as learner's performance and prior knowledge. Also, researchers consider various targets of adaptation. In this paper, we identify several sources of adaptation that are suitable for machine task tutoring in AR. Accordingly, we choose four tutoring elements. Specifically we have avatars, animate, components and arrows. expectations, and subtask descriptions. To better organize these elements to deliver an efficient learning experience, we propose AdaptTutor, an adaptive AR tutorial system for machine tasks. We demonstrate the entire process using a laser-cutting machine task. In the first step, the expert creates a tutorial in AR through embodied demonstration. Next, the expert can preview the avatar and animate components and choose to edit the tutorial. Such as adding expectation or subtask description, now we have four tutoring elements. When learner starts to follow the tutorial, A adapt, Twitter adjusts the tutorial elements in terms of five possible levels of detail. When the level is five, the system shows all four elements. Next, hide avatar and show the other screen. Next only show the expectations and subtask description. Next only show subtask description. And finally, no elements. We build an adaptation model based on deploying that finite state machine to adjust the level of detail. 1st. The lender should open the machine, lead. the current level of detail is fast screen. The system detects that the lender is stuck and increases the level of detail to four, so that an additional animated component appears. Now the system detects the correct operation and adjusts the level of detail to three for this step and all other similar operations. The next operation is picking up the cardboard. The system recognizes that the lender is not paying attention to the target. and increases the level of detail from four to five to bring out the AR avatar. Following the avatar, The lender finds the cardboard and picks it up. As the learner repeats, the tutorial adapttutor gradually decreases the level of detail according to their performance at level two and one. No step by step hint is provided, so the learner is encouraged to recall and perform that task by themselves. Here, when they forget to adjust the laser head and try to close the lid directly, the system increases the level of detail to inform them. In the end, with the help of adapt tutor, the lender masters the task without any tutorial. To evaluate the performance of the adaptation model, we conducted a two-session remote user study in VR. 24 users learned two machine tasks using AdaptTutor and a non-adaptive system as the control group. The non-adaptive tutorial shows all four tutoring elements to the users all the time. The users first learned the tasks following the tutorials and then did a test without the help of the tutorials. The results show the adaptive tutorial leads to a better learning outcome in terms of completion time and mistakes. Please refer to the paper for more details. Thank you.

reference: Hello, everyone, my name is Dr. Miriah Steiger and I'm a director of global research for wellness and resilience in the content moderation industry. In this research article, we surveyed the psychological risks that content moderators face in the course of their profession. and describe a range of strategies for reducing the emotional labor involved in this work. Content moderators play a vital role in the functioning of social media platforms today by safeguarding users from exposure to inappropriate content. While one could ideally rely on machine learning to automatically detect and filter out inappropriate content, human interpretation is often required due to high accuracy requirements and cost of errors and the subjective nature of the task and complex ever-changing moderation policies and forms of offending content. Prior literature has estimated that over 100,000 paid human moderators are staffed globally, spanning internal reviewers, contractors from third parties, and outsourcing to online labor. Former research has revealed that prolonged exposure to some forms of offending content may impair moderators psychological functioning. which can be further exacerbated by metric demands. Potential adverse health effects can include alterations to beliefs or worldview, interpersonal conflict, and stress-related disorders, just to list a few. And given the necessity of human workers in performing this task, we adopt a social justice perspective to motivate the need to support such operations. Therefore, We make three primary contributions in this publication. To begin we discuss moderators, psychological symptomology. drawing on the occupations involving secondary trauma exposure to further guide understanding of both symptoms and support mechanisms. Subsequently, we review a combination of both programmatic and technological support for confronting these challenges, adopting the lens of the preventative care model and discussing treatment options, and examining ways to measure the effectiveness of psychological support. Our final contribution Our final contribution includes recommendation of best practices as well as directions for future research. By applying the model, we begin with discussing primary interventions, which apply strategies that limit symptom onset or prepare an individual to manage potential adverse situations. For example, While the 1st line of defense includes technological filters to limit human exposure, we noted that how challenging this detection is. to automate with sufficient accuracy. Therefore, programmatic interventions are a necessary form of additional support to prepare moderators by use of pre-employment risk disclosure and resilience training prior to any and immediately following exposure to content. Second-level interventions are essential as moderators will inevitably encounter triggering content. The fundamental purpose of secondary care is to reduce symptom severity following onset, thereby returning to a state of stability. Technological approaches such as alterations to image size and blurring or muting videos represent secondary support. And in terms of programmatic aid, ongoing resiliency skill-based training for workers is recommended. And finally, tertiary interventions provide treatment for following the manifestation of a psychological disorder, which requires an evaluation by a licensed professional. Those meeting severe criteria should be referred to community resources as they fall outside the workplace setting scope of practice. If appropriate, tertiary technological interventions such as virtual reality can be beneficial. They've been studied to treat stress-related disorders by increasing mindfulness and producing lower levels of anxiety, sadness, and anger. Across technological and programmatic services, we propose a variety of directions for future work with the potential to better protect content moderators as they safeguard social media platforms. Our authorship in this work spans academia and industry, bridging expertise in technology, social science, and clinical mental health. We come together and form an alignment to support the well-being of content moderators. We advocate for continued growth of academic industry partnerships engaging with these issues, advancing both scholarship and practice. We thank you for your attention and encourage you to reach out to us with any questions.

reference: The global pandemic has seen many of our everyday activities head online. We're going to look at a particular case, how two traditional folk clubs took to the internet. This is particularly interesting because as traditionalists, they were somewhat reluctant adopters of digital technologies. The Carrington Triangle has been running in Nottingham for over 30 years and here it is in its normal situation, a crowded upstairs room above a pub with people doing a sing-around, taking it in turns to sing and play. Like many similar activities, the Carrington Triangle took to Zoom. Initially, they were concerned with audio quality and especially the sound of traditional instruments. They chose Zoom because of its enable original audio facility that switches off a lot of the voice processing. Like many of us, they learned that muting discipline can be tricky and the host created various protocols for managing this. Their biggest disappointment was they discovered that they couldn't sing together in chorus. For reasons of network latency and bandwidth and Zoom's management of audio, people can't sing along together and hear each other. However, they did find new creative opportunities, use of backdrops for example, and the fact that it felt really good to play along with someone at home even if they couldn't hear you. A second example, Folk Beeston, has also been running for decades and again would normally take place in the back room of a busy pub. Folk Beeston took a very different approach to going online. They created a weekly show in a Facebook watch party. Members would create videos, send them in, they would be stitched together and then once a week everyone would watch them at the same time and text chat with one another. Over the course of 21 shows, they actually evolved multiple ways in which participants could contribute. Yes, they could send in videos, but they could also be hosts, they could interview each other, they could even contribute to the opening doors music as it was called. They also experimented by introducing a catch-up feature so that people could watch the shows afterwards. They were really pleased, they were proud of the material they produced and they really upped their production skills as a team and also the ability of members to make videos. But some production fatigue set in. It proved to be extremely time consuming to make a weekly show And there was also a constant pressure on performers to produce new videos of a a suitable quality. Our paper draws out three ways in which technology could better support their practices. Firstly, they could do with configurable performance modes. It should be easier to move between performing, chatting, watching a video and to configure muting and sound and many other properties. Secondly, we could build on this idea of playing along at home to have a more distributed layered approach to recording. Something that mixes live performance with a digital audio workstation. And finally, they really are in need of better production tools and workflows. The kind of things that professionals enjoy using could be made available to them. We consider the question of liveness that's been widely debated in fields beyond HCI. The bottom line, the members of our clubs tried but ultimately failed to replicate the same kind of liveness that they'd enjoyed face to face. But instead, they created something new. They combined elements of embodied performance and digitally mediated live experiences into a new format. What's notable is that that extended throughout the whole production process from pre-production right the way through to replay. We also discussed the question of appropriation. Now both clubs appropriated existing platforms for their purposes and we consider how these were more or less open to appropriation. In turn, the technologies transformed their musical practices. For example, having catch-up replays of the show seemed to lead to less repetition of songs than you might normally expect and an impact on their repertoire. A final question that we'll leave you with is what will happen after life returns to the new normal? Will any of these new online practices find their way back into the traditional face-to-face clubs?

reference: My name is Griffin Dietz, and in our work, we present Storycoder, a voice-guided app that introduces computing concepts to children through storytelling games. In recent years, we've seen a global push for computer science education for all children, including our youngest learners, for whom this early exposure can lead to increased interest in the field, The development of computational thinking and literacy skills and computing readiness that can support an entire educational career. Despite this, many of our youngest learners lack the advanced literacy, numeracy, and fine motor skills needed to use most traditional programming environments or computational thinking tools. A number of successful solutions seek to bypass these literacy requirements by leveraging symbolic block-based programming languages, tangibles, and programmable robots. However, these approaches often necessitate specialized hardware or educator support. In our work, we argue that children can learn computational thinking concepts in a way that simultaneously builds literacy skills by engaging with these ideas through storytelling. And further, aligning with the oral traditions of storytelling, it is possible to introduce these computing concepts using a smartphone-based voice interface, which allows even pre-literate children to engage with this material without necessitating any specialized hardware. Our formative design interviews and classroom observations, as pictured in this photo on the left, further highlighted the importance of prioritizing accessible, approachable, and engaging interactions. We therefore built StoryCoder, a voice-based smartphone application that introduces computing concepts to children through storytelling games. StoryCoder consists of six voice-based user flows, two targeting storytelling to guide children in creating and listening to their stories, and four story games that each uses storytelling as a domain to learn about a specific computational concept. For example, a child might begin by engaging with the Create-A-Story flow, in which the app scaffolds decomposition and abstraction as the child generates a story plan. It does so by asking guiding questions about the main character, location, and problem, and then encourages the child to tell the story with a beginning, middle, and end. Ok, we'll create a story before you tell the story. Let's make a story plan. I'm going to ask four questions. question one is the star of your story, a person or animal? Animal awesome. What kind of animal a dog sounds good. We'll tell a story about a dog. Once the child has created their story, they can play with that story to engage with key computing concepts, sequences, loops, events, or variables through one of the four computational story games. For example, in Word Events, a child learns that an event is something that happens that causes something else to happen. In this game, children select words in their stories to be events, which can then trigger recorded sound effects. Awesome. We will record a sound effect for the Word Event Flute. You can record any kind of noise. As soon as you tap on the microphone, start recording your noise. Whenever we hear the word flute, we'll play the sound. Every user flow underwent a design process that included Wizard of Oz testing prior to implementation and after development iterative testing to further improve the system design. Finally, we conducted an evaluation of the system with 22 children age 5 to 8. Each Each child participated in 04:30 to 60 min sessions over zoom on four consecutive days. Through these sessions, we found that older children told significantly better stories with the guidance provided by our app than they did without such guidance, as measured by the index for narrative complexity. In this chart, stories told in pre-assessment without any planning guidance are on the left, and we can see an increase in scores in the planned stories among older children in these dark gray boxes on the right. And in a post-study assessment, we found that children were able to recognize the four introduced computing concepts in a novel context, played back scratch animations. Both younger and older age groups performed significantly above chance on this concept recognition task, where chance is denoted by this dotted blue line. In our work, we developed Storycoder, and through it, showed that preliterate children can use a conversational voice interface to effectively learn computational thinking concepts through storytelling games. Thank you so much for your time and attention.

reference: Hi everyone, my name is Kupamagan Ramkapani. Today I'll be presenting our work on predicting how users lie online. This is the work I did with Garaf, Jose and Soren. First, why did we do the study? Data has become very important in our everyday life. It's useful for personalizing services, predicting and providing intelligence. Because of many benefits of data, some providers end up collecting more data than they require, in some cases leading to data misuse. As a result, data misuse has become a threat to data collection. Also, users end up feeling that they are being asked for more data than they want to provide. As a result, they develop ways of protecting their personal data. One way is through falsifying data. However, false data may be bad for everyone. It can lead to all sorts of things, wrong predictions for providers, and for users, it may affect the services they receive, or even disadvantage them. Existing literature on data falsification focuses on various areas. Some work has focused on reasons why people lie, the frequency of lying, or even factors that contribute to lying. These studies, however, have not explored the possibility of predicting whether an individual will provide false information. And also, none of them have explored how users actually lie in practice. Given the context and data attributes, we aim to fill this gap by exploring the following questions. First, we want to understand if it's possible to predict with high accuracy, whether an individual will provide truthful information or not. Secondly, we want to identify factors that influence provision of truthful information. And lastly, we want to understand how these lies are made. What did we do? Based on movie ticket purchasing scenario, we created a survey and asked 875 people to answer 50 questions. The questions focused on personal information of the participants, other people, and movies. For each question, we varied sensitivity, relevance, and effort. To determine sensitivity of our questions, or even to balance other contextual values, we ran several pre-test studies. We also used machine learning techniques and thematic analysis to analyze our data. Detailed methodologies provided in the paper. What did we find? We developed two models. Model one is all variables, while the second model used only contextual variables, which is effort, comfort, and relevance. Using all the variables, our classifier predicted truthfulness with an accuracy of 89.7%, with a recall of 0.962. The second model, however, performed slightly less than the first model, with an accuracy of 87.6%. This, however, shows that both classifiers can be used to predict whether an individual will provide truthful information or not. To identify factors that influence truthfulness, we used regression analysis. We found that contextual variables had the most significant effect on truthfulness, comfort being the highest. Regarding thematic analysis, we found that not all untruthful data is the same. Users use different strategies depending on what is being asked. We found that some users may provide invalid information. This is information that is completely untrue and does not follow any pattern or make any sense with regards to the question that is being asked. The second strategy involved following patterns or a format. Responses here can be valid and completely untrue, or valid but partially untrue. The third strategy involved users refusing to provide a response. In some cases, this may follow a pattern, for example, email addresses. We also show in our papers how users use these strategies with respect to the questions being asked. The most common strategy used was providing invalid information followed by refusing to answer. And most participants refused to answer or provided invalid information when asked for their social security number. To conclude this presentation, I will share some of our takeaways. Our study shows that it is possible to predict whether an individual will provide truthful information or not with a very high accuracy. Also, partially true information is not bad at all. We have shown that people providing names of towns is still useful with regards to their addresses. We have also shown that service providers can choose which questions to answer if truthfulness is important to their use of data. Our study also shows that putting validation influences how users may lie. Lastly, some strategies reflect how pets work. This can be leveraged and be used to educate users about pets. We share and explain all this in our paper. Thank you.

reference: Hello, my name is Ville Mäkelä, and in this video I will present our CHI paper Hidden Interaction Techniques, Concealed Information Acquisition and Texting on Smartphones and Wearables. People interact with their mobile devices frequently. For example, we continuously check our devices for notifications, and texting has become a fundamental form of communication. However, interacting with personal mobile devices, like smartphones and smartwatches, is problematic when there are other people nearby. This can result in privacy issues, but most importantly, using one's personal device is often perceived negatively, or their use might even be forbidden. For example, pulling out a smartphone can disrupt a conversation and upset others. In these situations, however, people often really do need to interact with their devices. As a solution, we propose what we call Hidden Interaction Techniques, techniques that allow interaction with personal devices without being noticed. In this paper, we explore two different Hidden Interaction Techniques in two different social scenarios. We particularly focus on the following questions. First, how effectively can users hide their interaction using Hidden Interaction Techniques? Second, what tactics do users employ to hide their interaction? Third, are users able to sufficiently attend to a social situation despite their interaction? We first formulated four design goals that Hidden Interaction Techniques should fulfill. The first goal is eyes-free interaction. The technique should be usable without looking at the device. The second goal is no visual output. The technique should not reveal that the device is being used. The third goal is natural deployment. The technique must work on a device that is naturally carried everywhere and that does not in itself attract attention. The fourth goal is ease of use and low effort. The user must be able to carry on another activity, like a conversation, while they interact. Based on these design goals, we explore two different approaches. As a lightweight scenario, we investigated whether VyprTactile feedback could be used to acquire simple information from a mobile device. People often check their smartphones for notifications, so here we particularly envision that VyprTactile feedback could convey to users whether they have any noteworthy notifications, like missed calls. So, instead of pulling out the smartphone and looking at it to check its contents, one could do so by simply feeling the phone and not necessarily even take it out of the pocket. As an advanced scenario, we explored how users could write messages without being seen. Because no existing text entry technique was fully compatible with our design goals, we developed the concept of hide-write, a novel text entry technique for smartwatches. It is based on a drawing metaphor, where users can draw characters on a dimmed watch screen one at a time. Again, in this scenario, instead of pulling out a smartphone to type, or using a smartwatch and closely monitoring the typing with traditional techniques, users can keep their watch out of sight and type without looking, or even hide the typing in plain sight by disguising it as idle fidgeting. We evaluated these two techniques in different social scenarios, a casual hallway discussion and a meeting. In both of them, one study participant was tasked with using one of the techniques without another study participant noticing. The other participant took on the role of the observer, who had varying levels of knowledge about the user's interactive task. Despite significant differences between the interaction techniques and the evaluated scenarios, We require we acquired remarkably similar results from both studies. 1st users were highly successful in hiding the interaction from the observer. Only a fraction of the interactions were noticed, and only when observers had some degree of prior knowledge. Second, users generally sought to identify ideal moments to interact with their device to go for as little disruption as possible. They typically interacted when someone else was speaking, so that the focus was less on them. Moreover, users typically attempted to hide their interaction using their body or furniture. Third, users were able to sufficiently focus on the social situation despite their interaction. Observers, on the other hand, reported that observing the user was very demanding while trying to keep up with the conversation. These findings also validate our four design goals, which we believe provide a good basis for designing new hidden interaction techniques. This concludes our presentation. Thank you for your attention, and for more details, please check out our paper.

reference: Hello everyone, my name is Brian Wang from the University of Toronto. Thank you for attending the talk from all over the world. Today, I'm going to introduce our paper, Soloist, generating mixed-initiative tutorials from existing guitar instructional videos through audio processing. This is a joint work with Man Yu Yang and my advisor Tovi Grossman. Learning instrument using online instructional videos has become increasingly popular. However, learning with pre-recorded video does not provide immediate feedback, and existing video navigations are not optimized for instrument learning, making the learning experience encumbered. To address these limitations, we present Soloist, a full-stack framework that automatically turns off-the-shelf video lessons into interactive tutorials. So, how can we create an interactive tutorial from a pre-recorded video? Firstly, Soloist uses a series of audio processing to extract musical information from the video. This information is then Is then presented on a front end interface for the user to interact with. the user can record their practice. Practice and soloist would automatically analyze their performances and compare them with the video to provide a guided learning experience. Soloist also provides three types of learning feedback, including audio replay, Melody visualization and the note correctness score, which we will discuss later. Let's first take a look at how Soloist enables video navigations tailored for instrument learning. Soloist uses a waveform navigator to visualize the instructor's narration voice and the instrument sound, helping the user locate where the guitar is being played. Moreover, Soloist automatically segments the video into demonstration regions. Clicking a region will play the specified interval, and the user can drag the boundaries to adjust the start and end of a region. Soloist provides a set of navigational tools to facilitate music learning with videos. For example, users can click on the loop button to play a region repeatedly. Clicking on the preview button and hovering the cursor on different regions will display their melodic lines in each region. Users can select a region and press the query button. Soloist will then display the regions containing similar melodies and hide the remaining ones. Another important feature of Soloist is to provide immediate feedback on users' practice. To practice alone a region, the user can select it and press the record button. Soloist will then analyze the user's performance and provide various feedback. The first type of feedback is melody visualization, which visualizes the melodic lines of both the user's recording and the instructor's demonstration. Many common mistakes of guitar performance, such as missing vibrato, can be therefore identified. Another type of feedback is audio replay. The user can play their recordings and the referenced audio simultaneously, and a mixing slider allows them to adjust the relative volume. Soloist also provides a score assessment based on the note correctness of the user's performance. Since the models we use for audio processing may have inaccurate predictions, we adopted a mixed-initiative design where the user can overwrite the score if they believe it's inaccurate. To evaluate Soloist, we conducted a technical evaluation on the video segmentation by comparing the segmentation results with human labels. The evaluation shows that our algorithm is reasonably accurate and outperformed all baselines across metrics. We also conducted a qualitative user study remotely with eight participants to obtain their high-level feedback. The results showed that the participants unanimously preferred practicing with Soloist compared to using traditional YouTube videos. With that, I wrap up my talk, and I'm happy to answer any questions. Thank you.

reference: Welcome, everyone. My name is Jared Duvall, and I'm excited to present our paper, Chasing Play on TikTok from Populations with Disabilities to Inspire Playful and Inclusive Technology Design, on behalf of my co-authors from the Computational Media Department at the University of California, Santa Cruz. There's an open call for everyday technology to be more playful. Play is valuable for its own sake. Play is an apt vehicle to bring about societal change and improve the quality of life of people with disabilities because it embodies the very qualities of growth and pleasure. It is biologically evolved to help us learn and build skills. It is naturally social, and the voluntary nature of play allows us to focus on the style of play over the outcome. Two mainstream ways that technology can be designed to accommodate users with disabilities are by creating technology that provides a specific service to people with disabilities, called assistive technology, or by making general technology more accessible to people with disabilities, known as accessible technology. It is vital to include people with disabilities in the design process in both of these cases. This paper is motivated by the need to include populations with disabilities to inspire design more broadly and more generally, looking at values other than efficiency and accessibility. We design better technology for everyone when we include people with disabilities early and often in the process. We use situated play design and metanography methodologies to scrape playful content from creators with disabilities on TikTok because the platform is rich with tacit design knowledge and cultural labor we can use to inspire technology design. We analyzed 285 TikToks and sorted them into seven non-mutually exclusive themes inductively. Our most common theme is everyday theatrical life sketches, where creators showcase dramatic sized performances of a day in the life of a person with a disability, often showcasing humor and elements of improv. Our second most popular theme is playful advocacy, where creators educated the general population about disability and proper social etiquette using lighthearted and creative strategies, such as singing. Our five other themes, debunking myths and stereotypes, gamification of therapy, impossible challenges, perks of my disability, and duet differences are interesting too. More details can be found in our paper along with our analysis of performativity on TikTok. Unsurprisingly, TikTok is a very performative and exaggerated platform, so we should keep that in mind when we chase play and create resulting designs that will likely value extroversion. We also present our analysis of the mediums these videos might inspire for technology. We ourselves generated a catalog of 20 design concepts and share eight of our favorites in the paper. These concepts range from arcade games to apps to immersive storytelling props and wearables. My personal favorite is beat rings, inspired by the TikToker above with a motor impairment who is snapping their fingers at different intervals. Beat rings use accelerometers to create music based on taps, snaps, and gestures streamed to a smart speaker. In the paper, we use speculative futures to imagine designs that may or may not be possible with today's technology and imagined how our concepts might impact society. We organized our concepts by target populations they might be intended for, the technology medium they might be used for, the themes they relate to, the potential for them to increase disability visibility, and their potential for therapy or assistive tech. In summary, we scraped content on TikTok from content creators with disabilities resulting in 285 posts containing play potentials that we sorted into seven emerging themes. We created a catalog of design concepts and speculate on how they could inform the design of future playful technology that supports people with disabilities. We discussed how our concepts have the potential to facilitate disability visibility, understanding, and empathy. Our contributions add to the larger body of work advocating for the inclusion of people with disabilities in the design process. We left out many details in this video, so we encourage you to take a look at our paper and join us in the online discussion.

reference: Hello everyone, this is Yujia. I'm an undergraduate student at the Georgia Institute of Technology. Today I'll be presenting the work understanding the usage of online media for parenting from infancy to preschool At scale. This is a joint work with Jin Niu Jiang and. and my advisor Di Yang. So, welcoming a new life into a family is an extremely exciting change in life. However, what society fails to discuss enough is the potential loneliness, social isolation, loss of identity, or increasing rate of depression that accompanies this change for new parents. The beam of light for new parents is the rise of online media, Which creates a new community for them and connect with other parents? Research shows that 75 % of new parents seek information or social support. from online social media platforms. The important role social media plays in new parents' lives motivates us to deep dive into investigating what new parents talk about on online platforms, how they engage with them, and thus we can get insights on how online media can provide more support for them. Due to the diversity of user-created parenting communities, we have chosen Reddit as our source of investigation. From there, we identified 49 parenting-related subreddits to collect our large-scale data set, Containing 600000 posts and 10 million comments from 420000 distinct users. So, we started by asking the question, what topics do new parents talk about online? While previous works sought to understand this through automatic models like LDA, their topic modeling methods are not very successful at capturing more nuanced parenting topics. Thus, we designed a generic parenting taxonomy that will cover more nuanced and subtle parenting topics with human annotations. We discovered that there are 30 topics parents talk about, as shown here in the slides. We extracted general topics like pregnancy, breastfeeding, potty training, etc., which aligns with previous work. However, the human approach we took enabled us to extract nuanced topics like mom's health, language training, and walk training. We were also able to distinguish between similar topics like child behavior issue vs. child health. The subtle difference between those will be very difficult to be realized through a simple keyword perspective. Next, we were able to use the state-of-the-art tax classification model BERT to assign one or more topic labels to each of our 600,000 posts. For example, regarding our Our model training process, or technical details about how we boost model performance? I highly encourage you to look at our paper. Taking advantage of our large-scale dataset with post-level topic labels, we were able to conduct analysis to understand parenting topic discussion. To highlight some of our findings, we analyzed the topic parents discuss with respect to the time they first joined the parenting community. We separate their participation into different time chunks, such as the first month since joining, first to sixth month of joining, etc. Here in the figure, we can see topics like child appearance, breastfeeding, and parent-computer interaction are discussed more frequently as time progresses, while others like sleeping, pregnancy, and mom health show opposite trends. We thus discovered that within one year of joining the online community, there is a gradual shift from parenting-focused topics to child-focused topics, which leads us to conclude that many parents tend to join the community during key development stages of their parenthood as well as for their children. Besides these findings, we also found interesting conclusions about the relationship between each topic and their same-name subreddits, gender differences between the topics discussed by new parents, the effect of different parenting topic discussion on parents' engagement of online platforms, etc. I won't talk about them in detail due to a time constraint, but highly encourage you guys to check out our paper. In conclusion, our work provides both theoretical and practical implications for the understanding of new parents' use of online media. First of all, our identification of a comprehensive 30-topic taxonomy is generic, which means it can provide a reference point for further research on different online parenting platforms beyond Reddit itself. In terms of design and usability implications, we prove the feasibility of a real-time autonomous topic classification system that helps users find the most relevant information based on the topic they are discussing. Thank you very much for watching, and please reach out to me if you have any questions.

reference: Hello, I'm Paritosh, a Ph.D. student at Clemson University. I'm here to present our paper titled Overlooking Context, How Do Defaults and Framing Reduce Deliberation in Smart Home Privacy Decision Making? This research is a collaborative effort between research groups at Clemson University, USA and Eindhoven University of Technology, Netherlands. The funding for this research is provided by NSF and NWO. Privacy decisions, especially in smart homes, depend on various contextual factors, such as which devices collect data, which devices receive that data, and how well that data gets stored. Ideally, we want privacy decisions of smart homes to be based strictly on these contextual factors. Our previous research found this to be true. Additionally, we also observed that the effect of contextual factors on privacy decisions is mediated by attitudes. These attitudes are cognitive appraisals towards contextual factors. Ideally, we also want the privacy decisions to be free from heuristics such as defaults and framing. This, however, is not the case. We show that defaults and framing not only have a direct effect on privacy decisions, but they influence cognitive appraisals necessary to arrive at those decisions. To investigate these effects, we conducted a web-based controlled experiment involving 1,132 US-based participants, recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk. Each participant was presented with 13 scenarios. Each scenario, including the one on this slide, was a combination of five different contextual factors, which had multiple levels. We tested 4,608 scenarios this way. This is how our participants saw the experimental conditions. They read the scenario and answered two types of questions. First, whether they would enable or disable this scenario, which is a behavioral question, and five more questions, which were about their attitudes towards these scenarios, such as comfort, appropriateness, and risk. The defaults and framing were manipulated specifically for decision question, and both had three different levels. Defaults were manipulated as enabled by default, disabled by default, and no default. Framing was manipulated as positive, negative, and neutral. While analyzing the data, we created a generalized linear mixed-effects regression model. In line with existing research, we noticed that defaults and framing do have a main effect on privacy decisions. We did not find interaction effects between defaults and framing. However, we did find two-way interaction effects between attitudes and defaults and attitudes and framing. The y-axis on these plots represents the regression estimates of the effects of attitudes on privacy decisions. If you look at the left plot, you will notice that the regression estimates of attitudes are consistently higher in absence of defaults. More interestingly, in case of framing, that is the plot on the right, the effect of certain attitudes, like appropriateness and usefulness, is higher in case of positive framing as opposed to neutral framing. This goes on to show that in certain cases, the framing can even reverse the effect of attitudes. Let's look at logistic regression plots. Ideally, for an attitude, what should happen is that the disabled default should be more effective compared to no default in presence of negative attitudes. That is, the negative default should support people to disable a scenario when their attitude towards that scenario is negative, and vice versa. However, what our data shows is that this is reversed. In case of comfort, the disabled default has almost similar effect as no defaults for participants with negative attitudes towards the scenarios, whereas the enabled default pushes people to make enabled decisions even when the attitude is negative. Our study also found three-way interaction between framing, collection concerns, and attitudes. You can find more details about these interesting results in our paper. Based on the results, we conclude that nudges can have unintended consequences. We show this using our results from interaction effects where the effect of cognitive appraisals on decisions is reduced in presence of defaults, pointing to the possibility that defaults and framing reduce deliberation towards the context. As for future designs of smart home privacy systems, the use of defaults is in fact a balancing act. On one hand, we need people to make numerous decisions in really short time. On the other hand, we also need to ensure optimal decision quality. One potential solution is to use user-tailored defaults. We discuss these in another research paper and we welcome you to take a look at it. Please take a look at our paper and feel free to reach out in case of any questions. Thank you so much for listening.

It can help elicit more details of participants' experiences and balance dynamics. In our fieldwork, Most Diads chose to be interviewed in their homes where caregivers were able to make participants comfortable and take advantage of probes at hand. to prompt more engaging responses. Let's look at this example in one of our interviews. When the researcher asked about what topics he would like to chat with others, the participant with dementia answered, I don't remember. These paintings were created by the participant in his art therapy sessions. They jogged his memories about art as his favorite topic. Indeed, in that interview, the caregiver brought his paintings to the table or pointed to those hanging on the walls. We can try to know more about participants beforehand and encourage proxies to prepare personal items. It will keep the focus on helping participants express their thoughts and in turn, balance power dynamics. reference: My name is Ab Mosca. Today I'll be presenting our work, Does Interaction Improve Bayesian Reasoning with Visualization? I collaborated on this project with Alvita Atli from Washington University in St. Louis and Remco Chang from Tufts University. This project focuses on better supporting Bayesian reasoning, a problem common to medical risk communication, which has been shown to be a difficult reasoning task for physicians and patients alike. In the visualization community, there has been a lot of prior work investigating the best visualization design to support Bayesian reasoning. However, despite all of this work, there is no clear consensus on the best visualization to use. In this project we ask the question, What what if we add interaction in the visualization community? we know there are certain cases where interaction is indisputably beneficial. In particular, when we're trying to visualize large amounts of data on a small screen, interactions such as zooming or panning are essential to reveal otherwise occluded or missing data. But Bayesian reasoning visualizations are a fundamentally different context. A Bayesian reasoning visualization only needs to communicate four values, true positive, true negative, false positive, and false negative. As long as the visualization shows these four values, a user has all of the information they need to perform Bayesian inference. In other words, adding interaction to a visualization like this will not reveal or add any otherwise missing data that is essential to performing Bayesian reasoning. To see if interaction is useful in this unique context, we ran two human subject experiments. Each of these experiments utilized three base visualization designs that range in the amount of perceptual grouping they use to communicate subpopulations of interest to the Bayesian reasoning problem. In experiment one, we test each of these base visualization designs in a static and interactive setting. The interaction we implement is called CBL. It consists of adding check boxes next to each legend label of the visualization that allow participants to show or not show different subpopulations of interest to the Bayesian reasoning problem. We call this interaction CBL because the visualization loads on the page with all check boxes checked off. In experiment two, we test a slight variation of CBL. In addition, we test an interaction we call CBNone, which performs identically to CBL, but the visualization loads on the page with all check boxes unchecked. Additionally, we test a drag interaction, which performs identically to CBNone. Finally, we implement a hover and tooltip interaction. These are designed to draw a stronger link between the textual and visual descriptions of the Bayesian reasoning problem. The experimental task we give participants is a canonical Bayesian reasoning problem. We analyze proportions of correct answers across the different visualizations. Our findings are surprising. Despite our best efforts to implement interactions that would aid in Bayesian reasoning, we find no situations in which participants assigned to interactive visualizations performed with higher accuracy than participants assigned to static visualizations. In addition, in experiment two, we stratified our analyses based on participants' spatial ability. And we find that for participants with high spatial ability, those assigned to the hover visualization performed with significantly worse accuracy than those assigned to a static visualization. All this is to say our main takeaway from this project is that in the case of Bayesian reasoning, a well-designed static visualization may be as, if not more effective, than an interactive one. I'd like to recognize again my co-authors as well as our funding sources. Thank you for listening. I look forward to taking your questions.

reference: Hi everyone, my name is Ronald Robertson and this talk is about characterizing problematic email reply suggestions. In email interfaces and other systems that provide suggestions for computer-mediated communication including chat and text, providing users with reply suggestions such as those pictured here may simplify or accelerate correspondence. While the success of such systems is typically quantified using the number of suggestions selected by users, this ignores the impact of social context, which can change how suggestions are perceived. To address this, we developed a mixed methods framework involving two phases. In the discovery phase, we used qualitative interviews to identify the social conditions in which email reply suggestions might be problematic. In the evaluation phase, we used crowdsourced experiments to characterize problematic email reply scenarios. In In this brief talk, I'll present findings from both phases and conclude with some final thoughts. We define an email reply scenario as the digital analog to the speech situation from speech act theory, where the meaning of an utterance depends on linguistic conventions, the social context, and the speaker's intentions. We break this down into four components for the purposes of our study. First is social ties, to indicate who is being communicated with. Then we have structural features, which include email gradients and sign-offs. Next is the email act, which is the social purpose of the email. And last are the reply suggestions, which were introduced in 2016 and typically appear as shown here. We identify two junctions at which suggestions can negatively impact users. The first can be described as direct, and occurs between computer and human when suggestions are rendered and viewed. If those suggestions are perceived as problematic by the user, they can damage trust in the feature or service. The second can be described as more indirect, and occurs between humans, when suggestions have already been selected and sent. These suggestions might be perceived as problematic by the recipient or recipients, which can then damage user relations and reputations. After coding our interview transcripts, we found three broad themes that center on usability, email content, and social context. Here we briefly examine these three themes and provide example quotes from participants. In the usability theme, we found that users liked using reply suggestions for email scenarios that required quick and template-like responses. In the email content theme, we found that users were sometimes concerned about sending replies that omitted structural features, such as greetings and salutations, which reply suggestions do by default. They were also worried about suggestions that were too short, especially for negative replies, in these two examples you see here, which generally require greater care and explanation. In the social context theme, we found a variety of factors that influence participants' perceptions of reply suggestions, including communication dynamics, relationship type, and norms and culture. Based on our interview findings, we identified categories of problematic email reply scenarios, then curated and validated a set of vignettes, which we show some examples of here on the left. We then recruited crowd judges to rate our vignettes, as shown here on the right, while we systematically varied the social tie and the presence or absence of structural features. Two main findings emerged from our experiments. First, not all problematic email reply categories are equally salient. This plot shows the email reply category on the y-axis, The Likert scale participants' rated scenarios on along the X axis and highlights the variability of each rating across their categories. Second, the type of social and tie evolved can affect how replies are perceived. This plot, again, has categories along the y-axis, but has social ties along the x-axis, and the cells are colored by how likely people were to send a reply from that category to that social tie without editing. It again shows variability by category, but also by social tie. We conclude by noting that there is a need to develop mixed-method discovery frameworks that can help to proactively surface problematic scenarios that we may be unaware of. Our findings indicate that current text recommendation systems for email and other computer-mediated communication technologies remain insufficiently nuanced to reflect the subtleties of real-world social relationships and communication needs. As one interviewee aptly described it, it's not just a relevance problem, it's a problem of empathy. Thank you for listening, and please check out the paper for more details and findings.

While the success of such systems is typically quantified using the number of suggestions selected by users, this ignores impact of social context which can change how suggestions are perceived. To address this, we developed the mixed methods framework involving two phases. In the discovery phase, we used qualitative interviews to identify the social conditions in which email reply suggestions might be problematic. In the evaluation phase, we used crowdsource experiments to characterize problematic email reply scenarios. In this brief talk, I'll present findings from both phases and conclude with some final thoughts. We define an email reply scenario as a digital analog to the speech situation from speech act theory, where the meaning of an utterance depends on linguistic conventions, the social context, and the speaker's intentions. We break this down into four components for the purposes of our study. The first is social ties to indicate who is being communicated with. Then we have structural features, which include email greetings and sign-offs. Next is the email act, which is the social purpose of the email, and last are the reply suggestions to introduce in 2016 and typically appear as shown here. Red identified two junctions at which suggestions can negatively impact users. The first can be described as direct and occurs between computer and human and suggestions are rendered and viewed. If those suggestions are perceived as problematic by the user, they can damage trust in the feature or service. The second can be described as more indirect and occurs between humans when suggestions have already been selected and sent. These suggestions might be perceived as problematic by the recipient or recipients, which can then damage user relations and reputations. After coding our interview transcripts, we found three broad themes that center on usability, email content, and social context. Here we briefly examine these three themes and provide example quotes from participants. In the usability theme, we found that users liked using reply suggestions for email scenarios require quick and template-like responses. In the email content theme, we found that users were sometimes concerned about sending replies that emitted structural features, just greetings and salutations, which reply suggestions due by default. They were also worried about suggestions that were too short, especially for negative replies. In these two examples you see here, which generally require greater care and explanation. In the social context theme, we found a variety of factors influence participants' perceptions of reply suggestions, including communication dynamics, relationship type, and norms and culture. Based on our interview findings, we identified categories of problematic email reply scenarios that curate and validate a set of vignettes to show some examples of here on the left. We then recruited crowd judges to rate our vignettes, as shown here on the right. While we systematically varied the social tie and the presence or absence structural features. Two main findings emerged from our experiments. First, not all problematic email replies categories are equally salient. This plot shows the email reply category on the y-axis, a likelihood scale participants rated scenarios on along the x-axis and highlights the variability of each rating across their categories. Second, the type of social and tie evolved can affect how replies are perceived. This plot again has categories along the y-axis, but has social ties along x-axis, and the cells are colored by how likely people were to send a reply from that category to that social tie without editing. It again shows variability by category, but also by social time. We conclude by noting that there is a need to develop mixed method discovery frameworks that can help to peractively surface problematic scenarios that we may be unaware of. Our findings indicate that current text recommendation systems for email and other computer-mediated communication technologies remain insufficiently nuanced to reflect the subtleties of real-world social relationships and communication needs. As one interview we aptly described it, it's not just a relevance problem, it's a problem of empathy. Thank you for listening and and please check out the paper for more details and findings.

reference: Our paper is Designing Ground Truth and the Social Life of Labels from a team of researchers at IBM. In machine learning, people try to predict an outcome variable called the ground truth on the basis of multiple predictor variables or features. The prediction takes place in a data science pipeline, which typically involves extensive data preparation or data wrangling, as well as modeling and quality assurance. In human-centered data science, we want to populate that pipeline by adding the people who are doing the work to learn about their uniquely human contributions to that work. In some cases, the outcome is not given in the data, and so we have to ask human domain experts to apply ground truth labels, which tell us what the human believes the outcome is. These labels might represent a medical diagnosis, or a business characterization of a social media post, or a user's intention when talking to a chatbot. We interviewed 15 people at IBM who worked in the area of ground truth labeling, and we applied grounded theory methods to make sense of what they told us. In the full paper, we report on seven emergent concepts that we found through our grounded analysis. For this brief presentation, we focus on the last of the seven concepts, which is how people designed ground truth labels. We identified three major patterns in the design of ground truth. In principal design, people had a plan, they carried out the plan, and there were few surprises. In medical labeling, the labeling vocabulary may be based on diseases, conditions, symptoms, medications. The labelers already knew what they were looking for, and they labeled strictly according to that prescribed vocabulary. In a chatbot project, labelers knew that there were exactly 30 actions that the chatbot could take, and therefore, they could apply exactly 30 labels to end users' input. The second pattern, iterative design, the teams anticipated the need to revise their labels as they did the labeling work, and they included revisions as part of their process. In a different chatbot project, the team anticipated iterations. We would cold label the conversations, evaluate what we did, discuss what went well, what went poorly, and then go back and do it again. One informant was teaching an algorithm to recognize types of structured documents. They noted that the tool generates examples where the system is uncertain what the label should be. After additional labeling from the user, the system refines the rules. Clearly, the automated tool needed human correction, and they built those human correction processes into their plan. The third pattern we called improvisational design of ground truth, in which people encountered unexpected challenges to their labeling activities. One intrinsic problem was that people didn't agree on the labels. Another problem was complexity. In a social media labeling project, the informant told us, we ended up doing the simpler ones because this is more explainable, less time consuming. Significantly, this team had to exclude certain complex data types, and thus their labeling outcome described only a subset of their data records. Extrinsic challenges often came from clients or from the terms of a contract. An informant reflected on how they modified their labeling vocabulary to meet their client's expectations. Client was happy. If we had had more time, more data, more annotations, we could have done a lot better. We usually work on six-week engagements. In these examples, we see that the scope and nature of labels in improvisational design may be constrained by unanticipated challenges. Ground truth labels may be determined in advance, or they may be malleable, changeable, and importantly, socially negotiable. People do the work of ground truth labeling, and they bring human strengths and human weaknesses to that work, and they or their organizations become accountable for that work. Far from the conventional interpretation of the word truth, we learned to think of ground truth as a worthwhile but necessarily social achievement. Briefly, we learned some lessons for tools to support labeling or annotating data. Those tools should provide features for human consensus, social convergence, and accountability. We learned to think about data as a crafted medium of design, and we learned that the design of data depends very much on who is describing the data and what kinds of data vision they bring to that task. And we realized that after labeling is done, the ground truth labels tend to vanish into the infrastructure and become merely the truth when the modelers compute predictions based on the labeled data set. The design of ground truth is a human process. We'll do better data science if we are aware of how humans necessarily intervene to contribute human discernment to the the data that we analyze. Thank you.

reference: In 2020, due to the global pandemic, many of us were forced to move to the online space, which disrupted our work. Our study title is The Show Must Go On. In this talk, I share our team's study findings regarding our transition to the online space for work to go on. Our group name is KidsTeamUW, where we work with a group of children aged 7 to 11 years old where we co-design new technology for children with children. In 2020, our team was no exception in putting a halt to all projects. While COVID-19 was a reason that forced us to explore online, we noticed opportunities to meet with new children who were not able to come to the in-person sessions due to consequences like transportation or mobility and health issues, and the only option was to join online. When working with children in the online space, many prior work explores the asynchronous space like in social media sites or three-dimensional gaming space. However, not all children or adults are familiar with working on such sites. Scholars also have done numerous work on building prototypes for play and devices for telepresence, but they're not mainstream consumer devices. In our study, we were working with a device we had and was familiar with. So our research questions started with how to conduct synchronous participatory design online with children. We went through a total of 10 co-design sessions conducted on Zoom. We analyzed video, interviews, and artifacts produced. In the data, the majority of the sessions were a total chaos of having days where children turned all their cameras off, bad internet connections resulting in both frustrated children and adults. We also had days children co-designed in the car and with their pet lizard. In some, many things did not go as planned. For instance, in our very first session, we asked the children to design the future of co-design over Zoom. And a child stated, I see no point in designing for the future of co-designing online as there is no future for it. We noticed doing synchronous participatory design online with children was like doing stand-up comedy, which needed to interact with the audience, and going live is that you had to deal with what happens in the moment. Therefore, in making sense of our data, we switched our lens to improvisation, making or doing something that is not planned beforehand. Talented artists often embrace disorder to make the most of any situation. We use a paper by Kang et al. presented at CHI 2018, which discusses how improvisation emerges in practice and explains five features of improvisation. So instead of how to, we change our focus to what to consider. And we created a framework that was generated through thematic coding, which introduces three themes. The first theme is project logistics, which discuss how the decision might be planned and implemented. Our two sub-themes are techniques of how commonly used techniques in person had to be modified in the online space. Next, we needed to think about what digital tools we can use to meet, share, design, and collaborate. Our second theme is people and setting. We state how in the synchronous online space, children were coming from multiple locations, which differed from parents dropping their child off to the lab. Therefore, children were influenced by the technological infrastructure such as hardware and software. But there were also spectators like parents, siblings, and pets all part of the session. In the final theme, people's online interaction, we note how it is important to state how the children's interpretation and reaction mattered. For instance, when children muted themselves, our researchers assumed that the child was disengaged. However, when we later interviewed this child, he stated how he muted himself as his mom had the dishwasher on. From this code, we learned it is more difficult to understand children's feelings as we have fewer cues and that children have more autonomy and freedom to just log off. In the paper, we share a conceptual model of how the three themes influence each other and connect them to Kang et al.'s five features in FROG. The model centers on users' interactions and moves beyond the dependence of technology. In a synchronous session, regardless of how well prepared the researcher is, there are moments for improvisation. We encourage our framework and research to be used in adding more reference to the unexpectedness to be ready for improvisation. Thank you for listening.

Accounts in such platforms are so-called accounts designed for sharing, or DS accounts. reference: Hi, I'm Kristen Shinohara from Rochester Institute of Technology, and on behalf of my co-authors Mick McQuaid and Nayari Hakobo, I am presenting our paper, The Burden of Survival, How Doctoral Students in Computing Bridge the Chasm of Inaccessibility. There is a shrinking pipeline of students with disabilities, where fewer undergraduate students with disabilities go on to pursue advanced degrees. Notably, 0.8%, or N of 15, of computing doctorate recipients reported having a hearing disability, and 3.6%, or N of 66, reported having a visual disability in 2017. By comparison, the NSF survey of earned doctorates reported more than 4,239 computing and mathematics PhDs were awarded in 2019. We sought to learn more about the experiences of blind, low-vision, deaf, and hard-of-hearing doctoral students in computing to better understand the challenges for graduate versus undergraduate student experiences. We also sought to learn from computing students for insight they may have into technical opportunities for improving accessibility. Prior research found that inaccessibility for computing graduate students was evident by the gap between what non-disabled peers had access to and how ineffective solutions were when they were made available. It was also found that accessibility issues for graduate students were complicated by domain-specific and advanced technical needs. We conducted an interview study with 19 doctoral students in computing and related fields. We interviewed 12 blind or low-vision and 7 deaf or hard-of-hearing students. Participants were enrolled in a computing-related PhD program within the last 10 years. We asked participants about accessibility issues they encountered and how accommodations were addressed. We found that workarounds to address tool incompatibility exacted a cost because participants employed trial-and-error solutions that did not always resolve issues. For example, B2 stated, I had intensive background in using MATLAB and I had to abandon that. Now I have started using Python and I would say that cost me at least two years. That delayed my research because I was easily writing codes on MATLAB. Changing to any other language means downgrading. Participants also had to self-advocate extensively to not only request accommodations but also to explain what accessibility issues were and to inform others about what kinds of assistance they might need. D2 put a point to it by saying, other people won't do things to make it easier for you. Managing social capital required extra effort of participants because asking for help also exacted a cost. Participants weighed who to ask and what to ask of them, and they were careful not to ask too much. B12 said, sometimes I find it burdening to ask the same one or two friends, hey, can you do this? Can you do that? It's not very comfortable to ask this from everybody, and you don't want to use up all of it. You want to be cognizant of the fact that they might be busy, and they will not say no. They will do it for you. Finally, grad school expectations compounded time and effort. Simply, academia rewards individual effort and productivity, and grad students are tasked with magnitudes more work than undergrads. Accommodations are typically just not scalable. As B10 said, I did not really use disability services a lot because, for one, every course will have maybe about 50 articles to read throughout the course, and then converting those 50 articles to text, the lead time they required was huge, and they will ask me to send all these articles a couple of months in advance. It was impossible, so I just did it for two or three journal articles, so it was not really effective for me. Taken together, the grad school experience includes many research tasks and social capital management, as well as coursework and programming and teaching. For many of these tasks, accessibility issues abound, which requires maneuvering accommodations, advocating, and asking for help, among other things. Oftentimes, accessibility tasks fall on students' shoulders, and they are responsible for requesting, arranging, and managing accommodations, including things like gaining access to data, managing ASL interpreters, or dealing with limited tool accessibility. We consider imagining equitable solutions, such as allowing students to direct and engage their own help and support, or educating faculty about the difference between difficulty and accessibility and normalizing asking for help, so on and so forth, until we have better supported our students. Though there will still be more to do, our findings suggest that such changes may make a difference. This work was supported by the NSF. We look forward to your comments and questions. Thank you.

reference: Hi, I am Malihe Ghajargan from Malmo University and I present Synthesis of Forms, Integrating Practical and Reflective Qualities in Design, on behalf of my co-author Jeffrey Bartzel from Penn State University. In the design processes, we often synthesize different kinds of forms and meanings in a single product. So, most objects do not have a single or simple meaning, but rather a layered and complex set of them. In this research, we were interested in how this complex layering of meanings might apply in contexts of reflective design. Everyday-use objects for reflection seem to require a synthesis of two very different forms, conventionally practical forms since they are everyday-use objects, and evocative forms since they make users think. We formulated the following research question. How objects synthesize a multiplicity of meanings and forms, and more specifically, how a single design form might achieve a synthesis of design qualities that we tend to view as logically exclusive, for example, practical functionality versus evocative critical reflection, and yet which we argue they are not exclusive when manifest in actual design. Our research has at At as its points of departure, the question of the relationship between practical and critical design. Throughout design theory, pragmatic and critical design are often presented as doing opposition. And although at a level of logic the distinction feels correct, we could not square this theoretical distinction with our own design practice. We present the design process that led to two reflective designs, Soleil and Couture. Both designs synthesize practical and evocative forms and qualities of design. Soleil is an An interactive table lamp for home environment, it also provides light based feedback intended to trigger sustainable urban mobility behaviors. During the sketching, I explored the forms that can represent Schultz's theory of implicit connections with Nature, a theory that modeled connections. in three parts, myself, my community, and my planet. So I envisioned the lamp structure in three distinctive yet interconnected parts. As functioning lights, the units reinforce their structure using light in two different modes, to arise and to accumulate. Couture is an interactive keyhook designed for home environment, specifically the home entrance. It also uses a mobile application to collect behavioral data. I used sketching to help me visualize forms that represent inclusiveness. In the final design, the inner circles represent the self, the middle circles represent the community, and the largest circle represents the planet. The objects' behaviors reflect those of the user. As the user attains sustainability goals, the circles rotate to reveal the marked portion of the circle, not unlike progress bars. Reflecting upon the forms of two prototypes, we return to the question that animated the project. How does the design act of form-giving help resolve the apparent contradiction between practical and evocative qualities? Both prototypes are examples of useful everyday objects. Their familiar physical forms make them intuitive and easy to use. logs, and conducting semi-structured interviews with community stakeholders. Through applying
these methods over the course of three years, we were able to pick up on more subtle findings.
