Woolen Network, which was initially established as a means of distributing information for young
people to try and combat rural urban flight and the social exclusion of youth in the area.

broadened the network's content, which dramatically altered community members perceptions of the network.
Secondly, because our study had two deployments, we were given insight into the different
configurations and approaches to administration management and maintenance of each display network,
which highlighted more subtle and hidden background tasks concerned with routine logistics and
coordination needed to keep the network alive. It also clearly illustrated the impact of researcher
involvement and the need for them to distance themselves in order for communities to adapt to
running technology independently. Lastly, by comparing the two different approaches taken by each
network administrator, we found tensions around how administrators were offering to share control
of the network, but ultimately how there was a reluctance to relinquish the control these administrators
had as the sole people responsible for each respective network. So with these points in mind,
let's move on to how community technology can be designed to be more sensitive to these findings.

platform, evidently these were not fully utilized, which resulted in single administrators
in charge of each network. In prior literature, this single point of contact or community
champion as it's normally termed is well suited to take on the role. However, when we consider
how this works, when scaling the technology, the effort of a single handedly creating,
scheduling and managing content, as well as sustaining the network of physical displays,
soon becomes overwhelming for an individual person.
There was a clear need to design technology with this long-term sustainability at the forefront
of its design, in anticipation of community adoption and in-built, templated processes
for distributing the effort and emotional labour and skills required to promote aspects
of ownership, governance and operation.

reference: Hello, and thank you for joining me. Today I present our work titled Assisting Manipulation and Grasping in Robot Teleoperation with Augmented Reality Visual Cues. My name is Stephanie and I am from the Westphalian University of Applied Sciences in Germany. A prevailing problem in robot teleoperation is the perception in manipulation tasks, even in scenarios where the operator and the robot are located in the same physical space, but not in direct proximity. Here, operators may have a fixed viewpoint due to safety reasons and teleoperation requires the operator to have a good understanding of the location of the robot relative to the workspace and the objects in it. That is why we propose to use augmented reality and elements from monocular depth cues, which are visual cues Cues perceived only with one eye, such as lighting and interposition, to present two designs of visual cues, we name them augmented visual cues. and they aim to enhance the operator's perception of the robot and the environment and improve performance in pick-and-place tasks. Our first design, Basic Cues, consists of indirect cues that do not require previous knowledge of the environment, and they indicate the position of the gripper in the workspace. The main characteristic is a combination of physical and virtual landmarks. We can see the cursor taking the color of the pointed area. The virtual color map reflects the current position of the gripper on the real color map, which now is moving in between two colors. The real and virtual color map help operators realize the position of the gripper relative to a target by matching colors. Our second design, Advanced Cues, provides explicit hints for interactions that are environment-aware. This means that we use object and pose recognition to provide explicit hints. The main element is a virtual copy of the grasped object, With which we named ghost Object. Here we can see the cursor with occlusion capabilities that allows to point to specific areas of an object, for instance in between objects. This is the ghost object displayed at the same position where the cursor is, allowing to visualize the position, pose, and space that the grasped object will occupy in a specific area. Object's shadows are not visible to the operator. Our robot-controlled concept involves the use of hands-free interaction through head movements to point and voice commands to commit an action. We use the Microsoft HoloLens One to display our visual cues and present basic robot controls for fine positioning that are virtually attached to the gripper. Here we can see our robot-controlled concept working together with our basic cues design. We evaluated each presentation of visual cue against a baseline without cues in a between participants experiment. Participants performed the pick-and-place task with three different objects. And we evaluated task performance through time, accuracy, and errors as quantitative measures. As qualitative measures, we asked participants to provide words to describe their experience and carried out an interview. To the collected information, we performed a sentiment analysis and a thematic content analysis. Our quantitative results show that the advanced cues led to less errors, shorter time, and higher accuracy compared to the no cues condition. The advanced cues compared to the basic cues resulted in less errors and a shorter time. The basic cues compared to the no cues led to higher accuracy. Our qualitative results from a sentiment analysis revealed that teleoperation without cues prompted mostly a negative sentiment. Our basic cues prompted equally positive and negative sentiment, which were supported by a thematic content analysis. Here, our basic cues were referred as futuristic and complex. The advanced cues prompted mostly a positive sentiment and were regarded as visionary. Both presentations of cues were considered innovative, interesting, and intuitive. Our take-home messages are that both basic and advanced cues help to understand the relation between the robot and the environment in a given workspace and assist teleoperation by increasing accuracy. However, the number of elements from our basic cues added complexity to teleoperation. On the other hand, presenting the future state of an object favored not only task performance but perception of teleoperation. Thank you for your attention and I will gladly reply to your questions.

And these were the technologies that were used to capture these signals. Trainees were assigned to either the experiment group or the control group. Initially, trainees had taken part in a media interview, whereby the journalist would provide communication skills scores. reference: Hi, I'm Seungwon Do, and today I will introduce about our paper, a simulation model of intermittently controlled point-and-click behavior. We simulated the mouse point-and-click behavior that is applicable both when a target is stationary or moving. We combined five modules to create a point-and-click model, which was learned through deep reinforcement learning. As a result, we proposed a simulation model that creates a human-like mouse trajectory and clicks behavior. In this video, the left is a video of a real person, and the right is a simulation model. Black is the cursor, and red is target. First, I will explain the point-and-click model. The point-and-click model consists of five modules. Let's talk about the motor control module. The motor control module creates a cursor-motor plan that can move the cursor to the target based on the prediction horizon time. The cursor-motor plan is calculated as minimizing the mean-squared acceleration of cursor movement. The second module is the click-action module. The click-action module determines whether or not to activate the click and its timing. The optimal timing of the click action is calculated by integrating two sensory cues given during the execution of the current motor plan. The third module is the visual perception. The visual perception module receives the The velocity and position of the target and the cursor, and the position of the hand from the environment. The outputs are the perceived values, including perceptual noise. The fourth one is the mouse module. The mouse module simulates the process of converting the motor plan of the cursor into the motor plan of the hand, and how the cursor will move when the motor plan of the hand is executed. The last module is the upper-limb module. The upper-limb module simulates the rotation of the mouse by assuming the arm is a two-dimensional three-degree-of-freedom manipulator with three revolute joints, and also simulates the Gaussian additive motor noise proportional to the hand movement speed. The modules require parameters, but the predictive horizon time and click decision change as the simulation processes, so optimization for these two values is necessary. For optimization, we conducted simulation-based learning with deep reinforcement learning. Among various deep reinforcement learning algorithms, we used DeepQ network. For the learning, the model is formulated as a Markov decision process. We set the state as the information of the cursor, target, and hand with the noises. For minimizing on acceleration of the hand and success to click, the network optimized the prediction horizon time and click decision. After 4 million episodes, the learning completed. Through the learning, we finally present the point-and-click simulation model. With the binning of data, we can show our simulation model faithfully reproduce the human trial completion time and click failure rate. Also, for the distribution of trial completion time and click endpoints, the simulation successfully reproduce the human performance. This is the phase plot of the relative motion between the cursor and the target. The simulation faithfully reproduces the trajectory of human on average and the trajectory variability within a participant. In the subjective evaluation study using the video with the trajectory removed, the participant hardly distinguished between the two trajectories of the cursor and target. We presented a novel simulation model of intermittently controlled point-and-click behavior. But we are aware of the limitations that the applicability of the model has not been explored and that the different variations of MDP formulations. We hope these limitations will be discussed and supplemented through future studies. Thank you.

reference: Hello, my name is Jiwon Kim and I'm here to present the finger text that's exploring and automizing performances for wearable, mobile, and one-handed typing. Have you also done this kind of texting while walking before? Yeah, probably. We know that many people are using smartphones while walking. Likewise, typing on a wearable device while walking also can happen, but it is challenging. Many prior works tried to solve this problem by single-handed text entry. Thanks to the dexterity of fingers and wrists, these were effective while there was a lack of consideration on mobility context. To address this issue, we built a touch-sensitive fingernail system. According to the prior work, this system enables the eyes-free, one-handed, fine-grained input in multiple nail regions. So this is our system, finger text. Using finger text, you can easily type the text even while walking. Let's have a look closer. To build the system, we had two considerations. One is, which fingernail regions can you use for a key? Following the previous work on design space of fingernail, we set these two key configurations. 10-key layouts utilize the side and tip regions of fingernail, and 5-key simplifies this as one key. Then second, we need to assign 26 letters to each key. In this case, we might use QWERTY or alphabetic layout. However, this method is in a different form with keyboard or smartphone typing. So we frame a hypothesis that there will be no learning benefit. Later, to answer this question, we conducted a matrix study. The goal was to gather the three matrix data to feed on keyboard layout optimization process. We measured the speed and accuracy for each pair of keys, and the comfort for each key on 5-recurve scale. As well, we did this for walking and sitting pose to figure out the effect of mobility condition. Interestingly, in terms of pose, we couldn't find the significant differences in speed between sitting and walking condition. In terms of speed and accuracy, the results are obvious. Double tap and short distance were quick and accurate, but little and long distance were slow and error-prone. For comfort, user felt comfortable for using thumb, index, and middle finger, while not for using middle finger. For confusability, if we allocate the high-frequency letters to the most comfortable region, it can cause such a confusion that couldn't get what the user wanted to type. To deal with this issue, using confusability matrix, we can consider how many possible words will be generated for each layout. With these four matrix, we conducted optimization using NSGA2 algorithm. We get the min-max of each matrix to normalize it, and then we conducted optimization to get the perfect optimal keyboard layout. From these optimums, we selected the layout with an emphasis on speed and comfort. So this is our optimization result. As you can see, less frequent letters like Q, J, G are located on the little finger, and lowers are located on the comfortable regions like thumb, index, and middle finger. Then, to verify whether the optimization is effective or not, we conducted comparison experiment. For this comparison, we conducted word repetition study with QWERTY layout baseline. In the study, participants made a word input 7 times consecutively for 20 words while walking. This approach boosted participants to make an expert level of input within a short period of time. In the result, we found a meaningful performance improvement for each five and ten key layout. optimized layout improved in both speed and accuracy over the QWERTY layout. Compared to the other text entry studies on wearables, FingerText showed a comparable and promising result as a viable design for mobility context. This is final shot of our prototype. reference: Hello, everyone, I am Shigeo Ushida at the University of Tokyo, in Japan. I am glad to present teardrop glasses, an eyeglasses style wearable device. that can influence the emotion of multiple people. How do you feel when you see a person is crying? I believe many of you feel hurt by seeing tears rolling down the cheeks in this presentation. we introduce a method for influencing the emotion of multiple people through artificial bodily changes, such as through the tears. Psychological studies in emotion have revealed that our minds and our bodies are related. American psychologist William James best expressed this notion. We feel sorry because we cry angry because we strike, afraid because we tremble. This means that not only our emotions trigger our bodily changes. But also our bodily changes to trigger our emotions. On the other hand, emotional contagion is a phenomenon. in which emotion is unconsciously and instantly transmitted among people. Emotional contagion occurs by observing another person's bodily changes or emotional expressions. Then, this fact led us to an idea that we may be able to induce specific emotions of people by making them believe that they are experiencing specific bodily changes. In this study, we focused on shedding tears as a bodily change due to the relations between tears and emotions. Then, Instead, the way enforcing actual bodily change to people, we artificially generated a suitable bodily change such as the tears. We develop a device that can press water drops near the inner corners of the whale's eyes to immediate tear drops. The flow of water can be remotely controlled via infrared communication. A syringe is used to store and refill the water. Two springs fitted on the left side of the device push the syringe. When the electromagnetic bulb opens, the spring pressure is released. And the water within the syringe flows into the region near the inner corner of the user's eyes. We employ this motor free mechanism. For the sake of the lightness and quietness of the device. The water from the syringe goes to two tubes that are located near the inner corners of the user's eyes. We conducted an experiment to confirm our assumption of artificially generated bodily changes to induce emotional contention. In this experiment, the participant group was asked to watch a 10 min slideshow consisted of neutral visual stimuli. Each group watched three different slideshows with different 3 conditions, including control condition, In which the participants watched the slideshow without the device, Glasses without tears, condition in which one of the participants wore the device. But no water came out from the device, and finally glasses with tears, condition in which one of the participants wore the glasses. And water dropped every 25 S. we measure the subjective rating of sadness and happiness through a self inventory questionnaire with dummy questions. Moreover, we estimate the positive and negative score of each participant through the analysis of texts gathered from the participants as impressions of the slideshow. The take is obtained after watching each slideshow. These are the results of the sadness and happiness rating over the participants. Each rating was corrected by subtracting the ratings in control condition to simply compare the effect of the pseudo tears. A significant difference is found in the sadness rating with and without tears condition. The difference is found both for wearers and non-wearers. This means that pseudo tears successfully influenced the sadness rating of both wearers and non wearers in contrast. Only the happiness rating of non wearers has a significant difference between with and without tears condition. There is no significant difference in wearers. Also, the positive negative score and the with tiers condition in no wears was lower than the other conditions, however. No influence was found in wears. Comments from some wears indicates that the presentation of tears caused them to feel good. It seems that the tears also have an effect on stress relief. We believe that such an effect of tears might influence the feeling of the wearers and cause differences in the feeling of between the wearers and non wearers. reference: Hi, my name is Franklin. Today I'm presenting our paper, True Assistive Devices That Save My Face, a study on perceptions of accessibility and assistive technology use conducted in China. Co-authors are Laura, Mingming, and Kai. Based on statistics and prior research, China has 83 million people with disabilities, which is twice as the U.S. But little research has explored the adoptions and social acceptability of assistive technologies in China. With the knowledge of large population of disabilities in China, only 7 % of them had an opportunity to use Ats. Beyond the low usage of ATs, there is a huge shortage of professional caregivers, which is equivalent to 1 over 185 of the number in Europe. In Chinese culture, some families consider disability as the wrongdoings and sins in the past. In our research, we are interested to understand what are the practices and challenges surrounding AT use by people with various disabilities in China, and what are the design factors that influence the adoption and social acceptability of ATs in China. To understand the research questions, we conducted semi-structured interviews with 26 people with various disabilities in China. Participants were recruited through China Disabled Persons Federation. In our interview, we found that people with disabilities in China have a strong preference for using ATs that could show others their independence with minimal assistance with ATs and maintain their faith and self-dignity. Due to the stigma of linking wrongdoings and sins from the past to disabilities, people with disabilities mostly consult their family members and friends around them to choose their ATs, which limited their choices and resources. We found that accessibility infrastructures forced people to use certain ATs. For example, we found that although China has the longest tactile paving, some people place their cars on them, which may cause safety issues, and people also park their bikes at the end of the ramps. Finally, we found that subsidy or insurance only covers certain brands or models of ATs. It does not cover customization and maintenance costs. Due to the cost of and lack of assistive technologies, we found that participants with disabilities in China tend to DIY and customize their assistive technologies to replicate existing commercial ATs, either built from scratch or they modify existing mainstream technologies. But there lacks professional and authorized technicians to control the quality. Under social interactions, Traditional Chinese stigmatizing terms such as using shatz to refer people with visual impairments. have derogatory connotations and sound humiliating to people with disabilities. Furthermore, people with disabilities in China tend to have clustering effects during employment, such as people with visual impairments often work as a massage therapist, and people with hearing impairments often work in a deaf cafe or restaurant. Although this helped with employment for people with disabilities, this situation reduced the interaction between people with disabilities and the public, Which might cause misperceptions beyond the clustering effect, We found that the high attendance rate of people with disabilities when to specialized schools in China. would increase the knowledge gap between people with disabilities and the general public, which may lead to unwanted help. Beyond the misperceptions that were found under Western context, we found that there are three other misperceptions of ATs that are unique in China, which are ATs should overcome inaccessible social infrastructures, ATs are symbols of permanent disabilities, and ATs with more functionalities are better. For example, one participant mentioned that some people recommended her to modify her wheelchair to adapt the inaccessible subway system, rather than how to make the subway system fully accessible. Based on our findings, we found that future research should focus on design ATs that maintain face or self-dignity in China. Future work should also explore low-cost fabrication technologies for DIY ATs and customizations in both urban and rural China. To reduce the gap between the general public and people with disabilities in China, future work should explore different media platforms such as vlogs and live streamings to reduce the misperceptions in the society. Finally, all participants were from the same province and they all live in urban areas. However, rural areas in China might have different accessibility infrastructures and misperceptions which may lead to more AT abandonment. Therefore, future research should explore people with various disabilities from different regions in China to understand different AT adoptions and challenges in social interactions. For more details, please read our paper. Thanks for listening.

My name is Tobias Kauer and this paper was written by Aaron Ridley, Marion, Dirk, Benjamin Bach and me. With our research, we want to better understand how people express their reactions to visualizations. Prior work has studies how experts use, for example, visualization annotation to achieve a shared goal like decision-making or participatory sense-making. However, visualization reaches ever-widening and increasingly diverse audiences with individual opinions and personal perspectives on the data. So, we are interested how these public audiences react to visualizations in the wild. We look at reactions of non-experts who do not share a goal when engaging with visualizations. Better understanding these audiences is key to understand how visualizations are used, how they can contribute to productive discussions, and what harm they can potentially cause. In our study, we look at audience reactions on Reddit. The subforum Data is Beautiful is a community of about 50 million people where visualizations are created, posted, and discussed by their members. We collected textual reactions on 20 popular visualizations and classified them using a granular theory approach we found. Ten distinct reaction types that refer to four different scopes, or basically areas of a visualization post. Among them were reactions like observations, conclusions, or hypotheses. These primarily express how people make sense of the data and. they have been discussed in prior work on social analysis and participatory sensemaking. Sensemaking is also connected to clarifications, where people ask about details in a post they don't fully understand, and Usually they get further explanations by other members of the audience, and this audience also provides additional information like. background knowledge, trivia information, or links to reading material to To further contextualize information that is displayed in the visualization, I want to talk more specifically about two groups of reactions. On the one hand, people express critique about the visualization and its data, they criticize, e.g. misleading and codings, and. They provide proposals how to improve this problem. More interestingly, people call out missing or clearly wrong data. and with that they help the broader audience who reads their comments to understand possible issues of data quality. The most interesting reactions to us were testimonies and opinions. Here, the reactions differ greatly from prior studies, because in them people position themselves according to their cultural, political, or social identity. Particularly in testimonies, people provide personal stories or biographic anecdotes, and with that they basically connect a relatable human story to the data that is visible in the visualization. To better understand why people react, we did a follow-up survey to investigate people's motivation and identified nine engagement drivers in two groups. On the one hand, people express personal perspectives and experiences. They share opinions or emotions, and they point out what is interesting to them. They add anecdotal evidence, and even more analytical reactions are used to match existing knowledge with the visualized data. They basically Compare what they already know and what they see in the civilization. On the other hand, people are well aware that their reaction informs the public discourse, and therefore they have an impact on how this data is discussed or made sense of, And what additional information the wider audience gets to contextualize the presented data? So what can we do with this knowledge? Our results help understand the role of personal perspectives on data, and they pose challenges for future participatory visualization interfaces. For example, how can type-specific annotations be used to better capture nuances of reactions like critiques, clarifications, or contextualizations? What is the potential of audience-driven storytelling, where people contribute personal stories and testimonies to a visualization, and thus they add a subjective perspective to data that is otherwise considered raw or neutral? And how can we use audience engagement to visualize the discourse around the data and guide people's attention to areas that are highly debated or commented on? With that, I'm looking forward to your questions, and thank you for your attention. Thank you.

reference: Hello everyone. Welcome to the presentation of our paper, What players want? Information needs of players on post-game visualizations, in which we explore the types of information players pay attention to and consider important, for instance, for training visualizations. My name is Günter Wallner and I am happy to present this work today on behalf of my co-authors Manex von Weiland, Regina Bernhaupt and Simone Kriegelstein. The motivation behind this work was that video games strongly rely on players being able to make informed decisions during gameplay. And as such, video games share a long history with visualizations that convey information about a game's state to the player, such as for instance health bars, deck trees, and many more. And over time, collecting of behavioral data of players has also become more and more easy, which led to new application areas of visualization in games, which go beyond using them as part of the user interface. And nowadays, players constitute a growing target audience of such behavioral visualizations of in-game data, also because of the rise of online gaming and e-sports, which spurred interest in visualizations for training and skill development even more. There currently exists however limited knowledge about which information players rely on to make in-game decisions. However, understanding which information is important and why, and which goals players pursue with visualizations, is essential in order to create visualizations that are actually useful and satisfy players' needs. And as such, we conducted a study to explore and understand such information needs with respect to post-play visualizations, and develop an inventory about important in-game information and for relevance across genres. The study was guided by three research questions, which were related to why players actually make use of post-game visualizations, which information players rely on during gameplay, and which information they consider important to include in visualizations. In order to understand how these are affected by different gameplay mechanics, these questions were investigated with players of three competitive online games, covering three popular genres, including Dota 2, a multiplayer battle arena game, PUBG, a battle royale game, and StarCraft 2, a real-time strategy game. We used a mixed-matter study, starting with semi-structured interviews of 16 players of the three aforementioned games, and which cover different aspects such as the game itself, the information they rely on for decision making, and the role visualizations are playing. These interviews were then transcribed and analyzed using thematic analysis to develop themes with respect to the three research questions. To quantify these themes and to assess their importance across a larger sample, we then followed up with an online survey, asking participants to rate the relevance of the different themes. Based on this, we developed an inventory of players' goals and information needs. Due to the time limit, I can't go into much detail today, also because the results partly vary considerable across the three genres, but these are for example the results with respect to the information players consider important to know about the enemy for decision making. And in the paper you can find similar detailed breakdowns for all the research questions I mentioned earlier. Today I I would rather like to reflect on five high level design implications for post play visualizations 1st of all. one needs to carefully choose the data to be included, as not all information is equally important, and the importance can also differ based on the genre or the game. It's also important to select appropriate representations for the data, which is in turn influenced by the data itself, and also by the task which should be supported. Post-game visualizations are also not restricted to the information which is visible during play, and as such they can take advantage of being able to include data which is otherwise inaccessible. And in relation to this, it's also important to keep in mind that certain information becomes more or less relevant after playing. And lastly, players show a high interest in visualizations of high-level concepts that go beyond simply showing individual low-level data, but which instead require the integration of different types of data. That's it from me for today, thanks for watching!

I'm very excited to talk to you today about Fabricade, which is a fabrication-aware design tool for 2D cutting machines. The main contribution of Fabricade is to support designers who use laser cutters by doing live packing during the design phase. This is in contrast to existing tools that do so at the very end. First, I will discuss the motivation for our work. Relative to other fabrication processes, laser cutting has a pretty low barrier to entry. Designs can be made with 2D graphics software and a lot of cutting materials can be found in local stores. But since laser cutting is a subtractive manufacturing process, it produces a lot of leftover material. Managing materials effectively is a challenge to both novice and expert users. So this motivated the question of how material management might affect the design process. To better understand this, we performed formative interviews with six designers who are experienced laser cutter users. Their main takeaways were that using leftover material is desirable but hard to plan around, buying new materials is not always an option, and when that happens, designs have to be adjusted in some way. So this provided the motivation for Fabricade, Which helps users plan their designs with respect to material constraints, and I will now do a quick demonstration of our tool. This is a birdhouse design made by one of our participants in the user study. As you can see here, each of the parts are assigned different colors which correspond to specific materials that the user has. The Fabricade UI on the right shows how the parts are placed onto the material sheets. The existing holes on the sheets are rendered in gray. So if I were to add a new shape, our packing algorithm would quickly calculate the new positions of parts for that material. Fabricade would warn me immediately if my design can't be made with existing materials. So here, I wanted to make four birdhouse faces. reference: Hello, everyone, my name is Eike Schneiders, I'm a Phd student from Aalborg University, and on behalf of myself and my co authors, Anna Marie Kenstrup. Jesper Kjeldskov and Mikael Besko, I'm presenting our paper called Domestic Robots and the dream of Automation. Understanding Human Interaction and Intervention. Robots are increasingly becoming a ubiquitous technology, found in a variety of settings such as industry, tutoring, the service sector, or in the home. The domestic context is the context in which people are most likely to have their first encounters with robots, yet little research focuses on the interaction with commercially available robots in the domestic context. With this study, we contribute to the HCI and HRI literature in two ways. Firstly, we increase the empirical understanding on domestic robots and how they are integrated into existing household routines, but also create new ones. And secondly, we identify opportunities and design implications for enabling improved automation using robots in the home. Since I won't have time to elaborate in great detail on everything in the paper, I invite you all to read it. In order to collect in-depth data, we performed a study involving multiple qualitative methods. We recruited 27 participants, representing 24 different households. During the recruitment, we focused on finding a varied mix of households, representing different housing sizes, number of floors, different robot types, as well as different degrees of domestic robots familiarity. We used three different approaches for the data collection, the first one being online interviews. This was primarily due to the countrywide lockdown due to COVID-19, which didn't allow the physical data collection through home visits to continue. The second approach were contextual technology tours on location. Here, not only the robots, but the entire infrastructure used to interact with it were discussed and demonstrated. Lastly, in order to get impressions from novel robot users, we deployed a hybrid floor-mopping and vacuum robot to three households to 10 days each. The robot deployed supported remote interaction through both voice interaction as well as remote interaction through an application, but also co-located physical interaction with interaction on the robot itself. The data collection resulted in roughly 19 hours of audio material, which was transcribed. Over 220 photos and small video clips provided by the participants, as well as digital and physical diary entries from households participating in the robot deployment. Using thematic analysis, we coded the transcribed interviews, resulting in a multitude of codes such as automation, new routines, or remote interaction. Our data analysis led us to three themes, namely work routines and automation, which covers observations in relation to the change of behavior in order to facilitate automation using the robot. Domestic robot automation in the physical environment, which is related to the additional need for adaption of the environment to make it more robot inclusive. And lastly, interaction and breakdown intervention, which focuses on the user behavior in relation to interaction and, at times, very creative ways to extend the existing infrastructure to prevent or recover from breakdowns. Due to time limitations, I will briefly present theme one. The first theme, titled work routines and automation, covers observations Observations made in relation to the introduction of new routines and the fragmentation of current ones. in order to facilitate efficient task automation in the home. The observation was quite new for most participants, who, on purchase of the technology, expected it to be plug and play. The manual task completion, like the lawn mowing or the vacuuming, was described as one coherent task, where obstacles were removed or pushed away while performing the task. Similar potential maintenance was typically completed directly as an extension of the primary task. These tasks Were, with the introduction of the domestic robot, divided into three separate tasks, namely preparation, such as decluttering the floor or the lawn. the activity of the vacuuming or lawn mowing itself, as well as the maintenance, which was not necessarily performed directly after the robot operation was completed. Thank you very much for your attention and I'm open to questions.

reference: Hi Kai, it is my honor to present our paper comparing perspectives on human and technology support for contact tracing. With COVID-19, the world has experienced a major global health crisis. Many countries have used contact tracing to help contain the spread of the virus, Since an estimated 13 % of people with Covid-19 are symptomatic, there are two major approaches in contact tracing. Digital contact tracing aims to identify, notify, and monitor close contacts while human tracers typically perform the same function by directly talking to people via phone or video. We thus study contact tracing to explore the role of self-tracking technology in public health crisis. Studies have examined how self-tracking data can be aggregated to understand community-level health behaviors, but we have less understanding of how self-tracking technology can encourage people to contribute to disease surveillance and response. We ask two research questions. First, how do people perceive the respective strengths and weaknesses of these two approaches? Second, how does the contact tracing strategy influence people's willingness to share information collected during contact tracing? We therefore deployed a mixed-method survey with 291 U.S. responses in August 2020. We will describe a few oral findings, but we encourage reading the paper for our full set. Collectively, participants did not express a preference towards human or technology, seeing each having strengths and weaknesses. One participant said, it doesn't make a difference to me personally. I understand fully why we need to have contact tracing, whether that is by human or technology. We need to gather the data and find a way to contain the virus. People perceive digital contact tracing as more effective for promoting privacy, convenience, and data accuracy. Human contact tracing offers benefits around data security, emotional reassurance, advice, and accessibility. For privacy, participants feel that technology allows for anonymity, providing people to be judged by human tracers for their COVID-19 status or background. One participant said, if you feel embarrassed about something you have done or somewhere you have been, it is easier to give the information to the contact tracing technology as it will not judge you. For convenience, participants feel that technology could save interaction burdens by tracking data passively. It can also measure data and skill. One participant said, I can report all of my data on my own time through an app. Technology has greater ability to capture data more accurately and avoid potential challenges brought by human entry. One participant imagined data inaccuracy brought by humans. Unreliable information from a person if their memory is not the best, if they forgot places they have been, or if they forget people they have been in contact with due to being distracted or diseases such as dementia. People's unwillingness to share data with technology was often due to data security concerns. Technology was associated with tech companies or the government at large, which were less trustworthy than the public health department and easier to be hacked. One participant said, app data is more frequently attacked than direct medical records. Information linked could violate HIPAA and privacy. For emotional reassurance, human tracers could empathetically understand people, carefully convey bad news, and help relieve negative feelings. One participant felt humans can feel empathy and emotions for people who have that disease. For advice, human tracers were able to provide further information about how to act when people are positive cases or close contacts. One participant said, I will want to ask questions and get verifications on things you do not understand or even ask what the next stage was. For accessibility, one participant worried that many people do not have access to telephones or internet access and are likely already to be an at-risk group. So this is a very dangerous method because it leaves out this population. Also, some people would have difficulties to interact with technology. Although the use of contact tracing had little influence on participants' overall preferences towards digital or human, participants preferred technology when needing to report their health data every day during self-quarantine. One participant imagined being bothered by human tracers every day, while another participant felt it would be easy to lock information data in an app. Considering different affordances of this two approaches and the varied contexts required for contact tracing, Our work suggests value in solutions that combine the benefits of both humans and technology, e.g. To support people that can reliably access smartphones and the Internet, the system can mostly utilize self tracking technology and skill. For those with accessibility issues issues, the system would mainly adopt the human tracing approach. Also, the system should involve a full range of stakeholders and more clearly indicate what stakeholders, such as technology companies or public health agencies, are involved in the deployment or have access to data provided. Thank you.

Thank you.

With a short presentation, I'm starting with the takeaway message. User preferences for system pace are correlated with user pace. But this paper is not about how lucky I am, but about interaction pace. I don't know if you've noticed, but the first time I played, I interacted rather slowly with the system. This gambling machine that automatically adapts its pace to the user's pace was described by Jack Lowney in 98. And more generally, it opens up a question, can automatic interface adaptation to user space of interaction benefit users? There are plethora of situations in which the system pace is contrived by predefined parameters. From timeout before folder expansion, window reorganization animations, mouse pointer transfer functions, to long presses. And most interfaces use fixed timeout. Sometimes systems allow users to change the values via some preference system menus, but those are often ignored. Consequently, users typically have a one-size-fits-all solution, too fast for some, too slow for others. reference: Hi everyone, we are Jay and Yanni. On behalf of our co-authors, we are presenting our CakeVR, which is a social VR tool that helps pastry chefs and clients to co-design customized cakes in a virtual space. This work is supported by the Dutch National Institute of Mathematics and Computer Science, CWI, Delft University of Technology and EU Horizon 2020 VR Together project. Rarely is there a celebration without a cake. Customized cake services enable clients to discuss their dreamed cake with pastry chefs. However, it is often challenging for them to clearly communicate the size and decorations of the cake by text and images. As you can see in this collage, based on the keywords and the reference picture given by the couple in A and B, chefs made the wedding cake shown in C and D. This collage illustrates the risks of miscommunication since the clients only saw the cake on their big day. It is stressful for the couple but also created pressure for pastry chefs. This challenge motivated us to explore the potential of social VR to support cake co-design between pastry chefs and clients to let them see 3D visualizations of their designed cakes in VR on the fly. We started with user research to gather design requirements for designing CakeVR2. We did contextual inquiries with five pastry chefs and their bakeries and interviewed four clients to learn about how they communicate to customize cakes. We found that the communication typically consists of three phases. The biggest challenge is in the second phase where chefs and clients were exchanging a lot of pictures and messages to discuss the delicate details of the cake design. We planned to bring the three phases of communication to CakeVR based on which we distilled eight design requirements such as the users are represented as avatars and the system must support audio-visual communication and 3D sketches. Based on the design requirements, we made a storyboard to describe the core functions and user scenarios of CakeVR, starting from preparation by uploading reference pictures and joining the virtual bakery, then exchanging initial ideas using the pictures and building virtual cakes together. Finally, chefs and the clients return to the virtual bakery to confirm the design. This picture provides an overview of the CakeVR system. A pastry chef and a client can remotely join the virtual co-design session by wearing a head-mounted display. The virtual co-design space can switch between the virtual bakery and a celebration location. In addition, CakeVR has a graphical interface to guide cake co-design and enable VR users to see what they design in real time. We implemented a mid-fidelity prototype in Unity based on the storyboard. With this prototype, we invited four pastry chefs and six clients for evaluations. They were asked to use CakeVR to co-design a cake. These images displayed their design process and design outcome. The evaluation results showed that most users found that CakeVR is easy to use and quick to learn. Another interesting finding is that, compared to clients, the pastry chefs were much quicker and more independent in making the virtual cakes and were actively exploring the functions of CakeVR. The clients spent much more time in consulting or watching than actually making the virtual cakes themselves. To conclude, we found that CakeVR improves shared understanding and communication between users as well as empowers non-designers to visually express their ideas. The users commented that emotion connection and creative virtual environment are essential for their engagement. Finally, the CakeVR system has the potential to be adapted to other use cases such as medical consultation and interactive museums. Exploring more use cases and investigating the factors that influence the co-design engagement will be our future work. Thank you for your attention. Please read our paper, CakeVR, a social VR tool for co-design cakes.

reference: I am Joona Bariström, and together with Torsal Vedalsgaard, Jason Alexander and Kasper Hornberg, we reviewed 20 years of virtual reality studies of object selection and manipulation. Designing experiments for evaluating interaction is tricky, even when the focus is in the basic interactions like object selection and manipulation. We have some standards and common practices for experiment tasks on object selection, such as this reciprocal task, disk transfer task and pin transfer task from FITCES studies almost 70 years ago. And we have the ISO 9241 part 9 standard for tapping tasks in 2D. However, in VR, these standards are harder to apply. There, the objects of interest are not limited to a two-dimensional display with its frames in front of us. And even if researchers have adapted the 2D ISO task into three-dimensional layouts, like we did in the spiral-shaped layout following Jens and Theodor's example, in VR, objects of interest can also be all around the space and around ourselves, and occluded by each other. To find out how should we evaluate object selection and manipulation in VR, we reviewed 20 years of studies on that. Our aim was to analyze the studies to form an empirical basis of best practices in VR studies. We reviewed studies of object selection and manipulation in VR, published between 2000 and 2019, in the central conferences and journals of the field. The 93 papers included in our sample consisted of 48 studies, and out of these, 30 studies 30 studies evaluated object selection and 18 studies object manipulation. One of our key findings was that such a seemingly mundane decision as laying out targets for a selection task is indeed difficult in the context of VR. The strategies studies used included, for instance, target pairs, like in the FITC's reciprocal tapping task, but placed like here, for instance, on frontal and lateral axes, in front of the participant. They also included 2D layouts, following the ISO standard layout, adapted for instance in a horizontal form here on the left, and a vertical form on the right. And the studies included 3D layouts with random arrangements of targets. The studies further vary in the use of distractor targets, occluding targets, shape and size of the targets, and many other factors of the experiment design outside the task. Our aim with this review was to help researchers, including ourselves, to design and conduct VR studies of object selection and manipulation. To begin moving from our findings toward common practices in VR studies, we synthesized our key observations in 10 recommendations for designing studies, and also a A checklist to support the use of the recommendations and making reproducible studies. We also discussed research directions for VR study methods. In particular, we find a need for tools that help to accumulate knowledge and findings of object selection and manipulation techniques. In our sample, 64.6 % of the studies use a completely new task rather than building on existing studies. and therefore comparison across those or meta-analysis of findings are currently difficult. Aiding tools for this would be, for instance, test suits and reference tasks. We hope to continue working on these first versions of the recommendations and the checklist on VR studies with you at vrevaluation.github. Thank you.

reference: Instructional makeup videos are extremely popular on YouTube, catering to a diverse audience and garnering millions of views. They're effective for conveying actions that are difficult to describe with words or static images alone. However, it's often difficult for people to follow along with an instructional makeup video using a timeline-based UI. In particular, the linear nature of the timeline makes it difficult for the user to follow along at their own pace, jump ahead or replay steps since there are no step boundaries, or to get a sense of how many steps there are, what kind of makeup is applied, and more without watching the video through first. In contrast, many of these limitations of instructional videos are affordances of traditional text tutorials, which allow users to easily follow along at their own pace. However, traditional text tutorials are much less expressive compared to video tutorials. Our work aims to combine elements of text and video tutorials to get the benefits of both. In order to do this, we need to first segment the video into steps. Prior research in cognitive psychology suggests that people mentally segment procedural tasks into object-action hierarchies. In a formative study of makeup tutorials, we found that the course-level object categories correspond to facial parts, specifically the eyes, broader face, and lips, while fine-grained action steps entail manipulations on these facial parts, such as apply the liner on the lash line. We also found that fine-grained action steps are defined by a product, such as bronzer in step 1, and an action, such as apply. A step change occurs when the product being used changes, for example, going from bronzer in step 1 to blush in step 2. Using this structure, we developed a pipeline that, given an instructional makeup video's input, automatically segments the video into a two-level hierarchical tutorial And visualizes the resulting hierarchy in a mixed media ui. Now I'll go through our ui in more detail. At the top left is the video metadata. and. and then below that is a video player. At the very bottom, the overview timeline gives a breakdown of the tutorial by facial parts sections. Finally, on the right is the steps panel, which displays all the steps. Users can browse the tutorial by scrolling through the steps in the steps panel and reading the summary text. They can also hover over the step thumbnail to preview the video of the step as an animation. They can click on a step to play it. As always, I've applied an eyeshadow primer all over the lid. We've also implemented the following voice commands with which users can navigate the interface. Notably, users are able to navigate with high-level intentions by searching steps, facial parts, products, and more. Now, I'll talk a bit more about how we segment the video into fine-grained action steps as well as core screen events. To first identify the beginning of a new action step, we look for product changes in both the audio and the video. For example, to find a new step boundary in the video, we leverage an observation that before creators use a product, they tend to introduce it visually by featuring it prominently in the scene as seen in this first row of frames. In contrast, when they use the product as seen in the second row, the face is shown prominently with an applicator moving over it. We first run an object detector to detect all products in the scene. Since frame F does not contain a product, we judge that it is not a product introduction frame. Next, we run face detection to see if there are any faces on the scene. Since frame A contains only a product and does not have any faces in the scene, we judge that it is a product introduction frame and thus marks the start of a new step. Otherwise, if there is a face but it's not overlapping with a product, as in the case of frame B, we also mark that as a product introduction frame. If the face and product are overlapping, we calculate the motion of the product against the face. If it's fairly still, as in the case of frame C, we mark that as a product introduction frame. Otherwise, we assume that the video shows a makeup application action and move on. After we have all the steps, we cluster them into facial part groups. For a given action step, we identify the facial part by looking for subcomponents in the step text. And then we group consecutive steps with a common facial part together. To validate our system, we had eight users use the system to follow two tutorials, one in our UI and one with the YouTube UI. Overall, users found that our UI was easier to navigate and felt more confident in their results when using it. Additionally, participants felt that the automatic step segmentations were fairly accurate. We also asked users to compare the hierarchically segmented tutorials with the one-level version showing only the action steps. All participants expressed preference for the hierarchical version. Many participants appreciated that the hierarchical version helped them to quickly get an overview of the tutorial. For participants who only wanted to follow part of a tutorial, the hierarchical version helped them to find sections of interest much more quickly. With that, thank you for listening and please find more technical details in our paper.

reference: Hello, I'm Katie Burns from Stockholm University. I'm here today to present the paper Queuing for Waste, Sociotechnical Interactions within a Food-Sharing Community, on behalf of my co-authors Pia Rosito and Jakob Talander. There's much engaging past work that investigates how digital technologies may be utilised to rescue and redistribute surplus food in different settings, from charity to commercial. However, in previous work, in most cases the exchange of surplus food is centred around a digital platform, and the majority of interactions take place online. We identified queuing as an important aspect of sharing events, both in terms of managing the flow of attendees, and for communicating activism. In this paper we focus explicitly on the situated interactions centred around queuing, and the potential role of digital technology within that space. These contributions were the result of an ethnographic study of Foodshare in Copenhagen, a grassroots initiative operating in Denmark since 2016. Foodshare in Copenhagen runs face-to-face food-sharing events with the goal of reducing food waste. These events are open to anyone who wishes to attend, which marks a profound difference from the sharing for charity model that we've seen in other studies. Our findings reveal how face-to-face food-sharing events increase the visibility of food waste as an issue, as attendees get the opportunity to see all of the rescued food, rather than just their individual share. We also found that through the labour of volunteers, donated food which would usually go to waste is instead reframed as valuable, and shared with attendees as a gift, rather than a commodity exchanged through monetary transactions. Finally, we were able to identify how the community's The communities shift from traditional queuing mechanisms. such as first-come-first-served line aggregation, to more dynamic mechanisms such as the randomised number system, or the picture-based system, reflect this notion of sharing food as a gift, and support the community's activist endeavour around food waste. Throughout the paper we borrow from scholarship on community economies, to engage in a discussion on how concepts of commoning and care can help us to rethink queuing. We ask designers to reflect on the potential effects of digitally-mediated queuing. While digitally-mediated queuing may make the flow of attendees more efficient, for example by digitising tickets and distributing them before events, this could also remove much of the face-to-face interactions that unfold before each event. Such interactions help to break with individualism and sustain mutual relationships among the different actors taking part in events. By considering the value of mutual relationships, we highlight how queuing can facilitate commoning, That is the possibility to care and manner manage together practices of food distribution. Moreover, we see how queuing at food-sharing events can become an opportunity to encounter others, and collectively benefit from shared resources, Rather than simply a mundane activity that must be optimised. To conclude, this paper shows queuing as an important aspect of organising activism, in that queuing practices intertwine with the framings and meanings associated with surplus food. With this in mind, the paper shows how changes in seemingly mundane practices like queuing Can incur significant changes in the dynamic sharing dynamics of a community. Thank you very much for listening, and I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

Of course, we have some coping strategies such as password managers and browsers which recall them. However, these do not explore the design of those passwords, so what movements, what shape, what interaction would make sense. So therefore, our aim was to discover those things. In order to do so, we conducted six experiments which we divided in three phases. The first phase focused on the movement space of embodied passwords, the second on the affordances and instruction, and the last phase on the memorability. During the first phase, we conducted two experiments where we explored which movements are suitable for passwords and which aren't, and the space in which they should take place. From this experiment, we learned that people preferred the twist, so the object on the left, as it reminded them of a combination lock, so they associated it with something safe, and it allowed them a variety of movements. reference: Hello everyone. This paper presents the image of the interface, a work completed in the University of Saskatchewan. It investigated how people use landmarks to develop spatial memory of commands in graphical interfaces. Graphical interfaces arrange commands visually as menus, toolbars, and ribbons, where each command appears at a specific location in the interface. In order to select commands, novice users must perform a slow visual search in the interface, because they have not memorized their locations. In contrast, frequent users already know where the commands are in the interface, so they can quickly recall commands from memory to carry out tasks on computers. But we do not precisely know how this location memory of commands is formed in graphical interfaces. Spatial memory is a particular type of human memory that allows people to learn objects' location in an environment. It enables people to retrieve the locations of already visited items from memory. One mechanism that helps people learn spatial locations in real life is landmarks. Landmarks play a critical role in developing spatial memory of an area as they provide reference frames to remember objects' locations. However, such landmarks are not available in standard desktop interfaces. Frequent users of these interfaces can recall the locations of commands from their memory, indicating that, over time, they have developed mental images of the interfaces. It is important for designers to understand what landmarks are present in these interfaces that help people develop spatial memory and what they can do to make graphical interfaces more memorable. So we explored the mental images of the interfaces that frequent users develop. We carried out a semi-structured interview with 20 people who frequently used four commercial desktop interfaces Microsoft Word, Adobe Reader, Facebook, and Adobe Photoshop. We refer you to our paper for the details about the study methods, design, and results. Now I present some key findings from our study. First, we found all participants developed cognitive images of the interfaces they frequently used. We observed that all participants recognized the general structures of the interfaces that arranged all commands in several groups. In addition, all participants described the visual appearance of commands. We calculated the accuracy of the cognitive images. Overall locations in Facebook and Word interfaces were more accurate at least 76 % than the reader and Photoshop. Which were less than 44 % accurate, we identified four landmark types that people heavily used while recalling commands' locations. First, the interface layout provides users a bird's-eye view of the interface. In our study, all participants used layout as a general reference frame for remembering relative locations of commands. Second landmark was the command group. We found that participants recalled command locations using the semantically divided command groups as a reliable landmark. And their absence made certain areas of the interfaces less memorable. Third, the corners and edges available in the interfaces were an obvious set of landmarks that people used while remembering the commands located near them. Last, the visual appearance of the command icons were used as landmarks. Although the shape, size, and the color of commands do not provide any special information, interestingly, participants frequently referred to these visuals while recalling any command's location. In summary, our results revealed that frequent users of the four applications do have strong images of the interfaces in their minds, and they could easily recall the locations of commands using the landmarks in the interfaces. We identified four types of landmarks available in the interfaces that people relied to remember command locations, indicating that landmarks can aid in developing spatial memory of commands in graphical interfaces. Our results suggest that designers can consider using these existing elements and features in the interfaces as potential landmarks in order to design more easily memorable interfaces and can incorporate the idea of landmarks in the current interface design practices. Thank you.

And in the canonical workflow, the software tools for defining geometry are actually distinct from the programs that tell the machine how to create that geometry. This abstraction has been widely adopted by HCI fabrication researchers. However, in non-traditional fabrication contexts, it does not always fit. In online communities such as Plotter Twitter, artists create bespoke tools and share hardware and software hacks. Practitioners engage in activities that cannot accurately be described as CAD or CAM, thus challenging the normative categories of digital fabrication. Critically examining where practitioners are creating their own software and hardware tools would allow HCI researchers to understand how makers and artists are pushing the boundaries of what can be produced with these tools. That brings us to our research, where we're examining the unique digital fabrication workflows displayed on Plotter Twitter. Our first research question is, how can we conceptualize the space of workflows on Plotter Twitter beyond the canonical workflow? And second, how does work from Plotter Twitter question assumptions of who uses digital fabrication tools, and how? To answer our research questions, we investigated how the canonical workflow steps could be applied to plotting workflows, and identified areas where they failed to capture the activities happening on Plotter Twitter. We developed a coding scheme to categorize workflow steps, and applied this coding scheme to tweets we collected using the Twitter Streaming API. Plotter Twitter artists display an incredibly diverse set of workflows for engaging with digital fabrication tools. We observed these workflows to be much more complex and dynamic than the canonical CAD, CAM, CNC pipeline. Artists navigated often unclear relationships between digital and material forms. For example, matching appropriate pens and pencils to different image colors required iteration and testing. There are no out-of-the-box programs for accomplishing this, so artists developed their own lightweight and flexible tools to aid in this process. We found Plotter Twitter artists particularly interested in extremely niche workflows, like this one for creating plotted Magic the Gathering cards. Despite plotters being exceptionally good at drawing vector graphics, we saw almost no use of traditional vector graphics programs such as Adobe Illustrator. Instead, artists would create their own programs to generate graphics, and string these tools together. They would also integrate tools such as image generators created by the community into their workflows. The online community is extremely supportive of the spread of bespoke tools, and we found the hashtag full of questions and answers, recommendations, and resources. On Plotter Twitter, the workflow itself has become a medium of exploration and creation. Plotter Twitter shows that post-anthropocentric fabrication practice is thriving. We call on HCI researchers to adopt a post-anthropocentric view of making by conceptualizing personal fabrication as more than a series of steps. It is fundamentally more complex than that. Reducing the complexity of a personal fabrication workflow to the vision where data becomes things leaves out the nuanced interactions between human experience, machine idiosyncrasies, material properties, and code. Abstracting a workflow to one where a human maintains seamless control over their tools is ultimately not how personal fabrication works in practice. All of this leads us to an important concession. As researchers and tool builders, we should not assume that we can predict how people will use digital fabrication technology when they are exploring niche areas and developing novel workflows. Instead, we should leave room for, and perhaps even encourage, niche and case-specific interpretations. As HCI researchers, this takes the form of studying practitioners, developing flexible tools, and perhaps most importantly, refraining from assumptions about who produces and how. Thank you for your attention, and we'd also like to thank all of the Plotter Twitter community members whose work appeared in this paper.

reference: Winning is making a series of good decisions. A well-executed plan that can lead to eventual success. Recent work in artificial intelligence has shown us that reinforcement learning can be a powerful tool for planning successfully. AlphaGo demonstrated its capability about five years ago, and improvements have been steady ever since. Inspired by this, our work studies how human-computer interaction can benefit from similar approaches. We focus on adaptive systems that respond to user input and context to make changes to the user interface. Adaptive interfaces have been on the receiving end of much criticism. Frequent and unexpected changes often cause annoyances and do not allow users to rely upon memory. As such, myopic algorithms do not typically take into account these costs or long-term benefits of changes. You could say that adaptive interfaces haven't really been winning so far. In our work, we aim to change this by developing a new method where interactive systems can use long-term planning to adapt their interfaces. Our method convincingly outperforms typical non-adaptive and adaptive baselines. We frame the problem of adaptation as a stochastic decision-making problem. Here, the system must decide what changes it should make, if any, by picking sequences of adaptations that can maximize utility. Given the noisy nature of user interactions, it should make these decisions while accounting for uncertainty. The problem can then be formalized as a Markovian decision process, where a state represents both the interface and the user, and adaptations are actions that lead to different states. The goal of the system then is to maximize utility by picking an optimal policy for making adaptations. In a game like chess or Go, a win or loss is evident from the game state. But that is not the case during human-computer interaction. Estimating utility is much harder here. For one, as we interact with an adaptive interface, the benefits of an adaptation cannot be immediately observed from interactions. Further, during our interactions, we also, as users, adapt and change over time. Also, while I might interact with the interface in a certain way, you may do it very differently. Let's consider a simple case where a person comes across an adaptive menu such as this one. Through interactions, they learn and build up mental representations of the menu. So an adaptation that was beneficial initially might become quite harmful when made at a later time. To plan adaptations, we need a way to properly estimate the value of different states. This could be done by learning from interaction data or through simulation with predictive models. In our work, we adopt existing models that are readily available for tasks such as pointing, typing, menu search, among others. Taking the example of menus, these models can be used to simulate how the user would search for an item and how an adaptation might affect this search process. These predictive models can then be used by a planning algorithm like Monte Carlo Tree Search to efficiently find adaptations. To speed up computations, we can also use pre-trained neural networks to obtain value estimates. To bring home the point, I'd like to show you a couple of examples of how our method adapts menus. In this simple case, the menu has five items that are adapted based on the user's changing interests. As you might notice, through sequential adaptations, the average selection time goes down drastically. As a second example, here we see the results after three rounds of adaptations in a more complicated 15-item menu. While reducing selection time is important for menus, other usability factors such as facilitating skill acquisition or increasing enjoyment could be addressed too. Our work showcases how human-computer interaction can benefit from advances in artificial intelligence. Through reinforcement learning, we can critically take into account how both the human and the computer might adapt over time. I'd like to conclude by saying that we are very excited to see how such methods are extended in the future to enhance our interactions in different domains. Thank you!

Traditionally, interaction on such ear-borne devices occurs by performing input either directly on the ear or in the immediate vicinity such as on the ear rim or the face of the user. In our paper, we take a completely different approach. We rely on the tensor tympani muscle, which is the second smallest muscle found in the human body. It is located in the middle ear and some people can contract it voluntarily to induce a dull rumbling sound, a phenomenon also known as ear rumbling. So we asked ourselves, can we use the rumbling ability for discrete interaction? Hence, we exploit the viability of tensor tympani contraction, developed a sensing device that can be embedded into a standard earbud form factor, implemented a recognition pipeline and conducted an application study using the ear rumble technique. We applied a lab validated online questionnaire and found out that 36 to 50 % of the population possess the rumbling ability. Out of those, over 80 % could perform ear rumbling in isolation to any other movement, and over 85 % could perform rumbling in quick succession. and also for prolonged times. So ear rumbling proved to be a great opportunity for interaction. As the eardrum displaces inward during contraction of the tensor tympani, a pressure change can be observed in the sealed ear canal of the user. Therefore, we built an in-ear pressure sensing device that also has audio capabilities. We initially proposed three simple gestures, a rumble which is a quick contraction of the tensor tympani, a double rumble by contracting the tensor tympani twice in quick succession and a hold rumble by holding the tensor tympani contracted for about one second. We also asked participants to perform multiple rumbles over the duration of five seconds to initially explore the potential for more complex interaction such as beat synchronization. From related work, we knew that changes in facial expression may also induce pressure changes in the ear canal, so we also collected a set of related activities. In total, we recruited 16 participants. Using the collected data, we built our recognition pipeline. We use a threshold-based approach for activity detection and then extract 35 features from each ear canal. We apply gradient-boosted decision trees for the final gesture prediction And achieve 95 % overall accuracy, we then applied the rumble technique. In two applications, a music player and for handling incoming phone calls, and we compared our technique. to traditional input based on buttons. Six users preferred using rumbling for interaction, but they wished for more immediate feedback as the current response time of our recognition pipeline is about 400 milliseconds. In our small sample, we could not identify any significant differences for the cognitive load. However, our results greatly highlighted the discrete nature of the interaction technique. In this video, you can see myself soldering an SMD part while skipping the song using ear rumble, which also underlines why users describe the technique as magical and almost telepathic. So, in conclusion, ear rumble proved to be a viable, discrete, and easy-to-use technique with ear balls that can be embedded into a standard earbud form factor. If you're interested in more details, such as ease of use, comfort, details on the recognition pipeline, or also reaction times, Please refer to our paper. Thank you. I don't know.
