reference: Hi, my name is Ningwen Chen, a student from Tohoku University, Japan. I will present the paper entitled Ping Pong Fly, an eccentric position control drone interface using mobile AR. Accurate controlling of the position and direction of drone is difficult because it requires high operational skills, which is not an easy task even for experienced users. Here are the reasons. First, insufficient depth spatial perception. Spatial perception means the ability to be aware of relationships with the environment around you and with yourself. In the left picture, the user feels the drone is above the target position. In fact, there is a 0.8m error. In real-world operations, sometimes it is dangerous because users even don't know where the drone is, let alone accurate manipulations. The second issue, insufficient spatial perception of direction, which will lead to a problem called mental irritation. In drone operations, generally you fly a drone like this. But sometimes you have to rotate the drone. If you forget to rotate the drone in your mind, operations like this would happen. We take the most famous interface joystick as example. You can see in the video to install the drone at 0.8 accurately, the user has to adjust many times, which is not so easy. To solve these issues, we searched some related works. We found that we can visualize the drone via AR, design the interface as eccentric interface, which is very intuitive, and use position control method to respond accurate and easy drone operation requirements. Inspired by related works, we found that a cast shadow like this seems to solve all these issues. If we control the drone through this cast shadow, it becomes eccentric interface, and we can control the drone's position directly, and also it can improve depth perception. Then we choose to use a mobile device to implement these concepts. Height slider bar is used to adjust height slides. Cast shadow is used to determine the ground position. And direction slider bar is used to rotate the drone. With such interface, we can pinpoint the drone's position. So we call this interface inPinpointFly. Based on the idea, we made a prototype and designed four interaction techniques. We found that they can cover most of the visual live site applications. First, dragFlight. Drag the cast shadow, and the flying drone will track the virtual drone in real time. Second, pointFly. Point the virtual drone to target position, and the drone will fly to there accurately. Third, trajectoryFly. First, draw a flying trajectory, and the drone will fly along that path. Last, waypointFly. First, designate some waypoints, and the drone will fly along the waypoint. During the flying process, User can also move in the direction slider Bar manually. Then we made studies to test the performance of Pinpointfly compared to joystick. This study focused on testing the positioning performance. User flies the drone from start point, and the timer begins. When the user feels the drone is above the target area, he says Ok, and the timer stops. The system will record the task completion time and distance error between drone and target points. The sideway task is almost the same to depth task. The only difference is the view perspective. Another study focused on videography performance. For those in circle task, participants are required to fly the drone while rotating it to take a video for the panda with different interface. You can see in the video to install the drone at 0.8 accurately, the user has to adjust many times, which is not so easy. To solve these issues, we searched some related works. We found that we can visualize the drone via AR, design the interface as eccentric interface, which is very intuitive, and use position control method to respond accurate and easy drone operation requirements. Inspired by related works, we found that a cast shadow like this seems to solve all these issues. If we control the drone through this cast shadow, it becomes eccentric interface, and we can control the drone's position directly, and also it can improve depth perception. Then we choose to use a mobile device to implement these concepts. Height slider bar is used to adjust height slides. Cast shadow is used to determine the ground position. And direction slider bar is used to rotate the drone. With such interface, we can pinpoint the drone's position. So we call this interface inPinpointFly. Based on the idea, we made a prototype and designed four interaction techniques. We found that they can cover most of the visual live site applications. First, dragFlight. Drag the cast shadow, and the flying drone will track the virtual drone in real time. Second, pointFly. Point the virtual drone to target position, and the drone will fly to there accurately. reference: This paper traces different conceptions of the body and Hci. It comes from a collaborative process by four design researchers. all with experience and training in a wide range of systematic and artistic body practices. We do two things in the paper. First, we present a broad updated survey of work dealing with the body in HCI. And second, we propose strong recommendations to support designers in designing for more than human bodies in complex times. Our paper situates conceptions of the body within the progression from first wave HCI to the emerging fourth wave. This is to provide designers with clarity around what we talk about when we talk about bodies in HCI. The intention is to support designers to gain greater clarity around the transforming design space of the body, Foster sensitivity to inclusive practices and contribute to an expanded corporeal ethics. This paper follows a distinct narrative arc from user to body, from body to bodies, and from bodies to more than human bodies. At each stage of the arc, we touch down in theories, methods and examples. We deploy lenses for clarity and we outline potentials and risks. The move from user to body is informed by phenomenology and driven by the awareness that everyone is embodied. The two lenses are the performative body. We look specifically to acting, improvisation and performance techniques to engage in user scenarios. The sensing body focus on sensory capabilities as a way for designers to use their body to inform the design process. Here we move from body to bodies, A pluralizing move, the datafied bodies lens understands bodies as a range of data objects, each with its own outputs and signals. Some see risks, others see potentials in surveillance, commercialization, optimization of human abilities and crisis management. The intersectionality lens is a way of understanding and analyzing complexity in the world, people and human experience, shaped by mutually intersecting factors of race, class, gender, sexual orientation and more. The move from bodies to more than human bodies is emerging in HCI. Diffraction replaces lenses for this area, accounting for how differences, contingencies and entanglements combine and recombine in the making of bodies. More than human perspectives emphasize the way bodies exist in dynamic configurations with things, spaces, organic and inorganic materials and beings. This points to a relational ontology. We no longer designing for or with. The ontological stakes are higher. We are designing bodies. We end by proposing five recommendations for designers as we move forward. 1. Attend to the embodied experience of the user. Consider users as complex beings with multi-sensory abilities. 2. The importance of clarity to concepts of the body in HCI. Be outspoken about the assumptions of bodies present in any design project. 3. Cultivate an intersectional sensibility. To avoid erasing or silencing some groups and to promote greater diversity. 4. Engage with theorists and practitioners from other fields. Collaborate with them, not just their theories. 5. Adopt a more than human approach to the body in HCI. Recognize that we are entangled with a wide range of beings. As designers speculate better futures, resonating with the ethics of more than human worlds, we can embrace both the richness and the limitations of bodies. This way we can continue to expand the diverse, entangled and interdisciplinary field of design to include an ontological expansion of bodies as we are and bodies as we can be.

reference: Hi, my name is Narges Portafarian. I'm a doctoral researcher at Saarland University, and together with my colleagues, we wanted to find a way to create epidermal interfaces directly on the body. So, we present BodyStylus, the first computer-assisted approach for on-body design and fabrication of epidermal interfaces. Current approaches for creating epidermal interfaces typically have three different steps, designing the interface on a computer, fabricating the design, and then applying it to the body. But this is fundamentally different from how traditional body arts and crafts are created. As you can see, traditional on-body arts and crafts, like henna or tattoos, are adjusted to the body as they are applied. We wish to do the same with electrical circuits and present an approach that considers both the functionality and aesthetics of the design. For our BodyStylus system, we took inspiration from the traditional handheld form factors of henna and tattoo arts. Our stylus consists of a new smart pen, which helps to track the position of the pen on the body. To make interactive traces, we filled the cartridge with sinter-free gold ink. It means it doesn't require curing after fabrication. In addition, we also added a micro servo motor, which allows automatic retraction. The overall setup I've just shown you allows ink on the body and simultaneously tracks the pen's location. However, it is not sufficient. Designing aesthetic epidermal interfaces on the filli is demanding. The user should consider the functionality of the created electrical circuits and the desired visual appearance. To support users in this task, we implemented guidance and constraints functions. Guidance provides the designer with options. We use a projector that projects visual cues on the skin. Constraints prevent mistakes through our computer-controlled handheld tool that switches between inking and non-inking mode. The concept of constraints has been presented in prior work in HCI, for instance by Zoran et al. Together, guidance and constraints provide a two-dimensional space for interacting with BodyStylus. As I mentioned, guidance assists the user to make a circuit, for instance by highlighting terminals to connect to, or helps to draw aesthetic elements. BodyStylus provides different levels of guidance for inking, minimal guidance, partial guidance, and full-detail guidance. The user selects a suitable level based on their expertise. As I explained, the inking tip of the stylus retracts whenever the user intends to violate the logic or aesthetic constraints. Here, for example, the user is going to create a short circuit, but the constraints prevent it. Constraints also have different levels. Without constraints, The user draws freely when the user selects a strong constraints. the system prevents any inking that was not planned. To summarize, the user can flexibly decide to benefit from more or less guidance or constraints. To evaluate BodyStylus, we invited two groups of engineers and makeup artists to use the setup. Both groups were able to adapt to the workflow. An observation we received was that, while artists found guidance more helpful, engineers preferred to use constraints more often. For more details, we invite you to have a look at our paper. BodyStylus enables fabrication on various body locations at different scales using various input and output modalities. In summary, I presented BodyStylus, a novel interactive approach that allows us to design and craft epidermal devices directly on the body. We use a handheld fabrication tool and self-sintering conductive ink. We leverage in-situ projected guidance and physical constraints to facilitate the creation of functional anesthetic epidermal devices. Thanks for listening! Looking forward to the discussion!

reference: Hello everyone, I'm Yueqin from Tsinghua University. Today I'm glad to introduce our work, ProxyMIC, convenient voice activation via close-to-mic speech detected by a single microphone. As we all know, voice interaction is convenient, efficient, and intuitive. But voice input still faces some challenges. First, the voice wake-up process can be lengthy. Second, such interaction can be tedious and annoying, especially doing multiple rounds of voice input. Third, users risk exposing their privacy, as their voices may be overheard or eavesdropped by a third party. Therefore, we propose ProxyMIC, a close-to-mic speech sensing technique for handheld and wearable devices. With ProxyMIC, users can keep the device close to the mouth and speak directly to the device without wake-up phrases or button presses. In addition, users can also whisper, directly interrupt, and realize multiple rounds of dialogue. In recent years, several works have been done to improve the voice activation process. They use a variety of sensors and device-related gestures to shorten the wake-up time for specific devices. The difference is that we only use one microphone. To implement a close-to-mic speech detector, we first conduct a pilot study to find what feature can be used. We found the most significant feature is pop noise caused by air being blown onto the microphone while speaking. This is an example. First, in 1st, in the time domain, the impact of the airflow on the microphone brings high amplitude. so the amplitude of close-to-mic speech with pop noise is usually higher than the background noise. Second, in the frequency domain, the pop noise area containing low frequencies is visible. So we adopt a two-stage approach to detect close-to-mic speech in time domain and frequency domain respectively. The first stage detector is based on the adaptive amplitude threshold with minimal calculation required. If the amplitude of audio signal exceeds the dynamic threshold, we will extract a one-second audio clip and hand this real signal input over a tiny spectrogram-based convolutional neural network for refined detection. We use smartphone to collect three audio datasets. They are voice commands dataset, background noise dataset, and seven days daily records. We use recall rate and false accept per week per user as matrix to evaluate our model. The result shows that the most false accept occurs when a person speaks from a distance and superimposes high-energy noise similar to pop noise. Recall rate is reduced in noise environment such as subway. In study 2, We conduct four analyses to understand the performance and the boundaries of Proxymac 1st, in order to understand what Cnn has learned. we calculated the silencing map and occlusion sensitivity map of voice input. We found that our CNN model mainly responds to pop noise in the spectrogram. Second, we tested different form factors. The result shows that watches and phones have similar performance due to the similar structures. For headphones and recording pens, there was less obvious pop noise due to their outer shells and the performance has been reduced. We also used a state-of-the-art ASR system to perform speech-to-text and calculate the word error rate of the voice command dataset. The result shows pop noise didn't significantly reduce the accuracy of speech recognition. For the privacy part, we invited six users, asked them to talk to ProxyMAC and make sure the ASR recognition is correct. When one person speaks, others sit on chairs at different distance, even stroke carefully, and write down what they hear. We found that whispering can efficiently protect privacy. Finally, we compared ProxyMAC to other traditional activation methods. Result shows that our method was significantly faster than the traditional methods, and the watches is faster than phones and headphones. For subjective feedback, our method has advantages in terms of speed and multi-rounded interaction. In summary, we present ProxyMAC, a novel sensing technique that uses pop noise and close-to-mic feature to perform efficient, user-friendly, and practical voice input by a single microphone. With this, I would like to end my talk. Thank you for your attention, happy to answer any questions.

reference: Hello, welcome to my talk. My name is Andrew. This is joint work with Nina, Alisa, Elena and Finale. So this talk is not just about the interpretability of machine learning models, but also how we evaluate the interpretability of machine learning models. We're introducing an interpretability evaluation method. That means we also need to think about how we evaluate those evaluations, which gets a little crazy, but bear with me. So the starting point of the story is that we train a machine learning model. Let's call it F using some machine learning method. We then want to explain that model to some user or group of users, and of course to do that we need to use some kind of interpretability method or visualization. And maybe we don't just have one model, but multiple, and we want to determine which is the most interpretable to this group of users. To do that, we employ some interpretability evaluation metric. It gives us a quantitative score for each model, or perhaps a ranking. And there are a number of ways people try to do this in practice. Some involve seeing how well the user can predict the predictions of the model. Others involve evaluating the coherency of the user's mental model of the model in some other way, or asking them to perform a downstream task that requires some meaningful form of model understanding. However, when we're doing research on interpretability evaluation, we need some way of evaluating whether the evaluation itself is measuring something meaningful. So although the main contribution of our paper is an interpretability evaluation method, we're also going to innovate a bit on how to evaluate evaluations. Another issue here is that most prior ML interpretability research focuses on classifiers, regressors, or more generally what are called discriminative models. Discriminative models are characterized by having relatively high complicated high dimensional inputs, like images, time series, text, or tabular data with lots of features, and relatively simple outputs, often just a single probability. There has been a ton of work on methods for learning interpretable discriminative models, or interpreting existing discriminative models, and also a moderate amount of work on how to best evaluate their interpretability. However, there's been a lot less for generative modeling, which is kind of the other main branch of machine learning. Examples include autoencoders, top models, or GANs. There's been relatively little research on how to interpret generative models, and almost none on how to evaluate their interpretability. One exception though is the literature on disentanglement, which provides a number of quantitative metrics for evaluating how well learned generative models match the ground truth model that generated the data, which is assumed to be interpretable. However, these kinds of metrics only work for synthetic data sets, and they haven't received much study in an HCI context. Our primary contribution is a novel method for both visualizing and evaluating the interpretability of generative models, which we call interactive reconstruction. In interactive reconstruction, we ask users to manipulate the underlying raw dimensions of generative models to reconstruct target instances to some degree of precision. We then measure whether and how efficiently they learned to perform this task over multiple trials. We designed this task to overcome potential pitfalls identified by interpretability researchers and more foundational work in HCI theory. And as promised, we attempt to rigorously evaluate our evaluation metric in several ways. The first way we evaluate our metric is by constructing data sets and models with ground truth. That is, we can justifiably assume a priori that certain models are more interpretable than others. We then test how well our method and baseline methods recover these ground truth rankings. Although I'll refer to the paper for more details, we find that we can recover this ground truth ordering from a number of different metrics associated with this interactive reconstruction task, such as the average rate of completion for each trial within a time period or the area under the curve of their error over time. The same ends up not being true for baselines, for reasons we explore in much more depth in the paper and back up the qualitative data. When we're dealing with real-world data where there is no ground truth, we evaluate our metric in a second way by comparing quantitative data from experiments on Amazon Mechanical Turk with qualitative evaluations of the same model and think-aloud studies of different groups of users. In general, we find really close agreement in basically all respects, including multiple subjective assessment tools, the consistency of the labels that users assign to model dimensions, and their raw qualitative feedback. Overall, we really take pains to validate that our metric is actually measuring model understanding, or at least something intimately correlated with it, and that this continues to hold for a variety of models trained with a variety of methods on a variety of data sets with a variety of characteristics. So overall, this lets us provide the first major comparison of interpretable representation learning methods on non-synthetic data. It also lets us evaluate how synthetic disentanglement metrics relate to human factors. If you're interested in learning more about this paper or our group, you can find more information at the links below. Thanks for listening and I'll be happy to take questions.

Some involve seeing how well the user can predict the predictions of the model. Others involve evaluating the coherency of the user's mental model of the model in some other way, or asking them to perform a downstream task that requires some meaningful form of model understanding. However, when we're doing research on interpretability evaluation, we need some way of evaluating whether the evaluation itself is measuring something meaningful. So although the main contribution of our paper is an interpretability evaluation method, we're also going to innovate a bit on how to evaluate evaluations. Another issue here is that most prior ML interpretability research focuses on classifiers, regressors, or more generally what are called discriminative models. There has been a ton of work on methods for learning interpretable discriminative models, or interpreting existing discriminative models, and also a moderate amount of work on how to best evaluate their interpretability. However, there's been a lot less for generative modeling, which is kind of the other main branch of machine learning. Examples include autoencoders, top models, or GANs. Based on phase 1, we evaluated in phase 2 the guiding cues and safety aspects of drone copter to ensure a reliable and smooth user experience during the user study. We selected and customized the chosen drone and implemented a framework for data collection for later analysis. Finally we performed a comparative user study in phase 3 to evaluate the performance and the user experience when guide copter is compared to a state-of-the-art audio guiding system. Due to the limited amount of time, we focus on results of phase 2 and phase 3 in the presentation of guide copter. To compare state-of-the-art audio cues as shown on the left side to the haptic forces of guide copter as shown on the right side, we projected the audio cues to directed forces applied via the drone to the pointing finger of the user. We see the advantage by design of guide copter to directly project guiding forces to the user's hand compared to an audio-based interface where the user has to translate the audio cues to motoric movements of the hand. reference: Hi, my name is Sarah Heitlinger, and I'm presenting on behalf of my co-authors, Lara Houston, Alex Taylor, and Ruth Catlow, and this paper is called Algorithmic Food Justice, co-designing more-than-human blockchain futures for the food commons. The global industrial food system encloses and extracts value from our planet's resources, concentrating benefits in the hands of a few major players. In the process, industrial agriculture is causing mass species loss, degradation of soils, and the disempowerment of small-scale farmers, ultimately threatening food security for all life on earth. This paper is concerned with the values that are driving these unsustainable social and environmental inequalities, and how digital technologies might intensify them, as well as how they might allow for fairer and more sustainable food systems. We describe a project that takes an algorithmic approach to creating a sustainable food justice system, and discuss our process of co-designing blockchain futures with urban agricultural communities in London, as a way to critically engage with alternative value systems that draw on the commons and more-than-human perspectives, which recognize the interdependencies between humans and non-human others within the food chain. It considers in particular how blockchain, the technology underpinning cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin, might offer ways to disrupt the prevailing paradigms and open up possibilities for more sustainable systems of value and governance in the context of food. So the project asked, how can we develop a more-than-human value system in order to redistribute value more equally between humans and non-human others? How might we develop new ways to sustain the food commons in order to manage resources more equitably? And how can we ensure that our algorithmic approach is inclusive in order to support participation and access for diverse marginalized citizens? We ran three workshops with participants that included community growers, organizers, artists, and technologists, where we critically experimented with algorithmic possibilities for new value systems that embed the interests of non-humans such as seeds, soil, and water in order to create more sustainable, inclusive, and just food futures in the city. In the first workshop, Mapping the Future Farm, we mapped the multi-species stakeholders and resource flows in the city farm now and 10 years in the future from the growers' expert knowledge. In workshop two, Now London is a City Farm, We used a gameplay technique called a lap, a live action role play. to explore what London would be like if all available spaces were turned over to urban farming. We used fictional scenarios to explore multi-species relationships, new economies, and radical decision-making processes for sustaining a city-wide food commons. In workshop three, we prototyped new algorithmic systems for a future food commons. We explored how blockchain affordances could help distribute resources more fairly between multi-species members, recognize the contributions and needs of diverse members, address some of the Address some of the injustices in the current food food systems and create a more balanced and fair food system. Participants worked in groups to create new blockchain-based organizations, or DAOs, and used paper-based syntax cards to determine the governance rules or smart contracts of those organizations and their multi-species members. These organizations allowed for new types of value exchange and governance. In the paper, we discuss how the speculative workshop methods created a space in which human exceptionalism and privilege within food systems were challenged, allowing alternative values and perspectives to surface. In the imaginaries produced in the workshops, the blockchain block blockchain provides the mechanisms to facilitate ecological repair and regeneration. by incentivizing the expansion and increasing the abundance of mutually beneficial relations. We also discuss how within the workshops food was reconfigured from a commodity to be exchanged for maximum profit to a more-than-human commons, in which different types of contributions and labors that are invisible within the dominant industrial food complex might be surfaced, acknowledged, and rewarded within a community. Thank you.

reference: Hello, I'm delighted to share with you our most recent research, which engages people with the sounds of the wild and features this guy, an eastern bristlebird. Eastern bristlebirds are rare and they're hard to see, and the population where I live in Queensland, Australia, lives among these tall tussocks grasses, which makes them really hard to find. We can find them, however, if we know how to listen for them. I spent two years learning calls using recordings of captive birds first, so you can imagine how excited I was when I first heard their calls in the wild. That's the picture you see here. And I'd like to introduce you to one of those calls. Isn't it beautiful? Music to my ears. Well, audio recordings are pretty easy to gather, as long as you can get to that rugged habitat. But making sense of the audio after you have it is the real challenge. We don't have a lot of knowledge about the calls of bristlebirds, which makes it extra difficult. I'd like to introduce you to another sound. Now when we get audio recordings, the fantastic benefit is that we have visualizations of sound as well. Have a look at the shape in that what we call a spectrogram and see if you can recognize when I play it again what that call sounds like and looks like. So we informed the design of the Bristle Whistle Challenge by our prior work in the lab. We designed and play tested a prototype as part of this paper. It includes mixed activities, including gameful, meaning structured and goal oriented tasks, and playful, meaning free form and exploratory activities. This was intended to inform design of nature engagement and conservation focused citizen science. One of the features of the Bristle Whistle Challenge was that participants were receiving guidance by a conversational agent. As you see here highlighted, that was Bob the Bristle Bird. He gave various comments throughout the entire challenge to assist people, and this provided sense making and emotional support. The gamefully matching of media was actually quite engaging for people when they were looking at spectrograms and audio or matching the different photographs to specific calls of particular species. It helped to hone in attention on the calls of the birds. The playfully exploring media included looking at photographs and spectrograms and listening to the calls as well, but without any particular tasks. It also included imagining what people might see as creative shapes in the spectrograms of calls. Do you see that flower shape in there like I do? Well, these types of activities piqued interest and elicited creativity in our participants. Then we explored how they might apply what they learned to quest for calls that they were meant to identify in unfamiliar spectrograms. It actually proved to be very useful, providing them all that variety of context ahead of time for identifying particular birds. And they enjoyed the experiences. It also revealed sensory and animal preference differences, which was quite interesting. And we recommended diverse design directions because, really, this is the tip of the iceberg. We need a lot more work to be done for creative and contextual audio encounters to build awareness of nature's wonders and saving species. We invite you to read the paper, view the challenge, and be sure and sing out for more info. Get involved in helping us save species by designing in ways that resonate with diverse audiences so that everyone can get involved. And with that, thank you very much for listening.

reference: Hello, I'm Taika Agustaitis, and I'm presenting on our paper, Online Transgender Health Information Seeking, Facilitators, Barriers, and Future Directions. Transgender or trans communities disproportionately experience barriers to accessing health care, which contribute to health disparities. There's also not enough information surrounding trans health needs due to many factors, including trans people's erasure in data and providers' lack of training. Outside of a health context, it has been shown that trans users engage with online platforms in novel ways to express their identities. Moreover, some health topics came up in previous qualitative work, but there weren't in-depth investigations. The purpose of this research was to explore the experiences of trans people accessing health information online, including how they use online platforms as tools to accomplish health information seeking tasks. We hosted asynchronous online focus groups to address our research questions. Participants were diverse across a number of domains, including age, gender, race, ethnicity, ability, and location of residence. The results reviewed several areas where people have information, Aspects of online help of online platforms that are facilitators and barriers to online health, information, seeking and presenting possible future directions. such as important features and stakeholders to integrate in planning and sustaining online platforms. And for time today, I will just review one facilitator and one barrier to online trans health information seeking. Some aspects of social media groups facilitated trans health information seeking, such as privacy settings. Groups having the ability to vet people via a questioning system make for the safest spaces you can find the most first-hand experience from other trans and gender nonconforming people. Privacy features were important not only to moderate the members who joined social media groups, but also helped participants manage how their identity is visible to others across the platform. Participants described being negatively impacted by platform-initiated censorship. For example, a topic that came up frequently was Tumblr's ban of adult content. Trans health educational content, as participant 21 mentions, was affected. Tumblr lost a lot of its credibility from heavy moderating and non-friendly behavior towards trans educational posts. Additionally, policies such as Facebook real name policy censored identity expression, inhibiting participation in online trans health communities. Participant 22 described, I used to have a 2nd Facebook account under an alternate name that I used to access transgender health groups. But Facebook deactivated it for suspecting me of having that 2nd account that wasn't under my birth name. Despite my pleas, they didn't give it back. The fact that I can only have one account under my birth name limits the amount of groups I am able to join. And also ensures I'm dead named within the trans groups that I'm in. Our research to our knowledge uniquely contributes an understanding of facilitators and barriers to online trans health information seeking. Trans users exemplify resilience in curating spaces for disseminating trans health information while navigating barriers. It is not known whether improving current systems, creating a new platform, or a hybrid is best, but our results and design implications in the paper provide potential future directions for any of these. Regardless of platform, policies that exclude or negatively impact trans people will be harmful to trans health and well-being. Therefore, small changes to platforms, such as the elimination of policies that negatively impact trans people, may contribute to better health outcomes. Here are our key takeaways that, if seriously considered in existing or new platforms designs, will improve online trans health information seeking processes. Please see our paper if you're interested in learning more. And also thank you to M-Cubed at the University of Michigan for funding this research.

reference: Hello, my name is Bronwyn Cumbo. I'm a postdoctoral research fellow at Monash University and I'll be presenting on some research our team carried out last year exploring the opportunities for online learning platforms to support the emergency homeschool context. Last year, COVID-19 swept across the globe and caused large-scale school closures and the transition to online modes of schooling from home. This new type of schooling was unprecedented, highly disruptive and likely to have long-term impacts on how we understand and practice schooling and the role of online platforms within that. The aim of our study was to better understand this new emergency homeschool context with a specific focus on families and how they have responded and adapted to the sudden imposition of school in their home. Research was carried out in Melbourne, Australia during the first round of state-sanctioned school closures that came about in April 2020. We recruited nine young families to the study, so nine parents and 11 children aged 5 to 10 years of age. These were all middle-class families and lived in a range of locations around Melbourne. We carried three research activities with the children. Firstly, an introductory online interview with parents and then parents and their child. Secondly, a 10-day photojournaling activity where children were invited to take a photograph each day of a part of the homeschool that was meaningful to them. And then a follow-up interview with parents and children using these photos as a prompt for discussion. We then transcribed and analysed this data, focusing on the roles and relations between people and place that emerged in the new context, and used these insights to generate five recommendations for designing and using online platforms specifically for this emergency homeschool context. There were four main findings that we report on in the paper, and I'm going to focus on the findings from the second theme, which is the increase in the roles and responsibilities of parents in the homeschool. I encourage you to read the paper to learn about our other findings. The introduction of the school to the home greatly increased parent labour in relation to their child's schooling. So we identified four new roles for parents. They were research providers, tech support, mediators and motivators of learning, and school administrators. The role of mediator and motivator was the most time-consuming role for these parents, particularly those with young children, as they had to be there to translate and interpret content shared by teachers and continuously encourage their child to do the work. Interestingly, many parents, particularly mothers, felt ill-equipped to support their child in their new role. So they expressed three main concerns. Firstly, they didn't know how to gauge their child's learning level, so what they were supposed to know and what was new. Secondly, they didn't feel that they had skills to teach. They were unsure as to when to encourage or reinforce learning or what was expected by teachers, as articulated by one mother who said, when do I applaud? When do I push? When the teachers tell us what's expected, what is actually expected, and what's just setting an end goal for children instead of a core expectation. Finally, many parents did not feel supported by the school, as teacher communications were directed at students, not parents, and contacting teachers was often a challenge. Despite these difficulties, parents were innovative and pragmatic in their approach to homeschooling. For example, some adopted a very flexible approach, adapting the subjects and timetables each day, depending on their child's mood, their time availability, and also what they considered to be important subjects. Other parents drew on their own experience of school to inform how they supported their children to learn. For example, some parents found their children were completing tasks too quickly, as teachers were not differentiating activities as they would in the classroom, so they would fill in the gaps, writing maths problems, or incorporating new forms of learning into recreational activities, so biology in the park or maths while cooking. Finally, many parents sought advice and emotional support from parent and teacher networks online. So what can we take from these findings to design platforms that better support parents in their emergency homeschool context? Firstly, there's an opportunity to design platforms that support parents better scaffold their child's learning across a diversity of subjects. We can also think about supporting open channels of communication between teachers and parents, challenging this black box mentality of schooling whilst also not trying to put too much extra work on teachers. Thirdly, we can think about leveraging place-based resources and social networks so parents can seek support beyond the school during these times. So what I've presented here is a slice of what was discussed in the paper. I encourage you to please read the paper if you're interested in this topic and contact me if you have any questions beyond the Q&A discussion. Thank you.

reference: We present Fits and Starts, a study on the enterprise use of AutoML and the role of humans in the loop. In recent years, new technology has emerged to automate various aspects of data science work. These so-called AutoML technologies were initially used to automate the model creation process, but in recent years, their reach has expanded to other aspects of data science work. While the goal of AutoML technology is largely to reduce the role of humans in data science processes, full automation is not yet possible. What is more realistic are varying degrees of automation that trade off between human labor and machine computation across various stages of the data science pipeline. In our research, we wanted to understand what the role of humans in the loop were within these automated data science processes. We were especially interested in understanding how data visualization was used. To answer this question, we carried out a series of interviews with industry experts. Our semi-structured interview process prompted participants with questions about their use of AutoML technology. When it was possible, these interview sessions were recorded and transcribed. When recording was not possible, study administrators took notes that were used in the data analysis. We analyzed the transcripts as well as our interview notes using a previously described framework for data science work. We recruited 29 industry experts to participate in our study. Participants in our study fell into two categories, analysts that were engaged in the day-to-day aspects of data science work and managers that oversaw data science teams. The majority of our study participants were analysts. These 29 individuals that we recruited collectively represent a variety of industrial sectors, from travel to government, software and manufacturing, among others. Participants used AutoML technology to varying degrees. Some were knowledgeable, meaning that they knew about it but were not planning on using it in their work. Others were experimenting, meaning that they were creating proof of concepts to understand how AutoML technology could help their data science work. And finally, others were actively using AutoML technology in their work. The majority of our study participants were either experimenting or actively using AutoML. Here's an overview of what we found, including the role of humans in the loop and especially data visualization. Overall, we found three primary use cases for AutoML technology. The first was to automate routine tasks. The second was to rapidly explore a potential data science solution. And the third was to democratize the data science process by making it available to those individuals that do not have data science, computer science, or statistical training. In our paper, we add more context around these scenarios. In particular, what bottlenecks are. In automating routine tasks, one of the limitations of AutoML technology is that data preparation is still very time-consuming and it can be challenging to correct and repair a model that you've deployed into production. We use participant quotes to emphasize these findings. And we similarly found bottlenecks and opportunities for rapid exploration, as well as using Automl to democratize data science work. We synthesize our work as a framework of automation across various aspects of data science work and according to different data science roles. What we found was that there was still a lot of human labor required to get AutoML technology to work, and the parts of automation that it was good at were only a small part of the data science process. We were also concerned to discover that data visualization is frequently abandoned in automated data science work. This was because it was just too difficult to create a data visualization or because data visualization tools did not integrate well with these automated processes. Here are some of the key takeaways from our work. First, we should think much more about augmenting data science rather than trying to automate it. And this is because AutoML is largely a misnomer. There's still a lot of human labor required to get it to work. Finally, for data visualization researchers, we need to think more about how we integrate our tools into data science environments. Otherwise, we're just going to be ignored. You can find more in our paper, which is available at this web link.

reference: Hi, my name is Sam Robertson, and today I'm presenting the paper Modeling Assumptions Clash with the Real World, Transparency, Equity, and Community Challenges for Student Assignment Algorithms, Which I wrote with co authors Tanya Nguyen and Niloufar Salehi, Many public school districts use matching algorithms to assign students to schools. These algorithms have promising theoretical properties, but districts have encountered challenges in practice. In this study, we explore why San Francisco Unified School District's algorithm Has not supported their goals of transparency, equity and community. We do this by comparing theoretical modeling assumptions to families, goals and constraints in the real world. In this analysis, we took a value-sensitive approach and combined policy analysis, 13 interviews with parents, and quantitative analysis of kindergarten application data. In this talk, I will start with a very quick overview of how these systems work. Then, I will summarize the challenges we found with respect to two of the district's goals, transparency and equity. I will do this by briefly explaining the theoretical properties that make the algorithms seem like a promising solution, and then contrast these to what happened in the real world. You can check out our paper to read more about the district's other goals, promoting quality schools And a sense of community, I will end the talk by outlining the implications of our work for the design of student assignment assignment algorithms and high stakes algorithmic systems more broadly. In districts with school choice programs, students have to apply to the schools that they are interested in. Usually demand for schools is unevenly distributed and. and not every student can attend their first choice school because of capacity constraints. Student assignment algorithms give school districts an efficient way of determining how to assign students to schools. These algorithms ask families to submit a ranked list of schools they would like to attend. Schools can also define priority categories for certain students, for example, siblings of current students. Researchers in the field of mechanism design have developed algorithms that find a good matching between students and schools, accounting for both sides preferences. But what is a good matching? In the next part of the talk, I will walk through some of the properties of these algorithms that make them an attractive solution to the student assignment problem, and how these properties have been challenged by real-world conditions. The district's first goal was to ensure that their assignment system was transparent and easy to use. Matching algorithms are often considered simple and transparent because they follow a clearly defined and explicit procedure. Plus, they are provably strategy-proof, meaning parents do not benefit from manipulating their preferences to try to improve their outcome. However, parents still found the system difficult to understand, and some believed that parents with privilege could gain the system to their advantage. Further, the main information that they needed was information about the schools, not information about the algorithm, and they found it difficult to find and navigate relevant school information. The second key goal for the school district was to promote racially and socioeconomically integrated schools, and to promote equitable access to high-quality education. The district hoped that the system would promote diversity and equity because it allowed all students to apply to any school in the district. Further, the district specified that the algorithm gives students living in areas of the city with underperforming schools priority access to their schools of choice. However, less than a decade after the system was introduced, diversity in schools had actually decreased and some schools were less diverse than the neighborhoods they were in. We found that part of the reason for this is that preferences remained segregated across the city, for example, because of transportation costs to schools further from home. The algorithm is optimized to satisfy preferences, so it's unable to create diverse assignments if the applicant pool at each school is not diverse. Based on our findings, we present recommendations for student assignment algorithms, which can be also relevant to other high-stakes algorithmic systems. E.g. one problem in San Francisco is that the algorithm is optimized to satisfy students preferences. but this objective doesn't align with distributive goals like classroom diversity. This suggests that there is a need to realign algorithmic objectives with community goals in mind. Another problem is that families have to do a lot of work to figure out how to express their needs and goals in the form of a ranked list of schools. One path forward could be to reconsider how families express their preferences to the district. This opens opportunities not only to make the process easier for families, but for the district to reduce the emphasis on individual outcomes and encourage community members to think about distributive outcomes like integration. If you'd like to learn more about this work, we hope you'll read the paper or come to one of our Q&A sessions. Thank you.

reference: The discourse around makerspaces is often one of great potential. Anyone can make anything. Included in this vision of making for all are older adults. Researchers are creating making technologies customized for older adults, and one study created a makerspace for older adults in a longer-term care facility. In this project, we ask, how do older adults themselves make sense of these movements? How would they drive the making initiatives that involve them? Our study took place at Nestern, a continuing care community in the United States with almost 200 residents in independent living. The business center, which housed computers and a printer, transformed into the makerspace over the course of this project. Ora, a resident of Nestern, was an initiator and driver of this project. Ora formed a committee, the Makerspace Planning Committee and invited invited residents to serve on it. This included individuals with technical. as well as arts and crafts expertise. Tara, a staff member, played a central role in the committee. The committee met monthly and was involved in decision-making around all the key aspects of the makerspace, from what equipment to purchase to the name. We interacted with 17 residents and one staff member over the course of this study. Of the participants, seven were members of the Makerspace Committee. We were invited to observe early in the process. A room had been identified, the committee had been formed, but many of the major decisions, such as which machines to buy or what to call the makerspace, had not yet been made. Our involvement over approximately eight months included observing committee meetings, interviewing residents, and conducting one focus group. Our analysis presents ways that residents made sense of and formed opinions about the makerspace during its formation. The first thing from our analysis concerns the openness of the makerspace. Makerspace discourse is broad. Anyone can make anything. And committee members tried to maintain this openness as they interacted with residents to shape the direction of the makerspace so that it could be tailored around community interests. But there was a distinct sense of uncertainty among many residents that may have resulted from this intention to keep it broad. When asked what kinds of activities they would want to do in a makerspace, one resident said, I can't think of a thing. When we asked another about the kinds of classes that they might want to take, they said, that's why I'm not that keen on it, because I don't know enough to imagine something. Residents we spoke to envisioned benefits for themselves from the makerspace, but were really interested in its potential in combating what they perceived as anti-technology sentiment they saw at Lestern, such as how residents rolled their eyes if someone pulled out a cell phone at dinner. researchers are creating making technologies,
customized for older adults,
and one study created a makerspace for older dogs in a long-term care facility.
In this project, we ask how do older adults themselves make sense of these movements?
How would they drive the making initiatives that involve them?
Our study took place at Nuster, a continuing care community in the United States with almost
200 residents in independent living, the Business Center which housed computers and a printer

around all the key aspects of the makerspace, from what equipment to purchase to the name.
We interacted with 17 residents and one staff member over the course of this study.
Out of the participants, seven were members of the makerspace committee.
We were invited to observe early in the process. A room had been identified, the committee had been
formed, but many of the major decisions such as what machines to buy or what to call the
makerspace had not yet been made. Our involvement over approximately eight months included observing
committee meetings, interviewing residents and conducting one focus group. Our analysis presents
ways that residents meet sense of and formed opinions about the makerspace during its formation.
The first thing from our analysis concerns the openness of the makerspace.
Makerspace discourse is broad, anyone can make anything, and committee members tried to maintain

That's why I'm not that keen on it, because I don't know enough to imagine something.

there are different entry points
or on-ramps to makerspace.

sewing machines and basic technology courses.

reference: Hi everyone, I'm Shirley Chen. I'm going to present an adaptive model of gaze-based selection. Gaze-based selection has been studied in HCI since the 1990s. While many significant advances have been made, we believe that further progress could be made with a cognitive model of eye movement and vision. In this paper, we proposed a reinforcement learning model that learns the gaze-based selection task from experience of the environment. In the model, the sequence of saccades and fixations is governed by an attempt to optimize a utility function, such as selection time, accuracy, or a trade-off between these two. Importantly, the optimization is constrained by the model of both motor system and vision system. In a gaze-based selection task, the user is often asked to move their gaze into a target region as quickly as possible. From a starting point, due to our low-acuity peripheral vision, a noisy estimate of the target position is made, as shown in location 2. Then, a eye movement is aimed towards location 2. However, due to the noise in our ocular motor system, the eye ended up at location 3. The process repeats until it reaches the target. In this case, it takes two saccades to reach the target. Similarly, in the model, the agent chooses an action as a saccade based on its current belief of target position. Given the action taken and the The task environment, a noisy observation is obtained. and used to update agent's belief of the target position. Meanwhile, the reward function is used to update agent's policy. A reinforcement learning algorithm is used to learn the optimal policy so that the sequence of saccades is governed by an attempt to maximize the reward function. Now let's look at some results. The selection time in a gaze-based selection task is usually composed of two parts, eye movement time and dwell time. Eye movement times are the time required to find and reach the target. This is sensitive to the size of the target. Specifically, the eye movement time decreases with bigger target sizes, as that the number of saccade required decreases. The second part is dwell time. In the experiment, a continuous 800 ms within target region is required to commit the target selection. However, it is known that even during fixation, human eyes do not remain perfectly still. The eyes jitter in a small area. For example, the data show that when fixating on a target region of 1.2°, this jitter causes the gaze to leave and re-enter the target area several times, Resulting in an actual target dwell time of a thousand and 75 milliseconds. ms, that is 275 ms longer than the dwell criteria of 800 ms. How does our model do? The model was only fitted to data of the smallest target size, but as you can see, there is an exceptional correspondence between the model prediction and the data. The model predictions of eye movement time, and final selection time, decrease the same rate as human data, our. Our model also predicts a number of other empirical findings in the literature, such as the effect of index of difficulty on the number of saccades. To conclude, we have reported a gaze-based selection model that adapts eye movement strategies to target size, target distances, as well as to noise in the motor and vision system. The model predicts a number of key empirical findings in the literature and provides a useful basis for guiding future research. Further work should explore using the model in design optimization. Thank you.

reference: What happens after death? Using a design workbook to understand user expectations for preparing their data. This paper was written by Janet Chen, that's me, and my co-authors Francesco Vitale and Joanna McRenere at the University of British Columbia. Consider the case of a woman who had to hack into her late mother's iPhone. Although her mother had shared the phone passcode only a month prior to the car accident, the passcode no longer worked. The daughter was locked out with no access. The device held more than the details required for planning a funeral and resolving financial accounts. It represented her mother's memories through digital photos, conversations, and notes. Like her mother, our devices are home to our most personal data, representing our memories and experiences. And our data is spread across devices such as phones, tablets, and laptops, which we accumulate over our lifetime. Nowadays with cloud storage platforms like these, we can store a lifetime of memories with little to no cost. But very few people prepare their data for eventual death. After all, it's hard. Dealing with a lifetime of data may be overwhelming, and current tools and stopgap measures like writing a list of passwords on a piece of paper may not be enough. To explore promising design directions for designing personalized and respectful death preparation tools for data, we ask the following research question. How can the HCI community support preparation of data in anticipation of death? We focus on three design directions. Nudging. How can we nudge users to begin the preparation process before it's too late? Control. Can we provide a flexible and desirable level of control over data? And collaboration. Can a collaborative process with loved ones help users choose meaningful data to leave behind? To answer our research questions, we first ran an ideation workshop to create a large number of design concepts as sketches. We grouped 12 concepts into a digital design workbook, which is a collection of related ideas. Each design concept has an illustration and description. Participants interpreted each concept however they wished. We used the design workbook as a probing tool in an interview study with 20 participants ages 18 to 80 years old. Using thematic analysis, we identified five themes that capture attitudes and expectations towards preparing data for death. Here is an overview of the 12 concepts in the workbook. In this video, I briefly discuss two key themes using two of the design concepts as examples. One of the key themes we identified from participants' reactions is that some wanted the process of preparing for death to feel personal and intimate. Designers could create tools for preparation to foster intimacy and involve loved ones in sensitive ways. Generation Cloud, the design concept shown here, lets people see data from family members and upload their own meaningful data over time. Participants said that they would cherish family data that creates connections across generations in their family. P14 said that he would feel motivated by Generation Cloud. That would be fascinating, actually. If I'm getting something out of it before, I can see more of the value of passing that on to my kids. Another key theme that we identified was that data cannot fully represent an individual. Take this concept, for example, Blast from the past, an Ai replica of an ancestor based on the aggregation of their lifetime data, participants reacted negatively to this idea. this idea, with P17 saying, that's not the way I want to remember someone. You've taken a complex human being and made them a literal digital icon. Instead, participants wanted control and agency over their self-representations after death by choosing what to share, delete, or keep private while alive. Based on the results of the thematic analysis, we present a set of design considerations for better tools focused on three areas that address our initial research questions. Normalizing preparing data for death, giving and taking control, and finding ways to introduce collaboration rather than conflict. In the paper, you'll find more details about each of these broad design directions. To summarize, our paper uses a design workbook with 12 concepts to understand user expectations for preparing their data for death. In the paper, we present the results of our thematic analysis and contribute a set of broad design directions. Thank you for watching.

reference: Hi, I'm Kristen Shinohara from the Rochester Institute of Technology, and on behalf of my co-authors, Jun-Chen Lee and Gareth Tigwell, I'm presenting our paper, Accessibility of High-Fidelity Prototyping Tools. High-fidelity prototyping tools enable user interface designers to quickly mock up interfaces, which can then be used to gather feedback and, during testing, to identify any usability and accessibility issues. Screen readers are tools used to read screen content out loud. Screen readers are often used by blind and low-vision computer users to access screen content. For example, we show here a screenshot of the Wikipedia page for Google. A screen reader might read the title of this page out loud as, Heading Level 1, Google. Increasingly, there is a drive to ensure that user interfaces can be used with a screen reader, but how accessible are prototyping tools for people who use screen readers and wish to design user interfaces? We conducted a study to examine screen reader compatibility with prototyping tools. Specifically, we sought to know what parts of prototyping tools are compatible or not with screen readers, which tools are recommended for use with screen readers, and what accessibility issues arise when using these tools together. There are a variety of screen readers and tools available. We tested how well VoiceOver on the Mac and Narrator from Windows worked with the prototyping tools Sketch, Adobe XD, Balsamiq, and UXPin. We assessed how well the screen reader could access GUI elements and controls, and how well tasks could be completed toward creating a simple prototype. For example, would a screen reader read aloud the function of a button and accurately provide information about what is happening on the screen? We found that Balsamiq had the best screen reader compatibility, but that overall most tools were not accessible by a screen reader. In addition, most issues were compounded by multiple problems, e.g. 42 % of buttons were accessible. but most did not have labels or had incomplete alternative text, often making it impossible to know what the button was for. Another example was poor focus order. For instance, a user may create an element by selecting an Add Shape button. After selecting the button, ideally the system would move on to select the new shape element on the canvas to aid with quick editing, but instead the system remains focused on the Add Shape button. We attempted to create a simple prototype using screen readers. Across six different tasks, including creating elements, adding them to a canvas, renaming a canvas, and editing parameters, we assessed how well we could complete each task. Overall, we were unable to complete about half of the tasks, which amounted to failure in creating a prototype with each prototyping tool. Task analysis uncovered situations where multiple accessibility issues prevented 100 % completion of any given task, E.g. it was difficult to create elements because many were not operable by keyboard. or it was difficult to move elements due to lack of information about sensory characteristics such as the element's shape, size, or location. Finally, all tools failed to export prototypes. Our analysis determined that VoiceOver and Sketch had the best compatibility, with the second best conformance to accessibility guidelines, and the highest task completion rate. However, for practical purposes, Balsamiq was more efficient because it implemented templates that eliminated many steps that created problems for other tools. We found that while prototyping tools have some level of screen reader accessibility, they are not yet accessible enough to enable a screen reader user to effectively and efficiently create high-fidelity prototypes. Based on our analysis, we recommend that tool improvement should prioritize accessibility of individual widgets, such as the canvas, buttons, text fields, and should focus on addressing accessibility issues for individual tasks, such as focus order, input instruction, alternative text, or keyboard operations, to name a few. Our findings will inform future improvement in high-fidelity prototyping tools to better support designers with disabilities and toward improving the overall accessibility of interfaces. We look forward to your comments and questions. Thank you.

reference: Welcome to the presentation of our paper on designing programming error messages for novices, readability and its constituent factors. Let's now take a look at two students working in a typical computer lab. And run 45 errors. The name I does not exist in the current context. What does that even mean? I have no idea. Mine says no reference exception? That doesn't make sense either. Unfortunately, these kinds of frustrating experiences are all too common. Novice programmers struggling to make sense of cryptic programming error messages. Such error messages are a type of feedback produced by software called a compiler or interpreter, which indicate there is some kind of error in the source code written by a programmer. The cycle of program input and error message response represents a fundamental interaction between human and computer. While error messages can be confusing and frustrating even for professional programmers, they can be paralyzing for novices who are just beginning to code. Consider this example, which involves a compiler for the C programming language. This is a popular language used in many introductory programming courses. The student here is attempting to write the code statement shown on top, but they make a very small error. They have forgotten to include the comma between the two identifiers, Fahrenheit and Celsius. This missing comma generates an error message, shown here in red, which is not only cryptic and mostly unhelpful, it is simply difficult to read. We propose that improving the readability of error messages is an important first step in making them more usable. However, we don't yet have empirically tested guidelines for making messages easier to read. In this work, we set out to answer two research questions. The first, to identify potential factors that might affect message readability. And the second, to measure the extent to which they do. Now I'm going to give a brief overview of the three studies we ran, as well as discuss the results of study one. In study one, we asked participants to rate on a scale of 1 to 10 the readability of 60 error messages from three popular introductory programming languages, Java, C, and Python. In study two, we took a smaller number of messages and asked participants to explain in their own words what made them readable or not. And then in study three, we took results from study one and two and asked students to rate a set of error messages with respect to what we had found in the first two studies. The results of study one indicate that length and jargon were particularly important. The shorter messages were ranked higher, generally speaking, and the longer messages were ranked lower. Also, the messages with more jargon were ranked lower, while messages without jargon or acronyms were ranked higher. To elicit potential factors that influence error message readability, we asked students to tell us what they felt made certain messages easier or harder to read. Responses indicated themes around message length, jargon, sentence structure, and vocabulary. In a separate study, we found that all four of these factors correlated reasonably with a measure of understandability. We present four concrete design guidelines for writing more readable error messages and apply these to messages from our dataset. Here is an example from C. Future work includes the creation of a readability metric for programming error messages. Finally, we hope that the guidelines presented here will aid in the creation of new programming error messages, as well as guide efforts to revise or enhance existing messages. Our goal is to see programming error messages become more readable and therefore more usable in the coming years, easing a decades-long struggle between countless novices and their programming environments. Thank you very much for listening to this presentation. If you're interested, you'll find more details in the paper, and if you have any questions, please don't hesitate to get in touch with us.

reference: Hello, my name is Minyoung Yoo from Simon Fraser University in Canada. Today I present a paper that aims to understand how people with blindness look back on the past and to explore possible design implications that supports their experience of reminiscence. A growing trend of increasing digital possessions and personal data have allowed great possibilities of using them as meaningful resources to re-experience the past. However, there is very limited research on how people with blindness draw on their digital possessions to capture, share, and reflect on their life experiences. So we aim to explore two main research questions in this paper. What are the practices and experiences of reminiscence in the past life for people with blindness? What types of cherished possessions are involved? We conducted one-on-one, in-person field study with nine participants by visiting their homes. Field notes, photos, and nearly 17 hours of audio recordings are collected, and data was iteratively analyzed to surface three underlying themes. The first theme presents how people with blindness captures and remembers the past. The next theme introduces the ways of re-experiencing the past with personal possessions. And the last theme explores wishes and desires in reminiscence and imagines how emerging technologies could support the experiences in the future. Among these three themes, I focus on the second theme for this presentation. There is a long tradition of making audio recordings well before the era of smartphones and digital recorders. Lewis said, audio recordings for us are like photographs for you guys. Largely, there were two distinct types of memory-oriented audio recordings. Recordings of ambient sounds were often used to capture the emotional feeling and atmospheric timbre of an experience as a whole, often recorded as the soundscapes of trips and special events. On the other hand, focused sounds were captured to commemorate close social relationships, such as recordings of intimate conversations and guide dog snoring. However, tensions when sharing memories often resulted in frustration and anxiety. While participants cherished photographs as their symbols of memories, it was difficult to be in the same moment when sharing memories as they had to wait for others to describe the photo. Conversely, revisiting memories solely through audio recordings did not resonate well with excited loved ones. Overall, both groups needed the pacing of interaction. They needed time to listen, observe, and digest in order to be immersed in each other's experience. Building on the findings, we propose possible design implications in three different areas in the paper. For the time being, I briefly introduce two implications in connection to the findings covered in this presentation about sound and collaborative annotation. There's an opportunity of pairing audio recordings with personal metadata, such as timestamp, geolocation data, people, time of day, or season. We propose a cohesive digital repository that combines this metadata to generate creative ways of storing and interacting with personal audios. This will enable to explore and surface forgotten or yet unknown themes and patterns across the archive. In order to mitigate tensions regarding the pacing of interaction, a tangible device that presents digital media with reflective questions could encourage nostalgic conversations beyond the photo. This allows an appropriate pacing for the people with blindness and their loved ones as it supports recalling and sharing memories through dialogues and verbal descriptions. We acknowledge that it is important to respect reciprocity. We'll work closely with participants as if they are collaborators and co-designers throughout the research process. Next, we plan to engage with participants in co-design activities to discuss what kinds of possible future practices are desirable or undesirable. Thank you all for listening, and I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

Through a series of interviews, we sought to investigate trans health needs and how technology can be better designed for this population.
