Many trans people transition in a few different ways, which we will discuss further. Finally, dysphoria is a feeling of distress with one's assigned gender at birth, and can be reduced or eliminated through transition. We were interested in two primary research questions. First, we were interested in the role that technology plays when trans people navigate and deal with gender dysphoria. Second, we were interested in the ways that technology can support the transitioning process before, during, and after transition. To answer these questions, we conducted a series of semi-structured interviews with 21 trans participants from the United States. Participants came from a range of ages, identities, and backgrounds, and were at varying stages in their lives and transitions. Interviews were conducted both in person and over Zoom. We split up the interviews into five sections, although we did cross over certain sections when appropriate. First, to encourage participants to be comfortable with sharing their stories, we asked them about their experience with their gender and transition, if applicable. We then asked them about how they experience and manage dysphoria, how they define and relate it to their trans communities, and how they manage their health and self-care when needed. Finally, we discussed the role of technology in their lives and how they view technology itself. Our interviews gave us many insights, and here I will discuss a few key takeaways. These are just a few of the themes that we found in our interviews. The first theme we found has to do with identity. A third of participants remarked that their identity was fluid rather than static. Even among binary transgender individuals, many felt like their identities were not fixed. Similarly, many, but not all participants, saw their gender as something that is evolving as they learn and grow in life. Below is one quote from a participant in his late 40s who transitioned nearly 20 years ago. It's not something that starts and ends. I don't have any list of surgeries that I want to say I'm complete. No, I don't think of it that way. I feel like every single day I become. Designers should keep this in mind and not use gender as an essential and immutable aspect of the user's identity. However, it is important to add a caveat that while fluidity and evolution are constant themes in our findings, we do not want to imply that these identities are stable and current identities are in flux. The next insight is the way that our participants' lived experiences challenge normative transition narratives. The notion that transition is a linear process and that it has a concrete start and end point was not true for most of our participants. Many participants had to interrupt, postpone, or skip parts of their transition due to their life circumstances and due to the barriers set out by the current institutions. For instance, one participant was able to pursue all but one of the procedures for transition that he desired, but due to his financial situation and the limitation of current medical technology, chose to indefinitely postpone seeking this procedure. Furthermore, the type of transition that participants underwent varied. For instance, some participants chose to socially, legally, and physically transition, while others chose to only socially and physically transition. The last theme that I will discuss here has to do with dysphoria. Before I proceed, I just want to note that not all trans people experienced dysphoria. However, all of our participants did, and we were able to discuss their experiences. Dysphoria is an intensely personal experience, both in its manifestation and its mitigation. Participants considered safety and harms when managing their dysphoria. We did find that a center's agency, often from being able to access transitioning resources, reduces dysphoria for our participants. In addition, technology appears to be a way to facilitate dysphoria management for many participants. However, any dysphoria management method that is not transitioning is a temporary fix. We also discussed things like information seeking, resource management, and transmedicalism. For more detailed information, I encourage you to read the paper. However, in sum, our results show the lived experience of our participants and illustrate many concepts found in transgender studies. Our participants' lived experiences challenge normative transition narratives. Thus, for researchers and designers, a one-size-fits-all approach to transitioning dysphoria is not appropriate. Which I have done in collaboration with my co authors Gene Song and Jason Corso, Single, target video, Object tracking is a canonical task in computer vision. The task consists of three steps. First, the user provides a video. Next, a bounding box is drawn around a semantically meaningful object in the first frame of that video. Last, a model tracks the object given in the first frame through the remaining frames. From the perspective of this work, the last two steps each encode an important assumption. In the second step, we assume the first frame bounding box accurately describes the target in the input space. And in the third, while some evaluation methods do consider robustness to perturbation, it is generally assumed that equally good bounding boxes result in equally good object tracks. We examine these two assumptions, and their implications, under a crowdsourcing framework. Broadly, this work asks three major questions. Are the assumptions of video object tracking valid when used with crowdsourced data? Is the typical crowdsourcing goal of optimizing in the input space valid with respect to inference in video object tracking? And, if these assumptions aren't valid, how do we address these inconsistencies in a way that balances the number of queries, actual performance, and optimal performance? We begin by examining the assumption that the received bounding box accurately describes the target in the input space. Using data collected across 900 crowdsource initializations on the Otb 100 data set. More important, however, is the effect of these received initializations on the final object tracks. This is partially addressed in the assumption that equally good bounding boxes result in equally good object tracks. We see in the two displayed object tracks that for the same video, a slight change in initialization can result in substantially different performance. This is reinforced by an aggregate analysis which shows that additional error, the increase in error when a non gold standard seat is used typically decreases. the initialization approaches the gold standard, but the correlation is not definitive. Good initializations often result in poor performance, and poor initializations often recover and perform as well as the gold standard. These findings affect how current crowdsourcing strategies, typically based on some sort of consensus in the input space, would work on this inference problem. Through this analysis, we find two major shortcomings. First, Such strategies would require multiple queries on all initializations, even the 23.3 % for which the crowdsourced initialization performs as well as the Gold standard. Second, such methods optimize the wrong objective, as the goal is to optimize performance in the output space, and the correlation between input space and output space quality is not definitive. To address these shortcomings, we introduce smart replacement, which consists of a re-query function that determines whether or not to accept the first initialization, and a selection function that, after receiving the second initialization, determines which initialization to use for the final inference. Under this paradigm, we aim to re-query only if necessary, minimizing the total number of queries, and, if a second initialization is provided, optimize output performance by choosing between the two. We see that not only does smart replacement improve the overall performance of the model when compared to naively accepting the replacement initialization, but also changes which scoring function should be used for both re-query and selection. To summarize, we have shown that the assumptions used in evaluation of object tracking algorithms Namely, that the initialization will be good and that equally good initializations result in equally good outputs are too simplistic with respect to a crowdsourcing scenario. and that current crowdsourcing methods that focus on aggregating multiple inputs to find the optimal answer in the input space will both re-query many unnecessary initializations and optimize the wrong objective. We then evaluated potential methods for detecting and correcting bad initializations under our smart replacement paradigm, and showed the importance of this method, which not only improved overall performance, but changed the re-query and selection functions that should be used.

reference: Hello, I'm Verwitsch Boas, a PhD student at the Mixed Reality Lab based in the University of Nottingham. Together with my co-author, Hannel Wagner, we will discuss our paper, Selling Glossy Easy Futures, in this video. In this paper, we explore the descriptions of commercial self-care apps in the Google Play Store through a feminist lens. We define self-care for mental health as a set of personal practices that people can use to look after themselves. Examples include physical exercise, meditation, or creative journaling. Technology can be used to support self-care. Unsurprisingly, self-care apps are a part of many people's lives. Facilitating self-care through technology is a tricky undertaking, as many of its features are abstract and not easily captured, so designers must make opinionated choices about how to communicate and present these features. This means that self-care apps inherently feature many implicit and explicit values, assumptions, and understandings of self-care. Apps therefore actively shape culture, but equally are influenced by mainstream ideas about health at large. Within the Google Play Store, app descriptions offer space for apps to describe themselves, advertise their features, and call those to install them. This makes them an interesting data source to explore which values, biases, or ideas are encoded within them. To explore these ideas, we created a data corpus of app descriptions scraped from the Google Play Store. We decided to focus on the most ethical, privacy, and user-respecting apps within our dataset, which left us with a total of 69 apps to investigate. To make sense of these 69 app descriptions, we decided to use thematic analysis after Brown and Clark. We coded all app descriptions inductively through an intersectional thermalist lens. Through discussing and self-reflection within our research team, we arrived at two concrete themes. Based on these themes, we developed three questions to revisit the data with in an inductive manner. In the interest of time, we will focus on discussing our themes. Our first theme is Self-care as an Improvement Tool for Better, Happier Futures. Based on the app descriptions, doing self-care through apps seemingly leads to a better life. Self-care is not portrayed as a tool to just manage wellness, but it is shown as a device to work towards a negativity-free, better future. This presentation frames apps as experts that have all the answers we might need, a one-size-fits-all blueprint for our lives, without the need to ask us for input, disagreement, or nuance. All stress is individual and easy to handle is our second theme. Within our dataset, stressors were commonly showcased as merely individual matters of personal attitude and perception. This framing of stressors within self-care apps does not recognize external or outside factors which might influence your well-being. We will now discuss what these themes mean embedded within a wider context. Mental health is difficult to untangle, as it is influenced by many individual, cultural, and societal factors. Mental distress is also not a linear or universal experience. Both themes indicate that the app descriptions frame mental distress as personal failure. If well-being is something that hard-working people can easily achieve by themselves, we might not seek out further support or even go so far to dismiss our own self-care needs. For many people, self-care apps might be one of the first spaces where they encounter ideas about well-being and distress. An overly individual, prescriptive, and assumptive framing of mental health has thus the chance to actively cause harm. We will schedule two design recommendations that reimagine self-care apps and the descriptions for meaningful, beneficial engagement. Our first recommendation is self-care apps as future-making tools. Instead of seeing self-care apps as mediators between the distressed here and the healthy then, we encourage self-care apps to engage with adaptive care that is recognizant Of the app and flow of mental health within the individual person, to also move towards a co created, personalized and contextual futures. Our second design recommendation is self-care apps and their descriptions as transparent companions. We encourage the departure from addressing a potential client through a default normative lens. Instead, self-care apps should introduce and connect people to different levels and modalities of care. Ultimately, we advocate for a move towards relative, transparent communication of what apps offer instead of superlative and empty promises. Thank you very much for watching our presentation. If this research resonates with you, please stay in touch.

reference: The title and aim of this paper is co-activation detection in 10-finger typing on a virtual keyboard. One factor that has contributed to the slow adoption and use of virtual and augmented reality is the lack of a reliable high-throughput input method. Adapting the concept of a common keyboard to create a virtual keyboard is one way of tackling this problem, but this exposes a challenging input interpretation problem with many sources of noise. One particularly challenging source arises from the physiology of the hand combined with the lack of a physical surface on which to type. Without the physical resistance of keys, intentional finger movements can cause other fingers to move unintentionally, producing unwanted key activations. These events are known as co-activations and eliminating them improves the efficiency of information transfer and improves user experience. Determining an effective method for identifying them and implementing this method into an existing statistical decoder is the aim of this work. The first step was to review a dataset of 24 people typing on a mid-air virtual keyboard with all 10 fingers in virtual reality for approximately 45-60 minutes. This was done to identify the circumstances in which co-activations occur. We found that the ring finger produced the majority of co-activations observed as shown on the left. We also found that the majority of co-activations were caused by a finger lateral to the intended one. For example, for intended use of the middle finger, co-activations of the ring and pinky occurred most frequently as shown on the right. The review was also used to identify an initial set of features distinguishing co-activations from intended activations, of which two are shown here. On the left, the time interval between activations and on the right, the average correlation of finger velocities. In both plots, orange indicates co-activations and blue indicates intended activations. These features clearly show how co-activations can be identified and separated from intended activations. The features were then refined to retain the ones most suited to being implemented into an existing online system. These features were evaluated by training a neural network on a single feature and recording its performance. Low-performing features were removed, leaving a final set of four. The velocity of the finger producing the current key activation, the finger depth of the previous key activation, and the interval and correlation between the current and previous key activations. Three models were trained using the final features, a neural network, a support vector machine, and a naive Bayes. The performance of each is shown here, with all models achieving a high level of accuracy in detecting co-activations. The neural network achieved the highest F1 score and so was chosen to be implemented into an existing statistical decoder. The existing decoder calculates the probability that an input character was intended and uses this result to make more accurate autocorrections. The model's co activation prediction is incorporated into this probability. and and if the prediction exceeds a certain threshold, the character was removed. An example is shown here. First NOP is entered using the index middle and ring fingers. The user is trying to type the word notes, but has caused a co-activation with their ring finger and inserted the P into the input field. The co-activation module subsequently identifies and removes the co-activation before the remaining characters TEE are entered. Finally, the input is corrected to the desired word notes by the decoder. With the addition of this model, a reduction in character error rate by approximately 10 % relative and oh .9 % absolute can be achieved. This investigation has shown that identification and removal of co-activations from a text input stream can be completed with simple, lightweight features. Four features have been identified that can aid the detection of co-activations. Combined, these features can achieve a detection accuracy exceeding 97%. The module integrated into the decoder also demonstrates how co-activation detection can effectively reduce character error rates.
